full_judgment:
This second appeal by the defendant-appellants is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.12.67 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rangpur in Title Appeal No. 54 of 1966 reversing those dated 9.2.66 passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Rangpur.

2. Plaintiffs case, in short, is that the land hereinafter called the suit-property covered by Khatian No. 14 (Ext. 2) of Mouza Marichbari within PS Mithapukur originally belonged to one Farahtullah to the extent of eight annas, to one Shariatullah to the extent of four annas and to one Kamiran and Samiran each, to the extent of two annas. Then Farahtullah died leaving behind defendant No. 1 as his wife, father of defendant Nos. 2-4 as his sons, defendants Nos. 5 and 6 namely Tasiran and Farijan as his daughters. The defendant I as per kabala Ext. I sold her share along with that of her daughters defendant Nos. 5 and 6 (then minors) to the plaintiff as far back as in 1348 BS. The same kabala was executed also by defendant No. 7, son of Samiran purporting to transfer the whole of his share. Two years later, father of defendant Nos. 2-4 also sold 0.55 acres of land to the plaintiff vide kabala Ext. I(a). Thereafter in 1352 BS.Farijan Nesa sold her 0.45 acres of land as per kabala Ext. 1(b). Afterwards the plaintiff Amena Khatun herself sold to the defendant Nos. 12-15 1.34 acres of land in 1363 B.S. and 1364 B.S. vide Kabala Exts I(c)-I(d) out of her kabala purchased lands covered by Exts. 1-1(b). Since her purchase of the lands, the plaintiff has been in ejmali possession of the suit-land with the other co-sharers in the suit property. The lands sold to the defendant Nos. 12-15 are being possessed by themselves. But as the ejmali possession of the suit-land has been fraught with inconvenience and as the share of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 has been wrongly and collusively recorded in their names the plaintiff has been constrained to institute the present suit for declaration of her title to 1.26 acres of land and for partition of her total of 2.48 acres of land.

3. This suit has been contested only by defendant Nos. 2-6 by filing a joint written statement. They contended that the suit was without any cause of action, that the plaintiff's kabala so far as the share of defendant Nos. 5 and 6 was concerned was void ab initio, that the plaintiff never possessed any portion of the suit property, that the kabala purported to have been executed by Nasiruddin, father of the defendant Nos. 2-4 was not legally valid, because the alleged executant was a lunatic and that advantage was taken for wrongful gain by the plaintiff, that defendant Nos. 12-15 also did not possess any portion of the suit-property, that defendant Nos. 2-4 already purchased the shares of defendant Nos. 5 and 6 vide deed Ext. A and that the plaintiff has had no possession in the suit property, hence her name was not recorded in the khatians. It was further contended that in view of all these facts, the suit was liable to be dismissed with costs.

4. The plaintiff examined in all 9 PWs and the defendants examined 7 DWs in support of their respective cases.

5. The learned Munsif formulated the following three issues:

1. Is the plaintiffs kabala, so far as the share of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 is concerned, void?.

2. Has the Plaintiff acquired any title to and has she been in possession of any portion of the suit property, if so, to what extent?

3. To what relief (s), if any, is the plaintiff entitled.

6. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence on record decided issue No. I in favour of the contesting defendants and against the plaintiff. As regards issue No. 2 the Trial Court held that the plaintiff as per Ext’s. 1-lb was not entitled to get more than a total of 2.24 acres of land. But consequently upon her sale of 1.34 acres, vide Ext’s. 1(c) to 1(d) to defendant Nos. 12-15 she was not supposed to get more than 0.90 acres of land. As regards possession of the plaintiff in the suit land, the trial Court found relying only on the deposition of DW 4 that the plaintiff was in possession of some portion of the suit jota and as such was entitled to get partition with respect to only 0.90 acres of land appertaining to the jota. With the above findings, the trial Court partly decreed the suit on contest in the preliminary form against defendants No. 2-6, ex pane against the rest by his judgment and decree dated 9.2.66.

7. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and declared plaintiffs title to the extent of 1.26 acres of land and allowed partition of the total 2.48 acres of land in her favour in the suit jote by his judgment and decree dated 30.12.67.

8. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendants preferred the second appeal in this Court.

<u>9. Mr. Md. Shahjahan, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, has taken me through the judgments of both the Courts below and then submitted that so far the transfer of the shares of the properties of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the suit jote by their mother during their minority in favour of the plaintiff-respondent by a registered deed vide Ext. 1 was void ab initio and both the Courts concurrently came to the aforesaid finding on the basis of the decision of the famous leading case of Immambandi and others Vs. Mutsaddi and others reported in 45 IA 73. Hence, that finding is final and conclusive and cannot be disturbed in this second appeal. His next submission is that the lower appellate Court committed error of law in holding that the interest of the defendant Nos. 5-6 to the extent of 1.26 acres of land was extinguished under section 28 of the Limitation Act and the plaintiff-respondent acquired title of the said land belonging to the defendant Nos. 5-6 by way of adverse possession, and as such the impugned judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court cannot be sustained in law. In this connection he submits that the question of adverse possession was neither pleaded in the plaint nor any such claim has been proved by reliable evidence, but the lower appellate Court without due consideration of this aspect of the case and the evidence on record most illegally and arbitrarily observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Naturally it is now with defendants 2 to 4 to put claim to the interest of defendant Nos. 5 and 6. But in view, of my above discussion regarding possession, it is my considered view that the plaintiff was in possession of Ext. 1 land since her purchase in 1941 for more than 12 years and as the defendants 5 and 6 did not sue the purchaser (plaintiff) within 12 years from the date of sale or within 3 years from the date of their attaining majority, whichever is later, to restore and protect their title, their claim is barred under section 28 of the Limitation Act".</u>

<u>and upon such observation illegally declared the tight, title, and interest of the plaintiff over 1.26acres of land of defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the suit property. Mr. Shahjahan further submits referring to the plaint as well as to the evidence on record that it is the case of the plaintiff-respondent that she is in ejmali possession of the suit property and further by way of purchase by registered deed Ext. 1 not only from minor defendant Nos. 5 and 6 but also from defendant Nos. 1 and 7 the plaintiff became a co-sharer in the suit jote. But a co-sharer cannot claim title by way of adverse possession against another co-sharer unless ouster of the later co-sharer from the land in question is established by evidence. In the instant case there being no finding on discussion of evidence on record as to any such ouster of the contesting defendants 5 and 6 from the disputed suit-property, the claim of title by adverse possession by the plaintiff cannot be legally sustained and the interest of the said defendants can not be held to have been extinguished or barred under section 28 of the Limitation Act. In support of his contention, Mr. Shahajahan has referred to a decision in the case of Sonaullah Hawlader Vs. Apseruddin Bali and others reported in 7 DLR 514 wherein it has been held that by a Division Bench that-</u>

<u>"It is well-settled that there can be no adverse possession by one co-sharer against another until there is ouster or something equivalent to ouster.</u>

<u>Whether there was ouster, is a mixed question, and we think that this appeal should be reheard by the learned Additional District Judge, who is the final Court of fact".</u>

<u>Another decision in this connection in the case of Jogendra Chandra Kapali Chowdhury and another Vs. Arjun Chandra Kapali & others reported in 15 DLR 628 has also been cited wherein it has been held that :</u>

<u>"possession of a co-sharer to be considered from three aspects; (1) Among co-sharers themselves possession of one co-owner is possession of all, to claim adverse possession in such a case assertion must be notoriously and unequivocally hostile. (2) A stranger purchaser of an undivided share getting possession of some specific land stands on the same footing as the other co-sharers, the land purchased by him being the land to be allotted to the share of his vendor on partition. (3) A stranger purchaser from a co-sharer who sold the property and the purchaser possessing it openly as of right without any attempt at concealment so that any person interested may know about his exclusive possession on the basis of his purchase, in such a case the purchaser's possession is not that of a co-sharer but it is exclusive possession in assertion of his title on the basis of his purchase."</u>

10. Further contention of the learned Advocate for the appellants is that the suit property was not at all partitioned and as such the plaintiff failed to establish his exclusive possession in suit property in the share of defendant Nos. 5 and 6. His main submission is that the learned lower appellate Court without proper discussion of the evidence on record came to an arbitrary finding of possession for more than 12 years in the suit property by the plaintiff-respondent, and as a result there has been serious miscarriage of justice.

11. It is well-settled that even a finding of fact without discussing the evidence on record or contrary to the evidence on record is an error of law which may be a ground for interference in second appeal.

<u>12. Mr. Akrm Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that even if the claim of title by way of adverse possession is not pleaded in the plaint still it will not be a bar in allowing the claim of plaintiff's title by way of adverse possession if he is found in continuous possession of the suit land in assertion of his title for more than 12 years, hence, in the instant case, possession of the plaintiff in the suit land for more than 12 years extinguished the right, title and interest of the original owners i.e. defendants 5 and 6 under section 28 of the Limitation Act. In support of his contention, he has cited a decision in the case of Sadak Ali Vs. Surju Ali & others reported in 7 DLR 94, wherein it has been held that:</u>

<u>"Possession under a mistake or invalid title is as effective as that of a trespasser, and, if sufficient in the length of time and continuity, gives the holder a good title....</u>

<u>Under Article 142 of the Limitation Act. time begins to run against the rightful owner from the date of discontinuance of possession or dispossession, as the case may be, and under section 28 of the Limitation Act the right is extinguished, if no suit for recovery is instituted by him within the statutory period.</u>

<u>The mere fact that the plaintiff did not specifically claim title by adverse possession is no reason to disentitle him to the decree which he is otherwise, entitled".</u>

<u>13. Thereafter Mr. Abdul Mannan Khan another learned Advocate while agreeing on behalf of the plaintiff respondent has referred to another decision in the case of Lala Hem Chand Vs. Lala Pearey Lal and others reported in AIR 1942 (PC) 64 wherein it has been Held that:</u>

<u>"If the owner whose property is encroached upon suffers his right to be barred by the law of Limitation the practical effect is the extension of his title in favour of the party in possession. Consequently where the executor holds the property adversely to the heir for upwards of 12 years on behalf of the charity for which it was dedicated, the title to it acquired by prescription, becomes vested in the charity and that of the heir if he had any, becomes extinguished by operation of s. 28"</u>

14. Relying on this Mr. Khan contends that the plaintiff has acquired title to the share of defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the suit property to the extent of 1.26 acres of land by way of adverse possession, if not by their purchase by registered deed Ext. 1 and therefore, the lower appellate Court has rightly declared plaintiffs title to the disputed 1.26 acres of land and allowed partition of the total share of the plaintiff to the extent of 2.48 acres of land.

15. Before considering the above submission of the learned Advocates of both the sides, let me keep on record some admitted facts in this case. Firstly, defendant No 1 for herself and as mother guardian of defendants Nos 5 and 6 executed and registered the deed of sale vide Ext I in favour of the plaintiff Amena Khatun predecessor of the present respondents including the shares of defendants 5 and 6 to the extent of 1.26 acres of land during their minority. Secondly the plaintiff respondent purchased in all 3,82 acres of land vide Ext. 1, 1 (a),- 1 (b) and out of this 3,82 acres, she had sold out 1.34 acres of land. So, the plaintiffs present claim was confined to the extent of 2.48 acres of land only. The dispute is mainly with regard to 1.26 acres of land of the shares of defendant Nos 5 and 6. If the plaintiff could establish her right, title and interest over the disputed 1.26 acres of land, then she would get her entire 2.48 acres of land in the suit holding and if she could not, in that case she would be entitled to get only 1.22 acres of land. Now, let me see whether the plaintiff has been able to establish her title over the disputed land of 1.26 acres. It may be pointed out that the claim of title over this disputed property by virtue of the registered sale deed Ext. 1 executed on behalf of the minor defendants 5 and 6 has been lost, being void ab initio as has been concurrently found by both the courts below. Now, it is to be seen whether the plaintiff respondent has been able to establish title by way of adverse possession over the said property i.e. 1.26 acres of land. The decisions cited at the Bar are not disputed but main question is whether the plaintiffs claim for any exclusive and actual possession over the specific portion of the disputed land of the defendants 5 and 6 has been proved by sufficient reliable evidence to be open, notorious and in assertion of her title for more than 12 years. This question ought to have been properly discussed and decided on consideration of the evidence on record, but unfortunately the trial Court without doing so only observed as follows:

"Furthermore since by virtue of purchase of some portion of the defendant Nos. 2-4 and from some others the plaintiff has become a co-sharer with the other defendants, the plaintiffs plea of adverse possession of the land of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 is an absurdity."

and the lower appellate Court also without discussing properly the evidence on record observed as follows:

"It is now clear that the plaintiff has been in possession of Ext. 1 land since her purchase in 1941 and the defendants 2 to 4 have purchased the interest of defendants 5 and 6 in the year 1963"

16. Thus the question of adverse possession has not been property discussed and decided by the courts below.

17. In such situation, generally the suit is sent back on remand to the lower court for consideration of the evidence by way of rehearing and deciding the question involved as raised above. But this Second Appeal of 1968 involves a suit of the year 1964 and if the suit is again sent back on remand it will entail further delay of several years for its final disposal at the sufferings of the parties.

So, when both the parties have examined a number of witnesses in support of their respective cases and their evidences are already on record, I think, it is proper not to send back this suit on remand to the trial Court or to the lower appellate Court for rehearing and disposal but to decide the question involved i.e. the question of adverse possession here and now by this court on discussion of evidence. The plaintiff respondent has examined as many as 9 PWs and the defendants have examined 7 DWs.

18. About possession, PW 1 Abdur Rahman Talukdar on behalf of the plaintiff stated as follows:-

"Since after purchase of the s/1 plaintiff possessed the s/1 through adhiars, Jamsher, Jamattulla, Dasimuddin and Mafizuddin for 10/11 years. Thereafter she had the s/1 in direct khas possession for 5/6 yrs. For the last 7/8 yrs. the s/1 is again being possessed through adhiars Kasimuddin and Safaruddin among some other persons. Defendant Nos. 2-4 have also been adhiars with respect to the s/1 for 7/8 yrs. The land sold away to defendants 12/15 are being possessed by the vendor themselves. Defendant Nos. 5 and 6 never possessed the s/1 or any portion of the suit joie after execution of Ext. 1 "In cross-examination this witness stated that defendants 2-4 are co-sharers in the suit property. In CS khatian defendants 5 and 6 were co-sharers, the CS Khatian bears also the names of these two defendants."

19. PW 2 Dasimuddin Akand states that they adhi cultivated 3-3½ bighas of land under Amena Khatun for 10/11 yrs. Thereafter for 4/5 years she got the same cultivated by her servants. Solaiman among others has been cultivating the s/1 at present. In cross-examination this witness stated that the adhiars were not known to the husband of the plaintiff and Solaiman was never an adhiar with respect to the s/1. He gave the description of the boundaries of the suit land. He stated that he himself gave adhi crops to the plaintiff. PW 3 stated that defendants 2-4 had been cultivating as adhiars under Mvi. A Rahman, PW 1 for 5/7 years, previously Abdur Rahman Mia kept the suit land in khas possession for 3/4 years. Defendants 5 and 6 were 5-7 years old and they never possessed the suit land. In cross examination this witness stated that he was not adhiar under PW.1 at that time. He stated that defendants 2-4 had been cultivating the suit land as adhiars since after his surrender in 1390 BS. He stated that defendants 2-4 are nephews of defendants No. 5-6. PW 4 Najamuddin drummer stated that he had been cultivating as adhiar under PW 1 for 5/6 years. He stated that he did not know whether Rabeya and Jamila ever possessed the suit land. In cross-examination this witness stated that he did not remember in which year he had taken adhi. He also stated that he did not know the area of the land. He admitted that defendants 2-4 also possessed the suit land. PW 5 Sarafuddin stated that he was cultivating 12/14 kathas of the suit land under Abdur Rahman Mia, for 5/7 years and also stated that Rabeya and Jamila never possessed the suit land. In cross examination this witnesses stated that defendants 2-4 purchased some land from his share in the suit property and by virtue of that purchase. Nehaluddin and others had been possessing a portion of the suit land. He could not tell the month and the year in which he had taken adhi. PW 6 Abdul Gafur Munshi stated that he himself sold the entire share of his father to defendant Nos. 2-4 and that Rabeya and Jamila never possessed the suit land. He stated that he was adhiar under PW 1 in respect of some other lands. He admitted that women did not cultivate the land themselves and they cultivated by their brothers and husbands and that the homestead of defendants 2-4 stood on the suit property. DW 7 Ismail Uddin Akhand stated that nobody on behalf of the defendants 5 and 7 possessed the suit land. In cross examination he stated that he could not say which plots were cultivated by whom. DW 8 Yunus Ali stated that he was no attesting witness to Ext. 1. He had no land in the suit mouza. DW 9 Nasu Sk. stated that he filed Ext. lc-Id. He stated that defendant Nos. 2-4 possessed the suit lands other than the Kabala lands.

20. DW 1 Jamila Khatun, one of the defendants stated that her nephew used to possess and cultivate her share of the suit land and gave her paddy and jute and that the plaintiff or her husband did never possess her share of land

21. DW 2 who is defendants No. 6 (Rabeya Khatun) stated that the plaintiff or her husband never possessed the share of land of defendant No. 6. It isr nephew who used to cultivate and possess the land on her behalf. DW 3 Abdul Khaleque was a deed writer at Pirganj SR office. He proved Ext. A. DW 4 Nehal Uddin who is defendant No. 2 stated that he himself and defendant Nos. 3-4 were possessing the suit- land since the death of their father. He stated that defendants No. 5 and 6 were sisters and co-sharers in the jote and their shares were possessed by them and they also took registered kabala Ext. A from them. The ancestral property was not partitioned. He stated that they were never adhiars under Abdur Rahman PW 1 and Kasim Uddin, Safar Uddin, Jamatullah, Dosimuddin and Naja were never adhiars with respect to the suit-land and Abdur Rahman never held the suit land, He further stated that the suit land had been also recorded in the names of the defendants No. 5 and 6. In cross examination he of course stated that his father allowed defendant No 1 to enjoy the eastern portion of the biggest plot of the jote and that Rabeya and Jamila were given in marriage by his father at his house. And plaintiff possessed only the land sold by Farijan and his father. DW 5 Khabir Uddin stated that Jamila defendant No. 6 was his wife. He also stated that defendants 2-4 used to look after the interest of his wife. The defendants adhi-cultivated her lands and gave her adhi crops weighing 5/6 maunds. DW 6 Rais Uddin Mondal stated that the suit land had been in possession of Nehaluddin and his brothers. In cross-examination he stated that the suit property had not undergone any partition by metes and bounds. DW 7 Darasuddin stated that he knew Rabeya and Jamila and they took crops from Nehal every year.

22. Now, from the consideration and analysis of the above evidence, it appears that the plaintiff claimed possession over the disputed portion of the suit jote in three different ways, firstly, for 10/11 years through some bargadars and again through khas possession for 4/5 years and then again through the present defendants 2-4 but these defendants stated that they were bargadars under defendant Nos. 5 and 6 and used to give crops to the said defendant Nos. 5 and 6 and after their own purchase, they have been possessing suit property independently as their own. It is the case of the plaintiff that she was in ejmali possession of the suit property and admittedly there has been no partition of the suit property by metes and bounds. Furthermore, from the deposition of the DW 4, it appear that the suit property was recorded in the present khatians in the names of the Air Tran defendants including the names of defendant Nos. 5 and 6. It is of course true that the record of right cannot be a document of title but it may be used as documentary evidence to show possession. Now, title by way of adverse possession has been claimed by the plaintiff and as such the onus is upon the plaintiff to establish the conditions required for acquisition of title by adverse possession. In view of the decisions cited above, it is no doubt clear that in the case of a claim of title by adverse possession by a co-sharer against another co-sharer, ouster of the latter has to be proved and possession of the party claiming title by adverse possession must be actual and exclusive for a continuous period of more than 12 years in assertion of hostile title. From the evidence on record as discussed above, it does not appear that the plaintiff has been able to fulfill the above conditions by reliable and sufficient evidence. It is rather the case of the plaintiff that she possessed the suit property in ejmali with other co-sharers through bargadars, but she could not lead any evidence to prove ouster of the other co-sharers particularly defendant Nos. 5 and 6 from their portion of the suit lands.

23. In that view of the matter, I must hold that the interest of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in respect of 1.26 acres of land in the suit jote has not been extinguished or barred under section 28 of the Limitation Act and the plaintiff respondent has not acquired any right, title or interest over the said disputed portion of the suit land i.e., 1.26 acres of the suit land by way of adverse possession claimed. Hence the lower appellate Court has committed error of law in allowing the claim of acquisition of plaintiff's title to the extent of 1.26 acres of land in respect of the shares of the defendant Nos. 5-6 in the suit jota and directing partition of the same by metes and bounds along with other lands measuring 1.22 acres i.e. partition for 2.48 acres in total.

24. For the reasons stated above the impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are liable to be set aside. The plaintiff is entitled to get a decree only for his 1.22 acres of land in the suit property and not for the remaining 1.26 acres. The suit is accordingly decreed in part and the plaintiff can get partition of his 1.22 acres of land only by metes and bounds.

25. In the result, the appeal is allowed in part. The impugned judgment and the decree of the lower appellate Court are partly set aside and modified with the observation as above.

In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs. Let the lower courts records be sent down expeditiously.

End.

Sreemati Parul Kusum Roy ------ Petitioner.
Vs.

case_source: In the matter of An application under Article 102 (2) of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh.
full_judgment:
Aminur-Rahman Khan, J. : This Rule is directed against the order of the respondent No. 3, namely the Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Anowara dated 14.9.85 declaring the disputed properties as vested property on the recommendation of the respondent No. 4, namely Upazila Revenue Officer, Anowara and approving grant of lease thereof in favour of the stranger respondent nos. 6-9.

2. 8.23 acres of land as described in the schedule in para No. 2 of the petition belonged to Jogesh Chandra Roy. He died leaving one son Purcendu Bikes Roy, one widow of the predeceased son Sukendu Bikash Roy and a grandson Hrishikesh Roy who was the son of his another predeceased son Amalendu Bikash Roy. Parul Kusum Roy, the present petitioner was the said widow of Sukendu Bikash Roy. Hrishikesh Roy having lost his father in childhood was brought up by his 2 paternal aunts namely Parul Bala Roy and petitioner Parul Kusum Roy. After attaining majority Hrishikesh Roy relinquished his right in favour of his said 2 aunts namely, Parul Bala Roy and the petitioner by a deed of declaration dated 5.5.62. Subsequently Parul Bala Roy and the petitioner brought O.C. Suit No. 11 of 1962 against Hrishikesh Roy which was decreed on compromise on 2.11.62 and by the said decree the 8 annas rigihts of Parul Bala Roy and 8 annas right of the present petitioner in the entire disputed properties was declared. Parul Bala Roy executed a will dated 10.11.69 bequeathing her right in favour of the present petitioner and a probate of the said will was obtained by the petitioner on 29.3.79 after Parul Bala died on 9.3.70 at Anowara Upzilia. Thus the petitioner got the entire right in the 8.21 acre of lands which she had been possessing all through by living in Bangladesh and erstwhile Fast Pakistan and by paying rents up to 1389 B.S. But after that her offer of rents for 1390 B.S. was not accepted on behalf of the government.

<u>3. Thereupon the petitioner started Miss Case No. 3 of 1984 on 5.8.84, before the Respondent No. 4 who called for a report from the local Tahsilder. In the meantime V.P. Case No. 20 of 1985 was started on 20.4.85 on the basis of a report dated 20.85 of the V.P. Tahsilder. Respondent No. 2 called for a report on 10.1.85 in Misc Appeal no 15 of 1984-85 but respondent No. 4 with an ulterior motive and without making any report and also without complying with the stay order passed in the Misc. Appeal hurriedly started a V.P. Misc. Case and proceeded to complete the lease of the properties without giving petitioner any notice or opportunity of being heard. The initiation of the V.P. case and the approval of the lease in favour of the stranger respondents 6 to 9 and the declaration of the property as vested property were all arbitrary, illegal, malafide and without any sanction of law. Upon the said facts and circumstances the petitioner made this application under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

4. On behalf or the respondent Nos. 1-5 and on behalf of the respondents No. 6-9 who are the lessees it was submitted that the petitioner had no right in the disputed properties either by inheritance or otherwise. It was represented that Hrishikesh Roy being the son of Jogesh Chandra Roy's predeceased son Amalendu Bikesh Roy he along inherited the entire property. The said Hrishikesh Roy left for India before 1962 and since then never returned to this country and consequently he remained in India during the war of 1965 and all through, So his property i.e. the disputed properties were correctly listed as enemy property and rightly declared as vested property. Thus the grant of lease in favour of respondent nos. 6-9 was validly made and possession taken over by them.

<u>5. Mr. S C Das, the learned Advocate for the petitioner referred to the relevant documents annexed to the petition to show that Hrishikesh Roy had relinquished his sight by a deed of declaration dated 5th May, 1962 vide Annexure 'D' and the compromise decree in Other Suit No. 11 of 1962 which was a suit brought by the present petitioner and Parul Bala Roy against Hrishikesh Roy which was decreed on compromise on 2.11.62 on the basis of the compromise petition vide Annexure B and F. By referring to these documents Mr. S.C Das submitted that Hrishikesh Roy had no subsisting right in the disputed property since 2.11.62 in view of the compromise decree declaring the right of petitioner and Parul Bala Roy in the entire property in equal share and undisputedly they never went to India. So the respondent's claim that the property having belonged to Hrishikesh Roy and he having left for and remained in India during the war of 1965 and the property was thus an enemy property could not be sustained in law or was true in fact.</u>

6. In answer to that the learned Deputy Attorney General submitted that the said compromise decree having been obtained by fraud and collusion could not be legally recognised and that the right of Hrishikesh Roy subsisted and as such it was rightly and lawfully listed as enemy property and was consequently declared as a vested property. So the lease granted by the respondent No. 4 in favour of respondents 6 to 9 was legal and proper.

<u>7. In support of his contention the learned Deputy Attorney General referred to a decision reported in A.I.R. 1947(Lahore) 117 in which it has been held that a compromise decree can be challenged in law if it was obtained by fraud and collusion.</u>

<u>8. We have perused the decision and we find that the principle enunciated in the said decision cannot be applied to the facts of the present case which is quite different. In the referred case some co-sharers having interest in the property challenged a compromise decree obtained by 2 other co-sharers to defeat their interest and in that circumstances it was held that such a compromise decree which was obtained by fraud and collusion could be disputed by the other co-sharers who had interest in the said property. But in our present case respondent Nos. 1-5 who are government officials and the respondent Nos. 6-9 who are strangers to the lands and who obtained the disputed lease from the government in 1985 had no kind of interest in the disputed properties in the year 1962 when the compromise decree was passed. So they had no scope to plead that their interest was affected by the said compromise decree so as to give them locus standi to challenge a compromise decree on the plea that it was obtained by fraud or collusion. In the counter affidavit of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 all that was noted vide paragraph 6 of the affidavit was that the compromise decree that was obtained in 1962 by the petitioner and her sister in law Parul Bala Roy was illegal and void because of the fact that the same was obtained by practising fraud upon the court. But no where it was stated what was the manner in which the fraud was practised and also who practised fraud upon whom. Similarly it was nowhere stated in the counter affidavit that the petitioner had practised fraud on Hrishikesh. On the contrary it is found that Hrishikesh had first of all made a deed of declaration relinquishing his entire claim and share in respect of the disputed properties in favour of the present petitioner and Parul Bala Roy and in confirmation of the same he later compromised the suit agreeing and consenting to the declaration of the title of the present petitioner and Peru Bala Roy in respect of the entire disputed property. Thus it is apparent that no fraud was practised upon Hrishikesh Roy who was said to be the owner of the property.</u>

<u>9. Realising the position, the learned Deputy Attorney General submitted a clarification that fraud was practised upon the court in as-much as a transfer of right in favour of the petitioner and Parul Bala Roy was sought to be created by the compromise decree by avoiding registration of a transfer deed as required by section 17 of the Registration Act. This contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General does not hold good in view of the exemption provided in section 17(2)(VI) of the Registration Act by which a decree or order of a court on a compromise in respect of immoveable property, if such compromise decree creates transfer in respect of the subject-matter of the suit, that does not require registration. Thus the position is that the compromise decree holds good as there was no fraud by way of defeating the provision of section 17 of the Registration Act and the respondents have no legal scope or locus standi to challenge the said compromise decree which was passed in 1962 when the present respondents had no kind of interest in the subject-matter of the suit i.e. in present disputed property,</u>

<u>10. In view of the said decree we cannot but hold that the disputed property did not bear any right or possession of Hrishikesh Roy since after the decree dated 1962 and the right and possession remained with the petitioner and Parul Bala Roy who admittedly never left for India and were citizens of the then East Pakistan and later of Bangladesh all through. In that position the disputed property according to law could not come within the category of enemy property and the listing of the said property as enemy property as also the declaration of the said property as vested property were illegal and without jurisdiction. Consequently the impugned orders by which the said properties were proposed to be leased out to the respondent Nos. 6-9 and by which the said proposal were approved were also equally without jurisdiction. In other words the impugned orders had no lawful authority or legal sanction.</u>

<u>This rule is accordingly made absolute. The impugned orders are declared to have been passed without any lawful authority and to be no legal effect.</u>

B. B. Roy Chowdhury, J.—I agree.

End.

Vs.

full_judgment:
This is a suit for realisation of Tk. 79,88,201 upon allegations that the plaintiffs have sustained loss due to late delivery of the cargo, namely 32,148 tons of cement clinkers imported from Turkey in ships. MV KAVO DELFINI and MV KAVO ALKYON owned by the defendant No. 3, for manufacturing of cement in their factory at Chittagong, and that the defendants are liable to reimburse the expenses incurred by the plaintiffs for stevedoring & lightering the aforesaid two ships at the outer anchorage and that other claims are due from the defendants. The plaintiffs have originally claimed the amounts under various heads as under :

LIST OF CLIAIMS

1. Loss sustained due to failure to deliver expeditiously Tk- 33,00,000.00

2. Stevedoring expenses for Mv Kayo Delfini Tk. 3.81,294.50

3. Stevedoring and lightering of clinker for Mv Kayo Alkyon Tk. 12.90,810.00

4. Claim on BG for US $ 88,400 ... Tk. 22,35,865.00

5. Short supply of 44 M. tons of Clinker from Mv Kayo DelfinJ Tk. 48,124.00

6. Re-loading charge of 5006 M. on from dump-yard to jetty conveyor belt @ Tk. 12,50 per MT .. Tk. 62,575.00

Total ...Tk. 79,88,291.00

In the trial, however, the plaintiffs have omitted the claim of Tk. 22,35,865.00 in respect of item No. 4 on account of Bank Guarantee. The plaintiffs have also given up their claim in respect of short supply of 44 in. tons of clinker being Tk. 49,124.00.

2. The plaintiffs have alleged that the plaintiff No. 1 entered into a contract on 31-10-83 (Exhibit 2) with defendant No. 5 for importing 40,000.M. tons of cement clinker for manufacturing cement @ U.S. $ 44.20 per M ton. In terms of the contract the defendant No. 5 agreed to discharge clinkers at the cement grinding factory jetty at Chittagong at its costs, risk and responsibility. The defendant No. 5 shipped a total quantity of 32,148 M. tons of clinkers by two chartered ships, namely, the aforesaid MV KAVO DELFINI and MV KAVO ALKYON owned by the defendant No. 3. The plaintiffs have alleged that in spite of requests and reminders from them the principal defendants neglected and failed to discharge the clinkers from the ships within a reasonable time although they arrived on 11-4-84 and 25-4-84 respectively; that the plaintiffs have suffered loss of production due to delay in discharging the clinkers which are used for manufacturing of cement, and thus they have suffered loss as claimed above. The plaintiffs have also alleged that they at their own expenses and costs have lightened the ships to as to enable them to reach the cement clinker jetty by engaging lighters and stevedores for discharging the clinkers at the outer-anchorage, and that the defendants are liable to reimburse the aforesaid amounts in item Nos. 2 and 3 of the list of claims to the plaintiffs.

3. Defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 and 6 have resisted the claim of the plaintiffs by filing two sets of written statements. The defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 in their written statement has alleged that all responsibilities for handling, clearing and discharging of the cargo from the ships were of the defendant No, 5 were to stow, load, trim, discharge and clear the cargo of the ships. These defendants have alleged that defendant No. 3 is not the owners of the two ships; MV KAVO DELFINI is owned by Navegederes Astrocielo Naviera S.A. Panama and MV KAVO ALKYON is owned by Intermarries Viatlentia Armodora, S.A. Panama and that defendant No. 3 are the Managers and agents of the two ships; in terms of charter party defendant No. 5 is solely responsible and liable to clear and discharge the cargo at their own costs, risk and responsibility. The defendants have averred that they are not liable to stevedore and lighten the ships at the outer anchorage and that in terms of the agreement between the plaintiffs and defendant No. 5, the defendant No. 5 is responsible for clearing, handing and discharging and thus for stevedoring the cargo and lightening the ships for safe arrival of the vessel at the clinker jetty site. The defendants have further alleged that they have no responsibility for alleged late delivery of the cargo resulting in the alleged loss to the plaintiffs. They have nevertheless denied that the plaintiffs have suffered loss on account of late delivery of the cargo at the clinker jetty site. In the written statement they have denied their liability as regards various claims made by the plain-tiffs and the quantum of the alleged claims as, in the plaint.

4. The defendant No. 6 in the written statement has denied their responsibility and liability to pay any amount to the plaintiffs. They have also alleged they are the agents of defendant No. 5, the charterer and hence as agents of the known principal they have no liability in respect of the claims; the substantive case of the defendants is that though they were appointed agents of the ships by the Charterer, the defendant No. 5, for declaring, handling and clearing of the two ships, the charterer failed to remit necessary funds for the purpose, and in view of paucity of funds the defendants could not carry on their works as agents of the ships expeditiously; defendants have stated that for declaring, handling, clearing of MV KAVO DELFINI they have incurred a total expense of Tk. 14,82,589.75 for port disbursement and cargo expenses for lightening and that out of the said amount defendant No. 3 had paid to the defendant Tk. 6,07,131 92 leaving a balance of Tk. 8,75,457 83 and that the defendants are liable to pay the said amount to this defendant. As regards vessel MV KAVO ALKYON the defendants, have claimed a total amount of Tk. 6,20,217.45 on account of port disbursement and agency fees, etc. and the defendants are liable to pay the same to them.

In the trial the following issues have been frame for decision:

1. Is the suit maintainable under the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the Court ?

2. Is the suit barred under the principles of waiver, estoppel, and acquiescence ?

3. Is the suit bad for mis-joinder and non-joinder of parties ?

4. Has the plaintiffs any cause of action against the defendants ?

5. Are the vessel MV KAVO ALKYON and KAYO DFLFINJ owned by two separate owners ?

6. Were these defendants responsible for arranging delivery of the cargo to the plaintiffs as per contract between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 5 dated 31-10-1993?

7. Were these defendants liable to compensate any alleged loss of the plaintiffs ?

8. Are the plaintiffs entitled to any relief against the defendants in the instant suit and, if so, against whom and in what sum?

9. Have the defendants Nos. 1, 3 and 4 suffered loss and/or damage as a result of delay caused by the plaintiffs in taking delivery of their cargo from MV KAVO ALKYON ?

10. Is the counter claim of the defendants maintainable in the Admiralty Jurisdiction?

11. Are these defendants entitled to the decree as prayed in the counter claim and, if so, in what sum ?

5. Issues Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4 have not been pressed at the trial and accordingly issue Nos. 1 and 4 are answered in the affirmative and issue No. 2 and 3 in the negative. We are now taking up all other issues together for decision for the sake of brevity.

6. It is not dented that the plaintiffs entered into a contract with defendant No. 5 to purchase and import cement clinkers for manufacturing cement at their cement-clinker grinding factory at Chittagong. It is also not denied that the defendant No. 5 is the suppliers and shippers of the cement clinkers. The defendant No. 5 is also the charterers of the two ships. MV KAVO DELFIN and MV KAVO ALKYON which together carried 32,184 metric tons of clinkers from Turkey in terms of a contract between the defendant No. 5 and the plaintiffs. It is not denied that in terms of the contract the defendant No, 5 is to beat all costs and expenses for clearing and discharging of the cargo at the cement clinker jetty at Chittagong Port. It is also in evidence that in terms of charter party between the owners of the two ships and defendant No. 5 the responsibility for discharging of the cargo of the ships was upon the defendant No. 5 on the unimpeachable facts and important evidence of the case viz, the contract of sale (Exhibit 2) between the plaintiffs and defendant No. 5 and the charter-party (Exhibit G F) between the defendant No. 5 and the owners of the ships, the defendant No 5 is liable for the claims made by the plaintiffs in this suit.

7. Dr M Zahir, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has strenuously argued that apart from the responsibility of defendant No. 5 for due discharge of the cargo both under the terms of sale of the clinkers and under the charter party, in which the plaintiff are not parties, the other principal defendant as well are responsible for due discharge of the cargo at the clinker jetty site. In this connection he has referred to the bills of lading in respect of the cargo issued by the masters of the two ships, and has submitted that in terms of the bills of lading the owners of the ships are responsible for due discharge of the cargo to the consignee.

8. Mr M Hafizullah, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the ships (defendant No. 1), the alleged owners of the ship (defendant No. 3) and the agent of the alleged owners (defendant No. 4) has firstly submitted that the owners having not been impleaded in the suit no decree can be passed against them in respect of any loss arising out of the alleged late delivery of the cargo or expenses incurred by the plaintiffs for lightening and stevedoring the ships so as to enable them to reach the cement clinker jetty. According to the learned Advocate, in view of the contract of purchase between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 5, the defendant Nos. 1, 3 & 4 or the owners of the ships are not liable for any of the claims made by the plaintiffs. According to him, the contract of purchase having specially mentioned that the seller, who is the charterer as well of the ships, was to notify the plaintiffs about the particulars and age of the ships before their sailings and when the plaintiffs were aware before the ships sailed with the cargo that the ships were of bigger draft and it could not enter into the jetty without lightening of the ships at the outer anchorage, the plaintiff were not entitled to reimbursement of the expenses incurred by them for lightening the ships. In this connection he has referred to the clauses 5.1, 5.2 and 5.5 of the contract of sale between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 5. According to him, in terms of clause 5.5 the particulars of the vessel and its age were to be notified to the plaintiffs by the seller before the shipment would be made in the ships. This provision appears to have been made in view of the low draft at the cement clinker jetty of the Port.

9. Dr M Zahir, on the other land, has submitted that there is no cogent evidence that the provisions in the contract of sale regarding notifying of the plaintiffs about the particulars and size of the ships were intended for shipment of the cargo in smaller ships. He has submitted that in terms of two contracts of carriage as evidenced by the bills of lading the owners of the ships were responsible for due discharge of the cargo since the bills of lading were on liner terms basis. He has submitted that the ships having been chartered by the defendant No. 5 on time charter basis, the bills of lading issued by the master or his agents was on liner terms basis because the ship owners was on possession and control of the ships through its master.

10. In the trial the principal questions are whether the expenses allegedly incurred by the plaintiffs are recoverable from all the defendants or from which of the defendants, if all of them are not liable. Secondly, whether the defendants are liable for the alleged delay in discharge of the cargo or which of the defendants is liable for the delay, if all of them are not so liable. As I have indicated above, the defendant No. 5 is undoubtedly liable in respect of the claims made by the plaintiffs including reimbursement of cost of lightening of the ships and stevedoring of their cargo. As regards the liability of the defendant No. 6, admittedly they were appointed agents for handling, discharging and clearing of the cargo from the two ships. It has been alleged by the plaintiffs that since the defendant No. 6 has received the money from the plaintiffs for the work of lightening and stevedoring the cargo of the ships they are also bound to refund the amount under section 230 of the Contract Act.

<u>11. The agent cannot personally be liable for the work done by him on behalf of his principal in absence of a contract that the agent would be liable personally for the performance of the contract made between the principal and purchaser, The plaintiffs were aware although that the defendant No. 6 was an agent of the principal, defendant No. 5. It has been noticed that the principal of defendant No. 6 entered into a contract of sale of the cargo with the plaintiffs providing in the contract stipulations as to delivery of the cargo etc. to the latter. The principal being a known one, and with whom the plaintiffs have dealt with regarding the cargo, the agent cannot be personally liable. DW 2 the Accounts Officer of defendant No. 6 has deposed that the defendant could not carry out the work of lightening of the ships and Stevedoring of the cargo in view of absence of remittances from the defendant No. 5. He has denied that he obtained work order from the plaintiffs for lightening of the vessels by coercion. The witness has deposed that they did not start or continue with the lightening work of the ships because no fund was available to them from the defendant No. 5. For the reasons stated above, the defendant No. 6 cannot behold responsible for the failure of defendant No. 5 or of the ships to lighten them and discharging the cargo within a reasonable time. There is no evidence that although funds were placed in the hands of the defendant No. 6 by the defendant No. 5, they did not carry on the work of lightening and stevedoring but they forced the plaintiffs to have the work of lightening done at the expenses of the plaintiffs. In this view the defendant No. 6 cannot be held liable to refund or reimburse the expenses incurred by the plaintiffs for lightening and stevedoring work of the two ships. Both in terms of contract of purchase and performance guarantee given by the Banque Indosuez on behalf of the defendant No. 5 and in terms of charter party, the defendant No. 5 is liable to reimburse and pay the claims as the plaintiffs would be entitled to.</u>

12. As regards the liability of the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 the plaintiffs have claimed that these defendants as well are liable to reimburse the expenses incurred by the plaintiffs for lightening of the ships and stevedoring of the cargo. The case of the plaintiffs is that beside defendant No. 5, the master of the ship, the alleged owners and the local agent of the owners are equally liable for the claims of the plaintiffs the bills of lading in sod respect of the cargo was issued by the Masters of the ships on liner term basis.

13. It is not disputed that lightening of the ships by discharging of the cargo on the lighter-age vessels and stevedoring of the cargo at the outer anchorage were required for reaching the ships at the cement clinker jetty. It has been alleged that the plaintiffs have spent sum of Tk. 3,81,294,50 for stevedoring of the cargo or MV KAVO DELFINI and Tk. 12,90,810.00 for stevedoring and lightening work of MV KAVO ALKYON. It appears from the contract of purchase, which has been mentioned in the bills of lading that the supplier i.e. the defendant No. 5 was to inform the plaintiffs about the particulars and age of the ships before shipments. This provision in clause 5.5 of the contract of purchase was made so that bigger ships were not engaged by the defendant No. 5 for carrying of cargo from Turkey to Bangladesh since bigger ships would not reach the clinker jetty at the Port.

14. Dr M Zahir has submitted that irrespective of the contract of sale between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 5, in terms of the Bills of lading the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4 are liable to lighten the ships and stevedoring the cargo at the outer anchorage and bear all expenses for the said works. According to him, when the owners took the voyage and accepted the consignment they know that the vessels could not reach the cement clinker jetty at Chittagong, without lightening he ships at the outer anchorage requiring additional expenses. It, however, appears from the deposition of PW 2 that the defendant No 5 sent to the plaintiffs in advance the particulars of the ships but plaintiffs did not raise any objection as to the size of the two ships, since the seller is to bear the expenses of lightening of the ships in terms of the contract of sale (Exhibit 2). The learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has strenuously argued that even assuming that the seller i.e. the Defendant No. 5 is responsible, to pay for the expenses of lightering of the ships in terms of the contract of sale, the owners as well arc liable for them on the footing of the Bills of lading. According to the learned Advocate when there is no evidence that the plaintiffs had knowledge of the charter-party or its terms before shipments of the cargo, the plaintiffs as endorsees or consignees of the bills of lading for value are entitled to delivery or discharge of the cargo at the jetty named in the bills of lading, and the ships, their owners and their agents are responsible for safe discharge of the cargo in terms of the bill of lading, Extra 3 and 4.

<u>15. I have indicated above that the defendant No. 5 is undoubtedly liable for the losses suffered by the plaintiffs for breach of contract of sale of clinkers to them. Whether the aforesaid ship (defendant No. 1), the master of ship (defendant No. 2) Manager of the owners of the ships (defendant No. 3) and the agent of the defendant No. 3 (defendant No. 4) are responsible for the alleged loss in delay in discharging the cargo at the Cement Clinker jetty and reimbursement of the expenses incurred by plaintiffs for lightening the ships at outer anchorage so as to reach the Cement Clinker Jetty. The case of the plaintiffs is that the bills of lading of the cargo being on liner term basis as admitted by DW 1, and the master through its agent having signed the bills of lading evidencing the contract of carriage between the shipper and the owners of the ships, the owners of the ships are liable to discharge the cargo at the Jetty named in the bills of lading notwithstanding the charter-parties or the contract of sale between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 5.</u>

<u>In Payne's Carriage of Goods by Sea (Eighth Edition) at page 40 it is however said :</u>

<u>"Where the charterer is also the ship-per, the rights of ship-owner and charterer as such will be governed by the charter-party alone. The bill of lading cannot vary or add to the terms of the charter party unless it contains an expenses provision to that effect."</u>

<u>Payne also says:</u>

<u>"Further in the case of general ship, if a shipper know of the existence of a charter party, he is taken to have contracted with the charterer and can sue or be sued by him. If he did not, his contract is with the shipper."</u>

<u>It will therefore appear that when the charterer is the shipper of the cargo contract of carriage would be governed by charter party alone for determination of liability as between the shipper and the owner. The learned Advocate for the plaintiffs has submitted that the plaintiffs as endorsee or consignees for value were not aware of the charter party and its terms and hence terms of bills of lading shall determine the liabilities as between the plaintiffs acid the owners of the ships. This view appears to be a sound one assuming that the consignees i e. the plaintiffs had knowledge of the charter party yet his knowledge of chatter party would not absolve the ship owners from discharging the cargo at the jetty site. In this connection I refer to a passage in Note 1354 of Carvers Carriage by Sea 12th Edition which are:</u>

"Effect of notice of Charter party. Cases such as Fry vs Chartered Mercantile Bank show that an assignee for value of the bill of lading to whom the contract in the bill of leading has passed, does not lose his right to have the goods free of liens of the ship owner, not expressly reserved in the bill of lading, merely because he has notice of the existence of the charter- party. Nor because he obtains his title from the charterer himself."

<u>In the instant case the charterer being the shipper of the cargo the terms of charter-party would govern the contract of carriage as between the owners of the ships and consignee value. In view of the decision reported in (1925) 30 Commercial Case 117 (125-6) as noticed in Peyne's Carriage of Goods by Sea, right and obligation in a contract of carriage as between the shipper (where is the charter is the shipper) and the owners would be governed by the terms of the charter-party but the position as between the owners of the ships, through the master who has issued the bills of lading on liner terms basis and the endorsee or the consignee for value (not the agent of the shipper) is on a different footing. There may be a notion that when the shipper is the charterer of the ships and with whom the owners/masters of the ship entered into a contract of carriage as between the owners of the ship and the consignee of the cargo would as well be governed by the charter-party of the ships. This view is erroneous.</u>

<u>17. The rights and obligations as between an endorsee of the bill of lading or consignee of the cargo and the owners of the ship which carried the cargo would be governed by the bill of lading. In the instant case, notwithstanding the charter-party between the shipper and the owners of the ship, in terms of bills of lading the owners of the ships were responsible to discharge the clinkers at the jetty named in the bill of lading.</u>

18. In the case of Manchester Trust vs Furness reported in (1895) 2 QB 539, the Court of Appeal of England has held that the master was in fact the servant of the owner and that the endorsees were not affected with notice of the charter-party clause, and may sue the ship owner on the bill of lading. Carver in Carriage by Sea, referring to the decisions has said as follows:

In Manchester Trust vs Furness the shipment was made by charterers under a charter party which contained the following special clause. In signing bills of lading is expressly agreed that the captain shall only do so as the agent for the charterers ...."A bill of lading was given for the shipment, signed by the master, reserving freight" and other conditions as per charter-party and this was endorsed by the charter-party to their bankers as security.

The Court of Appeal affirming Mathew J held that notwithstanding the above clause, the master was in fact the servant of the ship-owners and the endorsee were not affected with notice of the clause, and could sue the ship-owners on the bill of lading "is to incorporate so much of the charter-party as relates to the payment of freight and other conditions to be performed on the delivery of the cargo" but there is no authority whatsoever for incorporating more than that. What is wanted in this case is to say that, by reason of the reference to charter-party, the holder of the bill of lading and the person who takes it in the ordinary course of business are to be treated as having notice of all the contents of the charter-party. There is no doctrine that goes to anything like that extent; and as regards the extension of the equitable doctrines of constructive notice to commercial transactions, the courts have always set their faces resolutely against it."

<u>19. In view of the above, I am of opinion that the holder of the bill of lading or any person who has obtained it in ordinary course of business cannot be treated as having notice of the charter-party and that equitable consideration that an endorsee or a consignee has notice of the charter-party cannot be entertained. The owners of the ships therefore, on the basis of the bill of lading are to bear the expenses for lightening of the ship at the outer anchorage and liable for compensation for the delay in discharging of the clinker at the jetty. In this view defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 5 are jointly responsible for the delay in discharging of the clinkers and they are liable to pay compensation for loss of production of cement, if there has been any. However, in view of the evidence in the minutes of the Board of Directors dated 28-2-84 (Exhibit 1(e) that as on 1-3-84 there was sufficient clinkers for production of cement in the months of April, May and June 1984, the claims on account of loss of production of cement due to delay in discharge of the clinkers cannot be sustained. There is, however, evidence from the deposition of PW 1 that fresh clinkers are necessary for mixing with the old stock for manufacturing cement and that in view of the shortage of fresh clinkers production suffered. In view of the evidence in Exhibit 1(e) it would not be reasonable to allow compensation for loss on account of delay in discharging of the clinkers from the two ships. Further, it is in evidence that there has been huge losses in 1982 and 1983. Hence, in my view, grant of compensation for loss of production is too remote a relief claimed by the plaintiffs.</u>

<u>In view of the above, I hold that the plaintiffs are not entitled to any compensation for loss of production.</u>

<u>20. Under the bills of lading in the instant case on liner terms basis the owners are responsible for safe discharge of the cargo as expeditiously as possible. It will appear from Note No. 362 of Carver's Carriage by Sea 12th Edition that in time charter possession of the ship remains with the owner. It is seen from the deposition of DW 1 a Director of defendant No. 3, who are managers and agents of the ship-owner, that the masters of the ships have been appointed by the owners and that they have paid their salaries. D.W 1 was also deposed that the bills of lading were on liner term basis and that who issues the bills of lading pays for the discharge of the cargo.</u>

<u>21. As of the question who are the owner of the ships I have perused the evidence produced by the plaintiffs and defendant Nos. 1, 3, and 4. It appears from the photostat copy of Lloyds Register of Shipping (Exhibit D) as well as the list of ship owners (Exhibit 12(3) that defendant No. 3 Gourdomiehalis Midin are not the owners of the two ships but are the managers or agents of the ships. Be that as it may, in view of my finding made above that defendant Nos. 1 and 5 are liable for the claims in respect of the cargo carried in the two ships under the contract of carriage as evidenced by the bills of lading, any loss suffered by the plaintiffs on account of delay in discharging the clinkers and the costs incurred by them for lightening and stevedoring of ships at the outer anchorage are recoverable from the said defendant Nos. 1 and 5. Apart from the liability arising out of bills of lading in respect of the cargo, defendant No.5 is also responsible under the performance guarantee bond given by the defendant's banker in favour of the plaintiffs, which however, is not the subject matter of the dispute in this suit.</u>

22. With regard to the expenses incurred by the plaintiffs for stevedoring of MV KAVO DELFINI it appears to me that the evidence adduced by the plaintiffs as regards the actual expenses incurred by them, could not be dis-credited by any evidence of rebuttal. I, therefore, hold that the plaintiffs are entitled to realise Tk 3.81.294.50 for stevedoring expenses of MV KAVO DELFINI and Tk. 11,88,074.50 paisa for stevedoring and lightening expenses on account of MV KAVO ALKYON actually incurred by the plaintiffs from the defendant No. 5. The amount of Tk. 11,88,074.50 is also recoverable from the defendant No. 1. The Defendant No. 1, however, is not liable to reimburse the stevedoring expenses of MV KAVO DELFINI since in an action against MV KAVO ALKYON claims in respect of KAVO DELFINI and which is owned by a different owner, cannot be realised under law. The defendant No. 1 is also not liable to reimburse the overage insurance premium paid by the plaintiffs since the latter were aware of the particulars and size of the ships before shipment. This amount is recoverable from the defendant No. 5 alone.

<u>23. As regards the liability of defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 4 they being the agents of disclosed principals they are not liable to answer the claims arising out of wrongs done by their principals or for breach of contract made by them. The real owner of MV KAVO ALKYON has furnished the bank guarantee and they could be proceeded against in this suit. In this view the submission of the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs that agents are liable for the claim against the principal cannot by sustained. The decision referred to by the learned Advocate in 8 DLR 349 is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case,</u>

<u>24. The plaintiffs have filed two applications one for impleading the actual owner of the ship as defendant. As the owners and parties interested in the ships instead of defendant No. 3. Although the owners and parties interested in the ship are necessary parties and they ought to have been added as defendant in the suit but since the application for addition or substitution in place of defendant No. 3 has been made at a belated stage and after completion of evidence this application cannot be entertained and it is accordingly rejected. The plaintiffs have also filed another application for adjusting the decree, if any, passed in the suit against the bank guarantee furnished by the actual owner of the ship KAVO ALKYON. Since a decree has been passed against the defendant No. 1, the ship, and the owners of the ship have given a bank guarantee to the extent of the claim in suit, in suit, in my view in accordance with the Admiralty Rules 12.17 and 33 read with original side Rules 11, 13 and 15 a decree passed against the Defendant No. 1 can be adjusted against the said bank guarantee furnished by the owners of the ship, But the adjustment against the bank guarantee shall be limited to the extent of the decree passed in favour of the plaintiffs in respect of stevedoring and lightening charge in respect of MV KAVO ALKYON. The other claims of the plaintiffs and the decree passed in respect of stevedoring of the vessel KAVO DELFINI, overage insurance premium and reloading charge as claimed in item 7 of the plaint cannot be adjusted from the bank guarantee furnished by the owners of KAVO ALKYON. It may be observed in this connection that the owners of KAVO ALKYON may however avail of their remedy for reimbursement and or realisation of the claims from the defendant No .5 in terms of charter-party.</u>

<u>25. As regards the counter claims made by the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 against the plaintiffs for delay and detention of the ships for nearly three months, since I have found that the owners of the ships as well as the ship, defendant No. 1 are liable to discharge the cargo expeditiously in terms of bills of lading, the counter claim against the plaintiffs on account of delay and detention of the ship for nearly three months in the port cannot be entertained and the claim is accordingly rejected. The owners of the ships as indicated above may, however, avail of their remedies for reimbursements and/or realisation of their claims in terms of the charter party from the defendant No. 5.</u>

26. In the result the suit is decreed against the defendant No. 5 for a sum of Tk. 24,00,465.00 (Taka twenty, four lac four hundred sixty five) only on account of stevedoring expenses for MV KAVO DELFINI and MV KAVO ALKYON; overage insurance premium, re-loading charges from dump-yard to jetty conveyor belt. Out of the said amount of Tk. 24,00,465.00 the defendant No. 1 is liable to pay to the plaintiffs jointly with defendant No. 5, the sum of Tk. 11,88,074.50 actually incurred by the plaintiffs by stevedoring and lightening of MV KAVO ALKYON and accordingly a decree for Tk. 1188 074.50 (Taka eleven lac eighty eight thousand seventy four and paisa fifty) only is passed Jointly against the defendant Nos. 1 and 5. The suit is dismissed as against defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 and 6. The counter claim of the defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 against the plaintiffs is dismissed. In view of the decree the owners of KAVO ALKYON are directed to reduce the Bank Guarantee furnished by them to the extent of Tk, 11,88,074.50 (Taka eleven lac eighty eight thousand seventy four and paisa fifty) only and it is extended for another one year. In view of the facts of the case there will be no order as to the cost of the suit.

Let the operation of this judgment and decree be stayed for 20 days from the date of drawing up of the order.

End.
