full_judgment:
Md. Sirajul Islam, J.: This appeal by the defendant No.2 is directed against the judgment and decree dated 7.3.90 and 17.3.90 respectively passed by the Subordinate Judge. First Court. Dhaka in Title Suit No. 43 of 1984

2. Plaintiff Mr. AKM Bashirullah filed Title Suit No. 43 of 1984 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka for partition of their ejmali properties by metes and bounds. The plaintiffs case is that the properties described in the schedule to the plaint originally belonged to Dr Muhammad Shahidullah , one of the most distinguished educationists and his wife Mrs. Marguba Khatoon. Mrs. Marguba Khatoon and Dr. Mohammad Shahidullah died in 1968 and 1969 respectively leaving behind seven sons and two daughters who are the plaintiffs and the defendants in the suit. The suit properties thus devolved upon the plaintiffs and the defendants after the death of their parents. The properties have not been paritioned by metes and bounds amongst these co-sharers and that some of the co-sharers have been enjoying lion's share of the suit properties. The plaintiff demanded partition from the defendants but no partition took place. Hence this suit for partition

3. The defendant No.2 contested the suit by filing a written statement. His case is that the plaintiff and the defendants are the legal heirs of Dr. Muhammad Shahidullah and his wife Mrs. Marguba Khatoon. But that the properties have already been partitioned by metes and bounds amongst the co-sharers. The suit has been brought on some frivolous allegations and hence it is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Subordinate Judge after considering the evidence of the suit and hearing both the parties has decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 7.3.90 and 17.3.90 respectively.

5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge the defendant No.2 had preferred this appeal against the other co-sharers. The respondents opposed the appeal.

6. It appears that admittedly the suit properties originally belonged to Dr. Muhammad Shahidullah and his wife Mrs. Marguba Khatoon, Admittedly. Dr. Muhammad Shahidullah and Mrs. Marguba died leaving behind seven sons and two daughters who are the plaintiffs and defendants in the suit As such the plaintiffs and defendants are the legal heirs of late Dr. Muhammad Shahidullah and Mrs. Marguba Khatoon in respect of the suit properties. Therefore it appears that each of their sons is entitled to 2/16 share in the properties and each of their daughters is entitled to 1/16 share in the properties. There is no dispute in respect of this quantum of share of the respective parties in the suit properties. By a perusal of the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge has allotted the saham of each of the sons and the daughters according to this quantum of share. Therefore apparently we do not find any wrong or mistake in the amount of share allotted to the plaintiffs and defendants by the learned Subordinate Judge in his judgment.

7. The only question raised before us on behalf of the defendant No.2-appellant is that the parties made a compromise of the suit and submitted a solenama in court at the time of hearing of the suit which has been marked as Ext. "A" but that the learned Subordinate Judge did not accept the solenama holding that the solenama has not been acted upon. It is the case of the defendant-appellant that this finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is not correct.

8. Syed Muhammad Dashtagir Hossain the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant. submitted that during the pendency of the suit the parties made a compromise the terms of which are embodied in the solenama (Ext. A) and therefore the compromise may be recorded under Order 23 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure and decree passed accordingly. Mr. MB Taz Mohammad the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff and the defendant-respondents on the other hand argued that no effective compromise has been made and that the parties have not yet got any possession in respect of their respective legal share and that the alleged solenama is vague indefinite and not acted upon. The learned Advocates for the respondents further submitted that the defendant No.7 did not sign the alleged solenama.

9. Under such contesting submissions. it is to be determined here as to whether the alleged solenama (Ext. A) is legal. fair and acceptable under Order 23 rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code.

10. Order 23 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure runs thus:

"(3) Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise or where the defendant satisfies the plaintiff in respect of the whole or any part of the subject-matter of the suit the Court shall order such agreement compromise or satisfaction to be recorded and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit."

11. By a careful reading of the above provision of Order 23. rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code. it will appear that this rule will be applicable only when the suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by a lawful agreement or compromise or when the defendant satisfied the plaintiff in respect of the whole or any part of the suit.

12. Mr. Taj Mohammad the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents submitted that the alleged solenama was signed on 1.3.86 but the defendant No.2 who is the appellant here kept it in his pocket and that he filed the solenama in court only on 31.1.90 the date of hearing of the suit and that during this 4/5 years no share was given to any of the parties according to the solenama by defendant No.2 who is possessing the major portion and that the defendant No.2 did not satisfy the plaintiff or any other co-sharer in respect of the whole or any part of the properties in suit.

13. Let us now see whether the alleged solenama is lawful and whether it has adjusted the suit or whether it has satisfied the plaintiff in respect of the suit property.

14. On a scrutiny of the alleged solcnama, it appears that it was signed on 1.3.86 but that it was filed before the court on 31.1.90 by 'defendant No.2 alone and not by any other parties. It further appears that the solenama does not bear the signature of any lawyer of any of the parties. No application was filed by defendant No.2 through any lawyer under Order 23 rule 3 CPC praying for recording the solenama or to pass the decree accordingly. It appears from the record that while the defendant No.2 was deposing before the court as contesting defendant on 31.1.90 he filed the solenama in court from his possession stating that they made the solenama on 1.3.86.

<u>15. It. therefore appears that the alleged solenama (Ext. A) was in the possession of the defendant No. 2 from 1.3.86 till 31.1.90. No explanation has been given from the side of the defendant appellant as to why this solenama was not filed before the court nor was any prayer made to the court to record the solenama during the period from 1.3.86 to 3l.l.90. This fact alone goes to say that the alleged solenama was not acted upon and that the plaintiff or the other co-sharers were not satisfied by the defendant No.2 in respect of the whole or any part of the properties in suit.</u>

16. Defendant No.2 alone claims to have made a compromise of the suit as per the alleged solenama. Therefore, the onus of proving before the court that the suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise as contemplated by Order 23, rule 3, of the Code of Civil Procedure lies on defendant No.2. But it appears that defendant No. 2 did not adduce any evidence to prove any adjustment of the suit or legality or effectiveness of the alleged solenama. On the other hand, the plaintiff as PW 1 said in his deposition that the suit properties have not been partitioned between them by metes and bounds and he demanded a saham of his 1/8 share in the suit properties according to Muslim law. This means that plaintiff (PW 1) did not as yet get his1/8 legal share in the suit properties. PW 1 further said in his cross-examination that the solenama has not been acted upon and that it was a tentative solenama, In view of all these facts and evidence, it will appear that the defendant appellant has failed to prove that the suit has been adjusted wholly or in part as per the alleged solenama.

17. It may be mentioned here that admittedly defendant No. 7 of the suit did not sign the alleged solenama. Mr. Syed Md. Dashtagir Hossain, the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellant, referred to the case of Thiruvengada Mudaliar Vs. Thaugavelu Mudaliar and others AIR 1928 (Mad) 594 and argued that the solenama may be accepted even if one of the parties did not sign in it.

18. It appears from the above cited case that, that was an application to enforce a compromise in a suit for partition relating to a Hindu family and the terms of the compromise were reduced to writing on a stamp paper. It was held therein that "a compromise of a partition suit is not necessarily ineffectual because every party to the action does not join in it. It is undoubtedly true that in some cases there may not be a valid and lawful compromise unless all the parties join in effecting it; but each case must depend upon its own facts," The learned advocate for the appellant next referred to a case reported in AIR 1934 (Patna) 582. IL appears that, that was a civil revision case against the order for compromise passed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that case his Lordship observed that the proper provision under which the Subordinate Judge should have proceeded was Order 23, rule 3. That case was also a case relating to Hindu undivided family, It was held in that case that "in an inquiry under Order 23 rule 3 the plain duty of the court is to come to a conclusion as to whether there was a lawful compromise arrived at between the parties concerned or not, and although the fact that the compromise has been signed by some of the parties and not by others may be given due weight, yet in arriving at the ultimate conclusion regard should also be had to other matters, such as the relationship between the two plaintiffs, whether they belong to joint Hindu Family".

19. The facts and nature of instant case before us are quite different from those of the two cases referred to above by the learned Advocate for the appellant. The instant case before us is not relating to any Hindu Joint family property but that it is a case of partition by metes and bounds of property belonging to a Muslim undivided family, the quantum of share of which is required to be divided according to Muslim law of inheritance. Moreover, non-signing of the solenama by one of the co-sharers is not the only consideration in this case. There are other factors involved in it for consideration.

20. It has been stated in a counter-affidavit filed by the respondent Nos. 2, 5 and 8 that the appellant never came up with any positive attitude for early disposal of the suit, rather he is making endeavour to prolong the process of the court and that that they signed a draft solenama prepared by the petitioner (appellant) on 1.3.86 and that it is an incomplete and ambiguous solenama.

21. On a further scrutiny of the alleged solenama (Ext. A), it appears that it is written in a plain paper and not in any cartridge paper nor in any stamp paper. It appears from paragraph 3 of the solenama that Muncipal holding No. 79 Begum Bazar, Dhaka has been jointly allotted to plaintiff Mr. AKM Bashirullah @ Mortaza Bashir and defendant No.4, Mr AKM Waliyullah and defendant No.8, Mr. ABM Raziyullah and defendant No. 1 Musammat Mahjuja Khatoon which has been specifically mentioned in the schedule 'C'. It appears fromparagraph 4 of that solcnama that Muncipal holding No. 10, North Brook Hall Road, pS" Sutrapur, Dhaka has been jointly allotted to defendant No.2 Mr. AFM Sofiyullah, defendant No.3, Mrs, Mabrura Khaioon and defendant 7 Dr. ABM Naquiyullah which has been specifically mentioned in the schedule 'D' and that the defendants have accepted the joint allotment. But lhe fact remains that admittedly defendant No.7 Dr. ABM Naquiyullah did not sign the solcnama and that admittedly he was not in Bangladesh. Therefore, the question of acceptance by defendant No. 7 does not arise. It appears from paragraph 5 of the alleged solenama that the properties mentioned in the Schedules 4 and 6 of the plaint situated at Mymensingh and Bogra respectively has been jointly allotted to defendants 5 and 6 specifically mentioned in the schedules 'E' and 'P'. It thus appears that the defendants 5 and 6 were being pushed out to Mymensingh and Bogra only. It futher appears that the pages containing the schedules of the solenama have not been signed by any parties.

<u>22. In view of the nature of allotments as stated in the solenama it appears that the allotments have been made jointly and not by metes and bounds and some of the co-sharers have been given the property of Mymensingh and Bogra only, Therefore, this solenama is not only a draft solenama written in the white plain papers but also it is unconscionable, ambiguous and prejudicial to the parties of the suit. The normal course in respect of a compromise is that whenever any compromise is made between the parties during the pendency of a suit, then the plaintiff or any other party docs not proceed with the suit but that they file a compromise-petition with a joint-prayer through their lawyers for recording the solenama and then the proceeding of the suit shall stop there. But in this case, it appears that not only the plaintiff proceeded with the suit but also the defendant No.2 (appellant) contested the suit all through till the date of final hearing on 31.1.90.</u>

23. Having regard to all the facts, circumstances and the evidence discussed above, we hold that the alleged solenama (Ext. 'A') is neither fair nor lawful nor valid rather it is an absolutely unconscionable, ambiguous and a vague solenarna prejudicial to the respective co-sharers. This solenama did not satisfy the condition bid down in Order, 23 rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure Hence. It is not at all acceptable.

24. Taking all the above facts, circumstances and the position of law into consideration, we arc of the opinion that the conclusion of the learned Subordinate Judge is correct and does not call for any interference.

25. In the result, the appeal is dismissed and the connected Rule being Civil Rule No. 131(F) of 1990 becoming infructuous is hereby discharged and the order of the stay granted by this court of 14.6.90 is also hereby vacated.

26. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
