full_judgment:
These Rules arising out of Civil Revisional application Nos. 170-204, 206-222 of 1985 are directed against the judgment and order dated 2.1.85 passed by the 1st Court of Munsif (S. C. C. Judge), Dhaka in the respective S. C. C. Suits.

2. The civil Rules arising out of civil revisional application Nos. 635-649 of 1985 filed by Shamsul Haque and others, on the other hand, are directed against the order dated 27.6.1985 passed by the S. C. C. Judge, (Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court) Dhaka in the respective S. C. C. Suits.

3. Facts being similar they are taken up together for hearing analogous and are disposed of by this one judgment.

4. Facts in short, are that Tamizul Haque, Anwarul Haque and Shamsul Haque and heirs of Azizul Haque and others filed suits as plaintiffs against the defendant opposite parties Md. Yunus Ali, Jamalud din, Md. Ishaque Sikder, Md. Momin Khan and many others starting from S.C.C. Suit No. 70 of 1983 before the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka. They have also filed a number of S.C.C. suits against 14 other tenants before the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, being S.C.C. Judge, starting from S. C. C. Suit No. 30 of 1983. All these suits were filed for eviction of monthly tenants by the plaintiff who are landlords of Haque Market premises for default of payment of rent.

5. The market is situated at 22, Chittaranjan Avenue, Dhaka. All these suits were filed by Mr. Tamijul Haque in two different Courts as plaintiffs for himself and as constituted Attorney for Anwarul Haque, Shamsul Haque, Hakima Khatun, Sadrun Nessa, Ayesha Khatun, Enamul Haque, Ainul Haque, Noor-e-Afshan (Minor), Husn-e-Afsan. All these suits had been contested by the respective tenants by filing written statements where material allegations were denied and it was stated therein by the respective tenants that Tamijul Haque had no authority to sign the plaint on behalf of other plaintiffs as he has no authority to proceed with the suit on behalf of other plaintiffs; that notice under section 106 of the T. P. Act has not been served. It has been further stated that the plaintiff No.3 revoked the alleged power of Attorney granted in favour of Tamij Haque and directed the defendant to deposit rent in the court in view of filing Title Suit No. 83 of 1984 in the Court of 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for partition of the suit property. It is the tenants' case that 73 shops that are in the said Haque Market has formed an Association know as "Haque Market Kapar Baboashai Samity" which always negotiated with the landlord and it was the practice in the said Market that in case of any shop transferred to a tenant the landlord used to realise an amount known as transfer fee from the transferee recognising him as tenant. All these matters used to be negotiated through the said Association. The landlords were not regularising the transfer of shop to tenants for a pretty long time in spite of receipt of transfer fee and rent and they were not also granting receipt thereof. They realised rent but did not grant any receipt. The plaintiff had realised from the defendant tenants of the said market an amount of Tk. 2,00,000/- (two lac Taka) and odd as transfer fee with no receipt. The tenants had paid the rent bonafide and also the transfer fee to the plaintiffs with the hope that the rent receipt will be granted but it was not granted and now pressure was being put upon the defendants to come to an unreasonable settlement with the landlord. All the tenants had paid their rents, other tenants including the defendants had remitted their rent by money order but the same having been returned undelivered, the defendants had been regularly depositing rent in House Rent Case No. 364 of 1983. It has been stated further that if the plaintiffs succeed in evicting the defendants and the other tenants of the suit market only technically on the ground of default they would let the shop to new tenants. It had been categorically denied that they were defaulters and they alleged that the contention of default being a myth, the suits are liable to be dismissed.

6. When the suits proceeded on these pleadings, Tamijul Haque, the plaintiff, filed an application before the S.C.C. Court under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that application it was alleged that after filing of the suit the plaintiff No. 1 had been diligently pursuing the suit but very recently plaintiff No. 3, namely, Shamsul Haque, his brother, has turned hostile towards the other plain-tiffs and Shamsul Haque has cancelled the power which he gave to the plaintiff No. 1 and hence for the ends of justice and proper adjudication of the suits it became necessary that the name of the plain-tiff Shamsul Haque be struck off from the list of the plaintiffs and the plaint be amended accordingly but as the suit is required to be disposed of in presence of Shamsul Haque his name should be transposed as defendant in the above suits. Vide Order dated 4.9.84 the petition was allowed and it was ordered that the plaintiff No. 3 be transposed as proforma defendant and necessary amendments made and 13.11.84 was fixed for requisites. The plaintiff filed requisites. Thereafter, it was ordered that the summons be is-sued upon the proforma defendant. When that was the case, on 2.1.1985 Shamsul Haque describing himself as plaintiff and proform defendant filed an-other power through another lawyer and submitted a compromise petition stating that the landlord and the tenants have come to a compromise and the solenama has been effected in this regard and the suit therefore be dismissed for non-prosecution in terms of the solenama and the Court was pleased to dismiss the suit for non-prosecution in terms of the solenama. The said order was passed on all the 52 S. C. C. Cases filed by Tamijul Haque against the tenants. Against these orders passed 52 Civil Revisional applications were moved by Mr. Tamijul Haque and these are numbered as Civil Revision Nos. 170-204, 206-222 of 1985.

7. Similar applications had also been filed before the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court (S.C.C. Judge), Dhaka in the other 15 S.C.C. Suits filed by Tamijul Haque but the Court rejected those petitions filed by Shamsul Haque for dismissing the suit for non prosecution. Against those orders passed in these cases Shamsul Haque had preferred civil revision applications before this Court being Civil Revision Nos. 635 to 649, 1985 which are heard along with other Civil Revision Cases, in which Mr. Tamijul Haque is the petitioner and are disposed of by this one judgment.

8. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate, had appeared for Tamijul Haque in all these Rules and Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appeared for Shamsul Haque in all the other Rules. Mr. Abdul Mannaf Talukdar, the learned Advocate, appeared for the tenants.

9. Mr. Asrarul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for Tamijul Haque, submitted that the learned Munsif erred in law in passing the impugned order of dismissal, causing miscarriage of justice for the reasons that the Court below failed to take into consideration that at the time of moving the application for recording a dismissal for non-prosecution on the ground of compromise outside the Court by the plaintiff with the defendant tenants, Mr. Shamsul Haque, though described himself as a plaintiff and also a proform defendant, by order of the said Court dated 4.9.1984 was transposed as proforma defendant and his name from the list of plaintiff was struek off and that being the position that petition of compromise was not maintainable because two groups of defendants cannot withdraw the suit on the ground of compromise between the parties and, as a matter of fact, even if Shamsul Haque was a plaintiff in the suit and was not transposed as a proforma defendant on that day one plaintiff cannot withdraw a suit without consent of other plaintiffs being barred under Order 23, sub-rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the Court acted illegally in allowing the compromise petition when all the plaintiffs were not before the Court for compromise. He has further submitted that admittedly by the original power of attorney where all the three brothers and others were given power to act for each other there were two minors, namely, Ebrarul Haque and Jabeen Afshan, son and daughter of late Azizul Haque and for a Court to pass such an order where minors are involved it had to make a specific order to the effect that it was for the interest of the minors, which was not done in the instant case and, alternatively, he argued that if the minors had become major by that time they, in fact, had executed a power of attorney in favour of Tamijul Haque on 30.10.82 and when Shamsul Haque withdrew the suit on 31.12.84 he had no power to act on their behalf and the Court had not taken into consideration all these facts because the order was passed totally ex parte without hearing the lawyer for Mr. Tamijul Haque. In this regard he further submit-ted that the petition for dismissal of the suit for non-prosecution was moved before the Court by a different lawyer and not by the lawyer who originally instituted the suit and the Court did not consider the fact that under Order 3, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure the previous power ought to be cancelled with leave of the Court by the executor of the power for any subsequent lawyer to appear and if the previous power given to the previous lawyer who instituted the suit had not been cancelled by leave of the Court by the executor, the appearance of the subsequent lawyer, presenting the application subsequently, was without the blessing of law being violative of the provision of Order 3, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He has further submitted that Shamsul Haque, brother of Tamijul Haque, had knowledge that had he been relegated to the position of a proforma defendant because he appeared subsequently in the suit by filing a Vokalatnama describing himself as a plaintiff and also as a proforma defendant and hence it is not true that proforma defendant Shamsul Haque in all these suits had no knowledge that he is no longer a plaintiff at the time when he presented the application to compromise with the defendants, as plaintiff. This has not been considered also by the Court of learned Munsif and there lies the illegalities. He lastly submitted that in the 15 S. C. C. Suits filed before the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka Tamijul Haque had a chance to appear, and the Court after hearing the parties rejected the application on valid reasons, which need be upheld by this Court and the order allowing the application passed ex parte the plaintiff petitioner need be set aside, the cases be restored to their original position and be sent on remand for hearing on merits.

10. Mr. Asrarul Hossain lastly submits that the general power of attorney has not specifically given any power to withdraw a suit though powers were given to file and prosecute.

11. Mr. Md. Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for Mr. Shamsul Haque, on the other hand, had submitted that on the day ie. 13.12.84 when Shamsul Haque has presented the application for recording a dismissal order for non-prosecution he exercised the power as conferred by the general power of attorney by all the plaintiffs in the suit in his favour and that the power to institute a suit by the Attorney will carry with it a power to withdraw or compromise even if the power of attorney is silent in this regard. He further submitted that his power existed because only on 6.1.85 from a notice in the daily newspaper he came to know for the first time that Tamijul Haque had cancelled the power given to him on behalf of himself and that he never received any notice of cancellation of the power said to have been sent and posted by Tamijul Haque on 30.10.84 and hence the power having existed on the day when he submitted the application for non-prosecution on 13.12.84 the said was validly done and acted upon. He has further submitted that the transposition of Mr. Shamsul Haque as proforma defendant who had no knowledge of such transposition, had not affected his right to act an attorney on the basis of the said power for all and the said transposition behind his back was bad in law. He has further submitted that the minors had not cancelled the power given to him on their attaining majority and therefore it would continue. As to the allegation that the minors after having attained majority had executed a power in favour of Mr. Tamijul Haque on 30.9.82 it is submitted by the learned Advocate that the same is ante dated and is of no legal effect. He has thus submitted that the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge need be set aside but the orders passed by the learned Munsif be sustained.

12. The instant case had been argued in extensio by the learned Advocate for a number of days.

13. In the instant case certain facts are admitted, namely, that at the time when Tamijul Haque instituted the S.C.C. Suits being fifty- seven (57) suits before the learned Munsif and 15 suits before the learned Subordinate Judge against the respective tenants for eviction on the ground of default of payment of rent, Mr. Tamijul Haque filed for himself and for all the plaintiffs which included his two other brothers and heirs of his late brother Azizul Haque and other family members. The plaint of those suits were verified by Mr. Tamijul Haque and every page was signed by Tamijul Haque under a seal which describes him as a constituted attorney for Anwarul Haque, Shamsul Haque, Hakima Khatun, Sadrunnessa, Sajeda Khatun, Ayesha Khatun, Enamul Haque, Ainul Haque, Noor-e-Afshan, Husn-e-Afshan. The plaint was signed by Tamijul Haque as the plaintiff. He executed power in favour of Advocates Mr. Khondker Nurul Islam, Abdul Mannan Talukdar and Giasuddin Chowdhury. It is on record that the tenants in those cases appeared by filing written statements denying the material allegations made therein, On 10th July, 1984 an application by Tamijul Haque was moved before the Court under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure with a copy given to the lawyers for the defendants, who received the copy with objection, wherein it was alleged that very recently the plaintiff No. 3 has turned hostile towards the other plaintiffs and has cancelled the power which he gave to the plaintiff No. 1, so it is necessary that the name of plaintiff No. 3 be struck off from the list of plaintiffs and he be transposed as proforma defendant. From the order sheet it appears that this application was heard on 4.9.84. On the day the defendant filed hazira, petition dated 12.4.84 was put up for hearing and it was ordered by the Court that the petition be allowed and was ordered that the plaintiff No. 3 be transposed as proforma defendant fixing 13.11.84 for requisites. On 13.11.84 the defendant filed hazira. Plaintiffs filed requisities and it was ordered that the summons be issued upon the proforma defendant and 15.12.84 was fixed for service return. Service having not returned, 15.1.85 was fixed for the same. On 2.1.85 Shamsul Haque appeared through a different lawyer with a solenama praying that the suit be dismissed for non-a prosecution on the basis of solenama. An examination of the said solenama filed in Court on 31st December, 1984 by Shamsul Haque for himself and as constituted attorney of Mr. Tamijul Haque, Anwarul Haque, Ayesha Khatun, and others did not show that any copy of the said application was served on the plaintiff Tamijul Haque who instituted those suits before the Court and not also on his lawyer at any point of time. From an examination of the Vokalanama it is seen that Shamsul Haque appeared for the first time in those suits on 2.1.85 instituted originally on 11.5.83 by his brother Tamijul Haque against their common tenants of the Haque Market, by executing a Vokalatnama describing himself as "plaintiff and proforma defendant" by authorising Mr. Ahsanuddin Ahmed, Advocate, to appear on his behalf. It also appears from records that a notice had been issued by the Court upon Mr. Shamsul Haque as a proforma defendant, asking him to appear and re-ply in the suit within 15.12.84. So, it appears that Shamsul Haque had knowledge that his name has been struck off and he had been transposed from plaintiff to the position of a proforma defendant. This order of transposition had not been challenged and that being so it is not understood as to why the learned Munsif failed to take into consideration the fact that Shamsul Haque cannot appear in this case as a plaintiff for recording an order of dismissal for non-prosecution when the other plaintiffs were neither informed nor present: nor there is any evidence to show that they had consented to the compromise. Moreover, Shamsul Haque being only a proforma defendant in the suit cannot possibly make a compromise with other defendants and withdraw from prosecution as a mere compromise between the defendants would not non suit the plaintiff.

<u>14. Under the provision of Order 23, rule, sub-rule (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure only one plaintiff cannot withdraw a suit without the consent of other plaintiffs. In the instant case though the plaint was verified by Tamijul Haque on behalf of himself and all others by virtue of a power of attorney, all others were independently named as plaintiffs, therefore, the provision of Order 23, sub-rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure would apply and the order passed allowing the suit to be dismissed for non-prosecution on the basis of solenama, on the application of one proforma defendant plaintiff, would be hit by the provisions of Order 23, rule 1, sub-rule 4.</u>

<u>15. In the instant case it is seen that the minors are in the picture and without any proof that the minors had become major by this time, which is a matter of calculation of age, an order passed for them must show that it was in the interest of the minors. In the instant case there was no such application of mind by the Court while passing the order. It appears that the minors having acquired majority had opted in favour of Tamijul Haque and had executed power of attorney in his favour on 30.10.82. That being the position on 30.10.82 when the minors executed a power in favour of Tamijul Haque, Shamsul Haque signed the power in the Court in those suits on 2.1.85 on behalf of those two also, namely Shamsul Haque, Noor-e-Afshan when they, by a power dated 30.10.82, appointed Tamijul Haque as their attorney. It is further seen that Shamsul Haque appeared in those cases after describing himselt as plaintiff and proforma defendant with the compromise application through a different lawyer than the lawyer appointed by Mr. Tamijul Haque, the plaintiff of those suits. The previous Vokalatnama of the filing lawyer was not cancelled and neither the previous lawyer had withdrawn and hence a subsequent lawyer representing a hostile interest would be incapable or representing all the plaintiffs, and any such compromise would not bind others. Further, in suit of this nature which is of a representative character, as originally instituted by one for all, a plaintiff would not be allowed to withdraw the suit on being compromised out of Court and to pray for an order of dismissal for non-prosecution and in the process non-suit others without their consent. If he would not like to proceed with the suit, having compromised and having disagreed with other plaintiffs he may go out of the suit, but that would not end the litigation as there will be other interested persons who may be allowed to continue with the suit. In cases like this when one of the plaintiffs did not want to proceed with the suit having compromised, or having become hostile or disagreed with other plaintiffs it is for the Court to act under Order 1, rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code by striking off the name of the non-willing plaintiff and transpose him as defendant and continue under Order 22, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure and it calls for no order for non suiting the other plaintiffs. All these were not considered by the learned Munsif while allowing the application filed by Shamsul Haque for recording order of dismissal for non-prosecution on the basis of compromise outside the Court. In that view of the matter, the order passed by the learned Munsif cannot be sustained in law and those need be set aside.</u>

16. In the result, the order dated 2.1.1985 passed by the First Court of Munsif (S.C.C. Judge), Dhaka is set aside. The S. C. C. Suits covered by those orders referable to Civil Revision Cases Nos. 170-204, 206-222 of 1985 are restored to its original file and number and they are to proceed in accordance with law.

17. The orders passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in S.C.C. Suits covered by Civil Revision Nos. 635-49 of 1985 are affirmed and the concerned S.C.C. Suits arc to continue in accordance with law.

18. The stay order granted earlier concerning these suits are hereby vacated.

19. The Rule arising out of Civil Revision Case Nos. 170-204, 206-222. of 1985 are hereby made absolute and the Rule arising out of Civil Revision case Nos. 635-649 of 1985 are discharged but Without any order as to costs.

Let the order be communicated at an early date.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Shanti Ranjan Karmaker, Advocate  ------- For the Petitioner. 
Mr. Md. Wahidullah, Advocate  ------- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Narayan Chandra Banerjce alias Bandapadhya ------- Defendant Petitioner
Vs.
Md. Salek Ali Shaik  ------- Plaintiff Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan, J: On an application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure by the defendant No. 2 Petitioner, this Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment & decree dated 20th March, 1982 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka reversing the decision of the Munsif 4th Court, Munshiganj passed on 31.12.79 in Money Suit No.1 of 1979 should not be set aside.

2. The suit being money suit No.1 of 1979 was filed by the opposite party Md. Sudek Ali Shaik @ Sadek Ali as plaintiff for the recovery of the consideration money amounting to Tk. 7,500.00 from the defendants. The plaintiffs case, in short, was that the plaintiff purchased the suit land measuring 63 decimals from the defendants for a consideration of Tk. 10,000.00 (taka ten thousand) only on 9.9.78. Subsequently, on scrutiny, it transpired that the defendants were owner to the extent of 1/4 th share only of the suit land. Accordingly, it was found that the plaintiffs kabala stands valid only to the extent of 1/4th share and no title passed to the plaintiff to the extent of remaining 3/4th share of the purchased land in question. So the plaintiff is entitled to get back Tk. 7,500.00 (Taka seven thousand and five hundred only) from the defendants. The suit was filed as the defendant did not pay back the money on demand made by the plaintiff. Only defendant No. 2 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that they got the entire suit land by way of gift from their father Dinesh Chandra Bandapadhya who became the exclusive owner in possession of the same and, accordingly, by the purchase from the defendants valid title passed to the plaintiff over the entire suit land. While owning and possessing the suit land the defendants sold the same to the plaintiff and the plaintiff is in ownership and possession of the entire 63 decimals of land. Moreover, the plaintiff was fully aware about the title of his vendors, the defendants from before the purchase. The point for determination in the suit was whether the defendants sold the land without having 16 annas right, title and interest in the same and, if not, whether the plaintiff is entitled to get back from the defendants an amount of Tk. 7,500 being the 3/4 share of the consideration money out of the total consideration money paid by the plaintiff for the land. In the case plaintiff has examined himself as PW 1 and the defendant was examined as DW 1. The learned trial Court after examination of the witnesses and hearing arguments by his judgment and decree dated 31.12.79 dismissed the suit on contest against the defendant No. 2 and ex parte against the rest without cost. In the trial stage it was pleaded that the suit was hit by section 35 of the Specific Relief Act and the learned trial Court found that in the instant case sale and purchase of the suit land was concluded on plaintiff's payment of the consideration money and the defendants executing and registering the kabala and at this stage there remains nothing to be revoked or annuled by way of rescission. The learned trial Court also found that the plaintiff has failed to prove the fraud alleged to have been practised against the plaintiff. It was also found that the plaintiff purchased the suit land being fully aware about the title of the defendants in the same and that the plaintiff has also been in undisturbed possession of the suit land.

3. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff preferred appeal before the District Judge and the said appeal having been heard by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka was allowed and the suit was accordingly decreed. The appellate Court below did not reverse the finding of the trial Court to the effect that there has been no fraud and, therefore, the finding of the learned trial Court to the extent that section 35 of the Specific Relief Act is not applicable in the instant case, was found to have been affirmed. The learned appellate Court also affirmed the finding of the learned trial Court that the plaintiff has still been in possession of the entire suit land since purchase and has been enjoying the usufruct thereof. The appellate Court, however, decreed the suit with the finding that the defendants had title only to the extent of 1/4th share of the suit land and with regard to remaining 1/4th share of the suit land the vendors themselves having acquired no title, could not confer any valid title to the plaintiff.

4. Mr. SR Karmaker, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner, after placing the judgment of both the courts, submits that the Court of appeal below approached the case from a wrong angle of vision and made out a third case himself and set aside the judgment and decree of the learned trial Court without reversing all the points raised, discussed and decided by the learned trial Court and hence the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below cannot be sustained. The learned Advocate further submits that it was nobody's case that 3/4th share of the demised property was vested property but the court of appeal below committed error of law and misdirected itself in assuming jurisdiction not vested in him in presupposing that the property is vested property and the defendants having no salable interest therein was liable to pay the compensation for damage in respect of the same. It is argued by Mr. SR Karmaker that the defendant's predecessor Dinesh Chandra Bandopadhya obtained 1/4th share by inheritance and 3/4th share by way of purchase from his three brothers vide kabala dated 8.10.71 (a copy of which was produced) and the defendants after obtaining right, title and interest in respect of the entire suit land from their father being in ownership & possession sold the same to the plaintiff. The learned advocate also argued that the plaintiff having been a borga cultivator under the father of the defendants and, thereafter, under the defendants was well aware about whatever title they had in the suit land before and at the time of purchase and, therefore, fraud could not be attributed to the vendors.

<u>5. By referring to the case of Dalsukharam Saheba Vs. Mulchand Ashram reported in AIR 1928 (Bom) 427 (Rele. page 429). Mr. Karmaker submits that if the plaintiff with ordinary care could have discovered that there was defect.of title, then he cannot plead that there was failure on the part of the defendant to comply with the obligation laid down in s. 55(1)(a) Transfer of Property Act I find substance in the above submissions of the learned Advocate of the petitioner and I hold that the plaintiff is not entitled to say that there has been fraud on the part of the defendant in regard to the sale of the suit property to the plaintiff.</u>

<u>6. Mr. Md. Wahidullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, by way of supporting the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below, submits that the defendant's father Dinesh Chandra Bandopadhya was no doubt owner to the extent of 1/4th share of the suit land but the rest 3/4th share belonged to his other three brothers and they being non-residents of the country their portion has become vested property and the defendant having sold the said land on fraudulent misrepresentation of fact the plaintiff has not acquired any title in respect of the same and for that matter the learned court of appeal below has rightly decreed the suit for the recovery of the 1/4th of the consideration money. In support of his contention Mr. Wahidullah cited the case of Injad Ali and others Vs. Mohini Chandra Adhikari reported in CWN Vol XXVII page 1025 and the case of Allahdino Bacha Vs. Udhumal Amardenomal reported in AIR 1942(Sind) page 82; The case reported in the XXVll CWN 1025 is different and distinguishable from the present one as the suit under reference was a suit also for the recovery of possession the plaintiff being not in possession of the suit land but in the instant suit the question of possession is not involved as the plaintiff after obtaining possession from the vendor has remained in possession without being disturbed by anybody. In the other cited case reported in 1942 AIR 82 the following observation has been made:</u>

<u>"Where the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff by the defendant was not a nullity which the plaintiff could ignore and the defendant had title to at least part of the property and the plaintiff obtained possession of at least part of the property, the only case which the plaintiff could advance is that the sale deed is voidable because of material defect in his vendor's title not disclosed by the vendor, such non-disclosure amounting to fraud under section 55, Transfer of Property Act. Plaintiffs remedy in such circumstance is a suit for rescission of the sale deed, and for return of the price paid under s.38, Specific Relief Act. It is not open for him to ask for return of the price before conveyance is rescinded".</u>

<u>7. The fact of the present case discloses that the plaintiff purchased the property with open eyes having opportunity to know the title of the defendant and that the plaintiff having obtained delivery of possession has still been in possession in respect of the whole of the property. That being the position the principle laid down in the above referred case does not help rather it goes against the plaintiff as the plaintiff is not entitled to ask for the return of the portion of the consideration money before the conveyance is rescinded in a duly constituted suit.</u>

8. In the instant suit the suit land originally belonged to four brothers, viz. Dinesh, Jitendra, Bamkin and Sushen. Thereafter Dinesh became the owner in respect of 1/4th of the suit land by inheritance and the remaining 3/4 by way of purchasing the share of his three other brothers. While in ownership and possession of the suit land, Dinesh gifted the land to his three sons who are the defendants in the suit and the deed of gift was accordingly executed on 28.2.78 and registered on 4.3.78 in favour of the defendants. The gift deed contains a recital to the effect that Dinesh acquired property by way of inheritance from his father and also by way of purchase from his brothers. Furthermore, the present plaintiff being a borgader under Dinesh Bandopadhya and thereafter under the defendants was quite aware about whatever title defendants had in the suit land and, therefore, the question of defendants playing fraud does not arise. The next point raised by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party is that the other three brothers of Dinesh having left the country their 3/4 share in the property has become vested and non-resident property and the defendant having acquired no title therein could not confer any title on the plaintiff by the sale in question. The plaintiff examining himself as PW 1 deposed that he saw the father of the defendants possessing the entire suit land. He said that he has been possessing the suit land and nobody ever questioned his possession. Thus it is found from the admission of the plaintiff that since purchase the plaintiff has all along been in possession of the suit land without any interference from any quarter. The plaintiff has failed to produce any scrap of paper from the vested property authority at any stage of the suit appeal and revision in support of the contention that 1/4 portion of the suit land has become vested property. The apprehension that the land will be taken by the vested property authority appears to be so vague and remote that such apprehension cannot give rise to any cause of action for the plaintiff to get any relief, particularly when the plaintiff has been owning and possessing the property without being disturbed or challenged by the vested property authority or anybody. I do not find any element of fraud being practiced on the plaintiff by the defendant in the transaction. The suit seems to be a misconceived one and the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief in the same and the suit was, therefore, rightly dismissed by the trial Court. The learned court of appeal below committed error of law in setting aside the judgment of the trial Court without adverting to all the points raised and decided by the learned trial Court making out a third case and hence the impugned judgment cannot be sustained in law.

9. In view of the above, the Rule is made absolute and the judgment and decree of the court of appeal below is hereby set aside and the decree of the trial Court is hereby restored.

There will, however, be no order as to cost at this revisional stage.

End.

lawyer:
Jamiruddin Sircar with Mujibur Rahman, Golam Afzal ------ For the Petitioner. 
T. H. Khan with Md Awlad Ali ------ For opposite party.
parties:
Abdul Hakim Khan ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
Begum Safia Khatun ------ Respondent.
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff has arisen out of a judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd, Court, Dhaka reversing those of the learned Munsif, 6th Court Dhaka, passed in a suit for permanent injunction to restrain the defendants from constructing the building beyond the approved plan and for mandatory injunction for demolishing of the building constructed beyond the plan.

2. The plaintiff instituted the suit alleging that the suit plot i.e. CS plot No.151 belonged to one Yusuf Ali who sold six kathas of land out of the said plot to the plaintiff by a kabala dated 11-2-69; the plaintiff also purchased kathas of land in the plot in the name of his son by a kabala from one Mustafizur Rahman on 13.6.74. The plaintiff has alleged that he purchased in total 6½ kathas of land. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 purchased 5½ kathas of land from the said common vendor Yusuf Ali on the western side of the plaintiff's land. When the plaintiff began construction of his residential building the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 raised objection and ultimately they filed a suit for permanent injunction. The dispute between them was amicably settled in terms of a compromise in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 170 of 1970, and that in terms of the compromise the boundary will was erected in 1972 at the joint cost of both the parties. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 laid foundation of their multi-storied building on their land without keeping any space according to the requirements of Building Construction Act, 1953. They started construction keeping a space of only 1' (one foot) to 9" (nine inches) from the common boundary wall; the defendants raised construction of the building up to 10' (ten feet) height; by construction of the building the plaintiff's right of easement of use and enjoyment of light and air has been obstructed and infringed and thereby an atmosphere uncongenial for human habitation has been created, the plaintiff requested the defendants to restrain from erecting the building but failed; he brought the matter to the notice of the authority concerned but all the attempts of the plaintiff ended in failure. Hence, the suit.

3. The defendant No. 1 and 2 have contended, inter alia, that they purchased the land comprising 9.07 acres of land (5 kathas) by a registered deed dated 17.3.59 from Yusuf Ali, the vendor of the plaintiff and Mustafiuzur Rahman. Since the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the last purchasers the excess land in the plot are in possession of the defendants; the suit plot was not partitioned by metes and bounds which are in ejmali and hence the defendants filed the suit for partition and declaration being T.S. No. 393 of 1982. The defendants filed a suit for permanent injunction against the plaintiff being T.S. No. 190 of 1970 which ultimately ended in compromise in Mis. Appeal No. 170 of 1970 at the intervention of the local Chairman and others but the compromise could not materialize due to the war of liberation. The plaintiff illegally constructed structures without approval of the D.I.T. and are causing great loss and inconvenience to the defendants. The D.I.T. passed an order for demolishing of the illegal structures of the plaintiff under Memo No. NAA/ DIR/ 2-C-284/82/3591 dated 12.7.82. The defendants having obtained loan from House Building Finance Corporation and after due approval of a plan from D.I.T. they have laid foundation to the building and raised pillars up to roof level. The plaintiff's suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Munsif decreed the suit. He has found that the defendant's plea that they have some lands beyond the boundary wall is baseless and vague. He has also held that the defendants have not kept 4' feet space from the boundary wall between the land of the plaintiff and the defendants. The learned Munsif has observed that the defendant No. 2 (D.W.1) has admitted that distance between their construction and the disputed boundary wall is 1 foot to 2 feet 8/9 inches from south to north.

On appeal the court of appeal below has reversed the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit upon view that the plaintiff is not entitled to a decree as he has not acquired easement right over the land of the defendants requiring the latter to keep 4 feet space between their construction and the disputed boundary wall. He has also held that if there is any violation of the Building Construction Laws and Rules the D.I.T. can take action under section 187 of the Town Improvement Act. The Court of appeal below has found as follows:

"From the evidence on record it appears that the plaintiff and the defendants are the owners of their respective purchased land and they have been in possession of their purchased land as such the plaintiff cannot get any decree for mandatory injunction for the alleged violation of the Building Construction Rules inasmuch as there has been no breach of obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff. Moreover, no right of easement of the air and light accrued in favour of the plaintiff."

5. Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff has firstly submitted that the defendants being obliged under law to keep vacant 4 feet space i.e. 9 meter at the back of their constructions from the common boundary wall and admittedly a space of only 1 foot to 9", inch having been left by the defendants in between the boundary wall and their constructions and this being clearly violative of the provision for the building construction Act and the Rules there under, the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law occasioning a failure of justice in holding that the plaintiff has not succeeded in proving his legal right requiring the defendants to keep a vacant space as alleged by the plaintiff. The learned Advocate has next submitted that in view of the provision of Building Construction Act and the Rules there under the plaintiff has acquired a right requiring defendants to keep a vacant space of 4 feet from the boundary wall, and the learned Subordinate Judge on misconception of law as to the rights and obligations of the adjoining shares of land with respect to construction of Building in urban areas, has committed an error in reversing the judgment of the trial court upon a view that the plaintiff cannot get a decree for alleged violation of Building Construction Rules. He has next submitted that by virtue of provision of section 7 read with sections 32 and 35 of the Easement Act the defendants are obliged under the law to keep some vacant space in between his building and the wall. He has further submitted that apart from acquisition of right of easement by prescription, under the Building Construction Act, 1952 and the Rules thereunder a legal obligation on the part of the defendants vis-a-vis a right in favour of the plaintiff has accrued inasmuch as that the defendants have to keep a vacant space of 4 feet from the comma boundary wall and as per the plan passed by the D.I.T. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff has lastly submitted that the defendants having committed tortious wrong in not keeping 4 feet space between wall and their building, the latter are liable not to proceed with the construction and to pull down their construction already made in violation of the plan and the Building Construction Rules. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in holding that the D.I T. having not taken any action against the defendants for making construction in violation of the plan and the Building Construction Rules the plaintiff is not entitled to maintain the action for injunction and demolition of the unauthorised construction.

6. Mr. T. H Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant opposite party has submitted that the plaintiff has acquired no easement right either under the provisions of Easement Act or under the provision of Building Construction Act 1952 and the Rules thereunder inasmuch as the plaintiff has not acquired any easement by prescription or under sections 7, 32 or 35 of the Easement Act as claimed by the latter. Elaborating his submission he has argued that the provision of sec. 7 of Easement Act is descriptive of several modes or classes of Easement Act and that the said provision has not created any right by easement. He has further submitted that the plaintiff has not acquired any legal right or right of action even if it is found that the defendant has made construction in violation of the Building Rules or of the plan sanctioned by the D.I.T. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the laws governing construction of building in urban areas under the Building Construction Act, 1952 or under Town Improvement Act, 1953, do not give an adjoining owners of a property any right of action in case of violation of the Building Construction Rules under the Building Construction Act 1953, or the approved plan as passed by D.I.T. The learned Advocate has next submitted that by special law, namely, Town Improvement Act penalties having been provided for violation of building construction rules or violation of sanctioned plan, the adjoining owners have no right to an injunction or demolision of any structure constructed in violation of the rules or the plan. According to the learned Advocate, special provisions in the aforesaid laws as regards penalty and punishments for violation of the Building Construction Rules having been provided any action at the instance of the plaintiff for an injunction or any mandatory injunction to demolish any structure would not lie. According to the learned Advocate variation of the building construction plan or the Rules has not given a right to the plaintiff to sue to restrain the defendants from making any construction in violation of the sanctioned plan or of the Rules. He has further submitted that the plaintiff having not sought relief by way of declaration of his right of easement over the defendants land no decree for permanent injunction or mandatory injunction could be legally given. In support of the case of the respective parties they have cited decision reported in A. I. R. 1952 Calcutta 74, A.T.R. 1936 Madrass 142 and A.I,R. 1943 Oudh 111.

7. The first question to be decided in this Rule is whether the boundary wall from which the defendants are allegedly required under the Building Construction Rules and the sanctioned plan to keep 4 feet vacant space is the common or agreed boundary wall between the parties. The learned Subordinate Judge has not adverted to this question and has not given his decision. The finding as to whether the boundary wall was the agreed one or not was not necessary according to him as he has found that the plaintiff has acquired no right of easement over the land of the defendants legally obliging the letters to keep 4 feet space between the wall and their construction. The trial court, however has found in favour of the plaintiff that the boundary wall was erected as per the agreement in Misc. Appeal No. 170 of 1970. The learned Munsif has held on perusal of evidence that the defendants' plea that the boundary wall was not constructed in terms of the agreement between the parties was baseless. From the conclusion of the learned Munsif it appears that the learned Munsif did not accept the plea of the defendants that beyond the wall there was some excess land belonging to the defendants. I have perused the evidence of the parties as regard the erection of the boundary wall, and the plea of the defendants that there was some excess land owned by them beyond the boundary wall, and agree with the findings of the learned Munsif in this regard.

8. Now the question is whether the plaintiff has acquired any right of easement in the land of the defendants requiring the latters to keep 4 feet space between the boundary wall and their constructions. Right of easements are generally acquired by contract, by prescription or by way of necessity. Under any category of easements the plaintiff has not acquired any right of easement over the land of the defendants a requiring the latters to keep 4 feet space between the wall and their constructions. The submission of the learned Advocate or the plaintiff petitioner that the plaintiff has acquired right of easements under section 7 read with sections 32 and 35 of the Easement Act are therefore not tenable.

<u>9. Let us now consider whether, apart from right of easement which the plaintiff has not acquired, has he acquired any legal right requiring the defendants to keep 4 feet vacant space in between the boundary wall and their constructions in view of the obligations or duty of the defendants not to commit breaches or violations of the Rules under the Building Construction Act, 1951 and the sanctioned plan? To answer this question we are to consider the law of Torts. According to jurists, Tort has been defined as an act or omission which is unauthorized by law and independently of contract infringing of either some absolute right of another, or some qualified right of another causing damage, or some public right resulting in some substantial and particular damage to some person beyond that which is suffered by the public generally and gives rise to an action for damages at the suit of the injured party (Under bills Law of Torts 15th Edition page 4) according to the Professor Winfield an authority on Tort, "tortious liability arises from a breach of a duty primarily fixed by law; this duty is towards persons generally and its breach is redressable by an liquidated damages." Where a statue imposes a duty for the benefit of the public at large rather than a class of public, then prima fade there is no right of action by an individual. But if private individuals were intended to be benefited and to be protected, an individual who would be benefited if the duty was performed can maintain action for Tort. (1935) 1 KB 75).</u>

<u>10. In the present case the duty of the defendants is to keep vacant space or to make constructions according to the building plan sanctioned by the authority and their duty is fixed by law. He has also a duty towards his neighbours. The defendants in the present case in my opinion, has a duty to make constructions according to building Rules and the sanctioned plan i.e. to keep 4 feet space between the wall and their constructions. It appears that violation of the Building Rules and the sanctioned plan are punishable under the Town Improvement Act. Similarly if these violations touch the interest of the neighbours, they are also actionable at the instance of the neighbours. A person may be criminally liable for wrong done under some law. He may as well be liable to in a civil action for wrong done to a private person. In my view the defendants have incurred liability under tort for infringement of the Building Rules under Building Construction Act, 1952 and the sanctioned plan. I also hold that the plaintiff has succeeded in proving that the defendants have violated the Building Construction Rules under the Building Construction Act, 1952 and the sanctioned plan and they are liable for the infringement and violation of the right of the plaintiff.</u>

<u>11. Now in the Instant case whether a prohibitory injunction requiring the defendants not to make further construction within 4 feet space from the boundary wall should be granted to the plaintiff and whether the existing construction within 4 feet space should be demolished or not. It appears to me that in the present case injunction perpetual and mandatory with regard to the structures already erected and their upward elevation should not be given. In my view the injury is not of a great nature and compensation would be an adequate remedy. It is to be considered that granting of injunction perpetual or mandatory by demolishing of the existing constructions for which the defendants had taken loan from the House Building Finance Corporation would be oppressive to them. In this view I hold that the compensation would be the adequate remedy for the violation of the right of the plaintiff instead of granting injunction as prayed.</u>

<u>12. It has further been submitted that the plaintiff is not entitled to any equity as he has not come with clean hands. Unless the plaintiff has come with clean hands he is not entitled to any relief in equity as he has allegedly violated the sanctioned plan. To determine the quantum of compensation the question of equity as between the parties should be considered. The defendants have alleged that the plaintiff has made unauthorised construction in 1970. The plaintiff has asserted that the constructions are of temporary nature. It has not been alleged that the plaintiff has violated any building rules or construction plan. This question however, has not been gone into by the courts below. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, in any opinion it will be just and proper that plaintiff be awarded a compensation of Tk. 10,000.00 only in lieu of perpetual and mandatory injunctions as prayed in the suit.</u>

13. In the result this Rule succeeds and it is accordingly made absolute. The judgment and decree of the court of appeal below is set aside, and those of the trial court are modified to the effect that the plaintiff shall get a decree of Tk. 10,000.00 as compensation instead of permanent injunction to restrain the defendants from making further construction and mandatory injunction by way of demolishing of the existing structure. The suit is, therefore, remanded back to the trial court for the purpose of passing a decree for Tk. 10,000.00 in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of requisite court fee on the amount aforesaid. If the plaintiff fails to put in the requisites court fee within three months from the date of arrival of the records in the trial court, the suit shall stand dismissed. The order granting status quo with respect of the land and constructions of the defendants are vacated. There will be no order as to costs of this Rule.

End.

lawyer:
Abdur Rab 1, Advocate ------ For the Petitioners. 
No one appears ------ For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Selimuzzaman @ Selim and others  ------ Petitioners 
Vs.
Deputy Commissioner, Sariatpur, District Sariatpur and others ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the order dated 20.8.90 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Naria, District Sariatpur, dismissing the Title Execution Case No. 23 of 1989 should not be set aside.

2. The following facts require special consideration for the purpose of disposal of this Rule. The plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 27 of 1987 in the court of the learned Assistant Judge, Naria Upazila, on 29.3.87 against the defendant opposite parties for a declaration that the order of the Naria Upazila Nirbahi Officer treating the suit land as a part of Chandipur hator bazar is illegal, void and without jurisdiction and there is no hat or bazar on the suit land and for permanent injunction restraining the said defendant opposite parties from treating the suit land as hat or bazar and also from holding any auction for the suit land and for mandatory injunction directing them' to remove the huts if any erected in any portion of the suit land. After filing the aforesaid suit plaintiffs filed an application for temporary injunction. Thereupon notices were duly issued upon the defendants. Ad-interim injunction was granted. The defendants appeared and took time to file written objection. On several occasions adjournments were taken but ultimately no written objection was filed challenging the application for temporary injunction and as a result the learned Assistant Judge, Naria, by his order dated 9.9.87 made the ad-interim injunction dated 30.3.87 absolute restraining the defendants from disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. Thereafter, the defendants filed application and prayed for adjournment in order to file written statement. On so many occasions adjournments were granted to the defendants to file written statement but no written statement was filed challenging the suit. Ultimately, the suit was fixed for ex parte hearing on 22.3.88. On that date plaintiff No. 2 was examined and several documents were proved and marked as exhibits and the suit was decreed ex parte in favour of the plaintiff’s petitioners restraining the defendants by way of permanent injunction from treating the suit land as hat or bazar and also from leasing out the same by auction to anybody.

3. Against the aforesaid ex parte decree dated 22.3.88 the defendants filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1988 was started. From the records it appears that in the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case the defendants failed to appear on several occasions. The learned Assistant Judge on three occasions issued notices upon the defendants directing them to show cause as to why their Miscellaneous Case should not be dismissed for default. In spite of giving so many adjournments and also of issuance of show cause notices thrice, the defendants did not care to appear in their own aforesaid Miscellaneous Case and as a result the Miscellaneous Case was dismissed for default on 18.12.88. It is stated that against the aforesaid order dated 18.12.88 the defendants did not take any steps whatsoever and the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 27 of 1987 became final and conclusive.

4. After obtaining the aforesaid decree the plaintiffs requested the defendant opposite-parties to obey it, but they were taking steps to willfully disobey the decree. Then the plaintiffs moved a writ petition being WP No. 768/89 before a Division Bench of this Court for enforcing the decree. After hearing the learned Advocate the Division Bench verbally observed that equally efficacious remedy lies in the Code of Civil Procedure under Order 21 rule 32. Upon such observation the learned Advocate for the petitioners took back the writ petition with the leave of the Court and thereafter moved the learned Assistant Judge for enforcement of the decree.

5. The plaintiffs then started Title Execution Case No. 23 of 1989 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Naria, for execution of the decree and filed an application under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure for enforcement of the decree for permanent injunction. Plaintiffs deposited all the requisites for issuance of notices upon the defendants. Ultimately, the learned Assistant Judge on 20.8.90 passed an order stating that for executing the decree for permanent injunction the execution case is not maintainable in the eye of law and as such the decree holders were not entitled to get any relief. With the above findings the execution case was dismissed. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid-order dated 20.8.90 passed in Title Execution Case No. 23 of 1989 the plaintiffs preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr. Abdur Rab-1, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law in rejecting the application under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure and dismissing the Execution Case. He submits that the defendants appeared in the suit, took several adjournments to file written statement, but ultimately no written statement was filed and as a result the suit was decreed ex parte. He further submits that Miscellaneous Case was started at the instance of the defendants on an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit on setting aside the ex parte decree, but ultimately the defendants did not take any steps whatsoever and as a result Miscellaneous Case was dismissed for default. Till today no step was taken by the defendants against the order passed in that Miscellaneous Case. He submits that the decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge for permanent injunction is still in force and defendants are bound to obey the decree for permanent injunction. It is submitted that the defendants willfully disobeyed the decree for permanent injunction and that is why the plaintiffs filed an application under Order 21 rule 32 CPC before the learned Assistant Judge for enforcement of the decree. The mode of enforcement of decree for permanent injunction has been incorporated under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure which runs as follows:

"32(1) Where the party against whom a decree for the specific performance of a contract, or for restitution of conjugal rights, or for an injunction, has been passed, has had an opportunity of obeying the decree and has willfully failed to obey it, the decree may be enforced (in the case of a decree for restitution of conjugal rights by the attachment of his property or, in the case of a decree for the specific performance of a contract or for an injunction) by his detention in the civil prison, or by the attachment of his property or by both".

Relying upon the provisions of rule 32 as quoted above Mr. Abdur Rab submits that the decree for permanent injunction is still in force and defendants are bound to obey the decree. Since they are not obeying the decree and enforcing it the plaintiffs filed this application under 'Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the learned Assistant Judge for enforcement of the decree as per provision laid down in Order 21 rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Rab submits that in this case defendants have got the opportunity to obey the decree inasmuch as they appeared in the suit, took several adjournments to file written objection and written statement, but ultimately no written objection or written statement was filed and suit was fixed for ex parte disposal and on the appointed day the ex parte decree was passed. He further submits that for setting aside the ex parte decree the defendants instituted a Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In spite of giving so many opportunities and so many adjournments, ultimately the defendants did not appear in their aforesaid Miscellaneous Case and as a result that Miscellaneous Case was also dismissed for default. So Mr. Rab submits that the defendants knew full well about the decree for permanent injunction and as such they had an opportunity to obey the decree but they are willfully disobeying the decree for permanent injunction. Mr. Rab has annexed several papers with this application namely, Annexure B-1, D, D-1, D-2, D-3 and E which clearly show that in spite of knowing about the decree for permanent injunction the defendant-opposite parties are willfully disobeying as well as ignoring the decree for permanent injunction, treating the suit land as part of Chandipur hat although it is a part of homestead of the plaintiff. Further, after dismissal of their Miscellaneous Case No. 18 of 1988 filed under Order 9 rule 13 CPC they are debarred from touching the suit land. So for enforcement of the decree the plaintiffs filed application under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was illegally rejected by the learned Assistant Judge.

<u>7. Mr. Rab submits that the learned Assistant Judge acted absolutely beyond his jurisdiction in rejecting the Execution Case inasmuch as he had no option but to take steps under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure in view of the fact that the decree for permanent injunction is still in force and the defendants are bound to obey it. Mr. Rab in support of his contention has referred to the case of Sashi Mohan Sen Vs. Ainullah, 1992 BLD (AD) 8. In the aforesaid case the question of enforcement of the decree for injunction came up for consideration before their Lordships. Their Lordships had considered the provisions of Order 21 rule 32 CPC and held as follows:</u>

<u>"A reference of Order XXI rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure shows that when against any party a decree for injunction is passed and he has the opportunity of obeying the decree and he willfully failed to obey it the decree may be enforced by detaining him in civil prison or by the attachment of the property."</u>

8. From the impugned order it appears that the learned Assistant Judge acted absolutely without jurisdiction in rejecting the Execution Case without taking any action under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Since the decree for permanent injunction still stands good the learned Assistant Judge being Executing Court has no option but to take steps under the provision of Order 21 rule 32 for enforcement of the decree for permanent injunction. So the impugned order of the learned Assistant Judge cannot be sustained in law.

9. In this connection the conduct of the defendant-opposite parties needs consideration. The plaintiffs filed the suit for permanent injunction for restraining the defendants from treating the suit property as hat and bazar and also from leasing out the same in auction to any person. The plaintiffs obtained the order of ad-interim injunction and ultimately temporary injunction. The defendants in fact did neither contest the application for injunction nor the suit and as a result the plaintiffs obtained ex parte decree for permanent injunction. It can be further noted that the defendants filed an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and a Miscellaneous Case was started but the defendants did not care to take appropriate steps and the learned Assistant Judge, after giving them sufficient opportunity, dismissed the Miscellaneous Case for default. The plaintiffs also issued notice through the learned Advocate informing the defendants about the decree for permanent injunction and to obey the same. Even then the defendant opposite parties are ignoring and disobeying the decree for permanent injunction willfully.

10. In this case a question may arise whether the suit for permanent injunction is at all maintainable or not. In this connection it may be noted that after filing the suit for permanent injunction the plaintiffs filed an application for temporary injunction with a prayer for ad-interim injunction claiming exclusive possession and title over the suit land. Ad-interim injunction was granted. Then the defendant-opposite parties took several adjournments to file written objection, but no written objection was filed challenging and/or denying the possession and title of the plaintiffs over the suit land. Ultimately ad-interim injunction was made absolute and temporary injunction was granted within the knowledge of the defendant opposite parties. Thereafter several adjournments were taken by the said defendants to file written statement, but ultimately no written statement was filed by them challenging and denying the averments of the plaint including the claim of title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit property and as a result the suit was decreed ex parte. Even before this Court in the present Rule the defendant-opposite-parties did not appear and challenge the title and possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land. From the above I am of the view that the plaintiffs have been in continuous possession of the suit land and as such their suit for permanent injunction is maintainable.

<u>11. Since the decree for permanent injunction is still in force the Executing Court has no option but to take legal steps as contemplated under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure, but without doing that the learned Assistant Judge illegally dismissed the Execution case. Mr. Rab submits that since the defendant opposite parties came to know about the decree for permanent injunction they are bound to obey and enforce it and as they are not obeying it and are willfully ignoring the decree for permanent injunction the Executing Court is bound to take action under the provisions of Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure. I find force in the above contention of Mr. Rab. It appears that the defendant-opposite parties have got sufficient opportunity to obey the decree but they willfully failed to obey it and as such an action under Order 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure is called for in the present case.</u>

12. It may be further mentioned that after issuance of the rule by this court notices were duly issued and served upon the defendant-opposite parties, but they did not appear and contest this Rule. Since some high Government officials are involved this court suo motu directed the Deputy Attorney-General Mr. AY Salehuzzaman to assist the Court in this matter after taking necessary instructions from the opposite parties. The learned Deputy Attorney-General appeared before this Court and twice took adjournments for taking necessary instructions, but ultimately he verbally informed this Court that in spite of his best efforts be was unable to get necessary instructions from the defendant opposite parties to contest this Rule and he has not even received any cooperation from the opposite parties to assist this Court. This conduct further shows that the defendant-opposite parties are bent upon to disobey the decree for permanent injunction willfully and they have no respect for the verdict of the Court of law.

13. In this connection it is to be noted that the defendant opposite parties are high Government Officials and public functionaries and as such it is expected that they will be more obedient and respectful to the Court of law. But this continuous adamant attitude not to obey the decree of the Court is really shocking, unwarranted and unwanted. They should remember that any person, whoever he may be and how ever high he may be, even the highest executive of the country, is equal before law, bound by law and answerable to law. Everybody is crying for Rule of Law and Rule of Democracy, but such cry is meaningless if the verdict of the Court of law is ignored and dishonored in this way.

<u>14. In the result, this rule is made absolute without cost and the impugned order dated 20.8.90 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Naria, in Title Execution Case No. 23 of 1989 is set aside. The learned Assistant Judge, Naria, after receipt of the judgment of this Court, shall issue notice, by name and designation, upon the (1) Deputy Commissioner Sariatpur (2). The Upazila Nirbahi Officer, Naria, Sariatpur and (3) Bhumi Karmakarta (Revenue Circle Officer) Naria, Sariatpur, directing them to obey and enforce the decree for permanent injunction passed in Title Suit No. 27 of 1987 within two weeks from date of receipt of the notice of the Executing Court, failing which the Inspector-General of Police, Bangladesh, Dhaka and the Superintendent of Police, Shariatpur shall get the aforesaid three defendant opposite parties arrested and detain them in civil prison for one month in Shariatpur Jail as per provision of the Order 21 rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure for enforcement of the decree. The learned Assistant Judge, Naria, is directed to report the matter to the SP Sariatpur and Inspector General of Police, Bangladesh, immediately if his notice is not complied with by the above defendant-opposite parties within the stipulated time.</u>

15. Let a photo copy of this Judgment duly authenticated by the relevant officer of the Court be sent to the Inspector General of Police, Bangladesh, and the Superintendent of Police, Sariatpur, for implementing and giving effect to this judgment of the High Court Division, Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

Let the LC records along with a copy of this judgment be immediately sent down to the learned Assistant Judge, Naria Upazilla, for implementing this judgment with due care and earnestness. After taking steps as per direction given above the learned Assistant Judge, Naria, shall report compliance to the Registrar, Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Dhaka.

End.
