VS
Begum Tofatun Nahar & ors ----- Opp. Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule issued at the issuance of the plaintiff- petitioners is directed against the judgment and order dated 15.5.86 passed by Mr. Md. Sayedur Rahman, District Judge, Bogra in Misc. Appeal No.10 of 1986 affirming those dated 29.1.86 passed by Mr. Ahammed Jamil Mostafa, Subordinate Judge, Bograin O.C. Suit No.377 of 1985 refusing the prayer for temporary injunction. 

2. Short facts giving rise to this Rule may be stated as follows :- The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Other Class Suit No. 377 of 1985 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Bogra for a declaration that the preliminary decree dated 26.8.84 and the final decree dated 8.12.84 passed in Partition Suit No.102 of 1976 by the same court arc collusive, fraudulent, malafide, null and void and not binding upon the plaintiff-petitioners. During the pendency of the suit, the plaintiff-petitioners filed an application on 28.9.85 under Order 39 Rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for a temporary injunction. The defendant opposite party No.1 - entered appearance and filed written objection to con-test and oppose the prayer for temporary injunction. 

3. The plaintiff-petitioners' case in brief is that the opposite party NO.1 filed Partition Suit No. 102 of 1976 impleading the predecessors of the plaintiffs namely Nazirul Islam as defendant No.1 and Nesarul Islam as defendant No.16 and others; that during the pendency of the suit the said Nazirul Islam died on 23.8.82 but no substitution was made to bring his legal heirs on record and instead, the Deputy Commissioner, Bogra was made a party defendant in the suit and thereafter Nesarul Islam died on 27.2.85 after prolonged illness by paralysis and Could not contest the suit after his appearance, but no substitution petition was made to bring his legal heirs on record; that the defendant No.1 very tactfully expunged the name of Nazirul Islam as defendant NO.1 from the plaint and managed to insert the Deputy Commissioner, Bogra as a defendant; that the plaintiffs arc the legal heirs and successors-in-interest or the said Nesarul Islam, the brother's son of the said Nazirul Islam and by suppressing the aforesaid facts, and also by practicing the fraud upon the Court the opposite party No. 1 obtained a preliminary as well as final decree in the Partition Suit behind the knowledge of the plaintiffs-petitioners; that the defendant Nos. 17-23 arc in possession of the suit premises as bharatia under the plaintiff-petitioners and the defendant opposite party has no right, title or interest in the suit land and that by impleading some unnecessary parties he has managed to obtain the said decrees and also the Advocate Commissioner's report, on the basis of which he has also managed to obtain the final decree on 8.12.84; that thereafter the defendant opposite party instituted the Execution Case No. 1 of 1985 in the said Court and in pursuance of which the charities i.e. defendant Nos. 17-23 were going to be evicted, but being obstructed by the plaintiffs and others that could not be done. It has been stated further that the decree in the partition suit was passed against a dead person namely Nesarul Islam, the predecessors-in-incrust of the present petitioners and as such the same is a nullity. 

 4. The defendant opposite party's case inter-alia is that the aforesaid partition suit, notices were duly served upon the defendants including the aforesaid Nesarul Islam, predecessor-in-interest of the present plaintiff petitioners; that the said Nesarul Islam appeared in the said suit, but being hopeless of any success did not contest the same and as such it was decreed in the preliminary form and on the basis of the said decree and the Commissioner's report a final decree was passed. Thereafter the plaintiff of the partition suit i.e. the defendant opposite party was in- ducted into physical possession of the entire suit premises on 14.9.85 by evicting the defendant Nos. 17- 23 through the process of Court and since then he is in peaceful possession of the entire suit premises. Further the whereabouts of the defendant Nazirul Is-lam or any of his legal heris could not be found, in- spite of best efforts. Hence the Deputy Commissioner, Bogra was made a party defendant in the partition suit and that defendant No. 16 Nesarul Islam was alive throughout the pendency of the partition suit. He appeared in the said, but did not contest. Be died on 27.2.85 after the passing of the final decree. So, it was not passed against a dead person as alleged. The further case of the defendant opposite party is that before the institution of the 'present suit, she has already made some pucca construction according to the plan passed by the local Municipality and the same awaits only completion; that the construction in no way would change' the nature and character of the suit property; that the plaintiffs-petitioners have no prima facie case and that the balance of conveniences and inconvenience is in favour of the defendant opposite party. 

5. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties in the matter of the application for temporary injunction and was pleased to reject the prayer for temporary injunction by his judgment and order dated 29.1.86 holding inter-alia that the plaintiff petitioners have failed to establish any prima facie case. Against the aforesaid judgment and order, the plaintiff-petitioners preferred an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 10 of 1986 before the learned District Judge, Bogra who was pleased to dismiss the same after hearing and affirm the judgment and order dated 19.1.86 of the learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and order dilled 15.5.86. Being aggrieved by the said decision of the learned District Judge, the petitioners filed a provisional application before this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

6. Mr. Kh. Saiful Huq, the learned Advocate appeared for the plaintiff-petitioners in support of the Rule and Mr. Mashih-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate appeared for the defendant opposite party No.1 and filed a counter affidavit to oppose the Rule. 

7. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff- petitioners firstly submits that the courts below erred in law in coming to a finding that the plaintiff- petitioners have no prima facie case without considering the documents filed by them and as such the finding is a perverse one and cannot be sustained in law. He further submits that Moksudar Rahman, husband of defendant opposite party No.1 admittedly was a tenant under the said Nazirul Islam and in that connection a suit arose and ultimately a second appeal is still pending in this court and as such the defendant opposite party No.1 is estopped under section 116 of the Evidence Act from denying the title of the landlord defendant No.1 of the Partition Suit without handing over possession of the suit premises. He also submits that the impugned decree of the said partition suit was passed against a dead person namely Nesarul Islam and as such it was a nullity in the eye of law and hence the plaintiff-petitioners have prima facie case. The further submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is that the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of granting injunction against the defendant opposite party No.1, but the courts below committed error of law in not discussing this important question and coming to a finding on the same. The learned Advocate also submits that unless the injunction is granted, the plaintiff-petitioners will suffer irreparable loss, but the courts below also failed to determine this question and as a result there has been a failure of justice. Lastly, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the prayer for temporary injunction is not with regard to possession but for restraining the defendant opposite party No.1 from making construction on or leasing out the suit premises and thereby changing the nature and character of the same till disposal of the suit. Hence, according to the learned Advocate for the petitioners, the impugned judgment and order suffers from legal infirmity and the same should be set aside and the Rule be made absolute. 

8. Mr. Masih-ul-Islarn, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant opposite party No.1 on the other hand submits that the finding as to the prima facie case is essentially a question of fact and in this case both the Courts below on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record have come to a concur- rent finding that the plaintiff-petitioners have failed to establish their prima-facie case The learned Advocate contends that the submissions made on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners to the effect that the decree in partition suit is a nullity as the same was passed against at a dead person namely Nesarul Islam, is not correct inasmuch as the said defendant No.16 Nesarul Islam died on 27.2.85 whereas the final decree in the Partition Suit was passed during his life time on 8.12.84. The further contention of the learned Advocate is that the impugned finding as to prima facie case cannot be termed as a perverse or illegal one as the same has been arrived at by the courts below on proper and sufficient consideration of the materials on record. About the question of operation of estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act against the defendant-opposite-party as canvassed on behalf of the petitioners, the submission of the learned Advocate for the opposite party is that MaksudarRahman, the husband of defendant opposite party No.1 might be a tenant under the said Nazirul Islam who was defendant No.1 in the partition suit, but this defendant opposite party No.1 who acquired the property in dispute by purchase from one of the co-sharers in the suit jute was or is not a tenant under the said defendant, So, the question of application of estoppel under Section 116 of the Evidence Act does not arise here in this case. The submission of the learned Advocate for the Opposite Party No.1 with regard to the finding about prima facie case in fine is that this is a concurrent finding of fact arrived at by the courts below on proper consideration of the materials on record and the same is neither arbitrary nor fanciful nor contrary to law. So, this court should not interfere with the same in its provisional jurisdiction under Section 115(1) of the C.P.C. In this connection he has referred to some decisions namely a decision reported in 28 D.L.R. (A.D.) 57 and also a decision in C.P.S.L.A.No.128 of 1975 in the case of Naimullah and another V s. Govt. of Bangladesh and others reported in the Bangladesh Supreme Court Digest 1972-1977, Volume I at page 65. 

9. As regards the submissions of the learned Advocate for petitioners on the point of balance of convenience and inconvenience and the question of irreparable loss Mr. Mashi-ul-Islam, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party No.1 submits that if there is no discussion or finding on this 2 points namely balance of convenience and in- convenience and irreparable loss, still then the impugned orders cannot be found to be bad or illegal, when both the courts below came to a concurrent finding on the primary and most important question to the effect that the plaintiffs have failed to establish their prime-facie case for temporary injunction. He, of course, maintains that the question of balance of inconvenience has been considered in this case, but not in so many words and express findings. He however, submits that in the counter-affidavit the defendant opposite party No.1, has categorically stated that the construction on the suit premises according to the plan passed by the local Municipality is almost complete, but because of the ad-interim order of temporary injunction made by this court at the time of issuance of the Rule, the finishing has been kept in abeyance and as a result, serious inconvenience has been caused to the defendant-opposite party No.1 and that her house-building materials are being wasted and apart from that the defendants opposite party No.1, the decree-holder of the Partition Suit is being deprived of the enjoyment of the fruits of her decree which she obtained about 4 years back. The learned Advocate's further contention is that the plaintiff-petitioner will not suffer any loss, not to speak of any irreparable loss as because the construction will be completed at the cost and risk of the defendant-opposite party No.1 and this will not change the nature or character of the suit premises in any way. According to his submission, there is no error of law in the impugned judgment and order of the learned courts below occasioning any failure of justice. Hence, the impugned orders cannot be interfered with and the Rule should be discharged with costs. 

10. I have carefully gone through the impugned judgments and orders of the Courts below and heard the learned Advocates of both the sides at length. This Rule arises out of an order passed in an application for temporary injunction under Order 39 Rule 1 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a suit for simple declaration. The principles governing the grant or refusal of temporary injunction are well settled. It is an equitable and discretionary relief which the Court can grant to a party in appropriate cases. It has been laid down in the case of Shahjada Muhd. Umar Beg Vs. Sultan Mahmood Khan reported in 22 P.LD.(S.C.) 139 relevant page 141, 144 that "the well settled principles for the grant or refusal for temporary injections are, firstly, whether the plaintiff has prima facie good case, secondly, whether the balance of convenience lies in favour of the grant of the injunction and thirdly, whether the plaintiff would suffer irreparable loss, if the injunction is refused." Now, in the light of the above principles, let us now examine this case and consider the submissions of the learned Advocates with regard to the first point on the question of prima-facie case, it appears that both the courts below on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record have concurrently held that the plaintiff-petitioners have no prima facie case. The submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners that the finding on prima-facie case is a perverse one appears to be wholly incorrect and untenable in law and facts. The finding cannot also be termed as arbitrary or fanciful when both the courts on careful consideration of the materials on record including the documents filed by the parties came to a concurrent finding that the plaintiff- petitioners have no prima facie case. I myself have also considered the materials on record and cannot but hold the same view. Therefore, I find no sub- stance in the 1st contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. 

11. The next submission of the learned Advocate about the operation of Section 116 of the Evidence Act as against defendant opposite-party NO.1 appears to be a misconceived one and the same has no bearing in this case in an application under Order. 39 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Besides, factually the defendant opposite party No.1 was or is never a tenant under defendant No.1 or defendant No.16 or the present petitioners and as such the question of application of the provision of Section 116 of the Evidence Act does not arise in this case at all

12. Now, with regard to the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners regarding the balance of convenience and inconvenience and irreparable loss, it may be observed that it is correct that the Courts below have not come to any specific findings on these points. but it has been submitted on behalf of the opposite party that when both the Courts have come to a concurrent, finding on the primary question that plaintiffs have no prima-facie case, then the absence of any specific finding on the other 2 points about the balance of convenience and inconvenience and irreparable loss have not caused any failure of justice. Of course the consideration of the said 2 points and findings thereon would have been quite material according to the principles laid down in 22 P.L.D. (S.C.) 39, had the plaintiff-petitioner been able to establish this prima facie case. But when plaintiff-petitioners have failed to establish any prima-facie case for temporary injunction, then even non-consideration of the other two points or absence of any specific findings thereon cannot cause any failure of justice or vitiate the impugned orders. So, this contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners also fails. Now, in the facts and circumstances of the case and on the materials placed before this Court, it is not understandable how the plaintiff- petitioners will suffer irreparable loss, if temporary injunction is not granted and how the balance of convenience and inconvenience goes in their favour. It has been submitted on behalf of the opposite party that the construction has almost been completed on the suit-premises which is being held in exclusive .possession and saham of the defendant opposite party. The present suit of the plaintiff/petitioners has been filed against the decree of the Partition Suit passed in the year 1984 in favour of the present defendant-opposite party and naturally a few years more may be taken up for its disposal and further, if the construction is completed on the suit premises by the defendant opposite party at her costs and by that any loss if at all is suffered by the plaintiff- petitioners; then that can be compensated by money and the loss cannot be termed as irreparable. It is also difficult to understand how such completion of the construction will change the nature and character of the suit premises, because it is a homestead non-agricultural land within the Bogra Town and the construction thereon has almost been completed. Further, it appears that in the application for temporary injunction no specification of the schedule land has been given by the plaintiff petitioners. So, on that score also it is difficult for the Court to grant temporary injunction because of the vagueness of the suit premises. 
	
13. Lastly the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the Courts below passed the impugned orders upon a glaring misconception of law and as such the same cannot be sustained and in support of this contention, he has cited two decisions reported in 36 D.L.R. A.D. page 248 and 1984 B.C.R. A.D.\ page 372. But while arguing, the learned Advocate for the petitioners could not satisfy me as to how and under what kind of misconception of law or from what : non- consideration of the materials on record, the courts below have passed the impugned orders and refused the plaintiffs' prayer for temporary injection. So, the aforesaid submission and the decisions are of no help to the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Rather, it is well-settled that power of granting or refusing temporary injunction is a discretion of the court and this court will not interfere under Section 115(1) of the C.P.C. in the matter of discretion, if it is exercised judicially and not arbitrarily or fancifully. If a decision is needed in this regard, then the decisions in the cases reported in P.L.D. 1970 S.C. page 139, 11 D.L.R. page 103, 21 P.L.D. Lahore page 89 may be profitably cited. Now, in this connection another decision of our High Court Division reported in 38 D.L.R. at page 227 and also a decision reported in A.I.R. 1963 Madhya Prodesh at page 209 may be cited. It has been held in those decisions that in a matter of temporary injunction, the question of prima-facie case is the most important one and also it has been held that justice requires that the decree-holder should not be deprived of the enjoyments of the fruits of his decree pending decision of an independent suit relating to the same property. So, in view of my above elaborate discussion on the facts and circumstances of the case and the submissions of the learned Advocates, I do not find any error of law in the impugned orders of the Courts below occasioning any failure of justice and as such the same do not warrant any interference by this Court in Revision . The Rule is, therefore, discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned order of the Courts below are upheld. The ad-interim order of stay granted by this Court is vacated. 

End.

full_judgment:
The Rule issued at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioners is directed against the judgment and order dated 28.12.85 passed by Mr. Md. Shamsher Ali, Subordinate Judge, Kushtia in Misc. Appeal No. 11 of 1984 reversing those dated 12.1.84 passed by Mr. Md. Monjur Kader, Munsif, Kumarkhali in Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 rejecting an application for dismissing the suit on the ground of non-maintainability.

2. The present petitioners as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 in the Court of Munsif now Assistant Judge, Kumarkhali Upazila in the district of Kushtia for setting aside an allegedly fraudulent and collusive ex parte decree passed against them on 27.8.79 in Title Suit No. 436 of 1973 of the First Court of Munsif, Kushtia. The case of the plaintiff-petitioners in short is that they purchased the suit land from one Bindu Bashini Saha, defendant opposite party No. 6 by two different Kabalas in 1973 and possessed the same since then. The contesting defendant-opposite parties created a forged, fraudulent bainanama and filed the aforesaid suit being Title Suit No. 436 of 1973 for specific performance of contract in the First Court of Munsif, Kushtia against the present petitioners and others including the said Bindu Bashini Saha. They obtained the impugned ex parte decree dated 27.8.79 in the said suit by showing false return of the service of summons upon the defendants. Hence the present suit for setting aside the ex parte decree.

3. The contesting defendants-opposite party Nos. 1-5 filed a written statement in this suit contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form and the same is not properly valued and stamped and is also barred by res judicata, waiver and acquiescence. It is also contended that one of the defendants in the Title Suit No.436 of 1973 Dilip Kumar Saha filed a case being Misc. Case No. 41 of 1980 in the Court of the learned Munsif, Kushtia under Order 9, rule 13 of the C.P.C. for set- ting aside the impugned exparte decree which is still pending. As such the present suit is hit by the principle of res judicata and not maintainable and. the same is liable to be dismissed.

4. On 16.11.83 the contesting defendant-opposite parties filed an application before the learned Munsif, Kumarkhali presumably under Order 7, rule 11 of the C.P.C. for rejection of the plaint of the suit mainly on the ground that it is barred by res judicata in view of the pendency of the Misc. Case No. 41 of 1980 for setting aside the exparte decree and also on the ground of incorrect valuation of the suit and non-payment of proper and sufficient court fees.

5. This application came up for hearing on 12.1.84. The learned Munsif, Kumarkhali upazila heard both the sides and was pleased to reject the same by his judgment and Order No.8 dated 12.1.84 holding, inter alia, that the suit is not barred by res judicata and the same does not suffer from incorrect valuation or non-payment of sufficient court fees and as such the suit is maintainable and not liable to be dismissed.

6. As against the said judgment and order dated 12.1.84 of the learned Munsif, the contesting defendant-opposite parties preferred an appeal being misc. Appeal No. 11 of 1984 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Kushtia and the same was transferred to the Court of the learned Subordinate Judge. Kushtia for hearing and disposal. The learned Subordinate Judge, Kushtia Mr. Md. Shamsher Ali heard the misc. appeal and was pleased to allow the same and set aside the judgment and order dated 12.1.84 of the learned Munsif by his judgment and order dated 28.12.85 holding, inter alia, that the Title Suit No.173 of 1983 is not maintainable as the same is barred under Order 7, rule 11 (d) of the C.P.C. and also hit under section 7(2)- VIII(a) of the Court Fees Act. Consequently he allowed the application filed by the defendant-opposite party Nos. 1-5 in Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 and dismissed the suit on the ground of non-maintainability by his aforesaid judgment and order. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order dated 28.12.85 of the Subordinate Judge, Kushtia in Misc. Appeal No. 11 of 1984, the present petitioners moved a revisional application in this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr. Hasan Foez Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, firstly submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law resulting in a failure of justice in not holding that the Misc. Appeal No. 11 of 1984 was not at all maintainable inasmuch as the learned Munsif did not reject the plaint of Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 under Order 7, rule 11 of the C.P.C. by his Order No. 8 dated 12.1.84 and as such it was not an order amounting to a decree to be appealable.

<u>8. Mr. Gazi Siddique Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the contesting opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that this point was not raised specifically by the present petitioners as respondents at the time of hearing of the said appeal and as such this can not be raised now. I have heard the learned Advocates and considered their submissions on this point. It is not disputed that while disposing of the application of the contesting defendants, the plaint of the suit was not rejected by the learned Munsif, rather the suit was found to be maintainable. It is also admitted that Order 43 of the C.P.C. does not provide for any appeal against an order passed under Order 7, rule 11. Had it been a case of rejection of the plaint then the Order could be deemed to be a decree as defined in section 2(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such appealable. On perusal of the impugned order of the learned Munsif and the relevant provisions of law, it is clear that the said order was not at all appealable, but the appeal was wrongly filed by the defendant/opposite parties and entertained by the learned Subordinate Judge. It may be true that this question of maintainability of the appeal was not specifically raised in the Appellate Court below, but this being a question of law, can be raised here before this Court. This Court in exercising its power under section 115(1) of the C.P.C. can even suo motu interfere into an illegal order in the interest of justice and correct the same. This view finds support from the decisions re-ported in 26 DLR (AD) 1 and 38 DLR (AD) 33 as cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners. Hence, the Misc. appeal was incompetent and as such the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners has substance.</u>

9. The next submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is that the learned Subordinate Judge committed serious error of law in holding that the present Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 is barred under Order 7, rule 11(d) of the C.P.C. so long as the Misc. Case No. 41 of 1980 under Order 9, rule 13 of the C.P.C. filed by one of the defendants Dilip Kumar Saha for setting aside the exparte decree is pending in the Court of the learned Munsif, now Assistant Judge Kushtia. Before considering the above submissions, it is better to quote the relevant portion of the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge which is as follows:—

"Perusing the certified copy of plaint of Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 it is evident that Ayezuddin Sk. and Monohar Sk. are plaintiffs in the Court of Munsif, Kumarkhali for setting aside the exparte decree of Title Suit No. 436/73 A.D. for Munsif, 1st Court, Kushtia. It is exposed from the argument of the lawyer of both the parties that the Misc. Case No. 41/80 A.D. is pending. As because, the Misc. Case No. 41/ 80 A.D. arises against the exparte decree of suit No. 436/73 A.D. and there remains provisions for appeal etc. against the result of Misc. Case No. 41 of 1980 A.D. it is clear that Title Suit No. 173/83 A.D. filed by Ayezuddin Sk. and Monohar Sk. is not maintainable. And the Title Suit No. 173/83 A.D. is barred under Order 7, rule 11(d) of C.P.C. so long there is Misc. Case No. 41/80 A.D."

10. From the above, it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge held the suit to be barred by res judicata. Mr. Gazi Siddique Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, by filing a counter-affidavit in this court has also submitted that the suit is barred by res judicata and as such not maintainable.

<u>11. Let me now examine the relevant provisions of law in the facts and circumstances of this case and see whether the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners or for the opposite parties is correct. The admitted position in this case is that an earlier Title Suit No. 436 of 1973 instituted by the present opposite parties against the petitioners and others was decreed exparte and thereafter one of the defendants started the Misc. Case No.41 of 1980 under Order 9, rule 13 of the C.P.C. for set-ting aside the said decree which is pending for disposal and some of the defendants of that suit are the present petitioners who have instituted a separate suit being Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 in the Court of the learned Munsif, now Assistant Judge Kumarkhali for setting aside the same exparte decree on the allegations of fraud and suppression of summons. It is not known whether issues have been framed in the above suit and the Misc. case and if at all framed whether such issues in both the cases are the same. But one fact is however admitted by the parties that no issue in the Misc. case or in the subsequent title suit has been heard and finally decided by any of the Courts. Mere showing that a matter directly and substantially in issue in both the suits or cases or proceedings, is not enough to attract the operation of the principle of res judicata. It has to be shown that such a common issue has been heard and finally decided by the Court in the earlier suit or proceeding. Apart from that, some other conditions have also to be fulfilled to attract the bar of res judicata under section 11 of the C.P.C. In the instant case the parties may be the same, the subject matter may also be the same, but there is nothing on record to show that the parties are litigating under the same title and the matter in issue in Misc. case No. 41 of 1980 is the same as in Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 and that any such issue has been finally decided after hearing the parties by the Court. It appears from the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge that he has held in view of the pendency of Misc. Case 41/80 under Order 9, rule 13 of the C.P.C. that the Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 is not maintainable. It is well- settled that as against an ex parte decree apart from the remedy under Order 9, rule 13 of the C.P.C. there are some other remedies open by way of appeal, review and also by independent suit on the ground of fraud. These remedies are concurrent. Of course, in a case of review under Order 47 of the C.P.C. if appeal is availed of, then review may not lie. In the present case, one of the defendants has, of course, sought relief by way of filing an application under Order 9, rule 13 of the C.P.C. but that itself cannot be a bar in seeking relief against the exparte decree by institution of an independent suit on the ground of fraud by other defendants of the suit, as the reliefs against an ex parte decree available under the law are concurrent. In this connection the learned Advocate for the petitioners has cited two decisions reported in 22 DLR(SC) 102 and in A.l.R.1957 Cal. 242. The principles enunciated in the above decisions are very much applicable in this case and as such, I find much force in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners and hold that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of aw in finding that the suit is not maintainable because of the pendency of Misc. Case 41 of 1980, the same being allegedly barred by the principle of res judicata.</u>

12. The next submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners is with regard to the valuation of the suit and payment of proper court fees. The learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that present suit is with regard to '72 decimals of land and as such it is valued at Tk. 3,500 and the learned Munsif rightly found this valuation and payment of court fees thereon as correct. In appeal, the learned Subordinate Judge has held that the suit i.e. Title Suit 173 of 1983 is hit by section 7-viiiA of the Court Fees Act for incorrect valuation and payment of insufficient court fees. Mr. Gazi Siddique Ahmed, learned Advocate for the opposite parties however submits that this finding of the learned Munsif is in-correct and that of the learned Subordinate Judge on this point is correct. According to him, the valuation of the suit ought to have been rectified and proper court fees ought to have been paid thereon by the plaintiff-petitioners. Section 7-viii A of the Court Fees Act runs thus:-

"In suits to set aside decrees passed for ascertained amounts-according to the amounts of the decrees sought to be set aside, or where such decrees are not for any ascertained amounts, the fee payable shall be the same as paid on the plaints of the suits in which the questioned decrees were passed:

Provided that, where such amount exceeds the value of land or interest, the amount of fee shall be computed as if the suit were for the possession of such land or interest."

13. The present suit is a suit for setting aside the exparte decree passed in a suit for specific performance of a contract. In the plaint of this suit, prayer has been made by the present petitioners for setting aside of the entire ex parte decree of the suit which was valued at Tk. 6000/- only. But for reasons unknown, the present suit has been valued at Tk.3,500/- only. From a reading of the impugned decree and the plaints of both the suits, it appears that Section 7-viii A of the Court Fees Act is very much applicable in this case and the present suit and the relief claimed therein has been under-valued also insufficient court fees have been paid thereon.

So, the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the suit is hit by section 7-viiiA of the Court Fees Act appears to be correct and that of the trial court is wrong. In that view of the matter, the present suit may, however, come within the mischief of Order 7, rule 11 of the C.P.C. as amended which runs as follows:-

"The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:-

(a) where it does not clisclon a cause of action:

(b) where the relief claimed is under valued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so :

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so:

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law: Provided that the time fixed by the Court for the correction of the valuation or supplying of the requisite stamp-paper shall not exceed twenty one days."

But in case of under-valuation of the relief claimed in the suit or non-payment of proper court fees, it appears from the statute itself that before taking any action under clause "b" or "c" of rule 11 of Order 7 of the C.P.C. some time not exceeding 21 days as per amendment must be given to the party concerned for correction of the valuation of the suit or the relief claimed and for payment of deficit court fees. Here in this case from the impugned order, it does not appear that the plaintiff-petitioners of the present suit were given any time by the court for correction of the valuation of the relief sought for in the suit and/or for payment of the deficit Court fees thereon. So, before compliance of that legal requirement, it can not be held that the suit is barred by or under rule 11 of Order 7 of the C.P.C. and as such not maintainable. In support of this view, a decision reported in 22 DLR (SC) 144 may be referred to. In this case the trial Court dismissed the suit under Order 7, rule 11 C.P.C. for its under-valuation and in and sufficient court fees. On appeal, the High Court found the order of the trial judge contrary to the provisions of section 149 and Order VII, rule 11 C.P.C. under which he was required to allow the plaintiff an opportunity to correct the value of the suit and pay deficit court fees which shall have the same force and effect as if such fee had been paid in the first in-stance. Their Lordships set aside the order of dismissal of the suit and remanded the suit for allowing the plaintiff to make good the deficiency in the court fee. The Supreme Court of Pakistan then in appeal dismissed the leave petition and upheld the judgment of the High Court.

<u>14. From the relevant provisions of law and the decision referred to above, it is clear that before rejection of the plaint of a suit on the ground of in correct valuation of the relief or non-payment of proper and sufficient court-fees, the plaintiff or plaintiffs must be given time as provided in law to correct the valuation of the suit and for payment of the deficit court fees. The learned Subordinate Judge has, of course held that Title Suit No. 173 of 1983 A.D. is barred under Order 7, rule 11(d) of the C.P.C. But this is not correct. Rule 11 (d) of Order 7 of the C.P.C. may be put into operation, only when the plaint is found to be barred by any law; but in the instant case except what have been stated above, nothing has been shown to establish that the suit is d barred by any law. So, the above finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is without any legal basis and hence can not be sustained in law. Having regard to my above discussion and consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the relevant provisions of law, I find that the impugned judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge suffers from serious legal infirmities and the same has caused a failure of justice and therefore should be set aside.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge, Kushtia is accordingly set aside. Let the suit be decided on merit by the trial Court if it is otherwise maintainable. The plaintiff-petitioners are directed to correct the valuation of the suit and pay proper court fees thereon within two weeks from the date of arrival of the records of the case to the trial Court and the notice thereof to the parties concerned. In the facts and circumstance of the case, there will be no order as to costs. Let the records be sent down immediately.

End.

caseno: Appeal from original order No. 91 of 1984 with Civil Rule No. 439(FM) of 1984.
lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Abul Quashem Bhuiyan, Advocate. ------ For the Appellant: 
Ashrarul Hossain with Syed Sakhawat Ali, Advocate. ------ For the Respondent No.1.
parties:
Bangladesh Power Development Board ------ Appellant
vs.
Sonali Bank ------Respondent
full_judgment:
Anwarul Haque Choudhury, J:- This appeal at the instance of the Bangladesh Power Development Board herein referred to BPDB is directed against the judgment and order dated 10.1.84 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Money Execution Case No. 4 of 1980. 	

2. Facts leading to this in short is that Sonali Bank, the plaintiff-decree-holder respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a Money Suit on 27.3.74 being Money Suit No. 26 of 1974 against Mis Conwell Ltd. and its Managing Director and one A.K.M. Moyeedul Islam as principal defendants, impleading BPDB and one of its Sub-Assistant Engineer-as pro- forma defendant No. 4 and 5 respectively on the allegations inter-alia that the said Mzs. Conwell Ltd. obtained an over-draft facility to the amount of Tk. 2,25,000/- from the former Premier Bank on hypothecating certain construction machineries belonging to the said company lying within the premises of Ghorashal Power Station and though the said advance was payable with interest at' 5% above the bank rate and the rate minimum 10% with quarterly rests and was payable and repayable by 31.12.71 but they did not pay. The further case of the plaintiff-decree holder was that the surety for the said over-draft and revival letter and the letter of continuity was duly executed by the Defendant Nos. 2 and 3 and also the demand promissory Note dated 21.10.71 in favour of the Premier Bank for Tk. 2,25,000/-. It is in the further case of the plaintiff that the proforma defendants No. 4 and 5 are denying and interested to deny the hypothecated tools and machineries as mentioned in Schedule 'A' annexed to the plaint and it is asserted that if they continue to do so the plaintiffs claim a decree against them as well, having used or taken away the hypothecated tools and equipment’s duly certified by them to be in their possession which they cannot do "without repaying the amounts due to the plaintiff." 

3. In that suit the plaintiffs claimed a decree for Taka 3,50,000/- with interest at the rate of 10% from the time of filing of the suit till realisation and also prayed for such other further reliefs to which the plaintiff would be entitled under law and equity. 

4. The said suit, in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka was contested by the Pro-forma-defendant No. 4. namely, the BPDB by filing a lengthy written statement in which it was stated inter-alia that there is no outstanding bill of defendant No. 1 namely, the Conwell Ltd. with the pro-forma-defendant and the bills were paid excluding the hire charges of the equipments of proforma defendant No. 4 which are to be realised from the security deposit of defendant No. 1 and from the tools and equipments lying with the proforma defendant. The value of the equipments and the amount of security deposit does not cover the total amount of liability of defendant No. 1 with defendant No. 4 and as a matter of fact defendant No. 1 have become liable to the pro-forma defendant No. 4 for an amount of Taka 14,00,000/- (Taka Fourteen lac) and the value of security deposit and equipment’s which are part of the contract do not cover the said total liability and the alleged hypothecation with the Bank of the tools and equipment’s being subsequent to the date of contract with proforma defendant No. 4 the said is illegal and inoperative in the eye of law and the plaintiff, therefore, cannot get the relief prayed for rather the Proforma-defendant is entitled to appropriate relief to-wards realisation of his amount of Taka 14,00,000, (Tk. Fourteen lac) with cost. 

5. It appears from records that no other defendant appeared in the suit to contest but only proforma defendant No. 4, who for reasons known to them all the time in the written statement described them as defendant No. 4 and not as proforma-defendant No. 4. It was further seen from the record that on 17.2.75 the plaintiff filed a petition for passing an order of attachment before judgment of the properties mentioned in schedule namely, the machineries and the equipment’s lying with the Bangladesh Power Development Board. The court thereon ordered to issue notices upon the defendants to show cause within 7 (seven) days as to why they shall not furnish security to the extent of the claim and why the schedule property shall not be attached pending judgment and passed an ad interim order or attachment on that date. 

6. It further appears that the said ad interim order thereafter was made absolute. Further, it appears that during the proceeding on 29.12.76 the suit was taken up for ex-parte hearing when P.W. Abdul Quayum was examined and certain documents were exhibited in court and 27.1.77 was fixed for ex-parte hearing. On 27.1.77 none of the defendants appeared and the court after examining the deposition of the witness and the papers filed by the plaintiff found that the case has been proved and ordered that the suit be decreed ex-parte with cost and interest and the plaintiffs do get Tk. 3,50,000/- from the defendants. The said decree was signed on 31.1.77. 

7. Against that judgment and decree which was ex-parate the proforma-defendant No. 4 preferred Miscellaneous Case No. 77 of 1977 under Order 9, Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. This said Misc. case was however dismissed and on appeal being F.M.A. No. 447 of 1979 before the High Court Division the Proforma defendant become unsuccessful. Thereafter, the plaintiff-decree-holder started the Money Execution Case No. 4 of 1980 for realization of the decreetal amount with cost and interest upto 31.12.80 amounting to Tk. 6,08606/- and prayed for attachment of the main Development A/C No. Spl. 36 of WAPDA-POWER DEVELOPMENT BOARD maintained in Sonali Bank, WAPDA Branch, Dhaka. 

8. In that money Execution case the Bangladesh Power Development Board namely, BPDB filed an objection on 31.7.82 contending inter-alia that the. money execution case is not maintainable against the Power Development Board because no decree was passed against the Proforma-defendant No. 4 and that the assets and all properties of M/s Conwell Ltd. was declared an abandoned Property vide notification dated 7.2.72 published in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extra-Ordinary dated 11.2.72 claiming that the alleged hypothecated tools and machineries of the said abandoned firm are not in the juridical possession of the Bangladesh Power Development Board and as the Government was not made a party in the said money suit and the Deputy Commissioner on 13.5.82 having taken over possession of the hypothecated goods, the decree cannot be executed against the Government also, they being not a party. That objection was heard on 10.1.84 and the Court rejected the objection petition filed by the Power Development Board holding inter-alia that the Sonali Bank instituted Money Suit No.26 of 197.4 against M./s. Con-well Ltd. and 4 others including the Power Development Board and got a decree in that suit against them and the court on examination of the papers and record found that the decree was passed against the Power Development Board also as they were in possession of the admitted hypothecated machineries and go-down of the other judgment-debtors and as such they by agreement, are bound to pay the decretal dues and the court found that the Execution case against the judgment-debtors including the Power Development Board can proceed. Against that this appeal is preferred before this court which is heard and disposed of by this judgment. 

9. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant in the instant appeal having placed the relevant papers and the impugned order, had argued that in view of the fact that no decree was passed against the Proforma-defendant Nos. 4 and 5 by the order dated 27.1.77 of the trial court and no money decree having been drawn up against the proforma defendants, the executing court erred in law in rejecting the objection of the proforma defendants against the execution of the money decree against proforma defendants. He has further argued that the impugned order suffers from an inherent illegality because the executing court found that the decree was passed against the Power Development Board, also as they are in possession of the hypothecated machineries when a reading of the decree itself would show that it was ordered that the plaintiffs are to get a specific amount from the defendants wherein the Power Development Board has been shown as a proforma defendant only and the expression defendants as used in the decree cannot be extended or made to include the proforma defendants because the executing court Would take decree as it finds it without any addition or alteration and cannot go behind the decree and write out a new order and decree in the name of inter-pretation, which was in fact done in the instant case and therefore, the said order need be set aside, being not warranted by law and according to the learned Counsel it ought to be held that the money decree is not executable against the proforma defendant No. 4. It has further been argued by the learned Counsel that there is nothing on record to show that any claim has been made against the proforma defendant No. 4 in the suit and that being so it cannot be said that the proforma defendant No. 4 would be bound by the judgment and decree arising out of a suit in which he has been added as a mere proforma without any claim against the said proforma by the plaintiff and as a matter of fact the said judgment and decree would not be a res-judicata between the plaintiff and the proforma-defendant in a subsequent suit, may be over the same matter and the proforma-defendant No. 4 being not bound by the decree, which as a matter of fact had been admitted by the Power Development Board in their written statement, it cannot be executed against the Power Development Board. That being the legal position the impugned order has no basis in the eye of law and need be set aside by allowing this appeal. 

10. Mr. Ashrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel appearing for the Bank who is the Respondent No. 1 in the instant appeal and who is also the plaintiff-decree-holder had argued that there is no illegality and the impugned order suffers from no illegality which would need interference by this court for the simplereasons that in the money suit instituted by the plaintiff a clear claim was made against the Power Development Board and it was to the knowledge of the Power Development Board and the said was to the effect that the Power Development Board are denying and are interested to deny the hypothecated tools and machineries and if they continue to do so the plaintiffs claim a decree against them as well, having used or taken away the hypothecated tools and equipment’s duly certified by them to be in their possession which they cannot do without repaying the amount due to the plaintiff and therefore it can- not be said that no claim was made against the proforma defendant No. 4 in the suit. Further, the learned Counsel submitted that the proforma defendant contested the suit and made an adverse claim in the hypothecated tools and machineries which, were subsequently attached before judgment and the BPDB being a contested party in the suit would be bound by the decree and it will be executed against the said proforma defendant No. 4. In this regard the learned Counsel referred to a number of decisions of the Indian Jurisdiction and particularly the one reported in A.I.R. 2947 (Bombay) page 217. In reply to that Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, has referred to the decision reported in A.I.R. 1960(SC) page 388 to which we would advert at the relevant portion of the judgment. 

11. In the instant case the question to be decided is whether the decree that was passed in the money suit against the defendants would be binding upon the Power Development Board also who was described in the plaint as a proforma defendant and whether in the facts and circumstances of the case it would be executable against them also. 

12. The term proforma means for the sake of form only but we find that the said expression does not appear in any provision of the Code of Civil Procedure where the terms are only plaintiff and defendant and no proforma. A defendant might be a necessary party whose presence is a must or be a proper party who though not a necessary party but yet a party whose presence would be required before the court, for the court to adjudicate all the points that are raised in a particular case before the court. In the instant case from a reading of the plaint it is seen that the plaintiff had made defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 as principal defendants. They are made so because defendant No. 1 Mis Conwell Ltd. is the firm which took the loan facility from the Premier Bank initially by hypothecating the disputed tools and the machineries belonging to the said firm but lying in the premises of the Power Development Board at Ghorashal Power Station. The defendant Nos. 2 and 3 has been made a party because they were the guarantors. Defendant No.4 was made a proforma because hypothecated machineries were in their custody and possession. But from a further reading of the plaint it is seen that the plaintiff claimed a decree against the defendant No. 4 as well  the plaintiff claimed that the proforma defendant No. 4 cannot go on possessing and using the hypothecated tools and machineries without paying the amount claimed. This is a clear specific assertion in the plaint. This is a matter on record and there is no denial to this. Going back to the written statement as submitted by the Power Development Board it is seen that they clearly understood this claim made by the plaintiff in the plaint and they came out with a counter claim stating that the tools and machineries are not with them for nothing but that the machineries and the tools which are hypothecated with the Bank and belonging to defendant No. 1, would. not cover the amount due to be paid to them by defendant No. 1 and in the written statement the Power Development Board categorically demanded Taka 14,00,000/- (Tk Fourteen lac) to be due from Mis Conwell Ltd. who are admittedly the owners of the tools and machineries hypothecated. They have not only made a counter claim but also challenged the legality of the hypothecation itself stating that the hypothecation being subsequent to their charge the said hypothecation being with the Bank was invalid and had no basis in the eye of law. It thus appears that the parties namely, the Plaintiff and the Power Development Board fought out the suit clearly understanding the issues and the claim they are making against each other as to the machineries and the godown belonging to the firm. If the proforma was for the sake of form only then they had nothing to deny and they could choose to keep quiet leaving others to fight the battle and in that suit a decree would not bind them. But in the instant case Power Development Board being the only defendant fought out the suit by filling a written statement and though the judgment and decree was passed in their absence it cannot be said that they being only proforma, the decree passed would not be binding upon them. 

13. The executing court would not go behind the decree and write out a new decree in the name of interpretation. That is the law and there is no dispute as to that. The executing court would, however, in the facts and circumstances of each case, be at liberty to interpret a decree and also the expression found in the decree, when there exists some ambiguity and uncertainty in the expression used, by taking into consideration the pleadings of the parties in the suit and the statements and averments made in the plaint itself. The court would do so to ascertain the precise meaning. In the instant case it appears that the executing court had gone behind only to ascertain the meaning and had to go to the pleadings of the parties and to the averment in the plaint made to the effect that the hypothecated goods and machineries are lying with the Power Development Board and if the claim of the plaintiff in those goods are denied they will be bound by the decree as well and a decree to the amount of the decrial amount be passed against them also. We had occasion to refer to the provision of the Code of Civil Procedure and we found that the expression proforma do not exist in the Code but only plaintiff and the defendants who may either be a necessary party or a proper party and thus a proforma party. But only because they were described as pro- forma they would not acquire any privileged position or any specialty if they choose to contest. 

14. In the case of Official Assignee Vs. Madholal Sindhu reported in A.I.R. 1947 Bombay at page 217, it was held that merely because parties were de- scribed as proforma defendants they would not occupy any peculiar or any privileged position different from that of an ordinary party. Their Lordships held in the relevant portion of the judgment, at last part of para 69 thus:- 

"The mere fact that no relief was claimed against him did not make him a proforma defendant. In any event once he had put in his written statement and joined in the litigation, he took the risk of any issue decided in that case becoming binding against him. At page 458 Edgily J. observed as follows:- 

"We think that the law contemplates that even a proforma defendant should ordinarily be bound by a decree which has been obtained in his presence." 

With respect, I agree with this view if it means that a proforma defendant who takes part in the litigation would be bound by the decision." 

15. We are in complete agreement with the observation made in the case under report which are in complete agreement with the view we have taken to the effect that a party though described as proforma in a suit would be bound by a decree passed in his presence after he has contested the suit by filing a written statement in which an adverse claim is made against the property in suit. He would be bound by the money decree in the instant case passed in his presence though he is described as a mere proper party namely, a proforma defendant. 

16. We also hold that it has never been laid down, as argued, that when there is a defendant against whom no relief was sought and who is not a necessary party in the suit and who took no part in the litigation but claim to stand by and see others fighting the battle, can still be bound by the judgment and the decree. If that being the position we would have allowed this appeal but we find that the position in the instant case is otherwise as in the instant suit a party was named a mere proper party and a proforma but against whom there is a claim made in the plaint categorically to the effect that the decree may be passed against them also and the proforma defendant having contested the suit by making an adverse claim and denying the claim of the plaintiff, the decree passed in the money suit in their presence would be binding upon them also, though they were mere proforma. 

17. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, has lastly submitted that the ex-parte order passed by the court below in the money suit had no basis because there is no evidence on record to come to a finding that the plaintiffs had proved his claim and further that the property being an abandoned property cannot be made subject to any attachment or sale in execution of a court's decree and more so when the concerned machineries are in the custody of the Deputy Commissioner at the present moment. There is little substance in it because we are not hearing appeal against the decree itself and if the Government is in possession they are to agitate at the time of sale of the property if it is abandoned. Mr. Ashrarul Hossain, the learned Counsel submits that this has also no basis in law because it has been decided in a number of cases by the Appellate Division of this court that if any claim exist prior to the coming in to force of the abandoned property that claim cannot be denied only because the property become an abandoned property subsequently as the property cannot vest in the Government minus the liability incurred. 

18. We are not on this point in this appeal be cause it is not an appeal against the decree but here we are to examine the order of the executing court and the matter for our decision in the instant appeal is whether the decree would be binding against the proforma defendant also which we find in the affirmative in the facts and circumstances of the case. 

19. That being the position, we find no sub-stance in this appeal which is, therefore, dismissed without any order as to cost. 

20. The order staying all further proceedings of the Execution Case (being Civil Rule No. 439 (FM)/84) is hereby vacated. The Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The execution case is to proceed in accordance with law. 

Latifur Rahman, J. I agree.

End.

parties:
Abdul Khaleque & others ---------- Appellants
Vs.
Siddiqur Rahman & others ---------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J. :—This appeal at the instance of the defendants respondents is against an order recording compromise under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts giving rise to this appeal, in short, are that Sarafatullah, predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos. 1-9 and respondent Nos. 10 and instituted Title Suit No. 69 of 1967 in the court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla against the defendant No. 1-Respondent No. 12, defendant No. 2-Respondent No. 13 and the present appellants who were defendant Nos. 22, 21, 20, 16 and 14 respectively for declaration of their title in the land in suit on the basis of lease, settlement and purchase in which they asserted their possession and they got their names mutated in respect of the said land. The suit was contested by the respondent No. 12 herein denying the title and interest of the plaintiffs contending that the dakhilas filed by the plaintiffs in support of their case were also forged and false created for the purpose of the suit. They also contended that original owners by executing a Bainapatra in their favour accepted Tk. 8000/- and delivered possession of the land to them and though no document could be registered yet they continued in possession thereof. The story of possession and dispossession set up by the plaintiffs was false.

3. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit.

4. The plaintiffs appealed. During the pendency of the appeal, the plaintiffs, appellants and respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed a compromise petition wherein the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs in the disputed properties were admitted by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. The learned lower appellate court on the basis of the said solenama passed the impugned order recording compromise.

5. At the hearing of the appeal a preliminary objection as to maintainability of the appeal was raised by the respondents. It was urged that the impugned order having merged with the decree of the lower appellate court an appeal lay against the decree and no appeal against the order recording compromise lies and as such this appeal is not maintainable. The learned Advocate for the appellant, on the other hand, submitted that the appellant had remedy both by way of appeal from the decree itself as well as from an order recording compromise under Order 43, rule 1(m) of Civil Procedure Code. He referred me to the decision in the case of Damodar Prasad and others Vs. Ram Charan Das and others, 1957 Pat 143; Haridas Sadhu Khan Vs. Iswar Ratneswar and others, 1933 Cal. 94; Ramnarayana Rao Vs. Ramkrishna Rao and another 1936 Mad. 358, Jarnail Singh Vs. Mst. Narain Kaur and others, 1936 Lah. 766, Mst. Kalpa Vs. Sita Ram and another 1955 All 187.

<u>6. There is divergent opinion on this point. In Bengali Coal Company Ltd. Vs. Apear Collieries Ltd. and others, 1926 Cal 412 it was held that no appeal lay against an order recording compromise passed under Order 23, rule 1 of the Code. Similar view was also expressed in the case of Onkar Bhagwan Vs. Gamna Lakhaji & Co. 1933 Bom. 205 wherein it was held that no appeal lay from the order recording compromise in pursuance of which a decree is passed. In the case of Sabitri Thakurain Vs. F.A. Savi and others, 1929 Pat 318,.a somewhat similar question arose as to whether right of appeal against the order passed under Order 23, rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code was lost by reason of a decree having been passed in accordance with the order. Construing provision of s. 97 of Civil Procedure Code vis-a-vis Or. 23, rule 3 of the Code it was held:-</u>

<u>"Therefore, to my mind, the right of appeal against the order directing a compromise to be recorded passed under Order 23, rule 3 is not lost by reason of the decree having been passed in accordance with the order."</u>

<u>The decision made in Bengali Coal Co. Ltd. was overruled in the case of Talebali Vs. Abdul Aziz, 1929 Cal 689 (F.B). The decision in Onkar Bhagwan was dissented from in .1936 Mad. 385. Wadsworth, J. in delivering the judgment observed "It seems to me therefore that the balance of authority in this Court is in favour of the view that an appeal lies against the order even when a decree has been passed in terms of the compromise". In the case of Umiashankar Naranji Vs. Shivshankar Prabhashankar, 1944 Bom (D.B) 239 the view expressed in Onkar Bhagwan was also not followed. Sen, 1. after reviewing a large number of cases on this subject held that "In our opinion though ordinarily where a decree has been passed after some contest between the parties such decree is appealable, where it has been proved that the suit has been adjusted by a lawful agreement, there can be no appeal against the decree under section 96(3), but there is a right of appeal against the order made under Order 23, rule 3". Though concurring but in a separate judgment in the same case Divatia, J. observed :</u>

<u>'The intention seems to have been that the propriety of an order recording or refusing to record an adjustment under Order 23, rule 3, should be decided by the appellate Court in an appeal from that order, because if a decree was passed according to the compromise, there could be no opportunity to test the order as there could be no appeal from such a decree by virtue of s. 96(3).</u>

<u>The recent decisions in 62 Cal. 229, as well as in 12 Pat. 359 also take the same view. That being so, I do not think that the Legislature intended to deprive the aggrieved party of the right of appeal against an order under Order 23, rule 3".</u>

<u>In Damodar Prashad & others V s. Ram Charan & others, 1957 Pat 143 it has been held that:</u>

<u>"Construing Order 43, rule l(m), with s. 96 (3) of the Code, it seems clear that the only appeal intended by the Legislature is an appeal against the "recording or refusing to record" the alleged agreement and not a further appeal again from the decree recording the compromise".</u>

<u>I need not discuss elaborately other decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the appellant in this case to burden the judgment as the trend of the decisions in the those cases is in the line of the decisions discussed above. Thus from the discussion of the cases above it seems to me that balance of the judicial pronouncement is in favour of the proposition of law that an appeal lies under Order 43, rule 1 (m) from an order made under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code. Being in respectful agreement with the aforesaid views of their Lordships I am of the opinion that even in a case where a decree has been passed in pursuance of an order recording compromise, the aggrieved party can take at appeal from order itself and a decree drawn in pursuance of the said order will not be a bar to the right of appeal given under Order 43, rule 1 (m) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Therefore, the preliminary objection fails.</u>

7. Now, it remains for me to decide the appeal on merit. The propriety of the order has been assailed on the ground that the Court below erred in law in recording compromise without noticing that the appellants before me were not parties to compromise. The learned Advocate for the respondents, on the other hand, submitted that the agreement Ext. A. was executed by Bonamali in favour of Afsaruddin Sarker, the defendant No.2, father of the defendant No. 1. The defendants appellants before me neither contested the suit nor took any appeal from the decree made in the said suit and they also did not challenge the compromise petition in the lower appellate court as they were not parties to the agreement and as such the learned Additional District Judge committed no illegality in recording compromise. It appears from the record that the suit brought by Sarafatullay, the predecessor in interest of the present respondent Nos. 1-9 and 2 others against the present respondent No. 12 Fazlul Karim (defendant No.1) and Afsaruddin, respondent No. 13 (defendant No. 2) and others was contested only by the defendant No.1 Fazlul Karim. At no stage before the trial court the present appellants did appear and contest the suit nor raised any objection to the compromise petition filed before the lower appellate court. The learned Advocate for the appellant before me, however, urged that an application was filed raising objection to the said compromise petition by the appellants. But from perusal of the aforesaid petition printed at page 168 of the Paper Book I find that the contention of the learned Advocate is not correct rather that application was under Order 41, rule 21 of the Code for re-hearing of T.A. No. 160 which was decreed on 16.4.1970 and it was not a petition of objection to the compromise itself. The learned Advocate for the appellants also argued that the agreement for sale was in favour of the present appellants whose names were mentioned in Ext. A and they being impleaded as defendants in the suit and not being parties to the compromise the learned Additional District Judge was wrong to pass an order recording compromise. He cited several decisions in support of his contention to which I shall refer shortly.

<u>8. True, the names of the appellants were mentioned in the body of the agreement and they were made defendants but on the very face of the agreement Ext. A itself it is clear that it was executed by Bonamali in favour of defendant No. 2 alone. The conduct of the appellants in dealing with the suit and the appeal are also circumstances enough to show that they were not interested in the result of the suit and as such did not take any step against the decree passed against them and also did not contest the compromise petition by raising any objection thereto. These facts also lend support to the contention of the learned Advocate for the respondents that although the names of the defendants were mentioned in Ext. A. they were not parties to the agreement. In defending their right, if any accrued under Ext. A, they ought to have appeared in and contested the suit from the very beginning in which they were impleaded as defendants and ought to have taken steps against the decree passed against them in the suit to vindicate their right arising out of Ext. A by way of appeal before the appellate Court. But the appellants did not do so. They also did not raise any objection to the compromise petition itself challenging the same on the ground of its genuineness and validity. Apart from that order recording compromise can not be said to be an illegal order inasmuch as the compromise effected between the parties is a lawful one. The learned Advocate for the appellants referred me to the decisions in the case of Ashfaqul Hossain 1923 Oudh. 252 and in the case of Ajoy Kumar Devi Vs. Manindra Nath Chakraborty, 32 Cal. 561 in support of his contention that the court below illegally recorded compromise under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code. The learned Advocate for respondents, on the other hand, submitted that the decisions do not apply in this case. In Ashfaqul Hossain, Dalal, J. has held that the court would refuse to accept compromise if the result of the compromise would be to deprive the other defendants of the fruit of their success. But the principle of law enunciated in that case has little application to the facts of the instant case. In that case the plaintiffs suit was a suit for specific performance of contract against one Syed Bunyod Hossain, the vendor defendant and two purchasers defendants. The trial court as well as the lower appellate court found that the agreement of the plaintiff was ante-dated and the defendant Syed Bunyod Hossain colluded in executing the agreement with the plaintiff to deprive the purchasers-defendants of the fruit of their purchase. It was also found that in the event of allowing the compromise the suit would be withdrawn and the plaintiff would bring another suit on the basis of his purchase against the purchaser to circumvent the law. But in the instant case neither there is any allegation as to collusion between plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1-2 for effecting the compromise nor there was any finding by the court on that count. The facts of the case reported in 32 Cal. 561 are quite distinguishable from the facts of the present appeal and therefore, the principle of law enunciated therein has little application to the facts of the case before me. Under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code where it is proved to the satisfaction that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise or where the defendant satisfies the plaintiff in respect of the whole or any part of the subject-matter of the suit, the court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction to be recorded and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit as Order 23, rule 3 does not confer any discretion on the court. In the instant appeal nothing could be pointed out before me by Mr. Karim that the compromise effected between the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1-2 was unlawful. If a party to a compromise denies having entered into compromise, the court will have to come to a finding as to whether there had been or not a compromise effected between the parties and to decide if the compromise was lawful. In this case there was no such denial and there being no evidence on record to show the term of compromise effected between the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 was unlawful, the court below was to pass the order recording compromise. This view of mine finds support from the case Mst. Kalpa Vs. Sita Ram & another 1955 All 187 (D.B) wherein it has been held that where the compromise was lawful, there would be no option left to the court but to pass a decree in terms of the compromise. The Bombay High Court went further. In Onkar Bhagwan Vs. Gamna 1933 Born. 205 it has been held that where recording of compromise was not challenged in the court below it must be held to have been done by consent. In the present case no such challenge was made by the appellants in the court below. Agreeing with the view expressed in Onkar Bhagwan and in view of the facts and surrounding circumstances of this case it can easily be said that the appellants had consent to the compromise in question even if it is assumed that they were parties to the agreement. In this view of the matter; therefore, it also can not be said that the order recording compromise is illegal.</u>

9. From the above discussion, I do not find any substance in this appeal. I dismiss the appeal.

However, there will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Ismail with Md. Omar Farooq, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md. Nurul Islam Chowdhury with Md. Abul Kalam Azad, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party
parties:
Tambia Khatun ----- Plaintiff-Petitioner
Vs.
Abdul Rouf Sowdagar ----- Deft-Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 23.3.88 passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 67 of 1986 should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts of this matter are that the petitioner being plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 106 of 1984 in the Court of Munsif, (now Assistant Judge) 2nd Court, Sadar, Chittagong on 15.8.84 for ejectment of the defendant opposite party on the ground of default in payment of rent and of bonafide requirement. The case of the petitioner is that the defendant-opposite party took bhara of the suit premises from the plaintiff as a monthly tenant for serveral years and then executed a bharanama agreement in 1981 and then again renewed the bhara by executing a renewed bharanama agreement on 1.11.83 in favour of the plaintiff. The defendant-opposite party paid rent upto May, 1984 and thereafter stopped payment of rent. The plaintiff-petitioner then served notice upon the defendant-opposite party under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act terminating the monthly tenancy on the expiry of 31st day of July, 1984 and then filed the Other Suit No. 106 of 1984 for ejectment The defendant-opposite party contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint and claiming himself to be a co-sharer in the suit house by purchase from one Halima Khatun and that he filed a partition suit No. 71 of 1985.

3. Thereafter when the ejectment suit became ripe for disposal, then the defendant-opposite partyfiled an application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of learned District Judge, Chittagong being Misc. Case No. 67 of 1986 praying for transfering the Ejectment Suit No. 106 of 1984 from the court of the Assistant Judge to the Court of the 1st Sub-Judge for analogous trial with Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985. The plaintiff- petitioner contested the Transfer Case No. 67 of 1986 by filing a written objection. The learned District Judge after hearing the parties allowed the transfer of the ejectment suit (Other Suit No. 106 of 1984) from the Second Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong to the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong with a direction for its analogous trial with Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985 vide his judgment and order dated 23.3.88.

4. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order of the learned District Judge, the plaintiff of Other Suit No. 106 of 1984 as petitioner has moved this court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr. Md. Ismail, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, submitted that the learned District Judge has committed an error of law and fact by transferring the Ejectment Suit No. 106 of 1984 to the Court of Subordinate Judge for its analogous trial with Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985 in view of the fact that the nature and character of both the suits are quite different from each other and that the laws applicable therein are also different and that the parties of both the suits are not the same. The learned Advocate further argued that the defendant-opposite party is an admitted tenant under the plaintiff- petitioner by executing bharanama agreement and paid rent to him upto May, 1984 and thereafter stopped payment of rent and filed the Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985 and then filed the Transfer Case No. 67 of 1986 with the sole purpose of delaying the disposal of the ejectment suit with the intention of depriving the plaintiff-petitioner from getting his suit house back from the tenant. The learned advocate argued that the defendant-opposite party took bhara of the suit house as a monthly tenant by admitting the plaintiff-petitioner as his landlord by contract and paid rent thereof for a few years and so the opposite party has no right to deny the title of the plaintiff-petitioner.
