<u>6. In support of his argument, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner referred to a decision in the case of Hajee Abdus Sattar Vs. Mahiuddin & others reported in 38 DLR (AD) 97. It appears that their Lordships have observed in that case the following:</u>

<u>"The estoppel as described in this section is known as tenant's estoppel or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person then neither he nor anybody claiming through him shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it."</u>

7. It has been further observed in that case that- "A device resorted to by tenant whereby he defaults to pay rent and when sued for evictien, sets up plea of no relationship of tenant and landlord such a plea is unavailing when original of tenancy is proved."

8. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner next referred to the case of Abdul Jahar Vs. Abdul Kader & others reported in 36 DLR 306 and said that in that case their Lordships have observed the following:

"An order of transfer or withdrawal may validly be passed in exercise of Court's judicial discretion for sufficient good reasons-The party applying for transfer, etc. must satisfy the court that a transfer, etc is conducive and convenient for both the parties."

9. Mr. Ismail has argued that the defendant- opposite party is an admitted tenant under the plaintiff-petitioner by executing contract and also by payment of rent and, as such, the disposal of the eviction suit cannot be delayed on the plea of its analogous trial with his partition suit having a distinct and separate character and therefore, this plea of analogous trial of two distinct suits cannot be good sufficient ground for transfer, rather it will put the plaintiff-petitioner, one of the parties, into most inconvenient condition.

10. Mr. Md. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party argued that the learned District Judge has wide power of transferring any suit from one court to another and, as such, the learned District Judge, Chittagong has not committed any error of law in transferring the Ejectment Suit-No. 106 of 1984 from the Court of Assistant Judge to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong. The learned Advocate further argued that in deciding this revisional application the only question to be considered is whether the learned District Judge has committed any error of law occasioning failure of justice, but that the facts of the case are not matters for consideration in this revisional application.

11. It is true that the facts of the case are not necessarily to be considered in deciding whether an order of transfer under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure has become legal or there has been any error of law in passing that order, But in deciding such a question in respect of an order of transfer of a case on the sole ground of an analogous trial with another case, it needs to be seen whether the facts and nature of the cases are conducive for such transfer on the sole ground of an analogous trial of both the cases.

12. By a perusal of the impugned judgment and order of the learned District Judge, it appears that the learned District Judge has made the following observation in his judgment:

"From the materials of the records, what I find is that the petitioner (defendant-opposite party of this revision) has rightly brought partition suit against the opposite party (plaintiff-petitioner of this revision). But it is not denied that he was the tenant for the disputed premises under the opposite party (plaintiff-petitioner of this revision). It may so happen that in the long run the petitioner may get his saham by partition, but it is difficult to say that the petitioner would get the disputed premises in his saham by partition. Ordinarily, it is "suspected that the opposite party-defendant (the plaintiff-petitioner of this revision) would get the disputed premises in his share and he (defendant opposite party of this revision) would get the remaining portion of his purchased land by partition."

13. From the above observation of the learned District Judge it will appear that he himself has found that the defendant-opposite party of this revision is an admitted tenant in the suit premises under the plaintiff-petitioner and that it is not likely that he would get the disputed premises in his saham by partition, although in the long run he may get a saham by partition in the remaining portion of this disputed property by his purchase. From the impugned transfer order of the learned District Judge, it further appears that the plaintiff-petitioner is in possession of the suit-premises since long before the purchase of the remaining portion by the defendant- opposite party and that the defendant-opposite party is an admitted tenant in the suit premises under the plaintiff-petitioner on payment of monthly rent, but suddenly stopped payment of rent from June, 1984. It is not known when the 'long run' as observed by the learned District Judge will come to its end for disposal of the partition suit, it may take a decade or even more. Under such circumstances, the transfer and tagging of the ejectment suit for analogous trial with the partition suit will amount to an injunction restraining the plaintiff-petitioner from enjoying the fruits of his suit premises. In this view of the matter I am of the opinion that the impugned order of transfer has become most inconvenient and prejudicial to the interest of the plaintiff-petitioner.

<u>14. It is argued on behalf of the defendant-opposite party that the District Judge has wide power of transfer of any case at any stage from one court to another for convenience and inconvenience of the parties. It is true that the District Judge has got such wide power of transferring a suit. But it is a settled principle of law as cited above that the convenience of transfer which is to be taken into consideration by the court is the convenience of both the parties, not only one of them. From the circumstances of the matter, it will appear that the impugned order of transfer as made by the learned District Judge will be convenient to serve the purpose of the defendant-opposite party to delay the disposal of the ejectment suit but it will be most inconvenient and prejudicial to the interest of the plaintiff-petitioner.</u>

15. Mr. Md. Ismail, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner next argued that the guiding principle of analogous trial of two suits are that the nature and character of both the suits must be same or similar, the parties must be more or less same and same set of witnesses will be there in both the suits on behalf of both parties and issues will be almost same in both the suits, but that none of these guiding factors are present in the ejectment suit and the partition suit. The learned Advocate further argued that the District Judge cannot also direct the transferee court for analogous trial of any transferred suit with another suit. In this connection, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner referred to the case of Dronavaijuls Vidyamba Vs. Vallabhajosyulla Lakshmi Venkayamma reported in AIR (Andhra Pradesh) 1958 page 218 wherein it has been held that "For whatever reasons of convenience or otherwise the order of transfer is made under section 24(2) CPC, it does not empower the court or contemplate any directions being given for the joint trial of the transferred suit."

<u>16. From the impugned order of the learned District Judge it appears that he has given a direction for analogous trial of the transferred suit No. 106 of 1984 (ejectment suit) with the Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985. From the facts and the nature of these two suits it appears that some of the guiding factors for analagous trial is present in this matter. The only question for decision in the ejectment suit is a question of relationship of landlord and tenant between the plaintiff and defendant and whether the defendant made payment of rent. Ejectment suit and partition suit are distinct and different from each other. In view of all the above, the learned District Judge appears to have committed an error of law and principle by directing for analogous trial of two suits of distinct and separate character.</u>

17. By a careful consideration of all the facts, circumstances and the principles of law discussed above, I find that the learned District Judge has committed an error of law resulting in an error in his decision occasioning failure of justice and that his impugned judgment suffers from infirmity and contradiction.

18. For all the reasons stated above, I am of the opinion that this is a fit case for interference by this court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

19. In the result, the impugned order of the learned District Judge dated 23.3.88 is hereby set aside and the Rule is, accordingly, made absolute without any order as to costs.

20. The learned Assistant Judge is directed to dispose of the ejectment suit being Other Suit No. 106 of 1984 as expeditiously as possible, preferably within three months of the receipt of this order.

Communicate this order to the courts concerned at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mohandra Lal Jaini Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1963 (SC) 109. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by Miah Abdul Gafur, Advocate on Record ----- For the Appellants. 
K. A. Bakr, Senior Advocate, Supreme Court, instructed by M. R. Khan, Advocate on Record ----- For the Respondent No. 1. 
Ex-parte ----- Respondents No. 2 to 17
parties:
Ful Chand Das and others ----- Appellants
Vs.
Mohammad Hammad and others ----- Respondents
case_source: From the judgment and decree dated August 28, 1974 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No. 38 of 1969.
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, J.—I have gone through the judgment of Shahabuddin, J and also those of Ruhul Islam, J and Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J who have concluded differently. In view of the concurrent findings of fact by the trial court and the High Court Division and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I agree with the judgment of Shahabuddin, J. I think it advisable not to state any views on the constitutionality of sections 4 and 6 of the Displaced Persons Ordinance, 1964.

Ruhul Islam, J.—On carefully going through the copy of the judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. and Shahabuddin Ahmed J, I find it difficult to agree with Shahabuddin Ahmed, J and although I agree with Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. as to the result of the appeal but I do not subscribe to some of his reasoning’s to support the conclusion for allowing the appeal. So, I consider it necessary to give my own reasons on the questions involved in the appeal.

2. This appeal by special leave arises from a judgment of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 38 of 1969 dated August 28, 1974 reversing that of the Subordinate Judge and dismissing the suit for cancellation of sale-deed dated February 7, 1964 on declaration that it is fraudulent, illegal and void.

<u>3. Plaintiff's case in short is that the plaintiff-appellants are members of the minority community having permanent residence in village Kazirgaon, P.S. Tejgaon, District Dacca, on the outskirts of the city of Dacca. They became victim of communal riots which broke out in January 1964; their huts and houses were burnt and their movable properties looted; they took shelter in the Refugee Camps opened by the Government in the city of Dacca After some time they returned to their village and after reconstructing their burnt down huts started living there. Defendant No. 1 Ganesh Chandra Chakra borty residing in the Dacca city appeared in their village and gave out to the villagers that he was a representative from the office of the Deputy High Commissioner of India in Dacca and told them that there was apprehension of fresh riot and so saying induced the plaintiffs and other villagers to migrate to India, where they would be properly rehabilitated. He proposed to the plaintiffs that they should leave the title deeds of their respective immovable properties with him for being kept in the Deputy High Commissioner's Office in order to protect their interests in their absence; and that the same would be necessary to enable them getting land and settle in India. The plaintiffs were at that time in such a state of mind that they readily agreed to his proposal and according to his instruction delivered to him their title deeds together with blank stamp papers and cartridge papers signed or thumb impressed by them. Thereafter the plaintiffs after obtaining migration certificates from the Indian High Com-mission Office left for India, but within 2 or 2-1/2 months they returned to their native village completely disillusioned as they did not get any help there. The plaintiffs asked defendant No. 1 to return their title deeds and the signed papers but on various pretexts he did not return the papers. After a few days the plaintiffs got notices from the District Sub-Registrar, Dacca directing them to appear and admit execution of a kabala in favour of defendant No. 2 Mohammad Hammad. Some of the plaintiffs appeared in the Registration Office and explained to the Sub-Registrar that no such sale deed had been executed by them. Then the plaintiffs approached defendant No 2 and told him that they never sold their land to him; and that they never executed any kabala in his favour, but he would not listen to them saying that he paid the consideration money of the kabala to defendant No. 1 for paying to the plaintiffs. They immediately filed petitions before the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca and the Relief Commissioner, Government of East Pakistan stating that they did not file any application for permission for sale of immovable property and if any such application had been filed should be rejected. The sale-deed was presented for registration without obtaining necessary permission from the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca/Board of Revenue, Government of East Pakistan. Ail application was filed before the Sub-Registrar stating that the vendors had filed applications to the relevant authorities for issuing necessary permission, and as soon as the same was granted, it would be produced for registration of the sale-deed. On December 9, 1964, defendant No. 2 came to the plaintiff's village and demanded possession of the property transferred to him claiming that he purchased their land on the basis of the kabala executed by them. The plaintiffs refused to comply with his demand when the plaintiffs were threatened that possession would be taken, if necessary, by force after December 31, 1964. In this background the plaintiffs instituted the suit. The suit was contested by defendant No. 2 by filing a written statement. It was stated, inter alia, that the Plaintiffs voluntarily transferred their lands to defendant No. 2 after due negotiation for a consideration of Rs. 14,900/- out of which Rs. 13,100/- was paid as earnest money and agreement for sale was executed by the vendor on December 28, 1963 and thereafter on February 9, 1964 the vendors executed the sale-deed in favour of the defendant on receipt of the balance consideration of Rs. 1,800/- and made over the sale-deed to the defendant. But on promulgation of the Displaced Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964 (Ordinance No. 1 of 1964) which put restriction on transfer of land belonging to the members of the minority community, the plaintiffs refused to register the sale-deed, whereupon he got the sale-deed registered by obtaining necessary per-mission from the competent authority as required under the said Ordinance. His further case is that the omission to mention about bainapatra in the sale-deed was due to inadvertence and mistake. The defendant, however, gave total denial to the case of the plaintiffs that defendant No. 1 on false representations to the plaintiffs got their title deeds and signed blank stamp papers and other cartridge papers which were converted into bainapatra and a sale-deed now sought to be declared as illegal and void. Defendant No. 1 also appeared by filing a written statement. His defence is that he had no concern with the suit lands or with the plaintiffs and he does not claim any interest therein and the properties transferred by the kabala executed by the plaintiffs. He also totally denied that he was ever acquainted with the plaintiffs. He also denied that he had any acquaintance with the, Deputy High Commissioner of India at Dacca.</u>

<u>4. At the trial the parties led evidence in support of their respective case. On consideration of the evidence the learned Subordinate Judge did not accept the case of the plaintiffs that the sale-deed was executed as a result of fraud and misrepresentation, and found it to be a genuine deed executed by the plaintiffs intending to sell their immovable property to defendant No. 2 Mohammad Hammad for consideration; and the trial Court did not find any collusion between defendant No. 1 and the defendant No. 2. But the trial Court found that in the absence of the necessary permission of the competent authority as provided in East Pakistan Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 the sale deed was not validly registered. On this ground the suit was decreed and the sale-deed was ordered to be cancelled. On appeal by the defendant No. 2 a Division Bench of the High Court Division concurred with the trial Court's findings of fact, but relying on a decision in the case of Chittaranjan Sutar v. Secretary, Judicial Department, Government of East Pakistan, 17 DLR Dacca 451, held that the sale-deed was not hit by the Ordinance as the relevant provision of the Ordinance, namely, section 4 which required permission of the competent authority for registration of the sale-deed executed by a member of the minority community, was declared ultra vires of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962. On this finding the judgment and decree of the trial Court were set aside and suit was dismissed.</u>

5. Leave was granted to consider the following two questions:

(1) Whether proper permission was obtained from the appropriate authority under the Disturbed Persons (Re-habilitation) Ordinance, 1964 for registration of the sale-deed in question ;

or

whether permission for registration was at all necessary in view of the decision by the Dacca High Court in Chittaranjan Sutar's case that "sections 4 and 6 of the aforesaid Ordinance were void ab initio being in conflict with the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution of 1962.

(2) Whether in view of the fact that the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 13 and 15 of the Constitution of 1962 having been suspended on declaration of Emergency from 6th September, 1965, sections 4 and 6 of the said Ordinance were revived and were in operation at the relevant time.

6. The learned Judges of the High Court Division have taken the view that sections 4 and 6 of Ordinance 1 of 1964 having been declared ultra vires of the Constitution of 1962 in the case of Chittaranjan Sutar, the sections became void ab initio, and consequently production of a certificate from the appropriate authority concerned was no longer necessary, and as such, the disputed sale deed was validly registered.

7. High Court's judgment is founded practically on two considerations. Firstly, sections 4 and 6 of East Pakistan Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 having been declared void in Chittaranjan Sutar's case, the said provisions not being in existence in the eye of law the impugned kabala in favour of defendant No. 2 never lost its legal validity on account of non-compliance of the requirement of section 4 of the said Ordinance ; and secondly, the learned Judges concurred with the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs failed to prove that the defendants 1 and 2 collusively created the impugned kabala Exhibit B. Section 4 of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 as promulgated on February 12, 1964 reads as under:—

"4. Restriction on transfer.—(1) Not-withstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force no transfer of any immovable property belonging to a member of a minority community shall be deemed to be valid and legal unless it has been made with prior permission of the Deputy Commissioner of the District concerned in connection with the provisions of sub-section (2).

(2) On receipt of the application, the Deputy Commissioner shall cause an inquiry to be made to ascertain whether the proposed sale has been brought about,—

(i) by coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence, misrepresentation or fraud ; or

(ii) in due course of business of the transferor. He will refuse permission in cases falling under clause (i) and may grant permission in cases falling under clause (ii).

(3) No instrument for transfer of immovable property of a person who is a member of the minority community shall be admitted to registration unless it has been accompanied by the permission of the Deputy Commissioner under sub-section (2)". Section 4 as substituted by Ordinance X of 1964, promulgated on October 10, 1964 reads as follows:

"4. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no transfer of any immovable property belonging to a member of a minority community shall be deemed to be valid and legal unless it has been made with the prior permission of the competent authority as specified in sub-section (2).

(2) For the purposes of sub-section (1), the competent authority shall be,—

(a) In cases where the applicant proposes to transfer his immovable property by sale or mortgage only for bonafide purposes of meeting 'an urgent and unavoidable expenditure,

(i) the Sub-divisional Officer of the Sub-Division in which the property is situated, if the property proposed to be transferred is agricultural land and the area thereof does not exceed one standard bigha or twenty five percent of the total area of all agricultural land held by the applicant, whichever is less,

(ii) the Deputy Commissioner of the district in which the property is situated, if the property proposed to be transferred is agricultural land and the area thereof does not exceed one acre or twenty five cent per of the total area of all agricultural land held by the applicant, whichever is less, or if the property proposed 'to be transferred is non agricultural land or any building or structure and the market value thereof does not exceed rupees five thousand and

(iii) in all other cases, the Relief and Rehabilitation Commissioner, or such other authority as may be appointed in this behalf by the Provincial Government by notification in the Official Gazette and

(b) in other cases where the applicant proposes to transfer his immovable property in any manner for any other purpose, the Commissioner of Relief and Rehabilitation, or such other authority as may be appointed in this behalf by the Provincial Government by notification in the Official Gazette.

(3) An application for permission for transfer shall be submitted, in such form as may be prescribed to the Sub-Divisional Officer in cases falling under sub-clause (i) of clause (a) of sub-section (2) and to the Deputy Commissioner in all other cases.

(4) On receipt of an application under sub-section (3), the Sub-Divisional Officer or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case may be, shall cause an enquiry to be made to ascertain-

(i) whether the proposed transfer has been agreed upon due to coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence, misrepresentation, inadequate consideration, or fraud and whether the purpose of the transfer, as stated in the application, is incorrect, or

(ii) whether it is a bonafide transaction and the purpose of the transfer, as stated in the application, is genuine; and shall refuse permission in cases falling under clause (i) and, subject to the provisions of sub-section (5), may grant permission in cases falling under clause (ii),

(5) All applications falling under clause (ii) of sub-section (4) in respect of cases under sub-clause (iii) of clause (a) of sub-section (2) or clause (b) of that sub-section shall be forwarded, by the Deputy Commissioner, after the enquiry, with a report to the Relief and Rehabilitation Commissioner or the other authority concerned.

(6) No instrument for transfer of immovable property of a person who is a member of a majority community shall be admitted for registration unless it is accompanied by the permission of the competent authority.

(7) No transfer under clause (a) of sub-section (2) shall be permitted more than once in a year. ( 8) A person aggrieved by an order refusing permission under sub-section (4) or (5) may, within sixty days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal from that order to—

(a) the Deputy Commissioner, if the order is made by the Sub-Divisional Officer;

(b) the Relief and Rehabilitation Commissioner or the other authority mentioned in sub-clause (iii) of clause ; a) of sub-section (2) or clause (b) of that sub-section, if the order is made by the Deputy Commissioner; or

(c) the Board of Revenue, if the order is made by the Relief and Rehabilitation Commissioner or any other authority; and no further appeal shall lie.

Explanation—In this section, the word "transfer shall include sale, exchange, gift, will, mortgage, lease, sub-lease or any other manner of transfer or any agreement for such transfer or change of management through a power of attorney or otherwise, but shall not include a mortgage to Government or to the Agricultural Development Bank or to the Agricultural Development Corporation or to a Co-operative Society of to such other organisation as may be notified by the Provincial Government in this behalf in the Official Gazette, for obtaining loans for agricultural purpose."

Comparative study of section 4 (original) and section 4 (substituted) shows that practically no restriction on transfer of immovable property by the members of the minority community was imposed by section 4 (original). Only restriction on transfer of immovable property by the members of the minority community was that registration of instruments of transfer was made conditional on the granting of prior permission by the Deputy Commissioner concerned after holding the necessary inquiry to ascertain whether or not the proposed transfer was in due course of business of the transferor; and transfer of immovable property without the prior permission of the Deputy Commissioner was to be deemed invalid. Ordinance I of 1964 was promulgated with the declared object to provide for the speedy rehabilitation of persons affected by the "civil disturbance" in East Pakistan in January, 1964 and for the protection of the immovable properties of the minority communities. Sub-section (1) of section 2 contains the provision for restoration of possession by way of rehabilitation of persons affected. It provides that any Magistrate or other officer specially empowered in this behalf by the Provincial Government by general or special order may, after such local inquiry and with such police or other help as he may consider necessary, evict summarily any person who may have occupied or taken possession in any manner whatsoever of any house, hut, structure or land which any other person has had to leave or has left on account of or in apprehension of the civil disturbance in January, 1964. Section 4 is concomitant to section 2 of Ordinance 1 of 1964. In the absence of section 4 it would be difficult for the authority concerned to give full relief under section 2. A person who had taken possession of any house, hut, structure or land on the basis of a document executed by the owner and registered, in a case as stated in section 2, would have a valid ground to resist his eviction. Sub-section (2) provided that on receipt of the application for permission the Deputy Commissioner was empowered to cause an inquiry to be made to ascertain whether the proposed sale has been brought about by coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence, misrepresentation or fraud; or it was in due course of business of the transferor. The Deputy Commissioner was required to refuse permission in cases by coercion, threat, intimidation, etc.; and he might grant permission where the proposed sale has been brought about in due course of business of the transferor. It is clear from sub-section (2) of section 4 that if the proposed sale had taken place in due course of business of the transferor, the Deputy Commissioner had no authority to refuse the permission; and he could refuse perimysium only in cases where the proposed sale was not in due course of business of the transferor. In other words, it was brought about by coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence, misrepresentation or fraud.

8. Sub-section (3) provides that no instrument for transfer in immovable property by a member of the minority community shall be admitted to registration unless it has been accompanied by the permission of the Deputy Commissioner. The restriction on the transfer of immovable property of a member of the minority community as provided in section 4, could not be said to be disadvantageous to a member of the minority community, because, it was necessary for his protection. The restrictions in the background of the civil disturbance in East Pakistan in 1964 could not be termed as unreasonable restrictions offending any of the fundamental rights of the transferors. The original section 4 was in operation till October 10, 1964 when it was substituted by section 5 of the Ordinance X of 1964 which incorporated some new restrictions. In sub-section (1) the expression "competent authority" was inserted in place of the expression Deputy Commissioner of the district concerned. Sub-section (2) provided that for the purpose of sub-section (1), the competent authority shall be,

(a) in cases where the proposed transfer of immovable property by sale or mortgage only for bonafide purposes of meeting of an urgent and unavoidable expenditure,—

(i) the Sub-Divisional Officer of the Sub-division in which the property is situated, if the property proposed to be transferred was agricultural land and the area thereof did not exceed one standard bigha or twenty-five percent of the total area of all agricultural land held by the applicant whichever is less; and

(ii) the Deputy Commissioner of the district in which the property is situated, if the property proposed to be transferred was agricultural land and the area did not exceed one acre or twenty-five per cent of the total area of agricultural land held by the applicant whichever is less, or if the property proposed to be transferred was non-agricultural land or any building or structure and the market value thereof does not exceed rupees five thousand. In all other cases the Relief and Rehabilitation Commissioner or such other authority as might be appointed by the Provincial Government by notification in the Official Gazette was the competent authority. The subsection (2) further provided that in other cases where the applicant proposed to transfer his immovable property in any manner for any other purpose, the Commissioner of Relief and Rehabilitation or such other authority as might be appointed in this behalf by the Provincial Government by notification in the Official Gazette. Sub-section (3) provided that an application for permission for transfer was to be submitted in the prescribed form to the Sub-Divisional Officer or to the Deputy Commissioner depending on the area of land pro-posed to be transferred. Sub-section (4) provided that on receipt of an application under sub-section (3), the Sub-Divisional Officer or the Deputy Commissioner was required to cause an inquiry to ascertain whether the proposed transfer has been agreed upon due to coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence, misrepresentation, inadequate consideration, or fraud and whether the purpose of the transfer, as stated in the application, was incorrect, or the proposed transaction was a bonafide one and the purpose of the transfer as stated in the application was genuine. The competent authority was empowered to grant permission or refuse permission in an appropriate case. Sub-section (5) provided that in respect of cases where permission was required to be given by the Relief and Rehabilitation Com-missioner, the Deputy Commissioner after holding inquiry was to forward the application along with a report to the Relief and Rehabilitation Commissioner or other authority concerned. Sub-section (6) provided that no instrument for transfer of immovable property of a person who was a member of minority community should be admitted for registration unless it was accompanied by the permission of the competent authority. Sub-section (7) provided that no transfer, of immovable property by sale or mortgage even for bonafide purposes of meeting an urgent and unavoidable expenditure would be permitted more than once in a year.

9. Section 6 of Ordinance I of 1964 as modified by Ordinance VI of 1964 provided that save as provided in the Ordinance no action taken, no decision made and no order passed in the Ordinance shall be called in question by any suit or proceeding in any court or tribunal. It further provides that no court shall entertain any suit for the Specific Performance of Contract relating to the transfer of immovable property of a member of minority community or for the declaration of title or enforcement of mortgage-security in relation to such property, except prior permission granted after such inquiry as it was considered necessary by the Board of Revenue and no such suit pending on the date of commencement of the Ordinance shall be proceeded with except with such permission. Sub-section (3) of section 6 which was added by the Ordinance No. X of 1964 provides that no immovable property belonging to a member of minority community shall be sold in execution of any decree of a civil court or of any certificate signed under Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913, except with the prior permission of the Board of Revenue. By Ordinance X of 1964 a new provision, section 6A, was added. It provided a penal provision. It provided that a transfer of immovable property which contravened the provisions of the Ordinance shall be null and void and the property so transferred shall stand forfeited to the Provincial Government.

10. Validity of section 4 as substituted by Ordinance X of 1964 and section 6 as amended by the said Ordinance was challenged by a writ petition in the case of Chittaranjan Sutar. The petition was heard by a Special Bench of the East Pakistan High Court. On examining the restrictions put on the transfer of immovable property by a member of the minority community, it has been found by the Special Bench that the restrictions are not consistent with the object of the legislation, namely, the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 ; and that the restrictions are unreasonable. The Special Bench has also found that the restrictions are discriminatory, vis-a-vis members of majority community, in the matter of the transfer of immovable property. It has been held that sections 4 and 6 are repugnant to Articles 13 and 15 of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed' under the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962. Article 13 provided the property rights of every citizen and Article 15 provided equality of citizens, that is, equal before law and equal protection of law.

<u>11. Judgment in Chittaranjan Sutar's case was given on July 1, 1965 and on the prayer made on behalf of the Government Certificate under Article 58 of the Constitution of 1962 was granted, as the case involved substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. An appeal to the Supreme Court was filed by the Government and ad interim order was made by the Supreme Court on July 3, 1965 staying operation of the judgment and order of the High Court. While the appeal was pending and the stay order was continuing, Emergency was proclaimed throughout Pakistan on the outbreak of war between India and Pakistan on September 6, 1965; and the Thirteenth Fundamental Right was suspended on September 6, 1965 and the Fifteenth Fundamental Right was suspended on September 16, 1965. While suspension of the Fundamenal Rights was continuing the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 expired by afflux of time on March 31, 1969 and appeal was withdrawn by the Government on June 10, 1970. It was argued before the High Court Division that in view of the suspension of the operation of the judgment and order of the Special Bench in Chittaranjan Sutar's case by the Supreme Court and the Ordinance expiring during pendency of the appeal of the Government along with the stay order, sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 continued to be operative. Secondly, it was argued that on the suspension of the Fundamental Rights concerned sections 4 and 6 revived, and the sections were operative when the impugned kabala was registered.</u>

<u>12. The learned Judges dealt with the second branch of the argument only, and replied saying that on the suspension of the thirteenth Fundamental Right on September 6, 1965 and Fifteenth Fundamental Right on September 16, 1965 by the Emergency proclaimed in the country on September 6, 1965, sections 4 and 6 of Ordinance 1 of 1964 did not revive, because, according to them, once a post constitutional provision is declared void being, in violation of any Fundamental Right, by operation of sub-article (2) of Article 6 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962, it is void ab initio and nothing revives when the relevant fundamental right or rights become inoperative on suspension. The learned; Judges while examining the question do not appear to have examined the effect of the declaration made in Chittaranjan Sutar's case on sections 4 and 6 of East Pakistan Ordinance No. 1 of 1964, particularly section 4 which had been substituted by a new section 4 by East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) (Second) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1964, (East Pakistan Ordinance No. X of 1964). It appears from the report of the Chittaranjan Sutars' case that section 4 of Ordinance No. I of 1964 as it stood on substitution was examined and on consideration of different restrictive provisions introduced therein, it was found that section 4 contravened the Thirteenth Fundamental Right. If section 4 (new) as introduced by Ordinance No. X of 1964 was void ab hallo, meaning it never came into existence in the statute book in the eye of law, and it did not affect section 4 of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 as it stood before substitution, So, original section 4 of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 should be deemed to have remained unaffected by the purported substitution made by Ordinance X of 1964. According to the original section 4 the sale-deed could not be registered without prior permission of the Deputy Commissioner which must be preceded by an inquiry to ascertain whether the proposed transfer was in due course of business of the transferors or it was by coercion, threat, intimidation, undue influence, misrepresentation or fraud; and the permission could be refused only when on inquiry it was found that the proposed transfer was not in the normal course of transfer. In view of the communal disturbance in the country in January, 1964 the Ordinance was promulgated to protect the interest of the members of the minority community. So whatever restrictions the section imposed on the registration of transfer deeds by the members of the minority community could not be termed unreasonable as contemplated in the Thirteenth Fundamental Right.</u>

13. In the absence of the required per-mission of the Deputy Commissioner the kabala which was presented before the District Registrar, Dacca on 2-9-64 for registration, could not be admitted to registration, and the Registrar kept the document pending. Defendant No. 2 then wrote a letter dated 18-6-65 (Exhibit C) addressed to the Secretary, Law (Judicial) Department, Government of East Pakistan, requesting him to direct the District Registrar, Dacca to register the kabala on the ground that Ordinance 1 of 1964 was not applicable to his kabala dated 7-2-1964 as it had been executed before the Ordinance came into force. The Law (Judicial) Department, by its letter No. 443-Judi, dated 3-9-1965 (Exhibit D) wrote to the District Registrar that "Government have no objection to the registration of these deeds provided all other formalities are observed by the party concerned". On receipt of this letter, the District Registrar registered the kabala on 8-9-1965. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of these facts found that the letter from the Law (Judicial) Department of the Government of East Pakistan could not be treated as the permission of the Deputy Commissioner as provided under section 4 of Ordinance I of. 1964, and, as such, the permission not having been granted by the competent authority, the kabala was not a valid document. The learned Subordinate Judge also noticed that the letter dated 3-9-1965 (Exhibit D) from the Law (Judicial) Department does not show that it really gave any permission as contemplated in the Ordinance, because it merely indicated that the Government had no objection to the registration of the sale-deed. This clearance to the registration of the sale-deed could not be treated as the prior permission as contemplated in section 4 of the Ordinance,

The trial Court took the correct view in respect of the letter from the Secretary, Law (Judicial) Department that it did not serve the purpose of the prior permission from the competent authority. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, however, did not consider it necessary to enter into discussion on this aspect of the case. Obviously they being of the view that declaration in Chittaranjan Sutar's case totally removed the requirement of production of prior permission from the competent authority reached the conclusion that validity of the sale-deed in, the absence of the necessary permission, was not lost. The learned Judges only examined whether there was any re-enactment of the sections declared ultra vires the Constitution when the constitutional impediment was removed by the suspension of the Fundamental Rights by the Emergency proclaimed on September 6, 1965. According to the learned Judges there was no re-enactment of the sections struck down by the Special Bench in the case of Chittaranjan Sutar. In this respect also the learned Judges were in error: Re-enactment of sections 4 and 6 was not necessary, because, firstly, in view of the order of the Supreme Court staying the operation of the judgment; and secondly, section 4 (original) becoming operative with the declaration of section 4 (new) as void. The following facts will clarify the position. Judgment was delivered in Chittaranjan Sutar's case on July 1, 1965 and a certificated appeal was filed by the Government in the Supreme Court and stay of operation of the said judgment was granted by the Supreme Court on July 3, 1965. Emergency suspending the Fundamental Rights was proclaimed on September 6, 1965. By East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) (Second Amendment) Ordinance, 1965 life of the Ordinance I of 1964 was extended upto June 30, 1966, By the East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) (Amendment) Act, 1966 life of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 was extended upto March 31, 1967. By East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1967 life of the Ordinance No. I of 1964 was extended upto March 31, 1968 Section 4 of the Ordinance I of 1964 was treated as operative in spite of the decision in Chittaranjan Sutar's case. By the East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) (Second Amendment) Ordinance 1967 which was published in the Gazette on December 22, 1967, section 4 of Ordinance No I of 1964 was amended. Amendment was as follows:

"4. Amendment of section 4 of E,P.Ord. No. I of 1964.—In the said Ordinance, in section 4,—

(i) in sub-section (4), the full-stop at the end shall be omitted, and thereafter the words and full-stop "within three months in the case of the Sub-Divisional Officer or within four months in the case of the Deputy Commissioner, from the date of the filing of the application" shall be added:

(ii) in sub-section (5)---

(a) after the word and comma "forwarded," the words and comma "within three months from the date of filing," shall be inserted ; and

(b) after the word "concerned" at the end, the words, "who shall dispose of the applications within three months from the date of their receipts" shall be added;

(iii) after sub-section (8), the following new sub-sections shall be added, namely

"(9) An appeal under clause (a) of sub-sections (8) shall be disposed of within two months, and an appeal under clause (b) or clause (c) of the said sub-section shall be disposed of within three months from the date of filing the appeal.

(10) Where an application is not disposed of within the period as specified in sub-section (4) or sub-section (5), or an appeal is not disposed of within the period as specified in sub-section (9) the authority concerned shall record, in writing, a good and valid reason there-of" ; and

(iv) the Explanation thereto shall re-numbered as Explanation 1 and after the Explanation so numbered the following new Explanation shall be added, namely:-

"Explanation 2--- In this section, the expression, 'the Deputy Commissioner' shall include Additional Deputy Commissioner and Joint Deputy Commissioner."

By East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1968, life of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 was extended upto March 31, 1969.

14. From the legislative actions taken in extending life of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 from time to time and also amending section 4, it is obvious that the Legislature treated section 4 of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 as very much in existence and operative.

<u>15. The learned Judges merely stated the fact that the Government of East Pakistan preferred an appeal against the judgment of the Special Bench in the case of Chittaranjan Sutar and obtained an order of ad interim stay on July 3, 1965 from the Supreme Court of Pakistan; and during continuance of the order staying operation of the judgment under appeal, Ordinance 1 of 1964 expired on March 31, 1969. From the above statement of fact it does not appear that the learned Judges took into consideration about the effect of the order staying operation of the judgment and order of the Special Bench in Chittaranjan Sutar's case on section 4 of the Ordinance. There is also no consideration about the effect of the certificate granted by the Special Bench under Article 58 of the Constitution of 1962. In view of the certificate the declaration of the Special Bench was made subject to the result of the appeal filed by the Government of East Pakistan in the Supreme Court of Pakistan. I am fully conscious that in view the withdrawal of the appeal by the Government the stay came to an end, and the judgment in Chittaranjan Sutar's case became operative on June 10, 1970. But withdrawal of the appeal did not have any bearing on requirement of production of prior permission from the competent authority before a sale deed executed by a member of the minority community could be admitted for registration. In Chittaranjan Sutar's case declaration on the question of validity of sections 4 and 6 of Ordinance 1 of 1964 was made as under:</u>

<u>"As however, we have found that the provisions of section 4 and 6 cannot be said to have imposed reasonable restrictions within the meaning of the Thirteenth Fundamental Right, those provisions are liable to be declared void, and in that sense they are also discriminatory so far as the Fifteenth Fundamental Right is concerned as section 6A cannot exist independently of section 4 and 6 that also falls."</u>

The learned Judges of the Special Bench concluded the judgment saying that "regard being had to findings above, this Rule is made absolute and it is declared that the order passed by the Respondent No. 3 refusing to accept for registration of the petitioners kabala dated 12th September, 1964 has been made without lawful authority and is as such of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to cancel the said order of refusal and register the kabala if otherwise in order in accordance with the provisions of the Registration Act, 1908. Then on the prayer on behalf of the Government of East Pakistan for a certificate under Article 58 certified that the case involves substantial questions of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution"

16. In view of the certificate granted by the Special Bench under Article 58 of the Constitution; and the order of the Supreme Court staying operation of the judgment and order of the Special Bench. I find it difficult to appreciate the view taken by the learned Judges of the High Court Division that section 4 having been declared ultra vires of the Constitution, the requirement of production of prior permission from the competent authority was no longer required, and in the absence of such requirement of Law validity of the impugned kabala was not lost.

<u>17. In my opinion finality of the judgment of the Special Bench in Chittaranjan Sutar's case was subject to the decision in the appeal preferred by the Government of East Pakistan on the basis of the certificate granted by the Special Bench under Article 58 of the Constitution. Beside that operation of the judgment and order of the Special Bench having been stayed by the Supreme Court on July 3, 1965, the declaration made in the judgment became ineffective. Consequently sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance continued to be operative.</u>

<u>18. Since section 4 as substituted by Ordinance X of 1964 was declared ultra vires the Constitution, and by operation of sub-article (2) of Article 6 of the Constitution it was void ab initio meaning it was non est, it means that section 4 (new) never came in-to existence. Such declaration obliterates the provision of law from the statute, as if it was never incorporated in the statute book. This state in the statute brings in another consequence, that is the provision of law which was repealed or substituted by the statutory provision declared ultra vires, automatically became revived. In the instant case as stated above section 4 (new) substituted section 4 (old), and section 4 (new) having been declared ultra vires of the Constitution being in conflict with the Fundamental Right; it became void ab initio. Meaning that section 4 (new) was no nest, as if it never came into existence A valid law cannot be substituted or repealed by an invalid unconstitutional law. But then what will happen on such declaration. The section of the law being ultra vires of the Constitution in meaning it was never incorporated in the statute book and the existing section or the law remained unaffected. In that process of operation of law section 4 (old) remained unaffected in the statute and it continued to be operative Principles of sound interpretation of statute does not contemplate a legal vacuum in the statute, and thereby making the statute unworkable. This view gets supports from Crawford: Construction of Statutes, paragraph 124. According to this authority if the amendatory statute is wholly void, the statute sought to be amended is not affected but remains in force. The paragraph reads as under:</u>

<u>"24. Effect of Invalid Amendments, Generally.—Of course, if the amendatory statute is wholly void, the statute sought to be amended is not affected but remains in force. It is as inoperative as if it had never been enacted; or the Act sought to be amended is, at least, reinstated in its effectiveness upon the established invalidity of the amendment."</u>

<u>Similar view expressed in Frost v. State Corporation Commission, (1929) 278 U.S. 515 has been referred to at page 592 of N.S.</u>

<u>Bindwa: Interpretation of Statutes (Sixth Edition). If the amending Act is ultra vires, the statute sought to be amended remains in operation, On the topic of Effect of invalidity of Amendment on Original Act, the said author stated the law as follows:—</u>

<u>"The rule that the invalidity of an amendment does not affect the original Act applies whether the amendment stands by itself as an independent enactment, or is incorporated in the setting of the original Act by a provision that the Act 'shall read as follows' ".</u>

<u>The author further stated as follows:</u>

<u>"When an amendatory exception to a statute proves unconstitutional, the original statute stands wholly unaffected."</u>

<u>19. Let me examine this question from another aspect: What is the effect on a statute repealed by an invalid Act. The following statement of Crawford: Statutory construction, paragraph 320, page 652 reads as under :—</u>

<u>"In order for repealing Act to be effective, it may be stated as a general rule, that it must be constitutional and valid, since a void or ineffective Act obviously cannot operate to abrogate a valid existing one."</u>

<u>I do not find any authority in support of the proposition that once a statute or provision in a statute is repealed by an Act which is subsequently found invalid, the statute or provision of law still remains repealed by implication. On this question Crawford states—'"Yet, the authorities seem generally to support the view that there will be no repeal by implication, where the repealing Act is invalid, even though the Act expressly states that it repeals all laws or parts of laws inconsistent therewith. After all, it is obvious that where the repealing Act is invalid there is nothing with which the existing law can be inconsistent and thereby repeat by implication." It has been indicated above that section 4 (new) introduced some restrictions on the transfer of immovable property by members of the minority community, which was found by the Special Bench as unreasonable and thus contravening Thirteenth Fundamental Right. Section 4 (original) is harmless, and there is nothing in the section to be in conflict with the Fundamental Rights. Section 4 (new) has been rightly found by the Special Bench to have no relation to the object of the legislation that is, Ordinance 1 of 1964 as promulgated on 12-2-1964, and it was in excess of the object, and the prevailing circumstances did not warrant the restriction. It has been noted above that section 4 was substituted by Ordinance X of 1964 on 10-10-1964 when communal tension completely subsided. It is also a recognized rule of construction that where a later statue which imposes a burden or condition is found to be ultra vires, the original enactment will, in the absence of indication of a contrary intention as it stood before additions or alterations, would be revived.</u>

<u>20. On consideration of the authorities referred to above it appears that there is no controversy on the question that when a mandatory provision proves unconstitutional, the amended provision stands wholly unaffected. That being the position section 4 as obtaining in Ordinance 1 of 1964 before its substitution by Ordinance X of 1064 remained unaffected, if section 4 (old) continued to be operative.</u>

<u>21. Considering the case from either of the two aspects that is, section 4 (new) as substituted continued to be operative in view of the order of the Supreme Court staying operation of the judgment and order of the Special Bench or by operation and order of the Special Bench or by operation of the rule of construction section 4 (old) remaining unaffected by the purported substitution by Ordinance X of 1994 which was unconstitutional. Consequently the provision of law requiring production of prior permission from the competent authority before the impugned sale-deed could be admitted for registration was very much in operation when the sale deed was registered. The High Court Division was completely in error in taking the view that in the absence of such requirement validity of the impugned sale-deed was not lost.</u>

22. According to defendant No. 2 an agreement of sale of properties was executed by the plaintiffs on 28-12-63, that is, only a few days before the communal riots started, and the sale-deed was executed by the plaintiffs on 9-2-64. Since possession of the plaintiffs in their properties was not disturbed and existence of the sale-deed became known to the plaintiffs much later only from the notices dated 2-9-1964 received by them from the office of the District Sub-Registrar, the plaintiffs could not seek relief under section 2 of the Ordinance after the kabala was registered, and they had to institute suit for cancellation of the kabala, on declaration that it was fraudulent and null and void. From the evidence led by the plaintiffs it appears that in Magh 1370 B.S. their village and neighboring villages were affected by communal riots and out of fear of their lives the plaintiffs came to Tikatuli in the Dacca City and they were given shelter in a camp by the Government at Qamrun Nessa Girls High School where they stayed for 13/14 days, and thereafter they returned to their village by trucks arranged by the Government and they reconstructed their burnt down houses. Then about 1½ months later defendant No. 1 went to their village and advised them to leave for India as there were chances of fresh riots. He asked them to hand over their property documents whit would be kept in the office of the Indian Deputy High Commissioner at Dacca. They were told that these documents would be necessary to protect their properties. He also stated that those would be necessary to enable the plaintiffs to get money, land, cattle, etc. in India. The plaintiffs being affected by riots were already panicky; and as such they being placed in such a situation easily responded to the proposal of defendant No. 1, They acted upon his advice, and brought their document of title of their respective property to defendant No. 1 at his residence in Warri and handed over the same to him. Defendant No. 1 asked the plaintiffs to put their signatures or thumb impression on some blank papers and stamp papers produced by him. He told them those would be used for making a Power of Attorney. According to the instruction defendant No. 1 the plaintiffs jointly put signatures and thumb impressions on the blank papers and blank stamp papers. Plaintiffs put their signatures or thumb impression on about 40 or 50 such papers as directed by defendant No. 1. The plaintiffs were given some slips by defendant No. 1 saying that the slips would help them .in obtaining migration certificate from the office of the Indian High Commissioner. It is also in the evidence that thereafter most of the plaintiffs left for India after obtaining migration certificates, but they returned within a period of 2/3 months completely disillusioned as they did not get any help there. They approached defendant No. 1 and demanded return of their documents and papers but on different pretexts he avoided returning the papers, saying that those had been deposited in the office of the Indian High Commissioner and ultimately defendant No. 1 told them that the documents could not be returned to them, because, they had sold their lands to defendant No. 2. Then the plaintiffs approached defendant No. 2 and explained to him the entire story, but the latter told them that he had purchased the lands from defendant No.1 In the meantime the plaintiffs received notices dated 2-9-64 from the office of the District Sub-Registrar, Dacca asking them to appear before the Sub-Registrar on 8-12-1964 to admit execution of the sale-deeds in favour of defendant No. 2 for Rs. 14,900/- Some of them appeared before the Sub-Registrar and informed him that no such deed of transfer had been executed by them. The plaintiffs under registered post sent petitions to the Relief Commissioner of the Government of East Pakistan and the District Magistrate, Dacca explaining the circumstances how they had gone to India for a short period handing over their documents of property to defendant No. 1 jointly signing or putting thumb impressions on some blank papers and blank stamp papers produced by defendant No.1; and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 collusively created a sale-deed to grab their property and presented it for registration. They requested the District Magistrate and the Relief Commissioner not to issue any permission under section 4 of Ordinance 1 of 1964 as prayed for by defendant No. 2. The plaintiffs did not get any reply. In spite of their pro-test the sale deed was registered on 8-12-1964. After obtaining certified copy of the sale deed the plaintiffs instituted the suit. The sale-deed shows that the lands of the plaintiffs numbering as many as 22, having no community of interest, and lands appertaining to different khatians under different mouzas, were transferred by one document. Normally registration of such transfer of lands belonging to different persons, having no community of interest is not allowed. The sale-deed itself (Exhibit B) sufficiently indicates that it was executed either in an abnormal situation and it was not "in due Couse of business of the transferors" or it was the product of fraud and conspiracy committed upon the plaintiffs. The agreement for sale dated 28.12.1963 and the impugned kabala dated 7.2.1964, even if taken as genuine documents clearly show that those were executed during the period of commotion when the members of the minority community being affected by the communal riots were forced to leave their villages and take shelter in the Refugee Camps opened by the Government in the city. It is not disputed that the plaintiffs were affected by the civil disturbance and they had to leave their houses and take shelter in the different camps in the city of Dacca, and after some time when they returned to their village they found their houses demolished and burnt down ; and after reconstructing their huts they started living there, but apprehending fresh riots they left for India after obtaining migration certificates from the Indian Deputy High Commissioner's Office, and within a period of 2/3 months they returned to their village and started living in their respective house. There was no obstruction to their taking possession of their property. As the plaintiffs were in possession of the properties purported to have been transferred by the impugned kabala there was no necessity of their seeking help of the law until kabala was registered in spite of their protest. However, their case did not fall within the ambit of sections 2 and 5 of Ordinance 1 of 1964. In this background the plaintiffs took recourse to a proceeding in the civil court. It appears that the learned Judges of the High Court Division did not take into consideration this aspect of the case. It is true that the plaintiffs failed to prove conspiracy between the defendant Ganesh and Hammad, but the circumstances are strong enough to show that the transaction did not take place "in due course of business of transferors". The plaintiffs in the wake of communal commotion became victim of conspiracy engineered by the defendants. The learned Judges omitted to consider the relevant evidence merely saying that this is another improbability The learned Judges observed as follows:—

"Take another improbability, according to the plaintiffs Ganesh created documents in favour of different purchasers but the document shows otherwise. Ganesh is not the purchaser in the deed. It is Hammad. The plaintiffs are executants of the kabala. Why Hammad. an honorary Magistrate and literate person will give money to Ganesh of about R s. 15,000/- is beyond our imagination. There is nothing in the deed to indicate that Ganesh was ever authorised by the plaintiffs to receive that money or he had any part to play in the transaction. The plaint case is so inherently improbable that it breaks down at every step, specially in the face of a registered kabala that we find no reason to interfere with the finding of fact of the trial Court.

23. On carefully going through the evidence I find it difficult to appreciate the reasons given by the learned Judges for taking the view that the plaint case is inherently imprbable and the case is so weak that it cannot stand, and it breaks down at every step.

24. The learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Judges of the High Court Division did not find any wrong in the sale-deed, but it does not appear they considered the unusual features of the sale-deed, that is, it was executed by 18 persons in 8 groups, having no community of interest, purporting to sell their lands described in 8 schedules; and the price of different classes of land as admitted by defendant No. 2 to have been fixed at a "thika" rate. Consideration of this aspect was very much necessary, because, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the sale-deed appears to have been executed when abnormal situation was prevailing in the country, that is, in January 1964. They also failed to note that the lands belonging to different persons appertaining to different khatians and mouzas were transferred by one sale-deed which in practice is never done. Normally such a transfer deed is not accepted by the Registration office for registration. The allegation of complicity of defendant No, 1 Ganesh in arranging transfer of immovable properties by the members of the minority community, in the back round of communal tension which started by the end of 1963 and the riots that followed, cannot be lightly rejected, but the trial Court as well as the High Court Division without giving any consideration to the situation prevailing at the relevant time treated the impugned kabala, as if it is the product of voluntary transfer by the vendors in normal circumstances. There is another important aspect which missed the consideration of the trial Court and as well as of the High Court Division; it is the failure of defendant No. 2 to take possession of the property alleged to have been purchased by him on 7-2-1964 on payment of the full consideration, and the vendors' documents had already been handed over to him. Recitals in the kabala show that on that day the vendors delivered possession of the properties purchased by him. It is not disputed that the plaintiffs left for India after obtaining certificates, and they were not expected to return to Pakistan. However, they returned after 2½-3 months. They left for India towards the last part or Baisakh or first part of Jaistha and returned in Bbadra.

25. The sale-deed was presented for registration on 2-9-1964 but it was not registered in the absence of necessary permission from the Deputy Commissioner as provided under section 4 of the Ordinance I of 1964, and it was kept pending. The defendant No. 2 wrote a letter (Exhibit C) to the Secretary, Law (Judicial) Department on 18-6-65 requesting him to direct the District Registrar to register the kabala on the ground that the Ordinance I of 1964 was not applicable to his kabala which is dated 7.2.1964, that is, before the Ordinance came into force. After clearance was given by the Law (Judicial) Department by the memo, dated 3-9-65 (Exhibit D) the kabala was registered on 8-9-1965. According to the learned Judges, there was no delay in presentation of the kabala on 2-9-64, although it was long after the alleged execution of kabala on 7-2-64. Obviously, the finding is based on the erroneous view that it was presented for registration on 2-9-64 after defendant No. 2 had obtained permission as required under the Ordinance I of 1964, although as stated above the purported clearance was given on 3-9-65. The evidence led by the plaintiffs fully supports the important features indicated above. In my opinion the evidence led by the plaintiffs and the defendants do not warrant the findings on the basis of which the suit has been dismissed.

26. P.W. 1 Tarani Chandra Das (plaintiff No. 4) deposed for plaintiffs 4. 8, 12, 7 (a) & 7 (b) P.W. 2 Nitya Nanda (plaintiff No. 1) deposed for plaintiffs 1-3 and 5, P.W. 3 Trinnath Das (plaintiff No. I()) deposed for plaintiffs 9-11 and 19 ; and P.W. 4 Kali Pada Das (plaintiff No. 14) deposed for plaintiffs 14 to 18. They uniformly stated that in Magh 1370 B.S. their locality was affected by communal riots; they left their village with their essential belongings and took shelter in different relief camps opened by the Government the City of Dacca, and after staying there for 13/t4 days they were taken back to their village by Government arranged trucks. They found their houses completely burnt down by the rioters. They reconstructed their houses and started living there. Towards the end of Falgoon or beginning of Chaitra defendant No. 1 came to their locality and told them that he had been sent by the Indian High Commission Office to tell the villagers that there was possibility of fresh communal riots and so, they should go to India to save their lives; and they would be rehabilitated there by the Government of India. Defendant No. 1 also told them that they should leave their documents of property with him at his residence in Warri, in the Dacca city, so that he could protect their properties and also arrange lands for them in India through Indian High Commission Office. Defendant No. 1 visited the locality on 3/4 days. So, towards the end of Chaitra or beginning of Baisakh they 15/20 of the plaintiffs went to the residence of defendant No. 1 at Warri in Dacca and handed over their documents to him, and he took their signatures and thumb impressions on blank papers and stamps. Defendant No. 1 then gave them slips, on the basis of which they obtained migration certificates from the Indian High Commission Office at Kakrail. The Migration Officer was a brother of defendant No. 1 and used to reside at his house in Warri. The plaintiffs left for India, towards the end of Jaistha and after 2/2½ months they returned from India in Bhadra because they did not get any help there as they had been assured. After returning to their homes they started living there. The plaintiffs received notices (Exhibit 1 series) from the Sub-Registry Office, Dacca. Some of the plaintiffs saw the Sub-Registrar and informed him that they had not executed any Kabala in favour of defendant No. 2. The plaintiffs approached defendant No. 1 and demanded back documents and signed papers, but defendant No. 1 did not return their papers. On the other hand, he offered them some money which they refused, They also sent petitions (copies-Exhibit 2 series) by registered post with acknowledgment receipts (Exhibit 3 series) to the Relief Commissioner and the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca. They also met defendant No. 2 and narrated every-thing to him. Defendant No. 2 told them that defendant No. 1 had taken money from him and given the documents in his favour. Thereafter the suit was filed. The plaintiffs categorically denied that they took any consideration money and executed the kabala in favour of defendant No. 1 on 7-2-1964. They also denied that the kabala was written by Monindra at their dictation or that Dhirendra, son of plaintiff No. I, attested in their presence. They further stated that Dhirendra's signature was also taken on blank papers.

27. In respect of the main events, on the whole, the evidence of P.Ws. 1, 2, 3 and 4 is uniform but with some discrepancies. P.W. 5 Niranjan Sarkar is a resident of the same village of the plaintiffs and he knows them. He stated that towards the end of Magh, 1370. B.S. after the riots when the villagers returned, defendant No. 1 visited their village several times and the witness saw him talking with some of the plaintiffs. In his presence defendant No. 1 told the plaintiffs that since there was apprehension of fresh riots in the locality, they should go to India where they would be rehabilitated with land, cattle, etc. by the Government. of India; and that he would obtain migration certificates for them. One day some of the plaintiffs went to the chamber of defendant No. 1 at Warri, but he did not accompany them. On the following day plaintiff Trinath went to defendant is house and he accompanied him and there saw the plaintiffs giving signatures and thumb impressions on blank papers. The witness also brought some papers but he did not give the papers to defendant No. 1 as done by the plaintiffs. P.W. 6 Radha Raman Roy who comes from the neighboring village which is at a distance of the mile from the village of the plaintiffs. He knows the plaintiffs. He also knows defendant No. 1 since after the riots of Pous/Magh 1370 B.S. He used to visit the plaintiff's village and used to go to the house of Tarani (P.W. 1). He saw defendant No. 1 visiting Tarani's house on 3 days. He also went to the house of Tarani to hear what defendant No. 1 said. Defendant No. 1 said that they should all leave for India because of the riots and that documents and signed blank papers should be left with him so that he could make necessary arrangements regarding law etc. in India. He stated that plaintiff Tarani informed him that defendant No. 1 would come to his house and he should be present there. He saw defendant No. 1 for the first time in the house of Tarani. He saw him on 3 days at Tarani's house.

28. In support of the defendant's case 5 witnesses were examined which included defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2. D.W. 1 (defendant No. 2) stated that on 28-12-73 the plaintiffs executed a bainama in his favour. It was written by Manindra Chandra Das, and some of the executants put signatures and some put their thumb impressions. On that day out of the agreed consideration of Rs. 14,900/-, he paid Rs. 13,100/-. The document was executed at his residence at 12/1, Nasiruddin Sardar Lane, Dacca. There-after on 7-2-64 the plaintiffs executed a kabala deed in his favour which was written by the same scribe Manindra Chandra Das and all the executants signed except Sashi Mohan and Gurakhanath and Sabitri Sundari who put their thumb impression and their names were written by scribe Manindra Chandra Das. D W. 2 Abdul Hafiz stated that he knows the plaintiffs who are residents of his adjacent village and he knows defendant No. 2. Plaintiffs village is 1 mile from his village. He was an attesting witness in the kabala (Exhibit B). The kabala was read over to the executants and then they put their signatures and thumb impressions. He saw defendant No. 2 giving Rs. 1800/- in the hand of Nityananda (plaintiff No. 1). There were 4/5 attesting witnesses present at the time of execution. He knows the deed writer Montazuddin (since deceased) who also attested the document. He also stated that Alek Chand, deed-writer was attesting witness. D.W.3 Ashutosh Das stated that he knows the plaintiffs who are residents of his adjacent village. He knows defendant No. 2 for the last 4 years. He was an attesting witness in the bainapatra in Exhibit 1. It was also executed in his presence. The scribe Manindra read over the document to the executants. He saw payment of Rs. 13,100/- by defendant No. 2 in the hand of plaintiff Tarani. D.W. 4 Ganesh Chandra Chakra borty (defendant No. 1) stated that he did not know the plaintiffs or defendant No. 2 before getting summons of this suit. He stated that he had no brother who was Migration Officer in the Indian Deputy High Commission Office at Dacca. He totally denied that after riots of 1964 he advised the plaintiffs to migrate to India or that he took documents or signatures from them by stating that he will arrange for protection or exchange of their property. He totally denied that he created documents in favour of defendant No. 2 in collusion with him or that he created bainapatra and false kabala out of blank stamps and papers, or that he realised money from defendant. No. 2 and misappropriated it, or that he went with defendant No. 2 to take possession of the suit lands. This witness, however, stated that they are 3 brothers, and Naresh Chakraborty is his full younger brother, but curiously enough he did not know if Naresh Chakraborty was an employee in the Indian Deputy High Commission office in Dacca. He could not say even whether Naresh was an employee of Government of India posted in Dacca. D. W. 5 Braja Ballav Biswas stated that he knows the plaintiffs and also knows defendant No. 2, He was present during the talk of sale of lands held between plaintiffs and defendant No. 2. He was present on 2 such days at the residence of defendant No. 2 where he was brought by plaintiffs Joydeb, Kalipada Aswani and Biswanath. He stated that after negotiation between defendant No. 2 and the plaintiffs on 2/3 days the price of the land was "thika-settled" at Rs. 14,900/- only. Plaintiff 1 is his taloi.

29. The High Court Division disbelieved the evidence led by the plaintiffs on the ground that "the plaint case is so inherently improbable that it breaks down at every step, specially in the face of a registered kabala. From judgment it appears that the improbabilities as pointed out by the learned Judges in the evidence led by the plaintiffs is that both the bainapatra and the impugned kabala were written by Manindra Chandra Das, who is a son-in-law of Tarani; and, according to the learned Judges, a son-in-law could not be expected to be a party in the conspiracy of the defendants to deprive the plaintiffs of their hearth and home. In making this re-mark the learned Judges overlooked the evidence brought out in cross-examination that Manindra was married with a daughter of Tarani long after the alleged execution of kabala on 7.2.74. Another improbability noticed by the learned Judges is that how such a big amount of money could be handed over by the defendant No. 2, "an honorary Magistrate and literate person" to defendant No. 1; and when under the kabala defendant No. 2 is the transferee, how defendant No. 1 could be said to have joined with defendant No. 2 to deprive the plaintiffs from their properties by illegal means. I fail to appreciate the logic of the reasoning. It is difficult to visualize the situation prevailing in December, 1963—January-February, 1964 in the then East Pakistan and if in the background of the situation then prevailing, the plaintiff's case is considered in that perspective, one would not find fault with the plaintiff's case as made out in the plaint and proved by evidence. With regard to the purchase of stamps for the bainapatra and the kabala the learned Judges noticed that the stamp papers were purchased by defendant No. 2 on 28.12.63 and 5.2.64 respectively, and these two days were mentioned in the application filed by defendant. No. 2 to the Judicial Secretary for permission for registration and that the application was filed on 18.6.65 long before the suit.

30.
