The judgment of the trial Court, as well as that of the High Court Division suffers from error of procedure also, in that the plaintiffs suit has been adjudicated treating it as an ordinary suit alleging fraud against the defendants, without taking into consideration as to whether the declaration sought for by the plaintiffs, in the context of the undisputed facts and circumstances as brought out by the evidence, it called for a decision in the light of section 4 of the Ordinance 1 of 1964, that is, to examine whether or not the impugned kabala was executed "in due course of business of the transferors". Even if it is accepted that the trial Court and the High Court Division arrived at the correct finding that the plaintiffs failed to establish fraud and conspiracy as alleged against the defendants, still their judgments fall short of the requirement of the law. In my opinion, in view of the pro-visions of the Ordinance 1 of 1964 which was promulgated to provide for speedy rehabilitation of persons affected by the civil disturbance in East Pakistan in January, 1964, and for the protection of the immovable properties of the members of minority communities, if it is found that the disputed transfer of immovable property has not been brought about "in due course of business of the transferors", but the abnormal situation prevailing in the country at the relevant time led the plaintiffs to execute the sale deed, a duty is cast upon the Court to adjudicate the dispute between the parties in the light of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and not as an ordinary suit alleging fraud.

31. If the evidence is considered in the context of the circumstances admittedly prevailing in December 1963-January 1964 in the wake of communal riots that took place, and the undisputed facts that the plaintiffs were affected by the communal disturbances in their locality and they had to leave their hearth and home and take shelter in the refugee camps in the city and their temporary migration to India and their returning back after a short stay there; defendant 2's failure to take possession of the properties and his failure to present the kabala for registration even after the plaintiffs returned from India and by one kabala more than twenty persons having no community of interest transferred their properties, it would appear that the evidence led by the plaintiffs cannot be brushed aside as wholly untrue, and, in my opinion, the evidence has sufficiently established the plaintiff's case that the transfer was not ‘‘in normal course of business". There might be some discrepancies in the evidence but the evidence read as a whole evokes credibility in the witnesses that they are not telling lies to support a false case, with a view to deprive defendant No. 2 from getting the property validly and lawfully purchased by him on the basis of a genuine deed of sale. Whatever weakness there may be in the evidence of the plaintiffs, the very fact that the kabala shows that the plaintiffs consisting of groups owning lands with houses in different mouz as and appertaining to different khatians, and having no common interest sold their lands by one kabala, and consideration was settled on the basis of "thika" price, is an important feature in the case, and this lends strong support to plaintiffs' case of fraud.

<u>32. In any view of the matter the plaintiffs suit must succeed, and it is not liable to be dismissed on the ground of paucity of evidence as remarked by the High Court Division. The suit must succeed, both on the ground that the impugned sale deed (Exhibit B) is not a valid instrument of sale, because it was registered in the absence of the required permission of the competent authority; and, secondly, on the ground that the sale is a product of conspiracy and fraud which could be easily perpetrated by the defendants taking advantage of the abnormal situation prevailing in the country. In the result the appeal is allowed with costs. Judgment and decree of the High Court Division are set aside and those of the trial Court are restored.</u>

<u>Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—I regret that I could not subscribe to she views expressed in the judgment of my learned brother Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.</u>

33. The plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration that certain blank papers signed by the plaintiffs were taken by the defendant No. 1, Ganesh Chandra Chakraborty and converted them into some documents of title, namely, kabalas in favour of different persons, should be declared null and void and for other reliefs by way of injunction restraining the defendants from entering into the suit land and disturbing with the possession of the plaintiffs thereon and also for directing the defendants to deliver blank stamps and plain papers, etc. The plaintiffs are schedule caste and members of the minority community. During the communal disturbance in or around Dacca City in January, 1964 the huts and houses in village Kazirgaon within P S. Tejgaon were burnt out and valuable articles were looted and the plaintiffs took shelter elsewhere to save their lives. After sometime they went back to their village when defendant No. 1, Ganesh Chandra Chakraborty appeared there posing himself as a representative of the Indian High Commission in Dacca and advised them to migrate to India. He asked them to sign on some stamp and blank papers apparently for the protection of their property. The plaintiffs gave him all their title deeds, together with stamp and blank papers totalling 15 in numbers signed or thumb impressed by them, and thereafter some of them left for India but returned after 3/4 months to their said village. Thereafter the plaintiff demanded back all their documents and papers from the defendant No. 1 who failed to do so. Some day later the plaintiffs got notices from the District Registrar, Dacca directing them to come and admit registration of kabala in favour of defendant No. 2, Md. Hammad. Some of the plaintiffs appeared and denied their execution of the kabala. Defendant No. I gave out that those papers have been converted into kabalas in favour of different persons on they will be paid in cash @ Tk. 100/- per bigha. Hence they filed the suit.

34. The defendants contested the suit. Defendant No. 1 denied the plaintiffs case and stated that he had nothing to do with the allegations made by the plaintiffs against him. Defendant No. 2 took the stand that the plaintiffs 1-17, of their own accord entered into an agreement on 28-12-63 for sale of a portion of the suit property with him (Ext-A.) and then executed a kabala for the same in his favour on 7-2-64 for adequate consideration on their free will. He got the required per-mission under Ordinance No. I of 1964 and the kabala was presented for registration on 2-9-64.

35. The trial Court held that the permission was not given by the proper authority as required under Ordinance No. I of 1964. On that ground it was 'held that the registration of the said deed was void. On merits the trial Court found that the plaintiffs have failed to implicate Ganesh in any fraudulent act and the kabaia admitted to be genuine and properly executed for consideration. Accordingly, the suit was decreed in. part and it w was declared that the kabala was null and void.

Defendant No. 2, Md. Hammad preferred First Appeal being No. 38 of 1965 and a Division Bench of the High Court Division allowed the appeal whereby the decision of the trial Court was set aside and the suit was dismissed with costs.

36. Leave was granted to consider whether proper permission was obtained from the appropriate authority under the Disturbed Persons Rehabilitation Ordinance, 1964 for registration of the sale deed in question or whether permission for registration was at all necessary in view of the decision of the Dacca High Court in Chittaranjan Sutar's case.

37. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury appearing for the appellants contended that the Chittaranjan Sutar's case has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case. Mr. Chowdhury submitted that the bainapatra which was executed, on 28-12-63 (Ext. A) was not mentioned in the sale deed nor was it mentioned in the application before the Judicial Secretary dated 18.6.65 for directing the Registrar to register the document It is to be noted that the Sub-Registrar refused to register the kabala. The Disturbed Persons Rehabilitation Ordinance, 1964 was promulgated on the 12th February, 1964 for the protection of the immovable property of the minority community and for speedy rehabilitation of the persons affected by the disturbance in January, 1964. The Governor was satisfied that circumstances existed which required this legislation.

38. The Ordinance contains only 8 sections. Section 1 gives a short title of commencement and duration; section 2 provides for restoration of possession; section 3 provides for an appeal; section 4 deals with restriction of transfer; section 5 provides for power of cancellation of instrument section 6 gives finality of orders section 6(a) provides for penalty; section 7 gives indemnity ; section 7(a) to (b) provide for conferment of certain powers on the Officers and section 8 deals with the power to make rules. Section 5 is in the following terms:—

"5. (1) If, on an enquiry under section 2, any Magistrate or other officer specially empowered under that section is satisfied that any person is in possession of any house, hut, structure or land under an instrument registered under the Registration Act, 1908, (Act XVI of 1908), within a period from the 1st January, 1964, to the date of commencement of this Ordinance, obtained under coercion, threat, intimidation, under influence, misrepresentation or fraud he shall refer, or the transferor may apply, to the District Judge within thirty days of the completion of the enquiry, for cancellation of the instrument.

(2) The District Judge shall, after notice to the transferee and hearing the parties, pass an order within a month of the receipt of reference or application cancelling the instrument and ordering restoration of possession to the person who is proved to his satisfaction to have been in possession thereof before the civil disturbance of January, 1964.

Provided that the District Judge may extend the time for good and valid reason to be recorded in writing

(3) When the person found to be in possession of any such property before the civil disturbance of January, 1964, is not traceable, the District Judge may order the property to be put under the management of the Evacuee Property Management Committee under section 3 of the East Bengal Evacuees (Administration of Immovable Property) Act, 1951 or under the management of such authority as may be specified by the Provincial Government in accordance with the rules made in this behalf".

39. Section 2 of the Ordinance deals with restoration of possession when a member of a minority community had to leave on ac-count of civil disturbance in January, 1964 the authority have been given summary power and effect in person and he can also direct restoration of possession to any person en-titled to the same. Reading of section 5 along with section 2 the conclusion to be arrived at that where any person is in possession of a house or land, etc. under an instrument registered between the 1st January, 1964 and 12th February, 1964, the Magistrate if he is satisfied that it was obtained by coercion or fraud, etc., shall refer the case to the District Judge for cancellation of the instrument. The transferor also has been given the same right but both the reference as well as the application shall have to be made with-in 30 days of the completion of the enquiry under section 2. It is unfortunate that the Courts below have taken completely different view of the law in its application in the facts and circumstances of the case. Sufficient evidence has been given that the plaintiffs were the members of the minority community and they were terrorised and the defendant No. 1 Ganesh had been posing himself as an agent and a savior and this man manipulated the blank cartridges and papers including the deeds of the plaintiffs.

<u>40. The defendant's own case was that a baina was made on 26-12-63 just 3 days before the legislative recognition was give to the civil disturbance which was obtaining in the country. It does not need much imagination that the land in or around Dacca City gradually appreciated in value and at time the speculative purchasers availed of the opportunity when such an advantage was clearly available, namely, communal commotion which would prompt he members of the minority community to sell their property even at a very low price. Precisely that thing has happened here. I stated further that Ganesh advised them to give him all their documents to be kept in the Indian High Commission. This evidence fully fits in the plaintiffs' case that out of fear they handed over those title deeds to Ganesh who arrived at their village after one and a half month of their return from Dacca city. These papers were later converted into title deeds of Hammad. Exhibit (B) dated 9-2-64 is clearly hit by section 5 of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. But, unfortunately, the Courts below have not scrutinized the things, nor the plaintiffs filed a petition before the District Judge for cancelling the documents which could be done within 30 days from the date of enquiry as contemplated in section 2. Instead, they filed the suit for declaration that the document is void. In that suit evidence was given by both the parties and the trial Court concluded that the plaintiffs' case on merit could not be proved but the document was void, inasmuch as it was registered without the permission of the Relief Commissioner as required by the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. Unfortunately the judgment of High Court Division also suffers from miss appreciation of evidence. Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—This appeal by special leave is from a judgment and decree dated 28-8-1974 of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 38 of 1969 reversing that of the Subordinate Judge and thereby dismissing the appellants suit for cancellation of a sale-deed dated 7th February, 1964, on a declaration that it is fraudulent, illegal and void.

44. Plaintiff-appellants are members of the minority community having permanent residence in village Mutually in the outskirts of Dacca City. In Magh, 1370 B.S. corresponding to January 1964, a communal riot broke out in and around Dacca, and their village was also a science of this riot and in consequence they took shelter in different places of the city including Qumrun Nessa Girl's High School and Jagannath College buildings. After about two weeks, when the riot subsided, they went back to their respective houses in the village. Sometime thereafter, one Ganesh Chandra Chakravarty, defendant No. 1, appeared in their village and posing as an agent of the Indian Deputy High Commissioner at Dacca advised them to migrate to India where they would be fully rehabilitated. He advised them to sign some stamp papers along with some blank cartridge papers which, he said, would be necessary for the purpose of their rehabilitation in India, and also to deliver title-deeds of their lands to him which would be deposited with the Indian Deputy High Commissioner for protection of their landed properties in their absence. Being thus assured and advised they signed about fifty stamp and blank papers and delivered them to Ganesh and thereafter most of them went to India. But after two or three months they come back from. India disappointed, and asked Ganesh to return those signed papers, but Ganesh after giving confusing replies and killing time, ultimately gave out that those papers had been converted into sale-deeds in favour of diverse person who could, however, pay the price of their land at the rate of Tk. 100/-per bigha. In December, 1964 one Hammad Ali, defendant No. 2, whom the appellants did not know, appeared in their village and told them that he had purchased their land under a kabala and asked for possession of the land. At about the same time they also received a notice from the Sub-Registrar's office to appear before him and admit the execution of any sale deed. They having realised that the blank papers had been fraudulently converted into a sale-deed filed the suit for cancellation of the deed as void and fraudulent.

45. The suit was contested by both Ganesh and Hammad. Defence of Ganesh was that of total denial of his connection with the transaction. Defence of Hammad was also denial of the allegation of fraud; his contention was that the plaintiffs had, of their own accord, entered into an agreement with him on 28th December, 1963, for the sale of their land and that in pursuance of the Agreement they executed the sale-deed on 7 February, 196 4, received full consideration thereof and left for India after delivering possession of the land to him. But on the promulgation of the Displaced Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964, (Ordinance 1 of 1964) which put restriction on transfer of land belonging to members of the monority community, the plaintiffs refused to register the sale-deed whereupon he got the sale-deed registered by obtaining per-mission from the competent authority, as required by the said Ordinance.

46. The trial court on consideration of evidence disbelieved the allegation of the plaintiffs that the sale-deed was got executed by fraud and misrepresentation but found it to be a genuine sale-deed duly executed by the plaintiffs selling their land to Defendant No. 2, Hammad, for consideration; the trial court did not find any collusion between defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2. But the trial court held that the sale- deed was not registered with the permission of the "competent authority" as required under section 4 of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and as such the sale-deed was invalid. On this ground the learned trial court decreed the suit and ordered for cancellation of the document. In appeal a Division Bench of the High Court Division concurred with the trial court's finding of facts that the sale-deed was a genuine document of transfer of land; but as to the validity of the sale-deed the High Court Division, relying on a decision of the erstwhile East Pakistan High Court in Chittaranjan Sutar's case, 17 D LR (DA) 451, held that the sale-deed was not bit by the Ordinance as the relevant provisions of the Ordinance, namely, sections 4 and 6 which required permission of the competent 'authority for registration of the sale-deed were ultra vires the Constitution of 1962 and that there having been no necessity for permission for registration, set aside the trial court's decree, allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit.

47. Leave was granted to consider two question. One is "whether proper permission was obtained from the appropriate authority under the Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964", for registration of the sale-deed in question, or whether "permission for registration was at all necessary in view of the declaration by the Dacca High Court in Chittaranjan Sutar's case (17 DLR 451) that "sections 4 and 6 of the aforesaid Ordinance were void ab initio being in conflict with the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by the Constitution of 1962"; the other question is whether, in view of the fact that the Fundamental Rights in Arts. 13 and 15 of the Constitution of 1962 were themselves suspended on declaration of Emergency from 6th September, 1965, sections 4 and 6 of this Ordinance revived and were in operation at the relevant time,

48. In the case Chittaranjan Sutar Vs. Secretary Judicial Dept.", 17 DLR 451, the vires of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964, particularly, Ss. 4 and 6 thereof came up for determination. This Ordinance was intended to provide for the speedy rehabilitation of members of the minority community affected by the civil disturbance in January, 1964 and for protection of their property.' Section 2 of the Ordinance provides for restoration of possession of properties of a member of the minority community by a Magistrate by summary eviction of persons "who may have occupied or taken possession in any manner whatsoever of any house, hut, structure on land which a member of the minority community has had to leave or has left on account of or in apprehension of, the civil disturbance in January, 1964". Section 5 provides that if any unauthorised possession as referred to in section 2 has been claimed under any instrument registered under the Registration Act within the period from January 1, 1964 to the date of commencement of this Ordinance i.e. 12th Feb,1964, the District Judge may cancel the instrument and direct restoration of possession to the person affected. Section 4 provides that no transfer of immovable property of a member of the minority community shall be valid unless it is made with prior permission of the competent authority such as the Deputy Commissioner of the district, if the area of land sought to be transferred does not exceed one acre. Sub-section (6) of sec. 4 requires permission of the competent authority for registration of an instrument of transfer of such property, Section 6 ousts court's jurisdiction to entertain certain suits relating to immovable property of a member of the minority community without permission from the Board of Revenue. Of these sections, section 4 (6) is relevant for our purpose. It is quoted below:

"No instrument for transfer of immovable property of a person who is a member of a minority community shall be admitted for registration unless it is accompanied by the permission of the competent authority."

49. In the case Chittaranjan Sutar, the petitioner was a member of the minority community. He executed a sale-deed on 12th September, 1964 transferring his land to another member of the same community and presented it to the Sub-Registrar who refused to accept it for registration on the ground that the sale-deed was not accompanied by permission of the competent authority as required in sub-section (6) of section 4 of Ordinance 1 of 1964. The petitioner challenged the Sub-Registrar's order in a writ petition before the High Court by raising the contention that Ss. 4 and 6 of the Ordinance were in conflict with the Fundamental Rights as to acquisition, holding and disposal of property, guaranteed by the Constitution of 1962 and as such no permission for registration of his sale-deed was required in the eye of law. A Special Bench of the High Court accepted this contention of the petitioner add declared Ss.4 and 6 of the Ordinance ultra-rides the Constitution of 1962, among others, with the following observation: Provisions of these sections place unreasonable restriction on a citizen's right to dispose of or acquire property and are violative of the Fundamental Right 13th and as such they are void and are also discriminatory tender Fundamental Right 15th."

The writ petition was therefore allowed, the impugned order of the Sub-Registrar was declared to be without lawful authority and he was directed to register the petitioner's sale-deed in accordance with the provisions of the Registration Act of 1908.

50. An appeal was preferred to the Supreme Court of Pakistan against the High Court's order under a certificate of fitness granted by the High Court and operation of the impugned under was stayed pending its disposal. But the appeal was withdrawn by the Government as the Ordinance itself expired in the meantime, and consequently the High Court’s order declaring Ss. 4 and 6 of the Ordinance ultra vires remained unaffected. In the instant case the High Court Division also examined this question but did not find anything to differ from the decision given in the Chittaranjan Sutar's case.

51. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, learned counsel for the appellants has contended that the decision as to interpretation of Ss. 4 and 6 as put by the erstwhile macca High Court and relied upon by the High Court Division is not correct in that sections 4 and 6, in his view, have put quite reasonable restriction on transfer of property of a weaker section of the citizens who badly needed the protection of law against transfer of their property in abnormal circumstances created by communal riot. Fundamental Right No. 13, he has pointed out, provides for reasonable restriction on transfer of property imposed by law. This Article is quoted –below:

Subject to any reasonable restriction imposed by law in the public interest, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property."

Article 15, it may be mentioned here, guarantees equality of all citizens before law.

<u>52. Mr. Chowdhury has further contended that the decision in the Chittaranjan Sutar's case even if it stood after the disposal of the appeal before the Pakistan Supreme Court is not binding upon this Appellate Division of Bangladesh Supreme Court and this Division may examine the question. There is no dispute that this Division may examine the question and arrive at a decision different from that which might have been given by the Supreme Court of Pakistan. Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 was promulgated in the public interest with a view to providing relief to the members of the minority community who had to leave their hearth and home in apprehension or on account of, the communal disturbance in January 1964. The learned Judges of the High Court, on careful examination of the various provisions of the Ordinance, found that the purpose of the Ordinance would be served by Ss. 2 and 5 which provide prompt relief in a summary manner and that the restriction on transfer of their property imposed by Ss. 4 and 6 was not necessary, particularly for an indefinite period for the realisation of its objective. The Ordinance was meant for a temporary period, upto December, 1964. But its life was extended from time to time till it expired in February, 1969 it is to be seen whether such a restriction on a citizen's property right was reasonable.</u>

<u>53. There is no hard and fast rule to determine the reasonableness of a legal restriction on any Fundamental Right but the reasonableness is to be judged with reference to prevailing circumstances, the evil sought to be remedied vis-a-vis the extent of the restriction and whether there is any check of the arbitrary exercise of power to impose the restriction. The Ordinance was intended to provide speedy rehabilitation of persons affected by the communal disturbance in January, 1964 and for the protection of their property during the disturbed period. But to impose a legal restriction on transfer of their property for an indefinite period extending over years cannot be said to be the objective of the Ordinance. Since Ss. 2 and 5 of the Ordinance could provide adequate remedy to the members of the minority community affected by the civil disturbance of January, 1964, legal restriction on transfer of their property as contemplated in Ss. 4 and 6 of the Ordinance are found to be unreasonable and as such these sections have been rightly declared ultra vices Article 13 and also Article 15 of the Constitution of 1962. We, therefore, find no reason to take a different view.</u>

<u>54. The next question is whether sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance which imposed restriction on the transfer of property revived when Fundamental Rights 13 and 15 were suspended during the Emergency declared on the 6th September, 1965. The answer is clearly in the negative. Ordinance 1 of 1964 is a post-constitutional legislation having been promulgated when Article 6(2) of the Constitution of 1962 was in operation. This Article provides that the State shall not make any law inconsistent with any fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution. Sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance which are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights 13 and 15 are "void" ab initio and as such these sections did not revive when the Fundamental Rights were suspended. Nor were these sections of the Ordinance re-enacted during the period when the Emergency continued. The position is different in the case of a law which is pre-constitutional, that is, a law which was promulgated when there was no constitutional prohibition as provided in Article 6 (2). A pre-constitutional law is contemplated in Article 6(1) of the Constitution. If this law comes in conflict with any Fundamental Right guaranteed by the Constitution, it will become void; it is not void ab-initio, and it will revive if the fundamental right is suspended and the constitutional prohibition is withdrawn. This principle of law is known as the "doctrine of eclipse". This doctrine is not applicable to Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. The Indian Supreme Court also held the similar view in "Mohendra Lal Jainl Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and other" AIR,1963- SC, 1019 where it has been held :</u>

<u>"The doctrine of eclipse would apply to Pre-Constitution laws which are governed by Art. 13</u>

<u>(1) and would not apply to post-Constitution laws which are governed by Art. 13(2).</u>

<u>" It may be mentioned that Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Indian Constitution correspond with Articles 6(1) and 6(2) of the Constitution of Pakistan. 1962. The High Court Division elaborately discussed this question and reviewing a number of decisions on the subject rightly rejected the contention that sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance get a new lease of life during the Emergency declared in September, 1965,</u>

Along with these stamp papers they said, they handed over their title deeds also to Ganesh. It is highly improbable that they would hand over their title-deeds to an unknown person and that also without any receipt. Again, Ganesh appeared in their village as they allege, not during the disturbances, but after one and half months, when they came back from the city and normalcy returned to their village. It is their case that some of them went to India but came back disappointed after two or three months which means in the month of May or June and demanded back their title deeds and signed stamp-papers from Ganesh. But what about those plaintiffs who did not go to India but remained all along in their houses; why did they not demand back their title-deeds and signed stamp-papers in the month of February but waited for the return of the other plaintiffs. If their signatures and thumb impressions had been procured by fraud and deception, they would not have hesitated to rush to the Police or Magistrate for immediate action under Criminal law.

59. Mr. K.A. Bakr, learned counsel for the respondent-transferee has submitted that when the Sub-Registrar refused to accept the sale-deed for registration the matter was enquired by the District Sub-Registrar who, after hearing the parties at length, registered the document on 8.9.64. Mr. Bakr has pointed out that Ganesh who allegedly committed a gigantic fraud in this case according to the plaintiffs, did get nothing as the sale-deed was executed in favour of a person with whom he got no relation whatever. Signatures and thumb impression on the sale-deed are admitted by the plaintiffs. It is for them to show that these signatures and thumb impressions were given under deception, inducement or misrepresentation of fact. But they have failed to discharge this onus. Both evidence and circumstances are heavily against them. The only thing that can be said in favour of the plaintiffs is that they executed the sale deed when the fear of fresh disturbances was not yet dispelled from their mind. But this fear or apprehension can hardly be a ground for assailing the transaction. Both the trial court and the first appellate court having taken into consideration all facts and circumstances of the case came to concurrent findings that the sale-deed, Ext-B, is a genuine document of transfer of land duly executed by the plaintiffs and that it was not procured by fraud, deception, undue influence or misrepresentation. The first appellate court, rightly observed in conclusion: "The plaint case is so inherently improbable that it breaks down at every step, specially in the face of a registered Kabala that we find no reason to interfere with the finding of fact of the trial court." This concurrent finding arrived at on due consideration of evidence is immune from interference. The contention of Mr. Chowdhury that the finding is perverse or is not based on due consideration of material points involved, has got no substance.

For the reasons given above we have no hesitation to hold that the sale-deed is genuine and duly executed for consideration.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

ORDER OF COURT

As the opinions in this appeal are equally divided, the judgment of the High Court Division is maintained. Consequently this appeal stands dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: This First Appeal is directed against the judgment and decree passed in Other Suit No. 70 of 1987 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong, decreeing the suit in favour of the plaintiff.

2. The defendant is the appellant before this court. Plaintiff-respondent instituted a suit for specific performance of contract alleging, inter alia that the plaintiff was the proprietor of Regal Housing, a Housing Project for commercial sale of built up houses and flats as well as sale of plots for residential housing. The defendant-appellant is a company incorporated in England and has been carrying on various business in Bangladesh. The defendant as per the paper advertisement as appearing in the Daily Azadi dated 23.2.87 called for tenders for the sale of 4'6291 acres of hilly land together with two one-storied buildings situated at Chatteswari Road, Chittagong, which is known as Tanneries Estate. The plaintiff became interested to purchase the aforesaid property and thereafter purchased tender form as well as terms and conditions of tender from the office of the defendant. The plaintiff submitted tender and offered Taka 2,87,00,000.00 and as per terms of the tender they deposited an earnest money of Taka 15 lakh vide a cheque dated 17.3.87. The offer of the plaintiff being highest was accepted by the defendant vide their letter dated 18th March, 1987. As per terms and conditions of sale supplied to the plaintiff with tender form the highest tenderer should be required to deposit 25% of the total tender-money within one month from the date of acceptance of the offer by the defendant. In accepting the offer of the plaintiff the defendant incorporated several terms and conditions in the letter of acceptance. As per terms and conditions of the tender the defendant as seller and the plaintiff as purchaser required to enter into an agreement for sale on receipt of the balance of 25% of the consideration money i.e. Taka 56,75,000.00. On receipt of the draft agreement the plaintiff had given some amendment in clauses 4, 6 and 12. But, the same were not accepted by the defendant. The plaintiff was always ready and willing to pay the balance of 25% of the tender price and even on 7.5.87 the plaintiff was ready to pay the same to the defendant. But the defendant did not accept it. The plaintiff fulfilled all the terms and conditions and as a result the defendant was bound to transfer the suit properties which were the subject matter of the auction sale.

3. Since there was a concluded contract in between the parties, the defendant was bound to execute and register the sale deed. As the defendant refused to execute and register the sale deed, the plaintiff was entitled to a decree. In the plaint the plaintiff made prayer to the effect that a decree be passed for specific performance of contract for sale of the scheduled property to the plaintiff on receipt of the balance consideration with direction to the defendant to execute and register the kabala in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of the balance consideration money within specified time failing which to execute and register the kabala through court on receipt of the balance consideration money. In prayer No. 2 an alternative decree was prayed for to the effect that a sum of Taka 2,15,00,000.00 in favour of the plaintiff against the defendant as compensation and refund of the earnest money with cost of the suit and interest at 20% per annum pendente lite till recovery.

4. On receipt of the copy of the plaint the defendant-appellant filed written statement in the court admitting the contract. Further, the defendant informed the court that this suit might be decreed in terms of the prayer of the suit for specific perfor-mance of the contract and balance consideration money should be given to the defendant in accordance with law. After this written statement was filed, the plaintiff filed an application for amendment of the plaint under Order VI rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure making a prayer that prayer-I be deleted. In prayer II the words" in the alternative" be deleted and the prayer II may be amended to the following effect that a decree for Taka 15 lakh be passed against the defendant being the earnest money illegally forfeited with cost of the suit. This amendment in the prayer portion only was allowed. Thereafter the defendant submitted written statement stating that as per terms and conditions of the agreement which are contained both in tender notice and tender form the plaintiff failed to fulfil the term by depositing 25% of the total value of the suit property within the extended time and since the plaintiff failed to fulfil the terms and conditions, the earnest money was forfeited according to the terms as contained in the tender notice itself.

5. Both the parties adduced both oral and documentary evidence and after considering the materials on record the learned Subordinate Judge passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff for a sum of Taka 15 lakh i.e. the earnest money which was given to the defendant at the time of submitting the tender. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant preferred this First Appeal.

6. Three issues were framed, namely:

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Is the plaintiff entitled to get decree for Taka 15 lakh from the defendant?

3. To what relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled to?

7. The plaintiff examined one witness and the defendant also examined one witness. Both the parties filed their respective papers and documents which were marked exhibits in the suit.

8. Plaintiff examined one witness, namely, Mesbahuddin Ahmed. In his deposition he stated that he seeing the paper advertisement purchased the tender form and terms and conditions at a sum of Taka 500.00. He offered Taka 2 crore and 87 lakh for purchase of the suit property and paid a sum of Taka 15 lakh as earnest money by pay order. He was required to pay 25% of the total price of the suit property within one month from the date of acceptance of the tender and time was extended for 20 days more to deposit the aforesaid 25% of the total consideration money. On 6.5.87 he went to the office of the defendant, but no understanding took place. He stated that in the tender form there was no clause for forfeiture. In cross-examination he stated that he saw the terms and conditions given in the newspaper. He was bound by the terms and conditions as given in the paper advertisement and tender form. It is not a fact that there was any term and condition that earnest money would be forfeited.

9. Defendant examined one witness as DW 1, According to the terms and conditions as given in the tender notice published in the newspaper the plaintiff submitted their tender with an earnest money of Taka 15 lakh. Since the offer of the plaintiff was the highest offer, it was accepted. He stated that within the stipulated time, the plaintiff failed to pay the 25% of the total consideration money and, as such, his earnest money was forfeited. In cross-examination he stated that there is nothing in the paper advertisement that the terms of the paper advertisement will be the terms and conditions of the form to be purchased from the office.

10. Tender notice published in the newspaper on 23.2.87 with several terms and conditions of tender is marked as Exhibit-1. In condition No. 20 of this tender notice it is stipulated that the intending purchaser will have to give a bank draft of Taka 15 lakh as earnest money by pay order with the tender form. In condition No.4 it is stipulated that within one month from the date of acceptance of the tender the purchaser shall have to pay 25% of the total consideration money and the terms and conditions of transactions would be settled by the seller for execution of the contract for sale, otherwise the earnest money would stand forfeited. Exhibit-3 is the tender form submitted by the plaintiff showing the offer of Taka 2 crore and 87 lakh. With this tender form he submitted a bank draft of Taka 15 lakh as earnest money. Exhibit- 4 is the terms and conditions which was given to the plaintiff with the tender form. In this Exhibit-4. condition No. 3 is similar to condition No. 2 of Exhibit-l i.e. provision of paying earnest money of Taka 15 lakh. Condition No. 4 speaks to the effect that the purchaser shall pay 25% of the total consideration money by bank draft or pay order and execute contract for sale of the suit property within one month from the date of acceptance of the offer. Terms and conditions will be prescribed by the seller.

11. Exhibit-2(a) is the letter dated 18th March, 1987 by which the seller accepted the tender of the plaintiff provisionally and directed the plaintiff to pay 25% of the total consideration money and terms of the contract for sale would be prescribed by the defendant on or before 18th or April, 1987. Exhibit-2(b) dated 9th of April. 1987 shows that the defendant accepted the offer of the plaintiff for a sum of Taka 2 crore and 87 lakh which was duly communicated to the plaintiff by the defendant vide letter dated 18.3.1987. By this letter the defendant also asked the plaintiff to deposit a sum of Taka 56,75,000.00 as the 25% of the consideration money as per terms of the tender bid. Defendant also asked the plaintiff to execute the contract by 18th of April, 1987 after making payment of the aforesaid amount. It is further stipulated that the earnest money of Taka 15 lakh would be adjusted with the price of the suit property. Exhibit-2(c) is a letter dated 16th of April, 1987 by which the plaintiff requested the defendant to extend the time for 20 days with effect from 18.4.87 i.e. upto 7th of May, 1987 for depositing of the aforesaid sum of Taka 56,75,000.00. By a letter dated 19.4.87 vide Exhibit-2(d) the defendant accepted the above request of the plaintiff and time for payment of the aforesaid sum was extended upto 10-00 AM of 7th May, 1987, but all other terms and conditions for sale would remain unchanged. Exhibit-2(e) dated 30.4.87 shows that the plaintiff requested the defendant to give a copy of the proposed agreement for sale. Exhibit-2 dated 3.5.87 shows that the defendant had given a copy of the agreement for sale to the plaintiff. Exhibit-2(f) dated 4th May. 1987 shows that the plaintiff made proposal for amendment of clauses 4, 6 and 12 of the draft agreement Exhibit-2(g) is the letter dated 5th May, 1987 by which the defendant requested the plaintiff to meet them on 6th May, 1987 for holding discussion.

12. Exhibit-2(h) dated 7.5.87 is the letter by which the earnest money of Taka 15 lakh had been forfeited. By Ext 2(i) the defendant refused to return the earnest money of Taka 15 lakh as the plaintiff failed to fulfil the terms of the contract by not paying 25% of the total consideration money within time. By Exhibit-2(j) the plaintiff gave a fresh offer for a negotiated sale or agreement or to refund the earnest money. Exhibit-2(k) is a lengthy letter written by the plaintiff to the defendant describing all facts stating that as per paper advertisement for sale of 4'61 acres of land with two buildings the plaintiff quoted the price of the immovable property at Taka 2 crore and 87 lakh and deposited a draft of Taka 15 lakh as earnest money and as per terms and conditions of the tender advertisement 25% of the tender amount shall have to be deposited within one month from the date of acceptance. Plaintiff further offered that they would pay the rest of the consideration money and asked for fulfillment of the contract failing which they would take legal action in the court of law.

13. Exhibit-A is the terms and conditions of tender as advertised in the newspaper where it was clearly stipulated that the person whose quotation would be accepted would have to pay 25% of the total price to the seller within one month from the date of acceptance of the quotation and execute the contract for sale on such terms and conditions as the seller would prescribe, failing which the earnest money shall stand forfeited. Exhibit-B(1) is the tender form and Exhibit-B(2) contains the terms and conditions of the tender. Exhibit-C is the letter of the defendant dated 9th of April, 1987 by which the defendant asked the plaintiff to pay the 25% of the tender consideration money and that the amount of Taka 15 lakh would be adjusted with the consideration of the suit property. Exhibit-C(1) is the letter of the plaintiff for extension of time. Exhibit-C(2) dated 30.4.87 is a letter of the plaintiff to the defendant seeking to see the proposed agreement Exhibit-C(4) is the proposed amendment of the draft made by the plaintiff. Exhibit-C(5) to C (13) are the correspondence in between the parties and some of which have already been made exhibits earlier. Exhibit-F is the proposed agreement for sale. These are more or less the oral as well as documentary evidence adduced by the parties in this suit.

14. At the very outset Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellant, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law and facts in decreeing the suit in favour or the plaintiff. He submits that the learned Subordinate Judge has misconstrued the oral as well as documentary evidence adduced by the parties and as a result an erroneous judgment has been passed in the instant suit. He further submits that the judgment of the trial Court shows that the learned Subordinate Judge had almost accepted all the submissions of the defendant-appellant, but abruptly he passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff decreeing the suit for refund of Taka 15 lakh. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that there was no contract at all and since no terms and conditions of the contract had been violated, the defendant was bound to refund the earnest money of Taka 15 lakh. Me. Chowdhury further submits that the term NO.4 as published in the tender notice for sale of the suit property cannot be construed as a term and condition of the contract, and, as such, that condition No. 4 as contained in Exhibit-1 i.e. the paper-advertisement inviting tender, is not binding upon the plaintiff.

15. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan has drawn our attention to the plaint of the suit. It was a suit for specific performance of contract and in the prayer portion there was an alternative prayer for refund of Taka 15 lakh, but main prayer was for a decree for specific performance of contract. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the defendant filed written statement admitting the grievance of the plaintiff and prayed that a decree might be passed in terms of the prayer in the plaint for a decree for specific performance of contract After the submission of the written statement the plaintiff cleverly filed an application for amendment of the prayer portion of the plaint and prayer No. 1 was deleted and only the prayer for refund of Taka 15 lakh was sought to be amended which was allowed by the court. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that none of the averments made in the plaint had been amended by the plaintiff and in absence of such amendment those averments are still there. Since the plaintiff equivocally made averments in the plaint itself that there was a concluded contract and the defendant was bound by the contract, Mr. Chowdhury, at this appellate stage, cannot retract from the earlier stand taken in the plaint and submit before this court that there was no contract at all. We find substance in the contention of Mr. Bhuiyan. Since the averments in the plaint made by the plaintiff-respondent are still there and have net been amended in any form whatsoever, the plaintiff-respondent cannot run away from the statement of the plaint and it does net leek nice from the mouth of the plaintiff-respondent to say that there is no contract at all. Since the plaintiff admitted that there was a concluded contract and the defendant was bound by the contract, we are .Of the view that there was a contract in between the parties for selling the suit property.

16. Let us new examine Exhibit-I along with Exts. 3 and 4. Exhibit-I is the tender notice and Exhibit-3 is the prescribed form for submitting tender and Exhibit-4 is the terms and conditions attached with the tender form, In the terms and conditions attached with the tender form there is no condition that for the failure of payment of Taka 25% of the total consideration money within one month from the date of acceptance of the tender the earnest money would be forfeited. Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury submits that the terms and conditions as contained in prescribed form for tender shall be binding, but the terms and conditions of the tender notice as advertised in the newspapers are net binding. It is difficult for us to accept the above contention of Mr. Chowdhury. It appears from the tender notice Exhibit-1 that the tenderer shall have to submit that tender with Taka 15 lakhs as earnest money, Had it not been binding on the plaintiff to deposit Taka 15 lakh as earnest money then what led him to deposit Taka 15 lakh at the time of submission of the tender. If one taka was less than Taka 15 lakh as earnest money, the tender of the plaintiff would net have been accepted by defendant. So, the terms and conditions of the tender as advertised in the newspaper are the primary terms and conditions which were binding upon both the parties. In the similar way the terms and conditions as annexed with the tender form are also binding upon both the parties. The terms and conditions as contained in Exts. 1 and 4 should be read together and the same should be interpreted as terms and conditions of the agreement for sale of the suit property binding upon both the parties. As such, we are of the view that the condition No. 4 as given in tender notice vide Exhibit-1 is binding equally upon the parties along with the other terms and conditions contained in Exts. 1 and 4

17. When there was an offer and acceptance, the agreement is complete. In arriving at an agreement both the parties are required to give some terms and conditions and if these terms and conditions are accepted, it is an agreement and if an agreement in enforceable under law, it is contract, New, from the Exhibit-1 to 4 as we have discussed above, in our view, there was a concluded agreement in between the parties and the terms and conditions contained therein are binding upon both the parties.

18. Mr. Chowdhury has drawn our attention to Exhibit-2(a), the letter of acceptance dated 18.3.87, and the learned Advocate wanted to submit that the tender was accepted provisionally. The word provisional is there in Exhibit-2(a), but from the other letters, Exhibit-2(b), 2(c), 2(d), 2(e) and 2(f), it clearly appears to us that though the word provisionally was used, the subsequent exhibits clearly prove that the offer of the plaintiff was accepted finally by the defendant. It is admitted position that the defendant did net deposit 25% of the total consideration money within one month from the date of acceptance of the tender or within the extended time granted by the defendant on the prayer of the plaintiff. Condition No. 4 clearly shews that for agreement for sale the seller would provide terms and conditions which will be binding open the purchaser. But the aforesaid exhibits show that when the defendant gave a draft agreement, the plaintiff proposed for three amendments of the agreement on its clause Nos. 4, 6, and 12 which were net accepted by the seller-defendant. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that all the terms and conditions as given in the draft agreement were very reasonable and the plaintiff was debarred from making any amendment of the draft agreement in view of the fact that condition No. 4 of tender notice Exhibit-1 clearly shows that the plaintiff would be bound by terms and conditions of the agreement to be settled by the defendant. We find substance in the contention of Mr. Bhuiyan in this respect also. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the plaintiff suggested several unreasonable amendments without paying the 25% of the total consideration money and as a result they violated the term No. 4 of Exhibit-1 and that is why their earnest money was forfeited.

<u>19. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that even if, in a tender notice like the present one, there is no condition for forfeiture, but if the tender is frustrated due to non-fulfillment of the terms and conditions by the purchaser, the seller is entitled to forfeit the earnest money. Me. Bhuiyan, in support of his contentions has referred to the case of Kunwar Cnlranjit Singh Vs. Har Swarup AIR 1926 (PC) 1. It is held by their Lordships of the Privy Council that earnest money is a part of the purchase price when the transaction goes forward. It can be forfeited when the transaction falls through by reason of fault or failure of the vendee. Mr. Bhuiyan has further referred to the case of Moula Bux Vs. Union of India, AIR 1970 (SC) 1955 and another case of Sree Hanuman Cotton Mills Vs. Tata Aircraft Ltd. reported in the same volume page 1986. In those two cases the principle laid down by the Privy Council had been approved, so Mr. Bhuiyan submits that since for the default of the plaintiff the earnest money was forfeited and since there is a clause in Exhibit-1 for forfeiting the earnest money because of the fault of the plaintiff the earnest money was legally forfeited. We find substance in the contentions of Mr. Bhuiyan.</u>

<u>20. The learned Subordinate Judge in his judgment has found that the plaintiff did not deposit 25% of the consideration money as per terms of the tender and PW 1 deposed before the court that the terms and conditions to the advertisement of the tender were binding upon him. He further found that clause Nos. 4. 6 and 12 of the draft agreement were sought to be amended by the plaintiff although there was a condition that the terms and conditions of agreement for sale would be settled by the defendant and the tenderer would be bound by those terms and conditions. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the plaintiff failed to show that any terms and conditions of the draft agreement for sale was unreasonable or absurd which could not be fulfilled by the plaintiff. We have also gone through the draft agreement for sale and we are of the view that there was no absurd or unreasonable condition attached anywhere in the draft agreement Exhibit-F. The learned trial Court further made observation to the effect that the terms and conditions of the tender were binding upon both the parties. In spite of above findings the learned Subordinate Judge illegally failed to put reliance upon the terms and conditions of the tender notice vide newspaper Exhibit-l and wrongly found that the terms and conditions as given in the tender form will be only binding upon the plaintiff and since there is no condition for forfeiture the condition of forfeiture contained in the tender notice is not binding. Such a finding cannot be accepted in view of the evidence we have already discussed above. We have gone through the judgment of the trial Court and we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has totally misconstrued the evidence both oral and documentary on record and illegally passed a decree in favour of the plaintiff. Since there was an agreement in between the parties for the sale of the suit property and since that agreement was enforceable in law and since the term of the agreement for depositing 25% of the total consideration money was violated the defendant legally forfeited the earnest money as given by the tenderer.</u>

21. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that in a case like this conduct of the plaintiff should be considered by the court. He has drawn our attention that though there is a condition that within one month from the date of acceptance of the tender the tenderer must pay the 25% of the total consideration money even then on the prayer of the plaintiff-tenderer the defendant extended the time for 20 days but with a condition that other terms and conditions would remain as it is. He submits that the plaintiff has proposed some unreasonable amendments in the draft agreement which they were not entitled to do. Further at any point of time they did not deposit the 25% of the total consideration money in favour of the defendant. The plaintiff in fact was unwilling to perform his part of the contract though the offer was accepted by the plaintiff. Mr. Bhuiyan has further drawn our attention to the written statement. which they first filed in the suit for specific performance of contract, admitting the claim of the plaintiff and made a prayer before the court for passing a decree as per prayer of the plaintiff. Upon such written statement the plaintiff with malafide motive very cleverly made an amendment to the prayer by making an independent prayer for a decree for refund of Taka 15 lakh only by deleting the prayer for specific performance of contract. This shows that the plaintiff had no bonafide intention to purchase the suit property. We find force in the above contentions of Mr. Bhuiyan. Had the plaintiff any bonafide intention to purchase the suit property, on the submission of the first written statement, he could get a decree for specific performance of contract and get the suit property. Above circumstances clearly show that the plaintiff had malafide intention to frustrate the auction sale just after acceptance of the tender of the plaintiff by the defendant In the facts and circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge had illegally assessed the evidence on record and passed a decree illegally, which cannot be sustained in law and, as such, the decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is liable to be setaside.

In the result, this appeal is allowed with costs and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are hereby set aside and the suit of the plaintiff is hereby dismissed.

Send down the LC records immediately to the trial Court.

End.
