full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Choudhury, J.—This Rule arises out of a proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and is directed against the concurrent decision of the courts below allowing pre-emption. This rule was issued for examination of the question whether the addition of parties made in compliance with the court's order would be subject to the law of limitation. But this question no more requires examination. The parties in the meanwhile have compromised the case and filed a joint petition of compromise. The question now before us is whether the parties can compromise the case and for the matter of that whether a Civil Revision case may be compromised by the parties. The matter has come to us on reference from a Single Judge of this Court.

We would, at the beginning, like to examine the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code relating to compromise. Order 23, rule of the Code deals with compromise. It reads as:

"Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a suit has been adjusted wholly or in part by any lawful agreement or compromise, or where the defendant satisfies the plaintiff in respect of the whole or any part of the subject matter of the suit, the Court shall order such agreement, compromise or satisfaction, to be recorded, and shall pass a decree in accordance therewith so far as it relates to the suit".

2. This rule enables the parties to compromise the whole suit or part of it and if the court is satisfied that the compromise or the agreement is lawful, the court is to pass a decree in terms of the compromise.

<u>3. Section 141 of the Civil Procedure Code has made the procedure provided in the Code in regard to suits applicable, as far as it can be made applicable in all proceedings in any court of civil jurisdiction. The consensus of judicial opinion is that the proceedings" as mentioned in the section refers to original matters in the nature of a suit, such as proceeding in probate, guardianship and so forth and do not include the execution and other proceeding which do not originate in themselves. The proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is in the nature of a suit. The right, title and interest of the transferee vests in the petitioner, if he is successful and as such the order passed in a pre-emption proceeding conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to the land in dispute and as such this is an original proceeding and the determination of the right of the parties are conclusive, whether it is called a decree or an order and the effect is the same. So we feel what provisions of Order 23, rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code would apply in a proceeding under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act whether it is in the trial court or in the appellate court.</u>

<u>4. The next question is whether a revision preferred against the decision of the lower appellate court under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is a proceeding. The revisional power as conferred by section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code may be exercised by the High Court either on its own motion or on the application of the parties. If, the High Court suo-moto calls for the record, the question of compromise by the parties does not arise. But the position appears to be different in a Civil Revision case preferred by the parties. There is no provision in the Civil Procedure Code to compel a party to proceed with a revisional application after the issuance of the Rule, if the party chooses not to press the rule and get it discharged for non-prosecution or default. In the absence of any compelling provision in the Civil Procedure Code, there does not appear to be any bar, if the parties by compromise wish not to proceed and have the compromise recorded in the court, if the terms of the compromise are lawful. There is no definition of the word "proceeding' in the Civil Procedure Code "Proceeding" as we understand it to have been used in the Civil Procedure. Code, is a prescribed mode of action for carrying into effect a legal right, it means and includes all the steps and measures for prosecution or defence of an action. A revisional application is a prescribed mode of step in the Civil Procedure Code either in prosecution or in defence of an action and as such the procedure provided for in the Civil Procedure Code shall also apply to civil revision including the provision for compromise on the strength of section 141 of the Civil Procedure Code provided that the revisional application arises out of a suit, appeal or original miscellaneous case or appeal therefrom to which the procedure provided in the Code would apply.</u>

<u>5. There is no direct decision on this point by any of the High Courts of this sub-continent. While dealing with the question of abatement some of the High Court’s found that the abatement procedure does not apply to the civil revision. References may be made in this connection to the following cases: (1) Mohd. Saddat Ali Khan Vs. The Administrator, Corporation of City Lahore, A.I.R  1949 (Lahore) 186; (2) Anandamoji Desai vs. Rudra Mahanit, 18 C.L.J. 141 ; (1) Manickam & others vs. Mr. R M. Mamanathan Chettier and others, A.I.R. 1919 (Mad,) 433 (4) Balulal & other vs. Mannillal, A.I.R. 1953 (Rajasthan). 169(5) Hafasji Ibrahim and others vs. Mangalgirji Mathurajlrji. But these decisions do not lay down any general proposition that section 141 of the Civil Procedure Code would not apply to civil revision or that a civil revision case cannot be compromised by the parties under Order 23 rule 3 of the Civil. Procedure Code, even if the terms of the compromise/agreement are lawful. We, however, are of the view that a civil revision case may be compromised under Order 23 rule 3 of the Civil Procedure Code.</u>

<u>6. Reference in this connection must be made to section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code. If the terms of the compromise are lawful and for the technical reason that the revisional application having not arisen out of an original miscellaneous proceeding the provisions of Order 23, rule 3 of the Code does not apply, the court for the ends of justice may record the compromise under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code, which exists for granting relief in appropriate cases in the absence of any other provision in the Code.</u>

7. In fine, we hold that a Revisional application may be compromised. In that view of ours the petition of compromise filed by the parties is accepted as the terms therein are lawful. The Rule is therefore, disposed of in terms of the compromise which will form part of the order of this Court. There will be no order as to costs.

Sultan Hossain Khan, J.—I agree.

End.

lawyer:
Md. Anser Ali with Abdul Majid ------ For the petitioners
B.N. Chowdhury with P.K. Bose and Mansur Habibi  ------ For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Azizur Rahman & ors ------Defendant-Petitioner
Vs.
Jugal Kishori Sarkar &  ------Plaintiff-Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant-petitioners is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge Rajsahahi, in Title Appeal No. 120 of 1979 affirming the judgment and decree passed by the Munsif, Rajshahi, in O.C. Suit No. 17 of 1975 decreeing the suit in the preliminary form.

2. The plaintiff opposite party brought the suit for partition of her 8 annas share in the suit land comprised of 4 plots with an additional prayer for purchasing the 8 annas shaft of the defendant-in the dwellings house in plot No. 492 under section 4 of the Partition Act.

3. The plaintiffs case was that the suit land belonged to Amritolal on whose death it devolved upon his two sons Jadab and Madusudan each having 8 annas share. Upon death of Jadab his 8 annas share deloved upon the plaintiff alone as his daughter and the 8 annas share of Modusudan devolved upon his only son and heir Jogobandhu. Plaintiff and his paternal cousin Jogobandhu jointly possessed the suit land including the dwelling house situated on plot No. 492. Jogobandhu transferred his entire share to the defendant in 1956 and 1957. Defendant being stranger and also having belonged to different that is muslim community the plaintiff is entitled to buy up the defendant's share in the dwelling house and joint possession being also inconvenient the plaintiff is entitled to have partition of her share of the other land. The demand for partition purchase having not been met this suit was brought.

The defendant No. 1 and 3 to 10 contested the suit.

4. The defence case was that there was already a partition between plaintiff and Jogobandhu and that Jogobandhu and after him his vendees namely the defendants have been separately possessing their share of lands. So there is no cause of partition. It was also pleaded that the plaintiff, since after her marriage having lived away with her husband she was no longer a member of her paternal family and she also did not possessed the dwelling house and as such she could not claim to purchase the defendants share of dwelling house under section 4 of the Partition Act. Further it was pleaded that no partition suit having been brought by the defendants the claim under section 4 of the Partition Act not lie.

5. Oral evidence were produced on the side of plaintiff and oral and documentary evidence on the side of the defendants.

The learned Munsif upon consideration of the evidence held that the defendants failed to show any previous partition and that the witnesses four the pin tiff and the defendants consistently proved that both the plaintiff and the defendants' vendor Jogobandhu used to live in the dwelling house and that the suit properties being undivided joint properties of both the plaintiffs and Jogobandhu the vendor of the defendants and Jogobandhu having transferred his share of the dwelling house to defendants who were strangers and belong to a different community so the plaintiff was entitled to have partition of her share of the suit lands and also entitled to purchase the defendants' share in the dwelling house and the homestead land on plot No. 492. With the aforesaid finding he decreed the suit and directed assessment to the value of the dwelling house by a pleader Commissioner.

6. The defendants preferred appeal Before the appellate court the defendants raised 3 points of objection against the decree namely that the plaintiff ceased to be member of the undivided family after her marriage elsewhere and that the suit was not brought by the defendants namely the stranger purchaser, and therefore the plaintiffs' claim under section 4 of partition Act could not be legally maintained. The third point of objection was that the learned Munsif did not himself assessed the value of the property as was required by law.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge upon a consideration of all the evidence and the judgment of the trial court in the light of the objections made by the defendants found that since the plaintiff not only owns the family dwelling house but also resides there so she being a member of the family had locus standi to claim purchase of the share of stranger defendants under section 4 of the Partition Act. He also held that the suit even though it was filed by the plaintiff herself and not by the defendant stranger she was entitled to lay her claim under section 4 of the partition Act. Lastly he held that the learned Munsif did not commit any illegality in assessing the value of the purchased share through a pleader Commissioner. The learned Subordinate Judge also referred to certain decision of the superior court in support of his finding. Thus he rejected all the points of objection raised by the defend ants and by concurring with the findings of learned Munsif he affirmed the judgment and decree that was passed by the learned Munsif.

8. The defendants-petitioners then obtained the present rule to challenge the judgment and decree that was passed in favour of the plaintiff.

Mr. Md. Anser Ali. the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioners raised several points of objection to support the petitioner's contention that the judgment and decree passed by the courts below suffers from; error of law and lack of jurisdiction.

Firstly it was submitted that the courts below did not properly cons per the defendants' plea that there was a previous partition between the plaintiff and defendants, vendor Jogobaddhu after which the plaintiff did not continue to be a co-sharer in the suit land and was not entitled to claim partition it was also submitted that the courts below also failed to consider that the plaintiff since after her marriage lived away with her husband and thus ceased to be member of his paternal family. In this respect it appears from the judgments of the courts below that the learned Munsif after considering the evidence clearly found that there was no proof of any previous partition between the plaintiff and the defendants' vendor Jogobandhu or with the defendants. It was also observed by the learned Munsif that the defendants themselves conceded to a decree for partition except only the claim for purchase under section 4 of the Partition Act. The judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge shows that defendants did not raise any please of previous partition.

9. Further it has been concurrently found by both the courts below upon the evidence of both the parties that the plaintiff continued to possess the suit land and resides in the dwelling house all through and that she jointly enjoyed the properties in her 8 annas share.

Mr. Anser Ali by referring to section 4 of the Partition Act submitted that the plaintiff could not be regarded as a member of the undivided family of her father after her marriage.

On the other hand Mr. B.N Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party contended that in order to be entitled to make a claim under section 4 of the Partition Act all that was necessary was that the plaintiff should own the house by having not divided the dwelling house with the members of her family in order to have her claim under section 4 of the partition suit.

<u>10. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury referred to several decision in support of his contention. In the case of Khtrode Chandra Goshal Vs. Saroda Proshid Mitra reported in XII CLJ page 525 it has been held that "undivided family" must be taken to mean, "undivided qua the dwelling house in question and to be a family which owns the house but has not divided it". The said decision has been followed in the case of Boto Krishna Vs. Akhoy Kumar reported in 115 C.W.N, page 450. In this case both the courts below have concurrently found that there was no previous partition between the plaintiffs and her paternal cousin and that both of them continue to live jointly in their paternal dwelling house. So upon the aforesaid facts the plaintiff has been rightly found to be entitled to lay her claim under section 4 of the Partition Act. So the points raised by Mr. Anser Ali in this regard does not stand.</u>

<u>11. Mr. Anser Ali next submitted that according to section 4 of the Partition Act only when the stranger transferee sues for partition then only the claim under that section can be laid. But in this case as the stranger transferees namely the defendants did not bring the suit for partition and the suit was brought by the plaintiff herself so section 4 was not applicable. Mr. Anser Ali is contention is apparently consistent with the wordings of the section. But this contention no longer holds in view of several decisions which have been cited by Mr. B.N Chowdhury In the case of Md. Magdu Bhuiva Vs. Jobhan Huq reported in 11 DLR page 355 it has been held that section 4 of the Partition Act will also apply in a case instituted by any other co-sharer because in a suit for partition all the parties are in the capacity of the plaintiff. In the case of Aid Habihullah Vs. Movi. Salek reported in 20 DLR page 489 the same principle has been followed. Besides that there were several other decision accepting the same proposition of law. So this points of objection raised by Mr. Anser Ali does not also stand.</u>

12. Thirdly, Mr Anser Ali submitted that since the defendants being stranger and members of different community have admittedly purchased 1/2 share of the dwelling house in as early as in 1956 and 1957 and have been continuously possessing the same house along with the plaintiff and since the plaintiff did not lay any claim under section 4 of the Partition Act during the long past 19 years the present claim is unreasonable and should not be accepted In reply to this objection Mr. B.N. Chowdhury submitted that for bringing a suit for partition or for making the claim under section 4 of the partition act law has not enjoined any time limit and as such the plaintiff has a legal right to avail of the benefit of section 4 no matter that there has been delay in laying such claim. It is undisputed position of law that there is no time limit for laying a claim under section 4 of the Partition Act unlike the claim for preemption under other law. So the plaintiff having the benefit provided by the law itself there is no scope for this court to refuse the claim of the plaintiff on the ground that the claim has been laid after much delay. So I am unable to accept the contention of Mr. Anser Ali. Mr. Anser Ali raised another objection on the ground that by the decree, the learned Munsif did not assess the value of the purchased share of the dwelling house and left the assessment with the pleader Commissioner and this was illegal. Section 4 of the Partition Act requires that the courts shall make valuation in such manner as it thinks fit. This means that the manner of the assessment of value has been left by the law to the discretion of the court. In this case if the court directed assessment of value by physical verification by the commissioner that did not mean that the final assessment would not he made by the court after considering the report of the Commissioner This aspect has been duly considered by the learned Subordinate Judge and I accept the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge that there has been no illegality on that count.

13. Lastly, Mr. Anser Ali submitted that the courts below granted decree allowing plaintiff opposite party to purchase under section 4 of the Partition Act the defendant-petitioners' share of the entire homestead land and building appertaining to plot No. 492 which totally measures 3.71 lands while dwelling but covered only 15 lands of the plots. But according to section 4 of the Partition Act plaintiff was entitled to purchase the defendants' share only of the dwelling house and not the entire land of plot No. 492. So the decree in that regard was illegal having been passed in excess of the jurisdiction of the court. Mr. B N. Chowdhury submitted that the entire plot being the homestead plot containing the dwelling house plaintiff was entitled to purchased the defendants, share of the entire homestead plot and the decree did not suffer from any illegality nor lack of Jurisdiction in passing the decree.

<u>14. On looking into the plaint as it is stood upon amendment by an application made by the plaintiff to insert the claim for purchase under section 4 of the Partition Act it clearly appears that plaintiff O.P, prayed for allowing her to purchase the defendants' share only in the dwelling house that stood on Plot No. 492. But the decree passed by the learned Mnnsif and affirmed by the learned Sub-Judge was in the following language:</u>

<u>The plaintiff is entitled to have the undivided homestead land and building of Jogobandhu appertaining to C.S. Plot No. 492 purchased from the defendants………………”</u>

<u>This certainly means that the decree al-lowed the plaintiff to purchase not only the dwelling house but also homestead land of plot No. 492 without specifying the extent of the homestead land and thereby indicating that plaintiff's purchase was allowed for the entire plot No. 492 which totally measure 3.71. Neither in the plaint nor in the evidence there was any disclosure from the side of the plaintiff as to how much land of plot 492 was actually covered by the dwelling house and the courts below neither noticed this nor sought to ascertain this. Mr. B N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite party submitted that the dwelling house as contained in section 4 of the partition Act will mean not only the structure of the house but also the attached land, garden etc. which are required for convenience use of the dwelling house. Mr. B. N. Chowdhury referred to certain decision for giving the meaning of the term dwelling house. In the case reported in 12 CLJ page 525 is have been held that the dwelling house embraces not merely the structure or building but includes also adjacent building, cartilage, garden Courtyard, orchard all that is necessary for the convenient occupation of their house. It must be reasonably held that the dwelling house as mentioning under section 4 of the partition act must indicate not only the structure of the house but also the adjunct land including courtyard which are essentially, necessary for reasonably convenient use of the dwelling house. In this case as I have already mentioned the plot No. 492 upon which the dwelling hat stands measure 3.71 i.e. over 1 Bighas lands. It cannot be conceived that the referred dwelling house of the plaintiff will cover the entire huge plot. So the plaintiff opposite party, under section 4 of the Partition Act will be entitled to purchase the share of the defendant-purchasers only so much land of the plot which is covered by the dwelling house and the adjunct land which are reasonably necessary for convenient and proper use of the house. Neither the plaintiff mentions the area of the dwelling house that is the actual quantum of land covered by the dwelling house and its adjunct land nor the courts ascertained or specified the same but gave a decree in favour of the plaintiff allowing her to purchase the entire homestead land that is the entire 3.71 land of plot No. 492. This was illegal being contrary to the provision of law and was also without jurisdiction. So on this ground alone the judgment and decree passed by the courts below can not be sustained and are liable to be set aside.</u>

15. Since however all the other points of fact and law have been decided in favour of the plaintiff opposite party so for ends of justice the suit should be remanded to the trial Court with a direction that he shall appoint a suitable Pleader Commissioner at the cost of the plaintiff to physically assess and ascertain the actual quantum of land covered by the dwelling house and the adjunct lands which are reasonably necessary for proper and convenient use of the blouse and also to visit the suit land and assess the value thereof and upon the report the learned Munsif shall determine the area of the dwelling house and its value either on the basis of the said report or on taking further evidence of both parties if necessary and thereafter to pass a decree in favour of the plaintiff according to law, and in the light of the observation made above.

16. The rule is accordingly made absolute and the judgment and decree passed by the courts below are set aside.

Send down the records to the Munsif, Rajshahi (Sadar) with a direction to dispute of the suit as early as possible.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No.114 of 1974 with Civil Rule No. 1060 (R) of 1974.
lawyer:
Nizamuddin Haider with H. N. Nondy ------ For the Appellant
Md. Abdur Rahim ------ For the Respondent
parties:
Haran Chandra Daradi ------Appellant
Vs.
Ejhar Molla & ors ------Respondents
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of plaintiff No. 1, Haran Chandra Daradi son of late Shashi Daradi is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Jessore in Title Appeal No. 96/70 reversing those passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Jhenidah in Title Suit No. 391/68.

2. Plaintiff appellant Haran Chandra Daradi who is the son of Shasi and the heirs of one of the original tenants, his sister Bhanu Sundari, plaintiff No. 2 and wife Brojabasi Dasi, plaintiff No. 3 together filed a suit for partition alleging that the suit land originally belonged to three tenants mainly Iswar Daradi, Kartik Daradi and Jagannath Daradi. According to the plaintiff these 3 persons were the original tenants. Iswar according to the plaintiff died leaving Feli Bewa, a childless widowed daughter and being a childless widow acquired no right of inheritance, but yet her brothers (cousins) namely Kudiram and Shasi Daradi (father of the present plaintiff) permitted Feli to possess the 4 annas 11 gondas 1 cara 2 krantis and 12 tils share in Khatian No. 444 and 929 and allowed her to posses 4 pies share in Khatian No. 764 just out of sympathy and not out of any right. The land was recorded in her name and she possessed the property accordingly. As to the other non-mentioning co-sharer namely Jadu Nath it is the plaintiff case that he had sub-let his land of the Khatian to tenant without, however, mentioning the name of those tenants. According to the plaintiff Feli Bewa had only 3.61 decimal of land in all those 3 Khatians but she transferred to Ananta Mondal and to a lady called Purna Bewa (her mother) an area totalling 6.10 acres out of those khatian whereafter Purna Bewa sold an area of .65 decimal of 'Gha' schedule property to defendant Nos. 6-11 and the rest to defendant Nos. 1 & 2. Plaintiff's further case is that Khokan, son of Khudiram, the heir of Kartik then sold from his share of .65 decimal to defendants 6-11 by registered kabala and sold the rest of his share to plaintiff No. 1 which was purchased in the name of his wife plaintiff No. 3 vide kabala dated 18th Chaitra 1365 B.S. It is the further case is that Baidyanath, brother of Khokan also sold from his share. 51 to defendant No. 5 and rest to one Saijuddin who in turn sold to plaintiff No. 2 sister of Haran, by a kabala dated 18th Chaitra, 1365 B.S. being Ext. 1 and Ext. A. Further case is that plaintiff No. 1 took settlement of rest of the land of Baidynath and Khokan, son of Khudiram and sold those to plaintiff No. 3 by kabala on the same date as stated already hereinbefore. Thus according to the plaintiff they are entitled to the share of 6.10 acres of land but their co-sharer are possessing in excess of their share. Hence the suit for partition.

3. The defendants Ejahar Molla and Tasirannessa being the wife of defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement alleging that the suit is not maintainable for defect of parties as heirs of Jadu Nath has not been made parties in the suit. They further alleged that Khudiram, son of Baidyanath never transferred his interest to Saijuddin and the plaintiff No. 2, sister of plaintiff No. 1 had created a false dakhilas through Saijuddin showing transfer of the said to plaintiff No. 2 by kabala of 14th Chaitra 1365 B.S. collusively. They also denied the settlement of Khokan's share, being another son of Khudiram, in favour of plaintiff No. 1 which was allegedly sold by plaintiffs I and 2 by kabala dated 18th Chaitra 1365 B.S. According to defendant Feli Bewa, daghter of one of the original tenant Iswar Daradi settled her entire share by patta dated 2.2.1944 to Puma Bewa and Ananta Kumar and defendant No. 1 purchased 2.09 decimal from them while defendant No. 1 again sold 2.08 decimal. It is further case of the defendant that Ananta Kumar also transferred some property to Abul Hossain Molla who thereafter transferred the same to defendant No. 1 in 1969 and the defendants are in exclusive possession to the knowledge of all and they are not possession the excess as alleged by the plaintiff, so the suit be dismissed.

4. On these pleadings the parties brought out the suit. The court of first instance framed the issues as follows:-

1. Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

2. Is the suit is maintainable in its form?

3. Have the plaintiffs their alleged Share and are they entitled to get partition to the extent prayed for?

4. What relief if any plaintiffs are entitled?

5. Has the suit been properly valued and stamped?

The court having found the suit maintainable in its present form filed by a member of minority community because of the repeal of Ordinance No.1 of 1964 since before and having found the suit properly valued and stamped found those in favour of the plaintiff. As to issue No. 1 as to whether the suit is bad for defect of parties, trial court have found that the defendants are claiming through Feli Sundari who being a childless widow would not inherit her fathers property but admittedly Feli was allowed to sue as owner her father's share on the death of her brother by both the parties and plaintiffs having admitted right, title and interest of the defendants, through Feli Sundar to the extent their predecessor-in-interest namely, Feli Sundari had in the property, the court of first instance proceeded to find the share of the plaintiff in the suit land and having found kabalas standing in favour of plaintiffs 2 and 3 being Ext. 1 and 1(A) both of 18th Chaitra 1365 BS and having found him pre-empting. 75 decimal of land he had already sold by Ext. C (4) being an area of 2 acres found him to be entitled to an area of 2.05 decimals and also found plaintiffs 2 and 3 to have purchased by kabala Ext. 1 and 1(a). Thereafter the court came to the plea of defect of parties and held that the same have not been too much agitated at the time of the trial and found that by amending the plaint the plaintiff explained that the heirs of Jadunath had leased out his share to others and in view of that the same was found not bad for defect of parties and hence maintainable. In that view of the matter he decreed the suit on contested preliminary form, plaintiff No 1. is to get 2.00 and plaintiffs 2 and 3 to get what they had by kabala Ext. 1 and 1(a).

5. When the matter went to appeal the defendants 1 and 2 objected before the court of appeal below stating that the trial court was wrong to observe that the issue on defect of parties was not too much agitated and hence that finding was wrong and the trial court should have dismissed the suit for defect of parties. On appeal, the plaintiff also filed a cross-objection on the ground that the c. s. khatian No. 444 and 929 were wrongly recorded and that the trial court was wrong in holding that Feli Bewa had annas 11 gondas 1 kara 2 kranti shares, claiming plaintiffs 2 and 3 as bonafide transferees and they acquired title also by adverse possession and further that the heirs of Khudiram and Jadu were not necessary parties as their lands were tenanted and their rent receiving interest had been acquired by Government. The court of appeal. below had occasion to examine the relevant khatians of the suit namely khatiati Nos. 444, 929 and 764 which were also examined by me at the time of hearing of this appeal. According to the these khatian Shasi Daradi, son of Jadu Nath Daradi had 2 annas odd share, Khudiram, son of Kartik another recorded tenant had 4 annas and odd share and Jadhunath son of Pitambar as original tenant had 4 annas share which meant Shasi, father of the plaintiff had 1/7th share and other 3 tenants had 2/7th share each in the land. On a reference to khatian No. 929 covering an area of 8.84 it is seen that Jadunath had no possession in the khas land in the khatian. Similar is the case in khatian No. 444. These khatians were accepted by the plaintiff to be correct khatian and correctly recorded at the trial court but it was alleged to be wrong only before the court of appeal below and the court rightly rejected that contention to be not considerable at the appellate stage. At the trial plaintiff No. 1 being P.W. 1 son of Shasi Daradi one of the original tenant had said that he had 2 and 5 annas and odd share in Khatian No. 444 and 929 which is the recording of the khatian. This being the case he may not be allowed to find a new case at the appellate stage. Defendannt also claimed that the khatians are correctly recorded, and in that view of the matter the court found the khatian correctly recorded with cogent reasons which I find reason to interfere in this appeal which is also not agitated before this Court. P.W. 1 stated before the trial court that he had 1/3rd share in khatian No. 764 and in that view of the matter the court rightly found that Jadunath had interest to the extent of .27, Feli .27, Khudiram and his to the extent of .27, Feli .27 Khudiram and his brother .27, and Shasi .17 in the Khas land under khatian No. 444 covering an area of 1.64 and the same is the case with the khas land of khatian No. 929 covering an area 2.84. It is seen on a reference to khatian No. 444 that Jadunath there in had been clearly recorded as a tenant having a share of more than 4 annas of the total area of 8.44 decimal covered by that khatian but he was recorded to be not in possession in the column kept for recording possession against the plot number. It is seen that those were possessed by Shasi Daradi, Khudiram and Feli and other 3 Riyats holding tenancy under Jamindary of Mohammad Shahi under Touji No. 178 appertaining to Mohammad Shahi Parganas within mouza Putimari, District Jessore. Jadu Nath therefore, is a recorded tenant along with other 3 tenants who are predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff and also of the defendant because in this case the defendants were claiming through Feli Bewa and plaintiffs claiming through Shasi and Khudiram son of Kartic.

Possession by a co-sharer is not a dispossession of the others, unless it is proved to the contrary to be hostile and a co-sharer in possession to the exclusion of other co-shares would be possessing for all. Hence merely because Khudiram was not recorded to be co-sharer in possession would not mean that Jadu Nath would lose his interest having adversely possessed by other which is nobody's case in this suit. The tenancy recorded in the name of khudiram was not rent receiving interest but a raiyati interest and because of the acquisition of the rent receiving interest of Mohammad Shahi Zamindary, Jadunath tenancy interest would not be extinguish and Jadunath would remain a tenant under the Government. His tenancy interest having subsistence even after acquisition of the rent receiving interest he would be a necessary party in any partition suit concerning the joint property covered by Khatian 444.

6. On a reference to C.S. Khatian No. 929, appertaining to Mohmmad Shahi Parga under Putimari Mouja, under Touji No. 4497 it is seen that there also the land was held under a Talukdari by tenants namely Shasi Daradi having 2 annas and odd share, Khudiram having 4 annas and odd share, Feli Bewa 4 annas and odd share and Jadu Nath also had 4 annas and odd share. In that khatian Jadu Nath's name was recorded against a number of plots and as to that he cannot be said to be a co-sharer not in possession.

7. In Khatian No. 764 under Mohammad shabi Pargana appertaining to Putimar Mouja of Jessore District, the land was recorded in the name of Shasi Daradi to the extent of 5 annas and odd, Khudiram 5 annas and odd share and Feli Bewa 5 annas and odd share. The name of Jadu Nath had not been recorded there. The plaintiff does not claim from Jadu Nath neither is the case of defendant that Jadu Nath had any share in that property under Khatian No. 764 Jadu Nath was not a necessary party being not the recorded tenant when that property under Khatian No. 764 is concerned but not to the land of other Khatian. In this view of the matter the court of appeal below hold that in a partition suit all the co-sharers were necessary parties and partition suit cannot be maintained without making all the co-sharers in the property a party and on that finding allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit though the court of appeal below found other grounds also reverse to the judgment of the trial court.

8. In a partition suit the law is this that all who had interest of the same property, claiming under the same right need to be made a party and in their absence, the suit would not be maintainable. This is based on the principle of substantial justice and for the purpose of doing away with multiplicity of suits. The court of first instance would have jurisdiction to pass a decree in a suit when the suit was maintainable but passing a decree in 4 suit which was not maintainable, being barred by law, would be a decree passed without jurisdiction because the proceedings would in such a case be carom non judice. This is not a mere irregularity of procedure but an illegality which cannot be cured because of obvious prejudice caused to the non-impleading parties.

<u>9. The learned Advocate appearing for the appellant having realised the gravity of the situation, therefore, filed an application before this Court praying for remand of the case to the Court of first instance allowing amendment of the plaint after impleading the necessary co-sharer parties which, according to the learned Advocate, crept in because of a bonafide mistake caused by the eminent local lawyers.</u>

<u>10. A case cannot be sent back on remand as matter of right. It is never sent back on remand as a matter of right for allowing the parties to change the nature and character of the suit or to correct mistake which initially had non suited the parties or for giving fresh evidence.</u>

<u>Under the law a defect in the plaint need be corrected at the earliest possible opportunity and any formal defect in a suit need be corrected immediately after it came to the knowledge of the party concerned but if a party chose to proceed with a suit in spite of the knowledge of the inherent defect in the suit, which would ultimately non suit him the party would be so proceeding and would be deemed to have proceeded with the suit with the knowledge of the legal consequence. Therefore, after long 15 years of filing of the suit in the court of first instance it would be an abuse of the process to allow the plaintiff to have the defect of parties corrected on remand which defect had been challenged by the defendant immediately in their written statement on 29.11.68, only 10 months after the suit was filed on 10.1.68.</u>

11. Mr. M.A. Rahim, the learned Advocate has cited a number of decisions in support of not allowing the case on remand Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, the learned Advocate had also cited a number of decisions in his favour,

In the case reported in 28 DLR at page 5 it was held that a formal defect of this nature must be corrected at the earliest possible opportunity and if necessary parties were not impleaded in a partition suit, whether objection or no objection, the decree would become infructuous at the option of the excluded parties.

In the case reported in 25 DLR page 97 it was held that the Party having persisted in holding the suit in spite of the defect of parties should not be allowed. to amend the plaint after an inordinate delay.

Mr. Rahim has cited some other cases of Indian jurisdiction which have been quoted with approval in the case reported in 25 DLR wherein it was held that to allow to amend after long years would be to allow him to file fresh suit after long years of limitation allowing him to take advantage of his own negligence and default. It was further held in those cases that if a suit would have been totally non-maintainable because of improper pleading under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act or for that matter for not making the co-sharers a party in partition suit, if cured after long years at the second appellate stage, would mean making the suit maintainable with retrospective effect by passing the law of limitation, in cases where the suit will be barred under the Limitation Act.

<u>12. This is a suit for partition and an amendment of the plaint as to parties would make the suit maintainable with retrospective effect from the year 1968 and hence it cannot be allowed now in the year 1983. It would have been done at the earliest possible opportunity and having neglected to do so with knowledge of its consequences it could not be said that it was a bonafide mistake for it to be cured by sending it back on remand after 16 years of the filing of the suit.</u>

<u>13. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider has referred to the case reported in I.L.R 44 Calcutta at page 929. In that case it was held by a Full Bench, of the Allahabad High Court that the court's power to remand is not restricted to the case specified under Order 41 rule 23 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the court by reasons of its inherent jurisdiction may order a remand if it becomes necessary for the ends of justice. It was further held therein that whether justice does require a court to invoke its inherent jurisdiction must be determined by that Court with reference to the facts of a particular case and the rule of law but a court cannot invoke its inherent jurisdiction where there is a provision in the Code whether by way of a remand or otherwise.</u>

14. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider has taken pains in expressing the ratio under reference by referring to the judgment of Teunon, J. in that case under report to the effect that a remand in such cases as to addition of parties may be made in case the trial had been vitiated by the court's erroneous decision on the preliminary question of non-joinder and because of the absence of the assistance which the added party was in a position to give. Reading the judgment as a whole it seemed that it was held by his Lordship that a trial be sent on remand to a de novo trial under Order XLI, rule 23, if the trial Court had disposed of the suit upon a preliminary point, and further held that the case would also be sent on remand when there was no proper trial because of the error caused by court in its procedural matters where, for example, a minor was termed as major or the trial has been vitiated by the Court's erroneous decision on a preliminary question of non-joinder.

15. In the instant case it is not a question of bringing in all the necessary or proper parties for the actual determination of all the questions at issue. It was rather a question of parties in a partition suit in the absence of whom there was no partition suit in existence in the eye of law. Therefore, the case referred to by the learned Advocate has no bearing to the facts and circumstances of this case. The application submitted for sending the case on remand is thus rejected.

16. The court of appeal below committed no error in reversing the Judgment and decree of the trial Court and it was reversed with cogent reasons. This appeal which has no substance is thus dismissed.

The judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are affirmed. But in the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost.

The order of injunction passed by this Court in Civil Rule No. 106 (s)/74 restraining the defendants opposite parties from interfering with the possession of the appellant in this appeal till disposal of this appeal is hereby recalled and vacated.

Send down the records as early as possible.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 94 of 1969.
lawyer:
Anil Chandra Sarker ----- For the Appellant.
Jane Alam ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
M. Akbar Ali (Plaintiff No. 1) ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Mrs. Rezia Sultana Begum and ors (Defendant Nos. 1-3) ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
A.T.M Afzal, J.—This appeal by the plaintiff arises out of a suit for money and is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 30-11-68 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge 3rd Court, Dacca in Money suit No. 89 of 1967 dismissing the plaintiff’s suit and decreeing the defendants counterclaim for Taka 50,000/- on contest with, cost against the plaintiff.

2. The plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit for realization of Taka 37,960/- from the defendants on the averments, inter alia, that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the proprietors of the business firm named M/S. Dacca Scientific Works defendant No. 3; that the plaintiff bad been working as a Manager of the said firm since' its inception and that he used to get a salary and commission on sale proceeds. A dispute arose between the plaintiff and the defendants with regard to the plaintiffs' dues and it was settled by and between the parties under terms and conditions embodied in a deed of agreement dated 7.9.66 executed by both the parties. The plaintiffs stated that in terms of the said agreement the plaintiffs dues were settled at Taka 41,000/ and the defendants agreed to pay the said sum in full by June 30, 1967 and that the mode of payment had also been mentioned in the said agreement. The defendant, however, did not comply with terms and conditions of the said agreement but merely paid a sum of Tk. 3,040/- only in all. The plaintiff served a demand notice through his lawyer on 26.6.67 calling upon the defendants to pay the outstanding dues of Tk. 37,960/- within one week from June 30, 1967 but the defendants did not pay the said amount and hence the suit.

3. The defendants contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. Besides denying the material allegations of the plaintiff they raised various pleas in bar of the suit. They denied that the plaintiff was the Manager of the firm since its inception. The defendant contended that the firm was started in October 1961 in a rented house at 22/2 Hatkhola Road, Dacca when the plaintiff was a lower division clerk in the office of the School Text Book Board at Rankinstreet. The plaintiff was asked by the defendant No.1 to look, into the accounts of the business and make correspondence of the firm in the evening after his office hours and was allowed to draw an allowance of Tk. 150/- per month.

4. The defendants asserted that the agreement dated 7.9.96 referred to by the plaintiff in his plaint was executed by the defendant under forced circumstances, coercion and without their free consent. The defendant set out the circumstances under which they were compelled to sign the agreement it was stated that the defendant's business firm manufactures and deals in scientific instruments, laboratory glassware’s chemicals etc. used in science laboratories of Educational Institutions. The plaintiff, as already stated, was a part time employee of the firm and was allowed to occupy a room in the premises of the firm at 22/2 and later on at 27 Hatkhola Road. The plaintiff was made a full-time Manager of the firm with a salary of Tk. 250/- and commission at the rate of two percent on sale with effect from 1st December, 1962. In October, 1964 the plaintiff demanded that his salary and. commission should be enhanced The defendants having found that it was difficult to replace him decided that his salary should be raised to Tk. 500/- per month and commission to 4 percent with effect from November, 1964.

5. Sometime in May 1966 it transpired that the plaintiff was arranging a secret business deal with some Japanese firm and this cast a serious doubt about the plaintiffs' motives in the mind of the defendant. At about the same time it was revealed that although a full-time employee of the defendant the plaintiff was a regular student of the Dacca University attending classes without the knowledge and consent of the defendant and he obtained an M.A. degree in History in 1964. The defendants further learnt that the plaintiff had been carrying on independent business from some time back and opened two firms of his own PIMCO Instrument and Victor Scientific Co. When the plaintiff realised that he could no longer conceal his activities, he gave a proposal to the defendants that he wished to open a firm of his own of scientific instruments while remaining their Manager. It was turned down by the defendants and the plaintiff became furious and turned hostile. The defendant's further asserted that in order to settled accounts with the plaintiff the defendants No. 1 asked him to hand-over all the papers, documents etc. but the plaintiff refused to comply with the said request. On the contrary realising the helplessness of the defendants the plaintiff made a fantastic demand that he should be paid a salary of Tk. 500/- per month and four percent commission on sale with retrospective effect. The plaintiff insisted that unless his demands were met be would neither vacate the premises nor hand over the books of accounts the documents relating to property etc. to the defendants. The defendants further contended that thus a deadlock was created and consequently an arbitration was held in which some basis of calculation of the plaintiff's salary and commission was arrived at.

6. It also alleged that the plaintiff continued to work for the benefits of his own firm at the cost and to the detriment of the interest of the defendants and as a result the defendants business sustained heavy loss. The defendants then served a pleader's notice to vacate the premises hut the plaintiff did not pay any been to it and continued with his nefarious activities. The defendants therefore felt that recovery of extremely valuable documents of property, books of accounts files, that from the custody of the plaintiff and his eviction from the firm premises became most urgent but be would pot leave nor hand over the documents. It is the positive case of the defendants that they had to sign the agreement in question under such extreme pressure and coercion put by the plaintiff upon the defendants. The plaintiff, it is said, handed over the documents and vacated the premises only after the execution of the said agreement.

7. The defendants further alleged that upon scrutiny of the books of accounts it was found that the plaintiff was accountable for a sum of Tk. 1,72,000/- under various heads as set out below :-

1. Unauthorised withdrawal of money Rs. 1,600/-
2. Loss due to unauthorised issue of receipts over Rs.20,000/-
3. Amount received from various sources but not accounted for Rs. 75,046/-
4. Money collected from Customers but not deposited into the firm's cash or into the bank or to the proprietors Rs. 34,379.30/-
5. Improper maintenance of cash book showing doubtful expenditure over Rs. 15,680/.
6. Articles belonging to the firm but retained and removed by the plaintiff Rs. 2,525/-
7. Refund of salary from December, 1962 to August, 1964 Rs. 5,650/-
8. Refund of overdrawn amount as commission Rs. 12,527/88
9. Dues on other headings-over Rs. 5,000/-
Total- Rs. 1,72,407.18
Relinquished Rs. 1,22,408.18
Total balance Rs. 50,000/.-


Claim.

The defendants claimed on the basis of the aforesaid account that the plaintiff was liable to pay the defendants Taka. 50,000/-, prayed for a decree accordingly and also prayed for a set-off of the said amount against the dues of plaintiff if any, as claimed in the suit. The plaintiff put in an objection petition against the defendants claim denying, the allegations of the defendants particularly as to withholding of books of account etc. and stating further that he had attended classes in the University during 1962-64 with full knowledge and consent of the defendant No. 1 and her husband. It was contended that the defendants claim under the various heads was false and baseless.

8. On the aforesaid pleading the following issues were framed at the trial for adjudication:- 1. Is the alleged deed of agreement vitiated by fraud, undue influence and coercion and is it enforceable in law against the defendant? 2. Is the plaintiff entitled to get any amount as claimed by him? 3. Is the plaintiff guilty of negligence to perform the duties as agreed between the plaintiff and defendants? 4. Are the defendants entitled to get a decree as claimed in the written statements as counter claim? 5.Are the claim of the plaintiff and counter claim of the defendants barred by limitation? 6. To what relief, if any, are the plaintiff and the defendant entitled?

[Discussion of witnesses evidence omitted]

9. The learned Advocate for the appellant has rightly challenged the finding of the learned subordinate judge in this behalf. Upon a reference to the impugned judgment it is found that the learned subordinate Judge was laboring under a serious misconception of the defendants case and the evidence adduced by them. The defendants nowhere alleged fraud but the learned Subordinate Judge took up for consideration as to whether the agreement Ext. 2 was, inter alia, vitiated by fraud. Similarly, he read many things in the evidence of D.W.I. which as we have indicated above, are not there. The subordinate Judge having realised that there was no evidence as to the demand of documents from the plaintiff went on to make surmise that it was natural for a prudent man like Mr. Fazlur Rahman D.W. l to have demanded the documents etc. from the plaintiff when the trouble began. The learned subordinate Judge then relied on the alleged admission of the plaintiff that demands were made before charge was made over as per Ext. 3. It is, however, found from the evidence that the plaintiff as P.W.l stated that it was not a fact that the defendants demanded the documents prior to granting to Ext. 2 and that it was not a fact that he refused to hand over papers before settlement of his dues. The subordinate Judge quite contrary to the evidence on record further found that there was no cogent evidence that any practical accounting was made in the salish before Ext. 2 was executed and that it was another circumstance to indicate and established undue influence and coercion. The evidence of D.W.1 as referred to above, completely belied the aforesaid finding of the subordinate Judge. We must say that we are disappointed with the poor appreciation of the fact and evidence made by the learned subordinate Judge with regard to the compromise agreement Ext.2 and for reasons to be referred hereafter we do not also approve of the other part of his judgment. In view of our discussion above we have no hesitation in setting aside his finding as to the compromise agreement and in holding further that the agreement in question was not vitiated by undue influence and coercion and as such it is perfectly enforceable in law.

10. The agreement Ext. 2 was between the pltff. And defdt. Nos. 1 and 2. If the defdts wanted to get out of the contract on the ground of undue influence and coercion it was absolutely essential for them to take oath before the court and depose it they so liked; but D.W. 1 flatly stated in cross-examination that he would not examine either defdt. No.1 or 2. Whatever might have been the consideration with D.W 1 to agree to the settlement, there is nothing on record to show that any undue influence or coercion was practiced upon the defdts to obtain the execution of the document Ext. 2. Even D. W. 1 did not say in his evidence that the defdts put their signatures in the agreement with any reservation. Since admittedly D.W. 1 was not a party to the agreement but he merely helped in the negotiation on behalf of the defdts, his evidence alone in our opinion, cannot be considered legally sufficient for the purpose of avoiding the agreement on the basis of alleged undue influence and coercion.

11. With regard to claim of defdts for Taka 50,000/- the subordinate judge found in his judgment that all the documents about the counter-claim were of dates beyond more than 3 years. Question arose whether limitation would be governed by article 62 or Article 89 of the Limitation Act. The defdts, contention was that since the plaintiff was their agent Article 89 was attracted and as such the counter claim was not barred by limitation even though it was made beyond 3 years. The learned subordinate judge upheld the contention of the defdts.

12. The learned advocate for the appellant has contended that the learned subordinate judge was wrong in holding that the plaintiff was an agent of the defendants. He has argued that there is a distinction between a servant and an agent and further that the defendts not having introduced expressly the concept of agency either in the written statement or in the deposition the plaintiff could not but be held to be servant of the defendants.

13. An agent has been defined by section 182 of the Contract Act to be a person employed to do any act for another or to represent another in dealing with third person. Notwithstanding this wide definition an agent is to be distinguished on the one hand from a servant, and on the other from an independent contractor. A servant acts under the direct control and supervision of his master, and is bound to conform to all reasonable orders given him in the course of his work; an independent contractor, on the other hand is entirely independent of any control or interference and merely undertakes to produce a specified result, employing his own means to produce that result. An agent though bound to exercise his authority in accordance with all lawful instructions which may be given to him from time to time by his principal, is not subject in its exercise to the direct control or supervision of the principal. An agent, as such, is not a servant, but a servant is generally for some purposes, his master's agent the extent of the agency depending upon duties or position of the servant, and in some cases an independent contractor may also be an agent (Halsbury's) Laws of England. (Third edition) Volume 1 page 145-146.

The Indian Supreme Court in the case of Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son Ltd. Vs. The Government of Hyderabad reported in 1955 S.C. Reports vol. I page 393 corresponding to A.I.R 1954 S.C. 364 noticed the aforesaid distinction between the different categories of employment while dealing with the subject of agency. In the case of Shalagram Jhajharia Vs. National Co. Ltd. & others, reported in 69 CWN 369 Bose C.J upon noticing the definition of agent as under the Contract Act observed that the relationship is to be determined not by name but by conduct of the parties and the purport of their dealings. It is, therefore, clear that it requires to be decided in the facts of each case whether a particular employment could be said to be one in the course of agency irrespective of by whatever name the employment is designated. In the instant case, however, we find it difficult to agree with the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the plaintiff was merely a servant of the defendants and not an agent for the simple reason that besides salary the plaintiff admittedly was used to be paid commission on the sale proceeds of the firm. This incentive by way of giving commission to the plaintiff shows that he was afforded a latitude in the matter of augmenting the sale of the firm and thus he could earn as much as he could work in his volition. In other words, be had a discretion in the matter of sale. There is nothing in the evidence to show that defendants could in any manner interfere with the plaintiff's job of selling on behalf of the firm.

14. We propose to examine the question of limitation on the footing that the plaintiff was an agent of the defendant. Article 89 of the Limitation Act provides for a suit by a principal against his agent for moveable property received by the latter and not accounted for. It prescribes a limitation of 3 years from the time when the account .is, during the continuance of the agency, demanded and refused, or where no such demand is made, when the agency terminates. There are two aspects to be considered in this particular case, firstly, whether the counter claim of the defendants was at all made bonafide and secondly, whether such a claim could be made without a proper suit for accounts. In the instant case there is absolutely nothing either in the pleading or in the evidence that account was even demanded of the plaintiff during the tenure of his service with the defendants. The plaintiff's service was admittedly terminated on and from September 9, 1966. The defendants can claim the limitation to run from that day provided it can be shown that something remained unaccounted for on that date. There is nothing in the evidence of D.W. 1 that anything remained due from the plaintiff on the date of agreement Ext.2. Admittedly the dispute between the parties arose since May 1966 and D.W. 1 had access to all the books of accounts of the firm He admitted in his evidence that he looked after the business of the firm though the management was with the plaintiff. 'The plaintiff stated in his evidence that he used to hand over the sale-proceeds of the firm to Mr. Fazlur Rahman daily. This statement of the plaintiff has not been challenged in cross-examination. P.W.3 Abdul Huq, an old pensioner of the neighborhood of the firm, deposed that he saw Mr. Fazlur Rahman to come daily to 27, Hatkhala Road in the evening and to examine all books of accounts. There is nothing on record to show that D.W. 1 laid any claim against the plaintiff at any point of time even during the arbitration when the claim of the plaintiff was being settled. That there was no claim of the defendants which was not accounted for by the plaintiff on the date of the termination of his service on 7.9.66 will be further evident from the defendant's own letter addressed to the plaintiff as late as on April 27; 1967 Ext. 5(e). Even in that letter the defendants made no claim whatsoever against the plaintiff although Mr. Fazlur Rahman stated in his evidence that with 4/5 months from September. 1966 he came to know of the fishy deals of the plaintiff after checking the books of account. D.W. 1 however, alleged in his evidence that he had made several demands from the plaintiff through third persons on the basis that huge amount was due from him but Mr. Fazlur Rahman could not name any of those persons nor he could give even the approximate time of making such demands. The predicament of this scholar witness is easily understandable. That the claim of the defendants is absolutely baseless can best be appreciated by the significant fact that the defendants never made any claim against the plaintiff until the filing of the written statement. From the circumstances of the case we felt absolutely certain that the counter-claim of the defendants was nothing but an afterthought and was advanced more on the theory that offence is the best form of defence. Since there is no material to hold that anything remained unaccounted for by the plaintiff-or that there was a claim even in that behalf on the date of termination of his service it is apparent that article 89 had no manner of application and thus the claim of the defendants could not escape the bar of limitation. The learned Advocate has rightly argued that the question of limitation as referred to above has been wrongly decided by the learned subordinate Judge.

15. The learned Advocate for the appellant has further argued that in the facts and circumstances of the case the Subordinate Judge ought not to have allowed a decree in favour of the defendants on the basis of their own accounting without specific prayer for rendering of accounts by the plaintiff. The submission of the learned Advocate seems to have considerable substance. The summary way in which the Subordinate Judge allowed the claim of the defendants betrays his lack of appreciation of the facts of the case and, particularly because the claim could not be allowed in that manner as admittedly the plaintiff had his own claim against the defendants notwithstanding the finding of the Subordinate Judge that the agreement Ext. 2 was obtained by undue influence and Coercion. Even otherwise, the learned Subordinate Judge while considering the defendants claim overlooked the material statements of the plaintiff that Mr. Fazlur Rhman used to receive the sale-proceeds of the firm daily and this statement of the plaintiff has remained unchallenged. The learned Subordinate Judge also ignored that Mr. Fazlur Rahman himself admitted in his cross-examination that he did not produce the payment register of the employed, the commission register sale registers of 1962-66, deposit and withdrawal register from different Banks, cash receipt of 1963-66 and the sale bills of 1963-66. It is in the evidence of Mr. Fazlur Rahman himself that he used to receive cash on many occasions of which he neither granted any receipt nor deposited the same in the Bank. We wonder how in the face of such evidence the Subordinate Judge could allow the claim of the defendants, particularly having regard to the manner in which it was claimed. Having gone through the evidence in the case we cannot help observe that the conduct of the plaintiff was above board in so far as the present transaction namely the agreement Ext. 2 was concerned. But we cannot say the same insofar as the defendant and their case are concerned.

16. In such view of the matter we are of the opinion that the defendants not having brought a suit for accounts they were not entitled to the relief in the manner claimed. In the circumstances of the case and in view of our findings above we do not consider it necessary to examine the defendants counterclaim on merit. We are clearly of the opinion that the learned Subordinate Judge illegally allowed the counter-claim of the defendants which is, accordingly, liable to be set aside

In the result the appeal is allowed, the impugned judgment and decree are set aside and the suit is decree with costs throughout in favour of the plaintiff. We direct that the defendants shall pay the plaintiff Taka 37,960/- and the decretal costs within two (2) months from the date of signing of the decree.

Ranadhir Sen J.-I agree.

End.

case_source: Appeal against the order of Mr. M. J. Chowdhury, Subordinate Judge of Zilla Kushtia dated the 9th day of November 1966 passed in Misc. Appeal No. 14 of 1966 affirming the order of Mr. A. H. Chowdhury Munsif 2nd Court Kushtia dated the 6th day of April 1966 in Misc. Case No. 100 of 1965.
full_judgment:
This second Miscellaneous appeal arises out of the lower appellate court affirming an order 1 of the trial Court dismissing a Miscellaneous case under section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure objecting to the execution of a com-promise decree passed in suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession of a disputed land. The main ground for objection was that the second term of compromise as contained in the solenama, Ext. A was not complied with by the plaintiff decree-holder and in such circumstances the compromise decree could not be put into execution. In accordance with the provision of solenama pursuant to the compromise decree which was passed by the trial court, the plaintiff decree-holder was obliged to execute a document within a given time in favour of the defendant-judgment debtor transferring a portion of the suit land as specified in the solenama itself. Admittedly, without complying with the terms of the solenama the plaintiff-decree holder put the compromise decree into execution when the defendant judgment debtor objected thereto on that ground. <u>The courts below dismissed the objection of the defendant judgment-debtor mainly on the ground that the executing court could not go beyond the decree as such. In a decree passed by a court on com-promise between the parties concerned where-in the terms of the compromise have been made as part of the decree, the executing court is obliged to see whether the terms of compromise have been complied with by the party concerned while executing the decree. The courts below in overlooking such omission on the part of the plaintiff decree holder evidently erred in dismissing the defendant-judgment debtor's objection to the execution case. For these reasons the judgment of the Sub-ordinate Judge of Kushtia passed on 9th November, 1966 in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 14 of 1966 affirming order No. 8 dated 6-4-66 passed by the second Munsif of Kushtia in Miscellaneous case No. 100 of 1965 arising out of Title Execution case No. 42 of 1965 is set-aside. The defendant judgment debtors objection under section 47 CPC is hereby allowed. The plaintiff-decree holder is, however, granted further time to comply with its obligation to transfer the agreed part of the suit land to the defendant judgment debtor by a registered deed of conveyance as referred to in the second term of the petition of compromise, Ext. A within two months from depositing the registration costs and stamp duty by the defendant judgment debtor before the executing court. The defendant judgment debtor shall deposit registration costs and stamp duty before the executing court within two months from the arrival of the records of this case along with the order of the court. If the defendant judgment debtor fails to deposit the registration fee and stamp duty, etc within the given time, the execution case shall proceed as usual against him. Even if after depositing the registration cost and stamp duty by the defendant-judgment debtor before the executing court. The plaintiff decree-holder fails to execute and register the deed of conveyance within the given time, as mentioned herein before, the execution case shall stand dismissed.</u>

<u>With the aforesaid direction this appeal is disposed of without any order as to costs. Let the records be sent down expeditiously.</u>

End.

lawyer:
Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed. Senior Advocate (Mahbubey Alam, Advocate with him) instructed by Md. Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant.
