case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 9.2.1984 passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Bench in Second Appeal No. 44 of 1980).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J : This appeal by the plaintiff by special leave is from the judgment and decree of a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, Camilla Bench, in Second Appeal in affirmance of those of the first appellate Court which allowed the appeal and dismissed the appellant's suit for partition. The trial Court decreed the suit:

2. The appellant's suit for partition being Partition Suit No. 34 of 1974 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Comilla, filed on 23.2.72, was based on the averments, inter alia, that the appellant's father Raj Kumar and the father of defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 Surya Kumar were brothers. They took joint settlement of the suit land, a tiny town property at Comilia, in 1934 and started living there together after erecting huts as monthly tenants of the land. Raj Kumar died in 1939. The landlords filed Title Suit No. 170 of 1940 in the 3rd Court of Munsif, Comilla for arrearrent and eviction against Surya Komar and the heirs of Raj Kumar including the appellant. The landlords did not press the claim for eviction and were satisfied with a decree for rent only on 5.9.50. It was further averred by the plaintiff-appellant in his plaint that both the plaintiff and the defendants had no title to the suit land on the date of filing of the said suit for eviction. But after the decree they continued to occupy and possess the suit land as tenants. The appellant in course of time became full 8-anna owner of the suit land upon the successive deaths of the other heirs of Raj Kumar. The appellant's mother shifted to her brother's house at Shimulia about 12 years, back and died there. The appellant worked and lived elsewhere at Com ilia town, but continued to occupy a kerosene tin shed in the suit land which yielded to decay about 9 or 10 years back. The appellant wanted to marry and raise a new hut on the suit land only to be obstructed by his uncle on the plea that the suit land had been recorded in his name. The matter was referred to the adjudication of the Union Committee but Surya Kumar would have none of.it. The appellant has since married and had been living with his wife at Comilla town elsewhere. Surya Kumar died in April, 1971 and his heirs, the defendant-respondents, went to Kachar following crackdown of Pak Army in 1971. The appellant also made good his escape to Tripura in 1971. In January, 1972 the appellant came back and occupied the disputed homestead where he is living now with his family members. The R.S. khatian has been wrongly prepared in the name of Surya Kumar. He demands 8 as share of the suit land by partition of the joint family homestead by metes and bounds.

3. Defendant-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filed a joint written statement contesting the suit. They contend that the appellant has no right, title and interest in the suit land. Surya Kumar alone obtained settlement of the suit land from the landlord. Raj Kumar did not erect any hut in the suit land. He died in the house of one Monohar Mistry in 1346 B.S. The appellant's mother died at Shimulia 16 or 17 years back and thereafter the appellant lived at Laksham and elsewhere. The disputed huts arc not in ejmali and the appellant has not acquired any interest in the disputed property. The defendants are in possession of the disputed property by inheritance from their father who had exclusive interest and title in the same. Since 1943 it is the father of the defendants who had been paying rents and taxes.

4. It is the concurrent finding of both the Courts below and the High Court Division that neither the plaintiff-appellant nor the defendant-respondents could prove by any documentary evidence that either Raj Kumar or Surya Kumar or both had obtained any settlement of the suit land from the landlord. The trial Court held that the plaintiff-appellant proved title by adverse possession and under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. Taking the view that the appellant was a co-sharer in the suit land the suit was decreed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla by his judgment and decree dated 29.4.74.

5. On appeal the learned Additional District Judge, Comilla by his judgment and decree dated 23.3.79 passed in Title Appeal No. 156 of 1974 re-versed the judgment and decree of the trial Court on the finding that the record of rights stands in the name of Surya Kumar and admittedly the appellant had no title to the suit land when the suit for eviction was filed in 1940 and, further, no documentary evidence being there that the tenancy right of the appellant's predecessor was perfected under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act the suit for simple partition was not maintainable without a prayer for declaration of title to the suit land. The appellant has no prima facie title to the suit land and no legal possession therein within 12 years from the date of filing of the suit on 23.2.72. The plaintiff's document Ext. 1, certified copy of assessment register of 1938-39, and the isolated piece of union tax receipt are also not connected with the suit property. By judgment and decree dated 23.3.79 the lower appellant Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit.

6. In Second Appeal No. 44 of 1980 the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division noticed both the Courts below took cognizance of the appellant's statement in the plaint that till 1940 the appellant could not acquire any valid title to the disputed property. The learned Single Judge held that in the face of this admission the trial Court was obviously wrong in holding that if any title accrued to Raj Kumar that might have been by way of adverse possession and under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, ignoring that Raj Kumar had already died in 1939. The lower appellate Court's finding the suit was not maintainable without declaration of tit to the suit land was upheld and the appeal was dis-missed by the judgment and decree dated 9.2.84.

7. Leave was granted to the plaintiff-appellant to consider whether the findings of the lower appellate Court as maintained by the High Court Division are based on misinterpretation of documents, Exts. 1-4 including rent receipt, assessment register and the plaint and decree of Title Suit No. 170 of 1940; whether in view of operation of section 7 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 a non-ejectable right of tenancy was conferred upon the appellant as a non-agricultural tenant when the landlord decided not to take possession and was satisfied only with a rent decree; whether the payment of rents by the appellant's predecessor, dismissed by the High Court Division as documents not creating any title, is an unchallenged evidence of the appellant's possession, especially when these are the basis of the trial Court's decision on adverse possession and when the trial Court's finding on adverse possession is undisturbed by the lower appellate Court and the High Court Division.

8. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellant, submits than there has been a total non-consideration of Exts. 3 and 4, certified copies of the plaint and decree in Title Suit No. 170 of 1940 both by the lower appellate Court and the High Court Division. Both the two Courts misread the statement of the appellant in the plaint that upto 1940 he and his predecessors had acquired no title to the suit land. The said two Courts also did not consider the appellant's evidence on continued possession from the creation of the tenancy in 1934 upto at least 1959. Exts. 1 and 2 have not been properly considered by the said two Courts.

9. Mr. M. Nurullah, the learned counsel for the defendant-respondents, submits, on the other hand, that Exts. 3 and 4 did not confer the status of non-agricultural tenant upon the appellant. The lower appellate Court has fully discussed the evidence on possession and found the appellant and the other heirs of Raj Kumar not possessing the suit land at least 12 years before the institution of the suit. Exts. 1 and 2 were also noticed and dealt with by the lower appellate Court.

10. The landlords who filed the suit for eviction in 1940 stated in the plaint Ext. 3 that the two brothers Raj Kumar and Surya Kumar obtained monthly tenancy of the suit land from Baisakh 1341 B.S. on a monthly rent of Tk. 2'50. The tenancy, therefore, started in 1934. The suit for eviction was filed in 1940. The decree, however, was passed on 5.9.50. The landlords did not press the prayer for khas possession of the suit land. The suit was de-creed for Tk. 22'50 being rent of the-'suit land from Sravana to Chaitra of 1346 B.S. at the rate of Tk. 2.50 per month.

11. This decree, Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits, brings the appellant within the ambit and protection of section 7(2) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, which is as follows :

"7. Incidents of certain Tenancies.— Not-withstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract.

(1)  (2) If the non-agricultural land comprised in any tenancy which has been or is created after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, (IV of 1982), has been held for a period of not less than twelve years without any lease in writing, or

(3)

(4)

(5)

(a)

(n)

then—

(i) the tenant holding the non-agricultural land comprised in such tenancy shall not be ejected by his landlord from such land except on the ground that he has used such land in a manner which renders it unfit for use for any of the purposes specified in section 4;

(ii)

and

(iii)

12. Mr. Islam submits that the plaint of Title Suit No. 170 of 1940 Ext. 3 unmistakably shows that the suit land was settled in 1934 not with Surya Kumar alone but with both the brothers and in 1940 when the suit for rent and eviction was filed the heirs of Raj Kumar were found to be in joint possession of the suit land and hence they were made defendants by the landlord. The decree was obtained in 1950, but the appellant's possession will be treated to be continuous from 1934 to 1950 in view of section 88 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 which is as follows :

"88. Application of the provisions of the Act to all pending suits, appeals and proceedings and unexecuted decrees, for ejectment—The provisions of this Act shall apply to all suits, appeals and proceedings including proceedings in execution for the ejectment of a non-agricultural tenant which are pending at the date of the commencement of this Act and also to all decrees passed for the ejectment of a non-agricultural tenant which have not been executed and are not barred by limitation and in respect of which no proceedings in execution are so pending, and the tenants against whom such suits, appeals or proceedings are so pending or such decrees have been passed shall not be liable to be ejected on any grounds except under the provisions of this Act."

13. This submission of Mr. Islam need not detain us for long. The father of the appellant Raj Kumar admittedly died in 1939. The interest of monthly tenancy did not devolve upon the heirs of Raj Kumar after his death in 1939. The definition of non-agricultural tenancy in the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 contained in section 2(5) is as follows:

"2(5). Non-agricultural tenant means a person who holds non-agricultural land under another person with consent of that person and is, or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay rent to such person for that land and also includes the successors-in-interest of the former but does not include any person who holds any such land on which any premises occupied by such person are situated if such premises have been erected, or are owned by the person to whom such occupier is or but for a special contract would be, liable to pay rent for such occupation ;

Explanation.—In this clause "premises" mean any building such as a house, manufactory, warehouse, stable, shop or but whether constructed of masonry, bricks, concrete, wood, mud, metal or any other material whatsoever and includes any land appertaining to such building."

<u>14. The said definition will apply prospectively so as to include the successors-in-interest of tenants. When the appellant's father died in 1939, no existing law conferred the status of tenants upon the successors-in-interest of tenants. Even the Bengal Act No. IX of 1940 did not do so. If the appellant and the other heirs of Raj Kumar continued to occupy the suit land after Raj Kumar's death in 1939, they could only be treated as trespassers, not as tenants. That is why the landlords sued them for eviction as trespassers. The protection of section 88 is not available to the appellant because on the date of coming into force of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 the appellant was not holding any land as a tenant. Nor is the benefit of section 7(2) available to the appellant because the non-agricultural land which he was holding since 1939 was not 'comprised in any tenancy'. The question of counting 12 years from 1934 does not arise at all. With the death of Raj Kumar in 1939 his successors-in-interest became simply trespassers.</u>

15. Mr. Mahrnudul Islam has made much of the observations of the lower appellate Court and the High Court Division to the effect that the appellant admitted in the plaint lack of acquisition of title upto 1940. The appellant averred that no non-agricultural tenancy right was acquired by both the plaintiff and the defendants when the suit for eviction was filed in 1940. The omission to notice the full statements in the plaint is not material, because the appellant's admission in the plaint, although meant to be applicable to both the plaintiff and the defendants, is nevertheless a correct statement insofar as the appellant is concerned, because he had never acquired the status of a non-agricultural tenant after 1939. After 1939 he remained a trespasser all throughout.

16. Mr. Islam has strenuously argued that by accepting a decree for rent the appellant has been admitted as a tenant by the landlords. This submission is also not correct. As already noticed, the decree in Title Suit. No. 170 of 1940, Ext. 4, was for Tk. 22'50 being rent for the months of Sravana to Chaitra, 1346, B.S. at the rate of Tk. 2'50. The decree was not passed for any rent after 1346 B.S. i.e. after 1939, when Raj Kumar died. Factually the appellant was not recognised as a tenant even in 1950 when the decree was passed.

17. Ext. 1, the certified copy of assessment register of 1938-39, is not connected with the suit property in any manner and Ext. 2, municipal receipt showing payment of rent on 4.4.69 for 1967-68 when the appellant was admittedly not in possession, is also of no use to the appellant. The lower appellate Court has duly considered these two exhibits and the appellant's contention that these two exhibits were not considered by the lower appellate Court is not correct.

<u>18. The appellant never prayed for partition on the basis that he or his predecessor acquired title to the suit property by adverse possession. Title by adverse possession has to be specifically pleaded and proved. The appellant's case was one of acquisition of title by settlement. The trial Court found that the case of settlement has not been proved, but it conferred title on the appellant on a gratuitous finding of adverse possession in his favour, unwarranted by pleadings. This gratuitous conferment of title was uncalled for in a suit for partition where the plaintiff's claim of title is to be looked into incidentally. If the precise title to which he lays his claim is not supported by the evidence on record, the Court can-not find out another source of title for the plaintiff by way of gratuitous relief.</u>

19. Hence on all counts we find that the impugned judgment does not merit any interference.

The appeal is dismissed with costs.

End.

lawyer:

full_judgment:
Nurul Huque Bhuiyan, J: This appeal at the instance of the defendants is directed against the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st. Court, Dhaka passed in Title Suit No. 301 of 1980 decreeing the suit for specific performance of contract. 

2. The plaintiffs respondents instituted the sun against the defendants appellants and preform defendant-respondent in the said court of the Subordinate Judge praying, inter alia:- (a) that a decree for specific performance of the contract be passed in favour of the plaintiffs and to direct the principal-defendants (defendants No. 1-3) to execute and register the deed of sale in respect of /12/- annas share of the suit firm in respect of the properties described in the schedule and/or reconstitute the partnership 10 the extent of that share in favour of the plaintiffs within the time to be fixed by the court; (b) that on failure of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to execute an register the necessary deed of sale and/or the partnership deed within the time fixed by the court, an order may kindly be passed for execution and registration of the same through court at the expense of the plaintiffs. 

3. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that the defendant No.1 Abul Hasan Khan and other 15 members of his family were the partners of M/s. East Pa- Kistna Aluminum and Iron Manufacturing Company, now Bangladesh Aluminum and Iron Manufacturing Company having office and factory at plot No. III and lO8/C, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka. In the middle of June, 1973 the defendant No.1 announced to sell out the /12/- annas share of the suit industry and the plaintiffs offered to purchase the said-/12/- annas share at a consideration of TIc 8,OO,000/-(Taka eight laces) being the highest market price at the time on conditions that the plaintiffs would deposit Tk. 45,OOO/-(Taka forty five thousand) as advance within 31st December, 1973 in the personal joint account of defendant No. 1 and his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan and after deposit of the said amount the defendant NO.1 would dissolve the then existing firm with his 15 relations (including Ehsanul Hasan Khan) and would reconstitute the said firm with defendant No. 1 and his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan as partners and thereafter the plaintiffs would sell out their residential house of Gulshan to make payment of the balance of Tk. 7,55,OOO/-(Taka seven laces fifty five thousand) and the formal deed of partnership would be executed between the defendant No.1, his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan and the plaintiffs. The further stipulation was that the plaintiffs would enjoy the profit and bear loss of the business proportionate to the aforesaid advance of Tk.45,000/- till execution and registration of the deed of partner- ship after full payment of the balance of Tk. 7,55,000/-. In pursuance of the oral contract the plaintiffs in good faith made payment of Tk.30,000/- on 19.6.73 in the name of the defendant NO.1 and Ehsanul Hasan Khan in A/C No. 19164 with the National and Grindlays Bank (now Grindlays Bank) and Tk. 15,000/- on 12.12.73 in the same account in the name of Ehsanul Hasan Khan. Since the payment of Tk. 45,OOO/-the plaintiffs were requesting the defendant No.1 to dissolve and reconstitute the partnership so that the plaintiffs could sell out their one storied building on 11 Kathas 8 Chhataks of land in Gulshan model town, Dhaka to make payment of the balance consideration of Tk. 7,55,000/- as early as possible. As the aforesaid 15 partners of defendant No.1 were residing at different places the defendant No. 1 could not act as per his agreement for some legal difficulties and as such the defendant No. 1 was taking time after time to reconstitute the partnership between himself and his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan. The plaintiffs were therefore constrained to wait in consideration of the actual legal difficulties of the defendant No. 1 in the way of performance of his part of the agreement. Ultimately on 24.4.78 the defendant No.1 reconstituted the firm between himself and his brother defendant No. 2 Maqbul Hasan Khan (who had also knowledge of the aforesaid contract with the plaintiffs) in place of his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan. Thereafter on 15.5.78 the defendants handed over the photo stat copy of lease deed (between the C & B and the then M/s. East Pakistan Aluminum and Iron Manufacturing Company) and some other papers to the plaintiffs and asked them to pay the balance of Tk. 7,55,000/- after selling out their aforesaid residential house at Gulshan as early as possible. The plaintiffs sold out their residential house at Gulshan in good faith at a consideration of Tk. 10,00,000/- (Taka ten leas) and received Tk. 1,00,000/-as advance in the first week of October, 1978. The plaintiffs thereafter got the partnership deed drafted on 7.10.78 and supplied a typed copy of draft to the principal defendant on 8.10.78 for their perusal and approval. The plaintiffs received another sum of Tk. 4,00,000/- on 18.10.78 and they offered the entire balance amount of Tk. 5,00,000/- to the defendants requesting them to execute the partnership deed and to receive the said Tk. 5,00,000/- and to allow some time for payment of the balance of Tk. 2,55,000/-. The defendants did not receive the same and asked the plaintiffs to pay the entire amount at a time. The defendants assured the plaintiffs of the execution of the partnership deed on the date of full payment of the balance amount at a time. The plain-tiffs obtained the Income Tax clearance certificate and expected the execution and registration of the sale deed of the Gulshan house and received the balance consideration of Tk. 5,00,000/- (Talca five laces) on 12.12.78. Since 12.12.78 the plaintiffs were offering the balance of Tk. 7,55,000/- to the defendants but the defendants refused to accept the same and deferred the execution and registration of the proposed deed. The plaintiffs issued a legal notice dated 24.2.79 upon the defendants. The defendants refused to accept the notice on 26.2.79. The further case of the plain-tiffs is that on a wrong advice they filed Title Suit No. 146/1976 in the said court of the Subordinate Judge for dissolution of partnership and rendition of accounts but the said suit was subsequently with-drawn with permission of the court to sue afresh on same cause of action. Hence the instant suit. 

4. The defendant Nos.1-3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that there is no privet of contract of any nature in respect of the suit industry between the plaintiffs and the defendants. The suit is not maintainable. There, is 110,CatISC of action for the suit. The suit is void. The defendant No. 5 M/s. Bangladesh Aluminum and Iron Manufacturing Company came into existence on 12.3.51 and till 24.4.78 the suit firm was constituted and reconstituted on several occasions on 12.3.51, 8.3.52, 1.2.53, 31.3.56, 28.4.56, 2.2.60, 1.4.63, 1.11.76, 31.3.78 and lastly on 24.4.78. The constitutions and reconstitutions were sometimes be-tween the defendants 1 and 2, sometimes between defendants 1 and 2 and their wives, sometimes between defendants Nos. 1 and 2 and their family members and lastly between the defendants Nos. 1 and 2. The reconstitution on 1.11.76 was between defendant No. 1, his daughter Mst. Hasina Khatun and defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 1 had 47-1/2% share, Mst. Hasina Khatun had 2 -1/2% share and defendant No. 2 had 50% share in the partnership firm. The said firm was renamed as M/s. Bangladesh Aluminum And Iron Manufacturing Company which was previously known as M/s. East Pakistan Aluminum and Iron Manufacturing Company. The defendant No. 1 had personal acquaintance with plaintiff No. 1 whom he gave personal loan of Tk. 45,000/- on different occasions. The plaintiff No. 1 returned this amount to defendant No. 1 by depositing the amount in the private account of defendant No. 1 when there was no talk at all of the alleged sale or of making the plaintiffs as partners. However, in 1978 for the first time a negotiation started between the plaintiffs and the defendant No. 1 for outright sale of the firm but the same could not be finalised and no contractual agreement to sell either in writing or oral was arrived at between them. When the defendants refused to enter into the agreement for sale of the firm and its as-sets the plaintiffs brought the Title Suit No. 146 of 1979 mala fide claiming them selves to be the partners and prayed for dissolution of the fine in order to create pressure upon the defendants. The present suit is false, frivolous and vexatious and as such liable to be dismissed. 5. The following issues were framed by the learned Subordinate Judge:-1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form 2 Is the suit void  3. Is there any privet of contract between the plaintiffs and the defendants 4. Is the agreement, &any, entbreegbld in lava '5. Is the suit bad for defect of parties ?‘ 6. Is the suit barred by limitation 7. Are the plaintiffs guilty of ladies 8. Are the plaintiffs entitled to a decree for specific performance of contract as prayed for 6. The learned Subordinate Judge decided issue No. 1 in the affirmative and issue No. 2 in the negative. On other issues he came to the findings that the suit was not bad for defect of parties, that the suit was not barred by limitation, that the defendant No. 1 on full authority of other partners decided in the middle of June, 1973 to sell /12/- annas share of the suit industry to the plaintiffs, that the terms and conditions set out in paragraph 3 of the plaint are true, that the shop at 29, Patuatuly, Dhaka was not closed after the liberation movement and the same was not looted, that the genuineness of the diaries Ext. W series were doubtful and the Ext. W series particularly Ext. W(3)(a), W(3)(b), W(3)(c), W(6)(a) and W(6) (b) were false and ante dated, that the wealth statements Ext. Z-Z(2) were procured and could not be re- lied upon, that the defendants failed to prove the loan, that the deposit of Tk. 45,000/- as per Ext. 1 and l(a) was nothing but payment of earnest money towards the total consideration, that mere omission of the word "accepted" in the plaint was not fatal, that the value of the /12/- annas share of the suit industry was Tk. 8,00,000/- in the year 1973, that a new partnership was constituted on 24.4.78, Ext. L (7) between the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 instead of defendant No. 1 and his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan but the agreement was not affected as defendant No.2 also had knowledge and consent about the agreement, that plaintiffs committed no mistake by selling the house which they acquired subsequently, that from 16.6.73 to the filing of the suit there was no laches on the part of plaintiffs in pursuing to buy the suit industry and they were always vigilant and instrumental to have the deed of sale registered but the defendants always deferred the matter, that the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 and other partners who assembled in Dhaka on 1.11.70 and had knowledge and consent of oral agreement made in the middle of June, 1973 and that the defendant No. I acted for himself as well as on behalf of all the partners and accordingly it was a case of assignment by all the partners and not by the defendant No. I alone, that the firm is a collective name of its members and it is not algal person with separate entity, and that defendant No.3 firm has had no legal entity other than the defendant Nos. I and 2 whose agreement is binding upon the firm, that the agreement was not vitiated by fraud, undue influence, misrepresentation, etc. that the assertion of the defendants that the talk of sale of the suit industry in 1978 was not finalised and when they re- fused the plaintiff-brought the suit is not convincing, that no evidence was adduced by the defendants that plaintiffs were friendly with defendants, etc. On the above findings the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit holding that all the issues were in favour of the plaintiffs. Against the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge the principal defendant Nos. 1-3 have preferred this appeal to this court. 
7. Mr. T.H. Khan, the learned Advocate for the appellants, has taken us through the plaint, written statement, evidence and the judgment under appeal. He has submitted that the alleged contract being an oral contract it was a vital necessity for the plaintiffs to mention in their plaint the dates when and the places where the talk of the alleged contract was held and the tender of balance consideration was made and the names of the persons who attended the alleged talk and tender and the omissions to mention these facts in the plaint are vital omission and the subsequent introduction of the dates, places of talk of the alleged contract and tender of the balance consideration as well as the names of the persons who allegedly attended the talk and tender for the first time in the cross-examination of P.W. I plaintiff NO.1 as noted below are after-thought and creation for the suit and these omissions and subsequent introduction make the plaintiffs' case of oral contract unbelievable. 

8, Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned Advocate for the respondents, has in reply submitted that the dates and places of the talk of the contract and tender of the balance consideration and the names of the witnesses need not be mentioned in the plaint as according to him the plaint gave the defendants sufficient notice as to what was the plaintiffs' case and as to what the plaintiffs would prove in the case: The plaintiffs re- lied upon the talk of contract arid the tender of balance consideration of money and the witnesses to the said talk and tender for establishing their claim in the suit and as such it was a vital necessity for the plain- tiffs to mention in the plaint the dates, places and names of witnesses and omissions to mention them in the plaint are vital omissions. The omissions of these facts and the subsequent introduction thereof for the first time in the cross-examination of P.W. 1 are, in our opinion, after-thought and creation for the suit and they make the plaintiffs' case of oral contract highly unbelievable. The dates and places o. the alleged talk of alleged contract and tender of balance consideration and the names of the persons who at- tended them are, in our opinion, material facts and the plaintiffs having omitted to mention them in the plaint' they can not be permitted to give evidence thereof at the trial in view of Order 6, rule 2, Civil Procedure Code without amendment of the plaint un- der Order 6, rule 17, C.P.C. and that the evidence given on these facts can not be looked into and the plaintiffs can not build up their case on these facts rich they failed to set up in their plaint. This view f Ids support in the case of Sarwar Khan Vs. Gulam sarwar and others, P.L.D. 1982 A,J. & K. 126. The zamed Subordinate Judge seriously erred in having .ailed to consider this vital aspect of the case. 
9. Mr. T.H. Khan has next submitted that the word "accepted" does not find place in the plaint but it was subsequently introduced in the evidence and as such the very foundation that could constitute the contract is missing in the plaint and therefore the contract is not a concluded one. !v1r.Moinul Huq has argued that the fact that the defendant No. 1 announced to sell and the plaintiffs offered to purchase as stated in paragraph 3 of the plaint means that the plaintiffs accepted the offer and as such the offer and acceptance are there and the contract is a concluded one, On perusal of paragraph 3 of the plaint we find that the plaintiffs did not make any offer and the defendant No. 1 did not accept any offer of the plain- tiffs but he only announced to sell and this can not be read as defendant No. 1 's accepting the offer and therefore the learned Subordinate Judge erred in assuming that the offer was accepted by the defendants and that the omission of the word "accepted" in the plaint was not fatal. We think that the omission of the word "accepted" in the plaint means that the very foundation that could constitute the contract is missing and this can not be filled in evidence as is sought to be done by the plaintiffs. As the foundation of the contract is missing in the plaint the contract is not a concluded contract and as such not enforceable. The learned Subordinate Judge wrongly applied the principle laid down in the case of Ram Singh Kundan Singh and sons and another Vs. Ram Chand Izards, A.I.R. 1925 Sind 342 namely, that in case of oral agreement payment of earnest money to vender would show that offer of purchase had been accrued by the vendor and the contract was concluded. III the case reported in A.I. it 1925 Sind 342 payment of earnest money was admitted by the Vendor but in the instant case the payment of earnest money is denied by the alleged Vendors, the defendants. The case in A.I.R. 1925 Sind 342 is thus distinguishable from the instant case on facts and as such the said case in not applicable in the instant case. 

10. In order to give an idea as to what is meant by "concluded contract" Mr. T.H. Khan has referred us to the case of Y.AJ. Noorul Hai and anothers Vs. S.P.L.K.R. Karuppan Chettiyar A.I.R. 1925 P.C. 232 wherein the Privy Council observed: "A contract is concluded when in the minds of each contracting party there is consensus ad idem and a modification or revocation of the contract requires a like consensus." Thus we find from the Privy Council decision in A.I.R. 1925 P.C. 232 that unless the minds of the contracting parties meet or concur there can be no concluded contract. We fully agree with Mr. T. H. Khan that the very foundation of the contract namely, "acceptance" is missing. Therefore, the con- tract is not a concluded contract and as such not enforceable. 

11. Mr. T.H. Khan has then submitted that in view of the reconstitution proposal in the alleged contract between the defendant No.1 and his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan, the reconstitution of the partnership firm between defendant Nos. 1 and 2 instead of between defendant No. 1 and his said son is a violation of the alleged contract and for this violation the entire contract fails. Mr. Moinul Huq's reply to this submission of Mr. T.H. Khan is that defendant Nos. i and 2 reconstituted the firm between themselves and the defendant No.2 had knowledge of the con- tract between defendant No. 1 and the plaintiffs and the other partners were silent and did not raise any objection after the dissolution and reconstitution and as such there was a new contract between defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the contract of 1973 was legally no voted in 1978 as per the provisions of section 62 of the Contract Act to which Mr. T.H. Khan says that story of novation should have been pleaded and evidence should have been adduced thereon. Section 62 of the Contract Act provides:- "If the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it, or to rescind or alter it, the original contract need not be performed." When the parties to a contract agree to substitute a new contract for it, it is known as no vatic or novation. 

12. in the instant case there is nothing on record to show that the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiffs i.e. the parties to the alleged contract agreed to substitute a new contract for the original contract and as such there was no novation in the instant case as per provision of section 62 of the Con- tract Act. Therefore, the reconstitution of the firm between the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is by no stretch of imagination a novation within the meaning of section 62 of the Contract Act. The alleged reconstitution of the firm was to be between defendant NO.1 and his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan as per the terms of the alleged contract but the reconstitution of the firm was between defendant Nos. 1 and 2 instead of be- tween defendant No.1 and his said son. The reconstitution was, therefore, in violation of the alleged contract and for this violation we think the entire contract fails. 

13. Mr. T.H. Khan has argued that the defendant No.1 had no authority to enter into the alleged contract on behalf of the other partners and as such the alleged contract is illegal. According to Mr. Moinul Huq, everything was a family arrangement between the partners and the defendant No. 1 had con- sent of all other partners and as such had full authority to enter into (he contract in 1973. 

14. Whether defendant NO.1 had authority and consent of ali other partners to enter into the contract is a matter of evidence and consent of other partners has to be proved in the case but nobody has proved consent of other partners in the case and in the absence of any evidence it can not be said that the defendant No.1 had authority and consent of all other partners. Therefore defendant No. 1 had no authority to enter into the contract in 1973 and the learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that a new partnership was constituted by deed of Partnership Ext. L (7) between the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 instead of defendant No. 1 and his son Ehsanul Hasan Khan and the contract was not affected as according to the learned Judge defendant No.2 had knowledge and consent about the contract. The learned Advocate for the defendants retired to the case of Addonzi Narayanappa and another Vs. Bhaskar Krishnappa (dead) and thereafter his heir- and others. In A.I.R. 1966 SC 1300 before the learned Subordinate Judge. Mr. T.H. Khan also has relied upon this case. In this case it was held that during the subsistence of the partner- ship no partner could deal with portion of the property as his own. In the instant case according to the plaintiffs defendant No. 1 entered into the alleged oral contract in the middle of June, 1973 which means that the defendant No. 1 as a partner of the partnership firm dealt with the property of the firm as his own. In A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1300 the question was whether one partner could deal with portion of the property of the partnership firm as his own during the subsistence of the partnership. In the above fact the principle of law laid down in the said case must be applicable in the instant case. The learned Subordinate Judge too erred in assuming that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and other partners of the firm assembled on 1.11.76 in Dhaka and they had knowledge and consent of the oral contract allegedly made in the middle of June, 1973 and that defendant No. 1 acted for himself as well as on behalf of all other partners. The learned Subordinate Judge erred in not applying the principle laid in A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1300 in the present case on the misconception that facts of the said case are not similar to those of the present case as according to him there is evidence that out of the 16 partners, 13 partners retired or withdrew on 1.11.76 and another retired on 31.3.78. As the partners excepting defendant No. 2 did not come forward to say that they did not authorize defendant No.1 to sell -/12/- annas share of the suit industry to the plaintiffs the learned Subordinate Judge held the erroneous view that it was a case of assignment by all the partners and not by defendant No.1 alone. In this connection it may be pointed out that there is nothing on record to show that all the partners assembled on 1.11.76 in Dhaka. Further, the other partners except defendant No. 2 not being made parties to the suit and there being no evidence on record to show that they had knowledge about the contract the question of their coming forward to say that they did not authorise defendant No. 1 to sell the /12/- annas share of the suit industry to the plaintiffs does not at all arise. The said finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is therefore not tenable. In the light of the decision in A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1300 we hold that the defendant No. l's alleged oral contract with the plaintiffs in the middle of June, 1973 dealing with the property of the partnership firm as his own is illegal, void and inoperative. 15. The learned Advocate for the plaintiffs referred to the learned Subordinate Judge the case of Scodayal Khemka and another Vs. Jahar Mull Man Mull and others, A.I.R. 1924 Cal 74. In this case it was held:-"A firm as such can not be a member of a partnership. A partnership under section 239 is a relationship which subsists between persons; but a firm is not a person, it is not an entity; it is merely a collective name for the individuals who are members of the partnership. It is neither a legal entity, nor is it a person. A firm name, in truth, is merely a description of the individuals who compose the firm. It is that, and it is nothing more." While commenting on this case the learned Suborders us Judge committed an error in holding that agreement (if any) of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is binding upon the firm defendant No. 3, inasmuch as defendant No. 1 entered into the agreement without authority or consent of the other partners. 16. Mr. T.H. Khan has further argued that the plaintiffs did nothing during the period from 1973 to 1978 in pursuance of the alleged contract and there was thus serious laches on the part of the plaintiffs in fulfillment of the contract. Mr. Moinul Huq has in reply said that the plaintiffs pursued the contract and went on requesting the defendant No. 1 to fulfill it but the defendant No. 1 could not fulfill the contract for some difficulties and that P.W. 1 is supported by other witnesses on this point. 17. We find that no step whatever was taken by the plaintiffs in fulfillment of the alleged contract from 1973 to 1975. The plaintiffs did not even send a letter asking defendant No. 1 to accept the money and to execute and register the sale deed during the long period from 1973 to 1978 and in such a situation the oral evidence of some of the P.Ws. on this point can not be relied upon. The laches on the part of the plaintiffs in failing to take any step from 1973 to 1978 to fulfill the alleged contract is truly serious and it strikes at the root of the plaintiffs' case of contract. The deposition of the plaintiff No. 1 as P.W. 1 in his cross-examination as: noted below to the fact that from middle of June, 1973 to 25.3.80 he was under the impression that he was a partner of the firm leads to the irresistible conclusion that the plaintiffs took no step towards fulfillment of the alleged contract during the period from middle of June, 1973 to 25.3.80. Therefore learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that from 16.6.73 to the date of filing the suit there was no laches on the part of the plaintiffs in pursuing to buy the suit industry and they were always vigilant and instrumental to have the deed of sale registered but the defendants al-ways deferred the matter. As regards non-disclosure of material facts and laches Mr. T.H. Khan has sub-mitted by making reference to the case of S.M. Wali Ahmed Chowdhury and another Vs. Mahfuzul Huq Chowdhury and others P.L.D. 1957 Da 209 that specific relief is a discretionary relief and the court must be that the persons seeking such relief came before it with an honest intention and made the fullest possible disclosure of all material facts within their knowledge and have not been guilty of any un-due laches. In this case it was held:-"The writ of quo warren to like all other prerogative writs is purely in the discretion of the court, and as in the case of all other discretionary reliefs the court must be satisfied in each case that the persons seeking this relief have come before it with an honest intention, made the fullest disclosure of all material facts within their knowledge and have not been guilty of any undue laches." Mr. Moinul Huq has in reply submitted that the decision in the said case being in a writ case it will not apply in the present case. The relief prayed for in the present suit namely specific performance of contract being a discretionary relief we think the principle laid down in the said case will be applicable in the present cast and in agreement with the said decision we hold that plaintiffs having not disclosed the material facts namely time, place and the names of witnesses as aforesaid, they have not come with honest intention and they are guilty of undue laches and as such the learned Subordinate Judge ought to have dismissed the suit.

(b)........................ 
(c)........................ 
(d)........................

The plaintiffs have to prove on evidence that there was usage or custom of trade showing that the defendant No.1 had implied authority to transfer immovable property belonging to the firm or to enter into partnership on behalf of the firm but the plaintiffs have not adduced any evidence to prove such implied authority of defendant No.1. D.W.1 is a formal witness. D.Ws. 2-3 have disproved the alleged contract between defendant No. 1 and the plaintiffs for sale of the /12/- annas share of the suit industry to the plaintiffs, the alleged advance of Tk. 45,000/- in pursuance of the alleged contract, the alleged tender of the balance consideration money, etc. and we have no reason to disbelieve them. D.W.4 who is an independent witness has consistently proved that M/s. Azad Store was looted before and after the liberation and we fully rely upon his evidence. The finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the terms and conditions of the alleged contract as set out in paragraph 3 of the plaint are true, is based on the alleged evasive reply of D.W.2 and D.W. 3 in cross-examination in respect of the terms and conditions and the alleged corroborative evidence of P.Ws. 1-3. The first evasive reply of D.W. 2 in cross examination according to the learned Judge is that although he denied that the plaintiffs proposed to purchase the suit property on the terms and condition stated in paragraph 3 of the plaint he did not deny that defendant No. 1 announced in the middle of June, 1973 to sell /12/- annas share of the suit industry. 33. The second evasive reply of D.W. 2 in cross-examination according to the learned Judge is merely that he could not understand the averments of the plaint in full and he was unable to read the averment made in paragraph 3 of the plaint. In the face of the denial of D.W. 2 as to the very existence of alleged oral contract he is not required to say about the alleged announcement of defendant No. 1 in the middle of June, 1973 to sell the alleged /12/-annas share of the suit industry and therefore his reply can-not be said to be evasive. The reply of D.W.2 that he did not understand the averments of the plaint or that he was unable to read the averments made in paragraph 3 of the plaint also cannot be termed as evasive. According to the learned Judge although D.W.3 denied that the plaintiffs offered to purchase the -/12/- annas of the suit industry for taka eight laces on the terms and conditions in paragraph 3 of the plaint he evaded to say the terms and conditions in his reply in cross examination by saying that he did not remember the facts in paragraph 3 of the plaint. The reply of D.W.3 in cross examination that he did not remember the facts in paragraph 3 of the plaint made after his denial of the plaintiffs' alleged offer to purchase he /12/-annas share of the suit in dusty for eight laces on the terms and condition stated in paragraph 3 of the plaint can never be read as evasive reply. As to the corroborative evidence of P.Ws. 1-3 it may be pointed out that we have al-ready disbelieved P.Ws. 1-3 on reasons and as such their evidence can not be relied upon. From the above discussion it is apparent that the said finding of the learned subordinate Judge is based on flimsy ground and as such not sustainable. 34. In view of the evidence of P.Ws. 5 and 8 and the kabala dated 23.2.73 Ext.9 executed by the defendant No 2 in favour of the of  Mi. Nabi -Bat-at-Law and power of attorney dated 22.12.72 Ext.AA(by virtue of which the defendant Nos.1 and 2 sold to P.W.8 M/s. Azad Store which belonged to their wives) both showing the address of D.W.3 at 29, Patuatuly, Dhaka the learned Subordinate Judge took the view that the evidence of D.Ws that the shop at 29 Patuatuly was closed after the liberation and the same was looted, could not be be-lieved and in that view of the matter he held that there was an agreement upon terms and conditions as stated in paragraph 3 of the plaint. On a close scrutiny of the evidence of P.Ws. 5 and 8 we have held that their evidence is not reliable on the score of their being interested witnesses. The Ext. 9 and A.A also do not prove that the particular point of time when the talk of the alleged contract was namely middle of June,1973 the M/s. Azad store was open. The learned subordinate Judge has not noticed evidence of D.Ws.2-5 on this point. The D.Ws. 2-5 have in our view consistently proved that no talk of sale took place at 29 Patuatuly. The learned Subordinate Judge erred in disbelieving them on flimsy and frivolous ground as noticed above. In the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record the learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that there was agreement on terms and conditions as stated in paragraph 3 of the plaint. While dealing with the question whether the deposit of '11c. 30,000/- on 19.6.73 and Tk.15,000/- on 12.12.73 in the joint account of defendant No.1 and his son Ehsanul Masan Khan was an advance in pursuance of the alleged contract or repayment of loan to defendant No. 1 by plaintiff No. 1 the learned Subordinate Judge started with the observation that D.W.3 (defendant No.. 1) suddenly produced some diaries Ext. V series and In-come Tax returns Ext. :Z series and the defendants adduced no evidence to prove the loan of Tk. 45,000/- although. D.W.2 stated in chief that the money i.e. Tk. 45,000/- was deposited to his account towards repayment of personal loan and this has occasioned a failure of justice. The learned Judge came to the finding that the genuineness of Ext. W series was doubtful on the grounds that the defendants did not adduce any evidence to prove the alleged loan of Tk. 45,000/- by defendant No. 1 to plaintiff No. 1, that the diaries Ext. W series were not filed in court in due time and that no explanation was given for state pro-ducked the same. D:W.2' Specifically stated in his deposition that the amount of Tk. 45,000/-was de-posited to his account towards repayment of personal loan and therefore the first ground namely that the defendant did not adduce evidence to prove the loan of Tk. 45,000/- falls through. By making reference to Order 6, rule 4, Order 8, rules 1-5 and Order 13, rules 1-2 of the Code of Civil Procedure and on relying upon the cases reported in A.I.R.1928 Nag 223 and A.I.R. 1931 Mad 512 cited by the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs before him the learned Subordinate Judge took the view that the Ext. W series was not filed in due time. Rule 4 of Order 6 of the Civil Procedure Code provides as follows:-"4 . In all cases in which the party pleading relies on any misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust, willful default, or undue influence, and in all other cases in which particulars may be necessary beyond such as are exemplified in the forms aforesaid, particulars (with dates and items if necessary) shall be stated in the pleading." 

35. Mr. T.H. Khan submits that Ext. W series and Ext. Z series are evidence and as such they need not be pleaded in written statement and therefore Order 6, rule 4 C.P.c., is not attracted. Mr. Moinul Huq, on the other hand, submits that the late production of W series is hit by Order 6, rule 4, C.P.C. On perusal of Order 6, rule 4 C.P.C. we fully agree with Mr. T.H. Khan that the Ext. W series being evidence they need not be pleaded in the written statement and as such Order 6, rule 4, C.P.C. is not attracted. It was argued on behalf of the defendants before the learned Subordinate Judge that the rules 1-2 of Order 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was repealed and as such they were not applicable in the present case. The learned Subordinate Judge took an absolutely wrong view namely, that the Ordinance No. 48 of 1983. (The Civil Procedure Code (Amendment) Ordinance, 1983) repealing rules 1-2 of Order 13 C.P.C. having come into force on 5.9.83 after the commencement of the hearing of the suit on 31.8.83 and in view of the fact that rules 1-5 of Order 8 C.P.C. provide that the defendants must produce the documents along with the written statement, the rules 1- 2 of Order 13 C.P.C. were applicable in the suit. Before the said amendment Ordinance came iron force rules 1-2 of Order 13 C.P.C. stood as follows:- (I) The parties or their pleaders shall produce, at the first hearing of the suit, all the documentary evidence of every description in their possession or power, on which they intend to rely, and which has not already been filed in court, and all documents which the court has ordered to be produced. 

(2) The Court shall receive the documents so produced: Provided that they are accompanied by an accurate list thereof prepared in such form as that (High Court Division) directs. 2. No documentary evidence in the possession or power of any party which should have been but has not been produced in accordance with the requirements of rule 1 shall be received in any subsequent stage of the proceedings unless good cause is shown to the satisfaction of the court for the non- production thereof and the court receiving any such evidence shall record the reasons for so doing." 

The rules 1-2 of Order 13 C.P.C, having been repealed by the said Amendment Ordinance which came into force on 5.9.83 before the judgment in the suit was delivered on 30.8.84, the said amendment applied in the suit and the rules 1-2 of Order 13 of the Code were not applicable in the suit as being repealed. The cases in A.I.R. 1928 Nag 223 and A.I.R. 1931 Mad 512 relate to the provision of rules 1-2 of Order 13 C.P.C. and as such they are not applicable in the suit after their repeal by the said Amendment Ordinance. The rules 2 and 5 of Order 8, C.P.C. amended by the Ordinance, are relevant to decide the point whether or not there was undue delay in filing Ext. W series. Rule -2 of Order 8, C.P.C. as amended by the said Ordinance No. 48 of 1983 runs as follows :- "Where the defendant relies upon documents in his possession or power as evidence in support of his defence or claim of set off he shall produce them in court when the written statement is presented and shall at the same time deliver the document to be filed with the written statement" -Rule 5 of Order 8. C.P.C. after the Ordinance. No. 48 of 1983 came into force runs-as follows:- "(5) A document which ought to be produced in court by the defendant when the written statement in presented, or to be entered in the list to be added or annexed to the written statement, and which is not produced or entered accordingly, shall not, without the leave of the court, be received in evidence on his behalf at the hearing of the suit. Provided that the court shall not grant such leave save in exceptional circumstances: 

Thus we see that under the amended rule 2 of Order 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure the defendant is not required to rile the document with the written statement and under the amended Rule 5 of Order 8. C.P.C. the document not filed under amended rule 2 may be received in evidence on the leave of the Court. Therefore the Ext. W series which were received by the learned Subordinate Judge are admissible in evidence and in such situation the delay in filing Ext. W series is not such as to make their genuineness doubtful. The last ground of the said finding namely, that there was no explanation for the delay in filing Ext. W series also fails in that the D.W.3 stated in cross-examination by way of explanation that he did not file the Ext. W series earlier because at the time of commencement of the trial the same were not necessary. In the above circumstances, the learned Subordinate Judge erred in finding that the genuineness of the Ext. W series is doubtful. This finding of the learned Subordinate Judge is further based on his view that D.W.3 wrote his name in all the diaries in one sitting and by the same pen and ink, that in the year 1969 and 1973 al- though the D.W.3 was not residing at 3/A/3, Quaid- e-Azarn Road yet he wrote his address as 3/A/3, Quaid-e-Azam Road in diaries for the year 1969 and 1973, that the hand writings in Ext. W(3)(a), W(3) (b), W(3)(c), W(6)(a) and W(6)(b) were not proved under the provisions of section 67 of the Evidence Act, that the case reported in 21 D.L.R.(SC) 357 decided that production of document without proving that person's handwriting does not constitute evidence and that under section 34 of the Evidence Act some entries in the books in course of business shall .not alone be sufficient evidence to charge any person with liability unless corroborated by other impartial evidence. 

In view of the cross-examination of D.W.3 that some of the diaries belonged to third parties and some entries are made by some third party but they have not been examined, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the Ext. W series particularly EXLW(3)(a), W(3)(b). W(3)(c), W(6)(a) and W(6)(b) are false and antedated. Section 34 of the Evidence Act runs thus "34. Entries in books of account regularly kept in the course of business are relevant whenever they refer to a matter into which the Court has to inquire, but such statements shall not alone be sufficient evidence to charge any person with liability." Section 67 of the Evidence Act runs thus:- "67. If a document is alleged to be signed or to have been written wholly or in part by any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's handwriting must be proved to be in his handwriting." 

In the case of M/s. Bengal Friends and Co. Dhaka Vs. M/s. Gaur Benode Saha & Co. Calcutta & another, 21 DLR(SC) 357 Supreme Court of Bangladesh held: "Entries in books of accounts regularly kept in the course of business are only declared to be relevant whenever they refer to a matter into which the Court has to enquire. But this does not dispense with the requirement of section 67 of the Evidence Act that if a document is alleged to have been written by any person, the signature or the handwriting of so much of the document as is alleged to be in that person's hand- writing must be proved to be in his handwriting. Mere production of the account books kept in regular course of business, therefore, does not constitute evidence of the transaction and accounts therein recorded." 

Section 34 of the Evidence Act and the case in 21 DLR (SC) 357 relate to books of account but in the instant case we are dealing with diaries. Thus section 34 of the evidence Act and the decision in 21 DLR(SC) 357 are not attracted in the instant case. D.W. 3 proved his noting’s in Ext W(3)(a), W(3)(b), W(3)(c), W(6)(a) and W(6)(b) in his examination in chief as noted above and D.W.3 having himself proved his writings in the said Ext. W series we think he is not required to prove his own handwritings in Ext. W series as per section 67 of the Evidence Act. Merely because some of the diaries are found to belong to third party and some entries are found to be made by third party and in the diaries of two years wrong address was given all the diaries do not become false or ante-dated. It is difficult to say if the defendant No. 1 wrote his name in all the diaries in one sitting and by the same pen and ink as opined by the learned Judge D.W 3 :)roved his noting’s of the payment of Tk.4500/- in Ext. Wf3)(a), W(3)(b) and W(3)(c) and his noting’s of receipt of Tk.45,000/- from plaintiffs No. 1 in Ext. W(6)(a) and W(6)(b) and there is no reason for us to disbelieve these noting’s in these diaries by defendant No. 1. For the above reasons the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the genuineness of the W series are doubtful and the Ext. W series particularly Ext. W(3)(a), W(3)(b), W(3)(c), W(6)(a) and W(6)(b) are false and ante-dated, is not sustainable. Ext. Z series including the wealth statements Ext. Z-Z(2) were discarded by the learned Subordinate Judge on the grounds that Ext. Z-Z(2) did not contain any court fee payable under section 76 of the Evidence Act read with Article 9 of the schedule 1 of the Court Fees Act or certificate of the Income-Tax Officer or any seal, signature or date of the Income-Tax Officer and that the defendants sub-mitted the wealth statement Ext. Z-Z(2) without demand notice under section 22(I)(A) of the Income Tax Act. Mr. T.H. Khan submits that the grounds for discarding the wealth statements arc very frivolous and the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the wealth statements Ext. Z-Z(2) were procured and could not be relied upon and that the defendants failed to prove the loan and that the deposit of Tk.45,000/-as per Ext. I and I(a) was nothing but payment of earnest money towards total consideration, is perverse. The D.W.3 (defendant No.1) during his examination-in-chief filed the certified copies of the Income-Tax returns for the years 1971-72, 1972-73, 1973-74, 1974-75 to prove the loan of Tk. 45,000/- paid by him to plaintiff No. 1 and along with the Income Tax returns he filed the wealth statements for the years which are marked Ext. Z-Z (2). D.W.3 proved the Income-Tax returns and the wealth statements and the grounds for discarding the said Ext. Z-Z(2) do not seem to be justified. 

37. The learned Subordinate Judge erred in holding that the value of the -/12/- annas share of the suit industry was Tk. 8,00,000/- in the year 1973 by discarding the testimony of D.W.2 on this point on the flimsy ground that his testimony was a solitary and uncorroborated testimony. 38.. As per the term of the alleged oral contract the plaintiffs were to sell out their one-storied residential house on 11 kathas and 8 chhataks of land in Gulshan Model Town but they admittedly sold an-other house which they acquired subsequently in 1975 instead of selling the said one-storied house of the plaintiffs. The said Gulshan house on 11 kathas and 8 chhataks of land admittedly came into existence in 1975 and in such situation the learned Advocate for the defendants rightly contended before the learned Subordinate Judge that the allegation of agreement to pay the balance consideration money by selling this house in the year 1973 could not be believed. Absolutely bypassing the contention of the learned Advocate for the defendants the learned Sub-ordinate Judge made an out of the way observation that the plaintiffs committed no mistake by selling another house which they acquired subsequently. We agree with the. learned advocate and hold the view that having regard to the fact that the house at Gulshan Model Town which was to be sold as per the term of the alleged contract in 1973 came into existence in 1975 and was not in existence in 1973 the alleged contract can not be believed. 39. We have disbelieved P.Ws. 1, 2 and 4 on reasons and as such their evidence can not be relied upon and the learned Subordinate Judge erred including that in relying upon the evidence of P.Ws. 1,2 and 4 to hold that the plaintiffs were insisting on several occasions to dissolve the partnership firm and D.W.3 was assuring them all the time to do the needful. The observation of the learned Subordinate Judge that the learned Advocate for the defendants could not show or make out any case that the agreement in question is vitiated by fraud, undue influence, misrepresentation, etc. is beside the point in the face of the defendants' case of complete denial of the alleged oral contract. The observation is just an idle talk. 

40. The learned Subordinate Judge is entirely wrong in saying that the assertion of the defendants that the negotiation started for the first time in 1978 for sale of his industry to plaintiffs was not finalized and as the defendants refused to sell the plaintiffs filed the suit, is not convincing merely because the plaintiffs deposited Tk. 45,000/- in the joint account of the defendant No. I and his son as per Ext. 1 and 1(a).

41. In the face of the testimony of D.W.2 that the defendant No.1 had acquaintance with the plain- tiff No.1 and the averment in the written statement that the defendant No.1 had personal acquaintance with the plaintiff No.1 and gave him' personal loan of Tk. 45,000/-, the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that no evidence has been led by the defendants that the defendants were friendly or in any way connected with the defendants or they had any business transaction prior to 1973 nor the defendants disclosed anywhere in their pleadings and evidence any sort of clement that leads a person to believe that the plaintiff No. 1 took loan from the defendant No. 1 is perverse. The said averment in the written statement and the testimony of defendant No.2 lead to the conclusion that the defendant No.2 had friendly business relation with the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant No.1 gave personal loan of Tk. 45,000/- to plaintiff NO.1 which the latter paid by depositing the same in the personal account of defendant No. 1 and his son, but when the negotiation between the defendants and the plaintiffs for the sale of the suit property by the defendants to the plaintiffs failed in 1978 and the defendants refused to sell the suit property the plaintiffs filed the false suit for specific performance of contract taking advantage of the deposit of loan of Tk. 45,000/- by plaintiff No.1 in the personal account of defendant No. 1 and his son as per Ext. 1 and 1 (a). The plaintiffs have to prove their own case and discharge the burden of proof which is on them. The learned Advocate for the appellant has V not advanced any argument as to defect of parties and limitation and as such the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge thereon are upheld. They can not succeed on the weakness of the defence case. The learned Subordinate Judge has seriously erred in disposing of the suit on the erroneous view that be- cause of the weakness of the defence case the plaintiffs' case is proved. From the evidence on record it is apparent plaintiffs have miserably failed to prove their case of oral contract by reliable, convincing and independent evidence. In the above circumstances, it is found that the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge suffers fro in flaw and illegality calling for interference. 
	
42. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed with- out any order as to cost. The Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is dismissed. During the hearing of the appeal the appellants have filed an application under sections 476 and 476A Cr. P.C. praying for directing the Deputy Registrar II of this Court to lodge a complaint in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka for prosecution of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 under sections 465, 468, 471, 193, 196/109 and 120B of the Penal Code for alleged of- fences of forgery of Ext. Wand Z series and their use in the suit and appeal by them. In the face of our findings in respect of Ext. Wand Z series the application is not maintainable. Accordingly, it is rejected. 

End.

caseno: Appeal from appellate Decree No. 79 of 1965.
lawyer:
B. B. Roy Chowdhury ----- For the Appellant. 
B. K. Das ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Archana Prasad Nandi ----- Appellant.
Vs.
Miss Chilia Randolph and others ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
The plaintiff's suit for specific performance of contract having been dismissed by the Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong and his appeal too having been dismissed by the Additional District Judge, Chittagong this Second Appeal has been preferred by him. 1 /2.

2. His case in short was that the suit property, a homestead land measuring 153 acres, including houses, structures, attached garden and appurtenances with all casement right thereof in Chittagong town belonged to the defendant No. 1, a Christian widow, her minor daughter defendant No. 2 and her stepson defendant No. 3 in equal 1/3rd shares. On 10-12-59, the defendant No. 1, on her own behalf and on behalf of her minor daughter, and-defendant No. 3 entered into a contract, vide Exhibit 1, for selling the suit property to the plaintiff for Rs. 6,000. The defendants 1 and 3 jointly received Rs. 2,000 as earnest money on that day and promised to execute the Kabala by 17-1-1961 after receiving the balances consideration money. They however subsequently changed their minds and did not execute the Kabala On 8-1-1961 the plaintiff served a legal notice on them offering the balance consideration money on receipt of which the defendant No. 3 alone executed a Kabala for his1/3rd share in the suij property on 27-1-1961 after receiving Rs. 1,480. This Kabala was registered after an appeal under the Registration Act. Plaintiff then transferred some portion of his purchased land to one Tofail Ahmed by a registered Kabala dated 4-5-62. Before his transfer to the plaintiff on 27-1-61, the defendant No. 3 had already transferred, some of the land in suit to defendants 4 & 5 who purchased the same knowingly of the plaintiff's contract with defendants 1-3. Plaintiff filed his suit not only against defendants 1-3, but also against defendants 4-5.

3. Defendants 1, 3, 4 and 5 filed separate written statements. Defendant No. 2, represented by a Court guardian, also appeared and filed a separate written statement. At the trial defendant No. 3 did not appear to contest. The contention of defendants 1 and 2 was that there was no agreement as alleged. The defendant No. 2 being a minor and the defendant No. 1 not being her legal guardian, the con-tract was void to the extent of the interest of defendant No. 2. Even if there was a contract, it was not enforceable as the plaintiff failed to perform his part of the contract. Defendants 4 and 5 contended that they were purchasers from defendant No. 3 for valuable consideration without any notice or knowledge of the plaintiff's contract.

4. Both the courts below held as a con current finding of fact that the plaintiff's contract, Exhibit 1 was executed by the defendants 1 and 3. They held that the defendant No. 1 was not the legal guardian of defendant No. 2 and therefore, the contract with regard to the share of defendant No. 2 was void and could not be enforced in law. The plaintiff having already obtained a Kabala dated 27-1-61 Exhibit 2 from the defendant No. 3, nothing remained with the said defendant to be transferred to the plaintiff now. Both the Courts below also held that the contract being a single and indivisible one, the plaintiff had given a good bye to its indivisible character by obtaining a separate kabala from the defendant No. 3. The trial Court held that defendant No. 5 had full knowledge of the plaintiff's contract, but the same could not be said of defendant No. 4. The appellate Court below held that the knowledge of defendants 4 and 5 should be decided in a separate suit between the plaintiff and the said defendants and that the trial court should not have recorded any finding as to the knowledge of the said defendant. Both the Courts held that the contract Exhibit 1 should not be enforced in law.

5. Mr BB Roy Chowdhury, the learned advocate for the appellant, has challenged the findings of the appellate Court below on the following grounds:

(1) That the contract is enforceable against defendant No. 2 as according to the customary law of the native Christian community, in the absence of the father, the mother is the legal guardian of her minor children in respect of both their person and properties.

(2) That even if it held that the mother had no power to enter into the contract, the contract is not void ab initio as far as the minor is concerned. It is void able at the option of the minor within 3 years of her attaining majority.

(3) That even if it is held that the contract is unenforceable against the defendant. No. 2 yet it is a divisible contract and it can and ought to be enforced against defendants land 3 in respect of their 2/3rd shares in the property, in terms of Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act.

(4) That the appellate Court below made an error of law in holding that the plaintiff did not perform his part of the contract.

(5) That defendants 4 and 5 were necessary parties to the suit in view of the provision of clause (b) of Section 27 of the Specific Relief Act and the appellate Court below was wrong to hold that the question of the knowledge of the plaintiff's contract should be decided in a separate suit between defendant No. 3 and defendants 4 and 5.

(6) That specific performance cannot be refused against defendant No. 3 on the view that he has already performed his part of the contract. because when he executed Exhibit 2 on 27-1-61 he had no subsisting interest in the suit property. His earlier kabalas to defendants 4 and 5 need to be cancelled in the same suit and the defendants 4 and 5 art to join with defendants 1-2 in conveying the suit property to the plaintiff.

With regard (o the first two submissions of Mr Roy Chowdhury, it may be slated at the outset that the law relating to the powers of a mother as guardian has been decided under Muslim law and Hindu law but has not received express and elaborate judicial treatment in this sub-continent in respect of communities other than Muslims and Hindus. The only text-book reference is to be found in the book of Trevelyan. The Law Relating to Minors, (5th edition, 1916) wherein it is observed at P 367:—

"The law applicable to persons other than Hindus and Mohammedans does not permit guardians, other than those appointed by the Court, or having power given to them by the instrument appointing them, to sell or charge the immoveable property of their wards. Where it be necessary in,the interests of minors to whom the Hindu and Muhammadan laws have no application, to sell or charge their immovable property, the best course is to apply for the appointment of guardian, and on such appointment being made to obtain the sanction of the Court for the sale."

6. BB Roy Chowdhury refers to two decisions, wherein, he claims, the powers of a Christian mother have received judicial elucidation. The first case is that of Bangrammal vs Lydia Kant reported in AIR 1934 Mad 605. Referring to an earlier decision of the Madras High Court, reported in AIR 1931 Mad 529, it was held therein that amongst the (Indian) Christian community an act done by a mere de facto guardian (such as a sister's husband) will not bind the minor and will be void against him. "But a mother", goes the decision "the father being dead, does not, we think, fall within this category, but is certainly, for many purposes, the natural guardian of her minor child. She is, for instance, entitled to the custody of the child and to the guardianship of its property." A Christian mother in the decision under reference alienated her two minor daughters shares by executing a sale-deed. One of the daughters on attaining majority, sued for a declaration that the sale was not binding upon her and for partition and delivery of her one-third share in the property. The Madras High Court held that an alienation by a Christian mother as natural guardian would be voidable, not void.

7. The next case cited by Mr Roy Chowdhury is that of Decosta vs Naddar, reported in AIR 1956 (Trav-Coch) 107. In this case too a Christian minor on attaining majority claimed that his mother was not competent to alienate the properties so as to defeat the title of the plaintiff. This decision followed AIR 1934 Mad 605. It held that the sale-deed affected by the mother is binding on the plaintiff unless he avoids it within 3 years of attaining majority. The following passage from Trevelyan's aforequoted book, in its 6th edition at PP. 167-168 (P. 60 of the 5th edition) was quoted in the decision:—

"Failing the father, the mother's custody of her children's property would be" treated as not unlawful. Failing the father and mother, and their appointees, no per-son, however nearly related, is of right entitled to the custody of minors, who are neither Hindus nor Mohammedans, or to the guardianship of their properly."

The Travancore Cochin decision interpreted the above observation as establishing that the mother would be the legal guardian of her minor children in the absence of the father among communities other than Hindus and Muslims.

Mr Roy Chowdhury has also relied upon Trevelyan's following observation at P. 168 of the afore-quoted book (5th edition):—

"An alienation by a guardian, which does not bind the minor, is not void, but voidable at the instance of the ward. Subject to the repayment of such money as he may have obtained the benefit of, the minor is "entitled, before or after attaining his majority, to recover such of his property as by the wrongful or unauthorized act has come into the hands of other persons."

From all the above, Mr Roy Chowdhury argues that the Courts below committed a grave error of law in holding that the defendant No. 1 was not a legal guardian of defendant No. 2 and that the contract with defendant No. 2 was void and unenforceable. He submits on the authority of the above decisions that defendant No. 1 was the legal guardian of defendant No. 2. She was competent under the Christian law to enter into the contract in question. It is not a void contract at all as far as defendant No. 2 is concerned. If the defendant No. 2 wishes she can avoid it within 3 years of attaining majority.

8. The validity of Mr Roy Chowdhury's contention may be examined now. It may be accepted that in the absence of the father, the Christian mother is the natural guardian of her minor children. It may also be accepted that it will not be unlawful for her to be the custodian of her ward's property. To that extent, Mr Roy Chowdhury's submissions may be taken to be correct and Mr BK Das, learned advocate for the respondents, does not dispute this contention.

<u>9. The present case, however, is not a case of completed alienation by a Christian mother of her ward's property. It is a case of specific performance of contract where alienation is sought to be completed with the aid of the Court. It is, therefore, not relevant far the purpose of this case to consider whether an alienation by a Christian mother of her ward's property is void or voidable. That question may properly be raised in a case where alienation is completed and is a past transaction and all that remains for the minor, is either to accept or avoid it on attaining majority. The two decisions cited are not, therefore, exactly on the point. The questioning this case is, where the natural guardian of a Christian minor's estate makes an executory contract for the sale of immovable property, can the contract be specifically enforced against the minor?</u>

10. The general principle is well established now that an executory contract for the purchase of sale of immovable property cannot be specifically enforced either by or on behalf of the minor or against the minor or against his property. A partial exception to this general principle is made with regard to contracts entered into on behalf of minors by guardians who have the power under the law to bind the minors by their, acts. This partial exception to the general principle has been well formulated in the case of guardians under Muslim law and Hindu law. But the forensic law of this sub-continent is scarce indeed in its treatment of this partial exception in the case of guardians amongst communities other than Muslims and Hindus.

<u>11.
