Mr BK Das submits, and it appears to me to be correct, however, that in granting or refusing specific performance of contract of sale of a Christian minor's property, the Court will be guided by the same considerations which govern the same relief is respect of a Muslim minor's property or a Hindu minor's property. The Court will require of the plaintiff to satisfy itself whether the contract was for the benefit of the minor, whether there was any legal necessity involved therein, whether it will be possible for the minor to avoid the contract on attaining majority. Section 27 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 imposes obligations upon all guardians of the property of award to deal there with as carefully as a wan of ordinary prudence would deal with it. Such a view will not be inconsistent with that Act. Even in Bangrammal's case, (AIR 1934 Mad 605) cited by Mr Roy Chowdhury and in the case reported in AIR 1931 Mad 529, it was inquired into whether the sale-deed was executed in the interest of the minor, Trevelyan also says at P. 167 of his aforequoted book (5th edition);</u>

<u>"Although a guardian may have power to sell or mortgage the estate of his ward, the Court will not decree against the minor specific performance of an agreement for such sale or mortgage, or any other agreement made by his guardian or the de facto manager of his property, unless it be quite certain that the agreement was for the benefit of the minor, that it will be for his benefit, that it should be enforced, and that it one which would be impossible for him to avoid in attaining majority".</u>

<u>12. It is clear that even though a Christian mother as a natural guardian of her minor children can enter into an executory contract of sale in respect of her minor children's property, in decreeing specific performance thereof the Court will have to be satisfied inter alia that the contract has endured to the minor's benefit No such case has been made out. It is neither averred in the plaint nor given in evidence that the contract is for the benefit of defendant No. 2. There is total absence of any evidence in this regard, which it was for the plaintiff to adduce. In view of the matter I am of the opinion that i that the two Courts below did not commit any illegality in refusing specific performance against defendant No. 2, although their reasoning there of proceeded along different lines.</u>

<u>That disposes of the first two submissions of Mr Roy Chowdhury.</u>

13. Mr BB Roy Chowdhury has submitted next that even if it is held that the contract is not enforceable against defendant No. 2, the contract is divisible and it car and ought to be specifically enforced against the defendants 1 & 3 in respect of their 2/3rd shares in the suit property, Mr Roy Chowdhury has invoked the provision of section 15 of the Specific Relief Act and has orally submitted that his reliant relinquishes al claim to further performance and right to compensation either for the deficiency, 01 for the loss or damage sustained by his client through the default of the defendants.

The contract in question, Exhibit 1, stands thus:—

"Received with thanks a sum of Rs. 2,000 (rupees two thousand only) by way of earnest money from Mr Archana Prasad Nandy S/o Birendrz Lai Nandy of Village Kanchana, PS Satkania, Chittagong." at present residing at 21, Alkaran Lane, PS Kotwali, Chittagong, out of the total consideration of Rs 6,000 (Rupees six thousand only) for which we agree to sell our properties shown in schedule below. We shall execute and get the kabala registered within 17th day of January, 1961, on receipt of residue of Rs. 4,000 (rupees four thousand only) from the said Mr Archana Prasad Nandy. In case of our failure to complete the sale by the aforesaid, date the said Mr Archana Prasad Nandy shall be at liberty to get the kabala executed and registered through Court I. Margaret Randolph, for myself and my daughter Chilia Randolph and IAP Randolph sign this document."

This document than contains case contract schedule of land agreed to be sold, recital of payment of Rs. 2,000 followed by the signatures of 4 witnesses and the signatures of defendants 1 & 3 in the margin.

14. It is to be noted that in the above con tract the defendants 1 & 3 have not given out that they were the sole owners of the suit property. I think they have made it fairly clear that defendant No. 2 has also an interest in the property. No one seems to have contracted for his or her share in the property. There is no mention of any share at all. It appears to be a contract for the sale of the whole property jointly by all the owners.

<u>15. The question is, can a part of the above contract be given effect to in terms of Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act? The general rule of equity is that the Court will not compel specific performance of a contract unless it can enforce the whole contract. This rule is embodied in section 17 of the Specific Relief Act. Under Section 17 a contract cannot be specifically enforced in part except under situations provided for under sections 14, 15 & 16 of the said Act, sections 14 & 16 of the said Act, con-cedes Mr Roy Chowdhury, have no application to this case. He submits that section 15 has full application to this case. Before I consider the application of section 15, let me set it out in full:—</u>

<u>"Where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, and the part which must be left unperformed forms a considerable portion of the whole, or does not admit of compensation in money, he is not entitled to obtain a decree for specific performance. But the Court may, at the suit of the other party, direct the party in default to perform specifically so much of his part of the contract as he can perform, provided that the plaintiff relinquishes all claim to further performance and all right to compensation either for the deficiency, or for the loss or damage sustained by him through the default of the defendant".</u>

<u>As one can see, there are several conditions for the application of section 15, Without going into those conditions the words in the beginning of the section "where a party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it" may be noticed. Sarkar says in his commentary on the Specific Relief Act (9th edition 1958) at P. 91, "These words suggest that section 15 is applicable only where the defendant made a representation that the whole of the property belonged to her, which eventually turns out not to be correct. The section has no application where the defendant contracted on his or her behalf and on behalf of somebody else (say, a minor) and it is found that the contract is not enforceable in law so far as that somebody is concerned". Sarkar has further observed in the next breath, "The Calcutta High Court has, however, applied section 15 in such cases also".</u>

<u>Both Mr BK Das and Mr BB Roy Chowdhury have submitted a few decisions, which only reveal the aforesaid contradictory positions of various High Courts.</u>

16. The earliest case on record is that of Abdul Hug vs Mohammad Yehia Khan, reported in AIR 1924 Pat. 81. An agreement for sale of certain immovable properties was executed by defendant No. 1 and by defendant No. 2 for self and as guardian of defendants 3 and 4. It was held that defendant No. 2 as de facto guardian had no power to convey to the plaintiff the shares of defendants 3 and 4. It was thereafter held as follows:—

"But here again the rule is firmly established that a contract for sale of property in one lot will generally be considered indivisible, for the reason that there is obvious injustice to take undivided parts of shares of the estate."

The decision goes further to state that for want of mutuality in the contract the plaintiff's present willingness to take a conveyance of the shares of defendants 1 & 2 cannot be conceded. That was not the original bargain struck between the parties. The decision quoted the following dictum of Lindley LJ in the case of Lumley vs Ravenscroft (1895) 1 QB 683 (H), "This case is not within the exception as to misconduct... but comes within the general rule that where a person is jointly interested in an estate with another specific performance will not be granted against him as to his shares." In interpreting Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act, the above observations of Lindley LJ obviously carried some weight. It was held on a consideration of sections 14-16, that it was impossible to give the plaintiff a decree for specific performance as against defendants 1 and 2.

17. Mr BK Das has cited the case of Rameswar vs Anandin, reported in AIR 1956 (Pat) 53. That was a case where the defendant contracted on her own behalf and on behalf of her minor daughter and it was found that the contract was not enforceable against the daughter. Following the earlier Patna case it has been held therein, "Defendant 1 did not make any representation that the whole of the property, the subject matter of the contract, belonged to her. She had made a contract on her behalf and on behalf of somebody else, and it has been found that the contract is not enforceable in law so far as that somebody is concerned. To such a case, section 15 has no application." The decision quotes the reasoning of the earlier Patna case and also quotes Fry on Specific Performance, Chapter XVI, Article 823, as follows, in support of its opinion:—

"823. A contract for the sale of property in one lot will generally be considered indivisible. Thus, in a case where. two undivided seventh shares of land were sold in one lot, the Court refused to enforce specific performance where a good title could be made to one seventh only and the purchaser of the entirety will, of course, not be compelled to take six undivided seventh parts of the estate. And so in a case where two persons were owners of an estate in undivided moieties and the plaintiff's sought to enforces an alleged contract by them to lease the coals under it, but could not prove any such contract against one of the owners, one ground on which the bill was dismissed against the other owner also was that he had never contracted to lease one share alone.

If he had held himself out and contracted as the owner of the whole, the case would have been different. But in the absence of misrepresentation or misconduct, the genera rule is that where a person is jointly interested in an estate with another person, and purports to deal with the entirety, specific performance will not be granted against him as to share."

As already said, the Calcutta High Court has applied section 15 in such cases also. Mr BB Roy Chowdhury has cited the case of Puma vs Gopendra, reported in AIR 1976 Cal 744. That was a case where A entered into a contract for safe of his share of property together with the share of his minor nephew B. On the view that A "was perfectly entitled to enter into an agreement with respect to his own share of the property, without reference to the interest of his infant nephew, it held that there is nothing in law to prevent the plaintiffs from enforcing the con tract as against A with regard to share of the property. Section 15 was therefore held to be applicable to the contract. This case neither gives any reason for the decision nor explains how the language of section 15 is applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case.

18. Mr Roy Chowdhury has cited next the case of Dihedral vs Monomohon, AIR 1957 Cal. 209 which is a case of lease. A contract of lease entered into by defendants 1-4 was found to be not binding on minor defendant No. 2. Specific performance was granted in respect of 3/4th share of adult contesting defendants but in this case also no independent reason has been furnished.

19. Mr Roy Chowdhury has cited another decision, the case of Imam Din vs Muhammad Din reported in AIR 1926 Lah 137. The High Court granted specific performance of contract against defendant No. 1 in respect of his own share in the suit property when it was found that he had no right to sell the share of defendant No. 2, his minor nephew. Section 15 has been made applicable to the case. No reason has been advanced for this decision also.

Mr Roy Chowdhury has cited next a decision of the Privy Council, the case of Abdul Karim vs Gladys Muriel, reported in 54 CWN 770. This was an appeal from West Africa decided in 1948 In this Decision the Privy Council says that Lindley, LJ's dictum in Lumley vs Ravenscroft (prey cited) that "where a person is jointly interested in an estate with another person and purports to deal with the entirety, specific performance will no be granted against him as to his share" "is seriously diminished by the circumstances to which they have adverted'. Lumley's case, the Privy Council seems to think, is no answer to the position where there is more than one vendor and one of the vendors cannot complete the contract. In this case the appellant had agreed to buy two houses which were owned by the 1st 2nd and 3rd respondents as tenants in common contract was unenforceable against the 1st respondent as she had no power to make the contract. The Privy Council held, on the authority of Horrocks vs Rigby (1878) 9 Ch D 180 and Attorney-General vs Day 1 Yes Sen 218 that the appellant can enforce it against the22nd and 3rd respondents in respect of their /1rd shares. Mr, Roy Chowdhury heavily relies upon this decision and submits that the present case is a case of more than one vendor.

20. It is no doubt apparent that to the extent that the decision reported in AIR 1924 (Pat) 81 and AIR 1956 (Pat) 53 are based on the afore-quoted dictum of Lindley of LJ., their validity can now be doubted on the authority of the just cited Privy Council case. But the Patna decisions did not rest on the dictum of Liodley, LJ alone. Section 15 of the Specific Relief Act has been connected with the dictum of Lindley, LJ Specific Relief Act has not been considered by the Privy Council whose decision is based entirely on a consideration of the English law on the subject. And I get it from the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Specific Relief Bill, "It seems impossible to elicit a Consistent doctrine from the English decisions as to the right of a purchaser or lessee to specific performance with abatement or compensation when the title of the persons agreeing to sell or lease is defective (Quoted in Sarkar's Specific Relief Act, 9th Edition pp. 89-90). That is why section 15 was introduced and it was a clear departure from the English rule as to abatement or compensation when specific performance of a part of a contract is decreed. It is difficult, therefore, to accept the Privy Council decision, cited by Mr Chowdhury, as an authority in support of his submission. As observed by the Privy Council itself in the case William Graham vs Krishna Chandra Dey, in AIR 1925 (PC) 45, Section 14 to 17 inclusive of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, are both positive and negative in their forms. Taken together, they constitute a complete code, within the terms of which specific performance of con tracts must be brought, if it is to be granted at all. Although assistance may be derived from a consideration of cases upon this branch of English jurisprudence, the language of the sections must ultimately prevail".

<u>21. I am inclined to agree with those decisions which hold that section 15 is applicable only where the defendant made a representation that the whole of the property belonged to him, which eventually turned out not to be correct. The section has no application where the defendant contracted on his behalf and on behalf of a minor and it is found that the contract is unenforceable against the minor. The object of enactment of section 15 is to Provide for abatement or compensation when the title of the persons agreeing to sell or lease is defective. However, I am not swayed by the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the legislation the section applies only when "party to a contract is unable to perform the whole of his part of it". A defendant who holds himself out not as the owner of the entire property and whose claim turns out to be correct is the party to the contract who is unable to perform the whole of his part of it, because it was his duty to convey the whole property of the plaintiff. Section 15 applies to him. But when a defendant contracts on his behalf and on behalf of a minor and it is found that the contract is unenforceable against the minor then that defendant is not a party to the contract who is unable to perform the whole of his part of it. It was no part of his function to convey the property of the minor to anyone, without fulfilling some conditions. He, therefore, does not answer the qualifying descriptions of a "party to the contract" in section 15, Specific Performance is not meant to be directed against him under section 15.</u>

<u>I am, therefore, unable to sustain the third submission of Mr BB Roy Chowdhury.</u>

22. The fourth submission of Mr BB Roy Chowdhury must be held to be correct. Time was not of the essence of the contract in this case and the very despatch of legal notice dated 8-6-61 offering to pay the balance consideration money was a good offer. In that view of the matter, the finding of the appellate court below that the plaintiff did not perform his part of the contract is not sustainable.

23. The fifth submission of Mr BB Roy Chowdhury is that the appellate court below erred in law in holding that the plaintiff and the defendants 4 & 5 have to settle the question of knowledge of the plaintiff's contract in a properly constituted suit. He submits that under clause (b) of section 27 of the Specific Relief Act, defendants 4 and 5 are necessary parties. They are persons claiming under defendant No. 3 by a title arising subsequently to the contract dated 10-12-59. In this very suit it is for those defendants to prove that they are transferees for value who have paid their money in good faith and without notice of the original contract. The trial Court below, Mr Roy Chowdhury further contends, approached the question of onus from wrong viewpoint. It fixed the onus on the plaintiff to prove that these defendants had notice of the contract and it found that defendant No. 5 had notice and defendant No. 4 did not have any notice. The appellate court below disregarded these findings of the trial Court and simply held that the trial should not have recorded any finding on the knowledge of these defendants and matter should be decided in a properly constituted suit between the parties. The ouster of defendants 4 & 5 from the frame of the present suit was illegal, he submitted.

24. Mr Roy Chowdhury has finally argued that the Courts below illegally refused specific performance against the defendant No. 3 on the view that he has already performed his part of the contract by executing kabala dated 27-1-61. That view was erroneous in law because on the date that he executed the kabala he had no subsisting interest in the property. Therefore, he never performed any part of his contract. It is necessary, therefore, Mr Roy Chowdhury submits, that it should be determined whether defendants 4 & 5 were bonafide transferees for value or not. If the determination is in favour of the plaintiff, the said defendants should be joined with the other defendants in executing a kabala in favour of the plaintiff. The kabala of defendants 4 and 5 should also be declared void in the same suit. Mr Roy Chowdhury has cited several decisions in this regard.

25. The view, however, that I take on the third submission of Mr Roy Chowdhury makes a detailed consideration of his fifth and last submission unnecessary. These would have been relevant considerations indeed if my decision way that the contract could be specifically enforced against defendants 1 & 3 in respect of their 2/3rd shares in the suit property. But I am clearly of the opinion that the plaintiff is plainly unable to enforce the contract Exhibit 1 either in its entirety or respect of the shares of defendants 1 & 3.

26. But that the defendants 1 & 3 executed the contract dated 10-12-59, and received Rs. 2,000 from the plaintiff as earnest money stand as a concurrently concluded fact. The plaintiff, therefore, cannot be denied any relief in this case. He should not be driven to a separate suit for realisation of the earnest money, of Rs. 2,000 from defendants 1 & 3. I therefore, pass a decree in favour of the plaintiff directing defendants 1 & 3 to return, to the plaintiff the earnest money of Tk. 2,000 with interest thereon at 11% per annum from 17-1-61 to the date of payment. Defendants 1&2 shall pay the plaintiff, costs in both the Courts below. There will be no order as to costs in this appeal. The appeal is disposed of in the above terms.

End.

caseno: Appeal from appellate decree No. 334 of 1964.
lawyer:
Miah Abdul Gafur ----- For the Appellant. 
Moksudur Rahman ----- For Respondents 2 and 3.
Nizamddin Haider ----- For Respondents 1(I) to 1(4) and 1(8).
parties:
Abdul Majid Howladar ----- Defendant Appellant.
Vs.
Hakimonnessa Bibi wife of Mvi. Azaharuddin Ahmed being dead some of her heirs. Azaharuddin Ahmed and ors ----- Plaintiff Respondents.
case_source: Appeal against the decree of Mr. K.F. Akbar, Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court of Zilla Baker gang dated the 31st day of May, 1963 passed in Title Appeal No. 332 of 1962 affirming the decree of Mr. M.A. Awal Munsif, 1st Court, Perojpur dated the 8th day of September, 1962 in Title Suit No. 104 of 1962.
full_judgment:
In this appeal defendant No. 1 calls in question a judgment of affirmance decreeing the plaintiff's suit for partition in preliminary form.

2. The plaintiff claimed partition or schedule 'kha' out of schedule 'Ka' land of the plaint. The schedule 'Ka' land of R.S, khatian No. 245 belonged in raiyati right Ensanuddin and others under Nabab others, and the same was auction solid in pursuant to a rent decree for arrears of accept and the plaintiff's father, Mujahar Ali, purchased the entire raiyat on 23.1.1936 and the sale was duly confirmed on 27.2.1936. Mujahar Ali obtained the sale certificate and delivery of possession. He died leaving a widow, Bakful, a son, Khoka and a daughter, Hakimannessa (the plaintiff). Khoka died leaving behind Bakful, Hakimannessa and paternal uncles, Atahar and Hatem (defendants Nos. 2 and 3 Bakful sold some of the lands out of her share to Atahar and Hatem. The R.S. Khatian No. 245 was recorded in the name of plaintiff's father. The plaintiff came to know that defendants Nos. 2 and 3 sold a portion of the suit land out of their share to defendant No. 1. Finding joint possession inconvenient the plaintiff demanded partition but was refused by the defendants on 15.2.62.

3. Defendant No. 1, and defendants, Nos. 2 and 3 filed two separate written statements. Defendant No. 1 contended that he paid the auction money and purchased the suit land in the name of the plaintiff's father and was in possession of the same. Defendants No. 2 and 3 along with the plaintiff agreed to execute a deed of release in favour of defendant 1 but on 30.7.52 a deed of release was executed and registered by defendants Nos. 2 and 3 only, and the plaintiff at the instigation of her husband's brother, Moslem Ali, refused to execute the same. Defendant No. l's son heated over the sale certificate and the copy of the writ of delivery of possession and the registration delivery ticket of the deed of release to his maternal uncles, defendants Nos. 2 and 3, in good faith. The documents were not returned to defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff procured the same from defendants. Nos. 2 and 3 through Moslem Ali. Defendant No. 1 got the suit land recorded in his name in spite of objection by Moslem Ali. The Government acquired some of the excess lands of defendant No. 1 including the suit land, but defendant No. 1 got the suit land released and paid rent for the same.

4. Defendants Nos. 2 and 3 contended that Mujahar was the real auction purchaser of the suit property and he got the sale certificate and obtained delivery of possession in the suit land. Their further case is that defendants Nos. 2 and 3 executed in favour of defendant No. 1 a khaikhalashi deed which was fraudulently converted into deed, of release and that as defendant No. I did not pay the consideration for the document defendants Nos. 2 and 3 withheld the registration ticket. These defendants prayed for their shares in the suit land.

5. The trial court held that the plaintiff's father, Mujahar, was the auction purchase of the suit land, that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land, that there was 710 contract for a deed of release and the alleged deed of release was purported to be a khaikhalashi deed, and that as the plaintiff did not execute the alleged deed of release she was not bound by it. The trial court decreed the suit in preliminary form against defendants I, 2 and 3 after allocating shares to the plaintiff and defendants 2 and 3 only.

6. The lower appellate court concurred in the findings of the trial court that Mujahar was the real owner and he was all along in possession of the suit property on the basis of the auction and that his name was recorded during the R.S. operation and after his death his heirs including the plaintiffs were in actual possession of the suit property. It further considered that defendants Nos. 2 and 3 by a registered kabala dated 20th Aswin, 1357 B.S. purchased a portion of the inherited share of the widow of Mujahar Ali and admitted there by the auction purchase of the suit property by Mujahar Ali, and subsequently they changed their sides and executed the Muktipatra in favour of defendant No. 1. The lower appellate Court, however, held that the Muktipatra was collusively created. It confirmed the judgment and decree of the trial court with the modification that the suit be dismissed with contest without costs against defendant No. I as he was not a co-sharer in the suit property.

7. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has contested that as defendant No. I claimed a hostile title and did not acknowledge the plaintiff and defendants Nos. 2 and 3 as co-sharers in the suit land the suit must fail. He has drawn my attention to the following observation made in the case of Annapurna Debya Vs. Golapmani Debya and others 25 C.L.J. 530.

"We need not discuss whether an adverse claimant, who has no community of interest with the parties to the suit, is in no view a co-tenant with them, but stands out on his own independent right and denies all right in his adversaries, can be drawn into a partition suit for decision of the question of title paramount. But, in any view, the principle appears to us to undoubtedly sound that where there is conflicting claim to share in the land under the same right under which partition is sought, the determination of the conflict is incidental to the partition and cannot be avoided before partition is directed. Such a case does not fall within the category of claims utterly hostile where each demands not a share but the whole".

8. Mr. Gafur has laid much emphasis on the first, and the last, sentence in the above observation and submitted that defendant No. 1 cannot be drawn in the present suit for partition. He has further submitted that the suit is bad for multifariousness as it has joined different causes of action and, the plaintiff sought, in the guise of a partition suit, a declaration of title and confirmation of possession against defendant No. 1 who he was not entitled in law to do so, and that the court had no jurisdiction to make any finding adverse to the title or possession of defendant No. 1.

9. Mr. Nizamuddin Haider, the learned Advocate for the respondents, has submitted that the question of maintainability was not pressed in the trial court and that the lower appellate court after considering the averment in paragraph 5 of the plaint, where it was stated that the plaintiff came to know that defendants Nos. 2 and 3 sold a portion of the suit land out of their share to defendant No. 1, rightly held that defendant 1 was a necessary party in the suit though at the time of hearing and in the decision of the suit it was found that as he had no title or interest in the suit property he was not a cashier in the same. Mr. Haider has further contended that even if defendant No. 1 was not a necessary party he was a proper, party in view of the plaint case.

10. In Gagan Chandra Hazra and another Vs. Surendra Nath Khamrai and other A.I.R. 1951 Cal. 410, K.G. Chandler and Sen, took the view that the presence of strangers was sufficient to take the suit out of the purview of a suit for partition and this view was followed by Mitter and Guha, 31, in Subodh Kumar Banerjee Vs. Soshi Kumar Benerjee 1958 C.L.J. 262. A contrary view was taken in Nilmoni Haider Vs. Upendra Nath Haider and others 61 C.W.N. 875, and Jugal Chandra Mondal Vs. Manindra Nath Mondal and others 62 C.W.N. 244, that, notwithstanding the presence or necessary presence of strangers, the suit may well be regarded, at least, as a suit to enforce a right to a share in any property on the ground that it is joint family property within the amended Art. 17(VA) of Schedule II to the Court Fees Act.

11. The following question regarding the court-fee matter was referred to a Special Bench of the Calcutta High Court in the case of Sm. Siba Rani Debi & others Vs. Ramandra Nath Mukherjee and others reported in 66 C.W.N. 828.

"Whether a suit, which otherwise satisfies the requirement of clause (VA) of Schedule II, Art. 17 of the Court Fees Act would go out of the purview of that Clause, if the plaintiff joins as a defendant a stranger, that is, a person who is not a co-sharer or co-owner for enforcing in his presence his (the plaintiff's) right to the share, claimed by him in the suit properties and if the determination of the question that the suit properties are joint properties, as claimed by the plaintiff, and of the plaintiff's title to the same as a co-sharer, as aforesaid, defends upon the construction or avoidance though not necessarily, cancellation, of some document or transaction in respect of the suit properties or any of them, in which the said stranger is or claims to be interested. If so, how is such a suit to be valued and stamped? The question was answered as follows:

"A. suit, which otherwise satisfies the requirements of clause (VA) of Schedule II article 17 of the Court Fees act, would not go out of the purview of that clause, merely because the plaintiff joins as a defendant a stranger, i.e. a person who is not a co-sharer or co-owner, for enforcing in his presence the right to the share in the suit properties claimed by the plaintiff, even if the determination of the question whether the suit properties are joint properties and whether the plaintiff has right to a share therein involve the construction of some document in respect of the suit properties or any of them in which the stranger is or claimed to be interested and or an adjudication that some document or transaction in respect of such properties or any of them is void, and or not binding on the plaintiff; provided that the determination of the above question does not involve the cancellation or setting aside of such document or transaction."

<u>12. The notion that disputed questions of title should not be raised in a suit for partition had its origin in England in the conflict of jurisdictions between Courts of Laws and Courts of Equity Courts of Equity which assumed jurisdiction in the matter of partition held back from determining doubtful questions with regard to the legal title and often stayed the suit for reasonable tine giving an opportunity to the plaintiff to establish his title in an appropriate action. The practice of English Court of Equity with regard to the bill of complaint for partition continued to exert great influence in our country long after the powers the Courts of Law and of Equity came to be administered by the same court. The Courts in our country refused to decide complicated questions of title in a suit for partition. However, questions of title came to be entertained when determination of such questions was found to be incidental to the partition and could not be avoided in a case where it was deemed just to direct a partition. Again, because of the requirement of presence of community of interest amongst the parties to a suit for partition a stranger could not be impleaded even when his preserve was found necessary for doing full and complete justice to the parties in one action. Widely, prevalent practice of benami transaction in our country caused great hardship to a plaintiff who sought partition and separate possession with regard to some joint property or joint family property standing in the name of a stranger, but was pushed to a troublesome and time consuming title suit. The Court Fees (Bengal Amendment) Act, 1935 (Bengal Act VII of 1935) for the first time introduced two specific provisions for suits for partition by incorporating paragraph VIA a in section 7, for the plaintiff who has been excluded from possession, and entry No. VA. in Article 17 of schedule II to the Court Fees Act 1870, for the plaintiff who is in possession of the property. The procedural phrase "to enforce a right to a share in any property," on the ground that it is joint family property or joint property," in both the provisions, has no doubt been meant to provide for adjudication of title in respect of any joint family property or joint property standing in the name of others including strangers. A plea of a defendant that as he entirely stands on his independent right and that he has no community of interest with the parties to the suit he cannot be drawn into a suit for partition will not affect the suit if it satisfies the bask requirements of a suit for partition.</u>

13. The present suit satisfied all the requirements of a suit for partition. The plaintiff prayed for partition of, and separate possession in, the joint property she was jointly possessing with defendants Nos. 2 and 3, and impleaded defendants No. 1 who was reported to have purchased a portion of the suit property from defendants No. 2 and 3. The allegations of defendant No. 1 that the plaintiff had no right, title or interest in the suit property and the suit was filed in collusion with defendants Nos. 2 and 3 to establish her right will not affect the suit.

14. Mr. Gafur's contention that the court has no jurisdiction in a suit for partition to make an adverse finding as to the title or possession of a defendant, who is a. stranger to the parties; has got no substance. A declaration as to title is inherent in the substantive relief of partition and separate possession granted in a suit for partition, and such declaration may involve as in the present case, construction of a document and an adjudication that the instrument is not binding on the plaintiff, and then an adverse finding as to the title or possession against a defendant may become unavoidable. In the present case both the courts below found that the plaintiff was not a party to the alleged deed of release and she was not bound by it.

15. Mr. Gafur has contended that in view of the fact that the suit land was released by the .Government after an objection by defendant No. 1 and the release order did not enure to the benefit of the plaintiff and defendants Nos. 2 and 3, the suit was not maintainable without making the Government a party. As the alleged excess land of the suit land had already been released by the Government in favour of defendant No. 1 and the Government had no abiding interest in the suit land it was not necessary to implead the Government in the suit.

16. Mr. Gafur has then contended that in view of the deed of release defendants 2 and 3 ought to be estopped from raising their plea against defendant No. 1 who ought to be alloted the shares of defendants 2 and 3. The trial Court found that the deed was prepared to by a Khai Khalashi deed, but the lower appellate court held that the alleged deed of released was collusively created in between defendant No. 1 and defendants Nos. 2 and 3. As the deed of release was found to be a collusive document defendant No. 1 cannot be allowed to benefit from his own collusion with defendants Nos. 2 and 3.

17. Mr. Gafur has also half-heartedly tried to reopen the finding as to the plaintiff's possession in the suit land. The courts below came to a concurrent finding that Mujahar, and after him his hers, including the plaintiffs were in actual possession of the suit property.

18. In view of the above, the appeal is dismissed with costs. Prayer for leave under Clause 15 of the Letters Patent is refused.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 325 of 1976 with Civil Rule No. 1174 (S) of 1975.
lawyer:
Md. Ansar Ali ------ For the Appellant. 
Akram Hossain Amin ------ For the Respondent.
parties:
Jasimuddin Mondal and ors------Appellants.
Vs.
Sunila Bibi and others------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 is directed against a judgment of affirmance in a suit for partition on declaration of plaintiff's title to the extent of ten annas ten gonads share in the lands described in schedules 1 to 3 And 5 to 12 and fourteen annas share in the land of schedule 4 and for recovery of khas possession and in the alternative, joint possession if the plaintiff is not found to be entitled to khas possession on partition by metes and bounds.

2. The plaintiff alleged that the land described in Schedules 1 to 3 and 5 to 12 previously belonged to Jamiruddin Sarkar to the extent of twelve annas share and Fakinnessa to the extent of the remaining four annas share. Jamiruddin had sixteen annas share in the land described in schedule 4 of the plaint Jamiruddin died leaving a son Chainuddin and a widow. Thereafter, the widow of Jamiruddin died leaving Chainuddin as the sole heir. Accordingly, Chainuddin acquired twelve annas share in the lands described in schedules 1-3 and 5.12 and sixteen annas share in the lands described in schedule. 4. Thereafter, Chainuddin died leaving plaintiff Sunila Bibi as daughter and pro defendant. No. 3 Sarifan Bibi as wife. Accordingly, the plaintiff acquired ten annas ten gonads share in the lands described in schedules 13 and 5-12 and fourteen annas share in the lands described in schedule 4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 are the heirs of Fakeness who acquired four annas share in the lands of schedules 1-3 and 5-12 and pro-defendant No. 3 acquired one Anna ten gondas share in the lands of those schedules and two annas share in the land of schedule 4. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 dispossessed the plaintiff on 20.5.60 although they have no title in the plaintiff's share of the land.

3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 dispossessed the plaintiff on 20.5.60 although they have no title in the plaintiff's share of the land. 3. Defendant No. 1 and 2 and defendant No. 5 and 11 filed written statement to contest the suit Defendant 5 and 11 ultimately did not contest the suit. According to defendant, 1 and 2, the suit is not maintainable in its present form since the disputed lands along with other lands were previously partitioned by a registered deed in 1348 B.S. By the said partition, the plaintiff obtained her share ascertained and the disputed land fell to the saham of the defendants and the plaintiff has no right, title and possession in the suit land. The contesting defendants raised a plea of defect of parties and a further plea that the entire properties of Jamiruddin were not brought into hotchpotch.

4. The suit was decreed twice previously and on appeal there was remand on both the occasions. After such remand, the plaintiff took necessary steps in terms of the order of remand and thereafter the suit was again decreed by the trial court granting partition on declaration of plaintiff's share in the following terms:-

"That the suit be decreed in the preliminary form on contest with cost against decants. 1 and 2 and exparte against the rest without' cost Puff's title in her 10 annas and 10 gondas and In 14 annas share in the lands in schedules Nos. 1-3 and 5-12 and in schedules. No. 4 respectively to the plaint be hereby declared. PM's, do get a separate Sahara for her share in the suit lands by partition by metes and bounds. She does get khas possession thereon by evicting the Defdts therefrom. On partition Defdts. 1 and 2 also do get a separate saham for their 4 annas share in the lands in schedule Nos. 1-3 and 7-12 by partition by metes and bounds.

"In reaching this conclusion the learned Munsif decided all the issues raised in the suit. According to the learned Munsif, all the properties held jointly by the parties have been brought into hotchpotch after amendment of the plaint on remand. The learned Munsif held that the suit was not bad for defect of parties and all the Persons interested in the disputed properties have been impleaded in the suit. Turning to the question of plaintiff's title to the suit land, the learned Munsif held that the plaintiff has ten annas ten gondas share in lands of schedules 1-3 and 5-12 by inheritance. The learned Munsif further' found that Jamiruddin had sixteen annas share in the land of schedule 4. According to the learned Munsif, the defendant No. I deposed in the suit as D.W. 4 and he admitted in his reposition that the plaintiff has acquired  share claimed by her in the suit land. The learned Munsif granted separate saham in favour of defendant No.1 and 2. In view of the finding on the question of plaintiff's title, the learned Munsif granted a decree for partition holding that the plain-tiff is entitled, to get separate saham in her share by metes and bounds and khas possession in the lands allotted to her on partition.

5. On appeal the learned District Judge affirmed the decision of the trial Court holding inter alia that the plaintiff is entitled to a decree for partition in respect of schedules 1-3 and 5-12 to the extent of ten annas and ten gondas share and fourteen annas share in the lands of schedule 4. The learned District Judge appears to have noticed the unfortunate development in the suit resulting in the successive orders for remand. The learned District Judge further noticed the legal effects of the exhibit A, the registered deed of partition dated 29.1.1942. According to the learned District Judge, the plaintiff was a minor and the said deed of partition was executed on her behalf by her mother and as such it was not binding on her and accordingly she had the right to at ode the same on attaining majority. The learned District Judge was of the view that the aforesaid partition was void and not voidable. As regards the age of the plaintiff, the learned District Judge reached a clear finding that she was minor at the time Exhibit "A was executed and the suit filed on 10.4.61 was within three years from the date of her attaining majority. The learned District Judge also noticed the evidence of D.W. 4 and the effects of his statement admitting title and share of the plaintiff as claimed in the suit. 6. Mr. Md. Ansar Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants contends that the learned District Judge erred in law in not holding that the suit was not maintainable without payment of ad-valorem Court fee on proper valuation of the suit. It appears that the question of Court fee and valuation of suit was never raised at any stage before this second appeal. It is true that originally the plaint consisted of four schedule and valuation of the suit was made in terms of the land involved. After remand, some other properties were included in the schedules to meet the objections raised by the contesting defendants and in terms of the order of remand by the Court of appeal below. After remand, prayer was made for amendment of the plaint and the same was allowed No further written statement was filed challenging the addition of properties and the valuation of the suit. This question was not raised at the trial or before the first appellate Court. Mr. Ansar Ali contends that the question of Court fee being a matter of revenue, the same could be investigated even in a second appeal. There is no doubt that this Court in the exercise of jurisdiction under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure may enter into such a question. In the instant case there is no material on record to indicate that a different valuation is possible. The defendants did not suggest any valuation according to their estimate nor there was any prayer before the Court of facts to ascertain the valuation of the suit properties in terms of section 8 (e) of the Court Fees Act. In the circumstances, in the absence of any materials on record, this Court cannot substitute an arbitrary valuation in place of the valuation stated by the plaintiff and accepted by the courts below while certifying court fees Mr. Ansar Ali has referred to the case of Nagendra Nath Sen Roy vs. Saiyad Ali Jamadar and others (1956) 8 DLR 100. The facts are distinguishable and there is no conflict that the Court has a right to correct the valuation. The question is not of right or jurisdiction of the Court but of materials on which the Court can decide this question in a second appeal. This question was not an issue since the defendants did not raise the same at any time before and pressed for determination of this question on evidence. In the circumstances, the contention of Mr. Ansar Ali does not appear to be of substance.

7. Mr. Ansar Ali refers to section 12 of the Court Fees Act. At this stage, it has no relevance. Unless there are materials on record to determine the valuation, section 12 of the Court Fees Act cannot be applied to recover the deficit Court fees on determination of proper valuation.

<u>8. The next question urged by Mr. Ansar Ali relates to the maintainability of the suit itself. The Courts below have concurrently reached a finding that the suit is maintainable Mr. Ansar Ali seeks to challenge this finding of the Courts below on the ground that the plaintiff is bound by Exhibit 'A' the deed of partition and that in the absence of a suit for avoiding that document on the ground of fraud, the instant suit for partition on declaration of title is not maintainable. Reference has been made by Mr. Ansar Ali in the case of Keramatullah Mia and others vs. Keramatullah Mea and others 23 Calcutta Weekly Notes 118. According to this decision, a dispute which has been resolved by a family arrangement cannot be reopened solely on the ground that one of the parties to the family arrangement was a minor". The facts of the case are clearly distinguishable. There is nothing on record to indicate that the partion in terms of Exhibit 'A' was in the interest of the minor and the same was a genuine transaction. The contesting defendants did not adduce any evidence to indicate that the previous partition was for the benefit of minor. There is no dispute that the partition deed was executed by the mother of the minor acting as a de facto guardian. The question is whether an act of de facto guardian binds the minor and whether the minor has any right to avoid an act of the de facto guardian. The law on the subject is char. Reference may be made to the case of Mir. Sarwarjan Vs. Fakhruddin Mahmed Chowdhury and others 39 I. A. page 1. Their Lordships of the Privy Council held that the guardian of a minor is not competent to bind the minor or his estate by a contract for the purchase of immovable property. The deed of partition by which a joint property was allegedly partitioned was not executed by a person lawfully authorised to represent the minor.' The act of the mother representing the minor as a de facto guardian 'cannot be conceived to be an act authorised to bind the minor for all purposes. A similar principle may be noticed in the case of Imambandi and others vs. Mutsaddi & others 54 1A7 3. It has been clearly laid down that the mother of the minor is not a legal guardian, has no power to deal with the immovable properly of the minor and alienation by such mother does not bind the minor. In the instant case the partition was effected by a registered instrument. Mr. Ansar Ali contends that the parties acted upon the said partition and as such it was not open to the plaintiff to undo the partition in the instant suit. There is nothing on record to indicate that the plaintiff acted upon. Exhibit "A Mr. Ansar Ali. however, points out that the plaintiff, after attaining majority, made certain transfers. The documents are on record. There is no recital there-in that she was in exclusive possession of the land transferred on the basis of the partition deed Exhibit 'A'. No evidence has been adduced by the defendants to show that the plaintiff accepted the partition in terms of the deed. In their circumstances, it cannot be conceived that the partition was binding against the plaintiff and that she acted upon in terms thereof. It has already been indicated that there is no material on record to justify that the previous partition was in the interest of the minor. In the circumstances, the contention of Mr. Ansar Ali does not appear to stand on a sound footing iii the instant facts. No authority could be cited that the plaintiff was estopped from exercising her right of partition on declaration of her title.</u>

9. The next contention of Mr. Ansar Ali relates to limitation. According to the learned Advocate, the plaintiff was aged about 30 years at the time of the deposition and the suit filed in 1961 was much beyond 3 years from the date of her attaining majority. In that way Mr. Ansar Ali contends that the suit was barred by limitation. The learned District Judge has considered this question with reference to Exhibits 2 and 2A. It has, however, been contended that there is nothing in Exhibits 2 and 2A to indicate that she was minor at the material time. On a scrutiny on those documents it appears that the learned District Judge was correct in construing exhibits 2 and 2A to indicate that the plaintiff was minor on 11-12-59. Reading the documents between the lines there is no scope for entertaining a doubt that she was not minor on 11-12-59. Mr. referred to the oral evidence D.Ws. 1, 4 and 5 to indicate Ansar Ali has of the plaintiff that the plaintiff was about 30 years on the date of her deposition. True, there are statements from which an inference may be made that the age may be more but it is difficult at this stage to decide this question conclusively without a reference to a conclusive evidence. Oral evidence adduced by the parties was assessed by the Court of facts. The learned District Judge reached a finding on assessment of evidence. This Court is not inclined to disturb a finding of fact reached by the Courts of facts. It further appears that the plaintiff alleged a case of dispossession on 20-5-60 and the instant suit was filed on 10-4-61. Therefore, it cannot be said that suit was barred by limitation. The plaintiff did not file the suit for declaration that Exhibit A was not binding on her or that the same was obtained by fraud and misrepresentation, since the plaintiff was a minor at the time. Exhibit A was executed; she is not the per-son to know that there was a fraud or misrepresentation at the time of execution of Exhibit A. Viewed from any perspective it does not appear that limitation has any role to play in the dispute.

10. The last contention of Mr. Ansar Ali relates to misreading and non-consideration of evidence. The learned Munsif, after remand decreed that suit on consideration of the evidence relating to the issues framed in the suit. In deciding those issues after remand, certain evidence was not relied upon since the defendant No. I in his evidence was not recalled after remand, admitted the title and share of the others. The case of defendant No. 2 is not inconsistent with that of defendant No. 1 and that they stand on the same footing. Therefore, the evidence of defendant No. I was an evidence in the suit and the Courts below appear to have relied on the said evidence in addition to other evidence on record, in deciding the extent of share and title of the plaintiff. It may not be an admission but the fact remains that the statement of defendant No. 1 was taken into consideration by the Courts below to decide the question of title and share claimed by the plaintiff. Mr. Ansar Ali has also complained of non-consideration of other question, namely, with reference to the evidence regarding the age of the plaintiff. As already indicated, this question has lost its importance in the suit as framed. It has already been pointed out that it is a suit for partition on declaration of title on allegation of dispossession some time in 1960. Therefore, non-consideration of that part of the oral evidence cannot be said to have validated the decision of the learned District Judge.

11. For the reasons stated above, none of the contentions raised by Mr. Ansar Ali appear to be of substance in the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs.

Mr. Ansar Ali the learned Advocate for the appellant prays for leave to appeal under clause 15 of the Letters Patent. The leave as prayed for is refused.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 14 of 1976.
lawyer: Serajuddin Ahmed-For the appellant, Chowdnury, Kazi Ebadul Hoque-For Respondents Nos. 1, 2(a)-2 (c) 3-7.
parties:
Madhari Mia ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Surjat Ali ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J -This appeal calls in question a decree dated 28.1.75 of Mr. M A Rashid, Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dacca dismissing the Title suit No. 92 of 1973 on the ground that it was bit by res judicata as well as barred by litigation, decree dated 31-8.67 of the Mnnsif, 1st Court, Dacca in T.S. No. 138/65 was found by the learned Subordinate Judge to have stood in the way of this suit. Hence the plain-tiff has come in this appeal.

2. Facts of the case, so far necessary for disposal of the questions raised before us, are that the plaintiff-appellant claimed to have purchased the suit land measuring a little over 3 acres within the vicinity of the Dacca Airport by a registered kabala dated 5.11.55 from one B. B. Basak and also to have gone into possession thereof since then. But the defendants respondents whose predecessors-in-interest had been owners of the land long, ago were, it has been alleged trying to disturb the plaintiffs possession puttin claims of title and possession. Thereupon a series of litigation followed between the parties. The plaintiff filed a suit being Title Suit No. 138 of 1965 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dacca for a permanent injunction against the defendants. The learned Munsif after hearing the parties dismissed that suit on 31-8 67 refusing permanent injunction on a finding that the plaintiff was out of possession of the land ever since he had purchased it. Thereafter the plaintiff filed the present suit; T. S. No. 92 of 1973, for declaration of title and recovery of possession. The defendants contested this suit denying the plaintiff's claim of title and possession altogether and questioned the very maintainability of the suit contending that it is barred by the principle of res judicata as well as by law of limitation. In view of these pleadings of the parties the learned from Original Decree No. 14 of Subordinate Judge decided the suit on the preliminary issues, without going into the merits, accepted the contention of the defendants and held that the decree dated 31.8 67 of the Munsif in the previous No 138 of 1955 for injunction operates as res judicata In this suit and further that the suit is barred by limitation. On these findings he dismissed the suit by the impugned decree.

3. Mr. Serajuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate, appearing for the appellant has seriously assailed the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge. He has contended that the principle of res judicata is not at all applicable to this suit firstly, because the court which had tried the former suit had got no concurrent jurisdiction with the court of the Subordinate Judge in which this suit was filed, and secondly, because the matters in issue between the two suits are altogether different. Mr. Serajuddin Ahmed has submit-ted that the former suit was a suit for injunction which was filed on payment of court fees of Tk. 25.00 whereas the subsequent suit is a regular title suit filed on payment of ad valorem court fee, for declaration of title and recovery of possession. As to the finding about the appellant's possession. Mr. Serajuddin has contended that this finding is not of the learned Subordinate Judge but is the finding of the Munsif arrived at in the former suit for injunction and as such on this finding it cannot be held that the present suit is barred by limitation.

4. Mr. B N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the respondents has supported the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge. He has argued that though the learned munsif had no jurisdiction to try the subsequent suit as a whole yet he had got jurisdiction to try a particular issue which is common to both the suits i.e. the issue of the plaintiff's possession. In the former suit for injunction, Mr. Chowdhury contends, possession was to be determined and this question was determined by the learned Munsif who found the plaintiff out of possession for over 12 years. This decision as to possession, M. Chowdhury argues, will certainly operate as res judicata in the subsequent suit. Both the learned lawyers have cited a great number of decisions in support of their respective contentions. We propose to Considers some of those decisions which appear to us to be relevant to the questions before us.

<u>5. Law as to res judicata has been laid down in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The relevant part of this section is quoted below: "No Court shall try any suit. or issue in which the matte has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such court". This law is called res judicata, Fundamental principle of res judicata is that a case which has been decided by a competent court shall not be brought before another coda by the same parties, for if such case is allowed to be fought again the successful party will be put to harassment and there will be no end of legal battle. A case must be decided finally and once for all and after it is so decided no further litigation between the same patties should be allowed this principle has been best elucidated by this court in a case in 10 DLR-621. The relevant part of the decision thereof is quoted below:</u>

<u>“The maxim is that no one shall be vexed twice over the same matter, which presupposes that the issue has been fairly and finally tried dusted, d in a former suit, which was independent of the proceedings, in which the same matter is again in dispute"</u>

<u>To bring a decision made in a former suit within the purview of this section one of the requirements is that the court which tried the former suit must have jurisdiction to try the subsequent suit as well In this case the former suit was tried by a Munsif who had no pecuniary jurisdiction to try the subsequent. Therefore, these two courts are not courts of concurrent jurisdiction. But Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has submitted that the learned Munsif had jurisdiction to determine the issue of possession in the former suit and he had determined this issue, and when this very issue of possession of the plaintiff has been raised in the subsequent suit this decision will operate as res judicata. In support of this contention he has referred to AIR 1945 Bombay, 45 and 67, AIR 1935, Calcutta 72, 13 DLR 89. In AIR, 945 Bombay, 45 it has been held.</u>

<u>"It is true that ordinarily the decision of an issue in a court of lower pecuniary jurisdiction will not operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit filed in a court of a superior jurisdiction, and tribal only by such court. But it is not open to a plaintiff to evade the bar of res judicata by joining several causes of action against the same defendant or defendants in a use tent suit instituted in a court of higher pecuniary jurisdiction. Where a decision has been given by a competent court in a previous suit, regarding part of the claim in the subsequent suit and between the same parties; then so much of the claim, which is common to the two suits should be excluded from the subsequent suit as barred be the principles of res judicata".</u>

<u>In the other case of the same AIR Bombay (1945) it has been held:</u>

<u>"Just as a plaintiff cannot evade the provisions of section 11 by combining several causes of action against the same defendant in a subsequent suit and instituting it in a court of superior jurisdiction, so also he cannot avoid section 11 by splitting up the cases of action of the previous suit, as to give jurisdiction to an inferior court".</u>

<u>In these two cases, the principle of partial res judicata was applied because in one case several causes of action were combined in the subsequent suit and in the other case cause of actin of a previous suit was split up into several causes for filing it in an inferior court. But in the case before us there has neither been any combination of causes of action nor splitting up of a cause of action into many. Moreover, in those cases, the nature of both the previous and subsequent suits was the same, whereas in the case before us the nature of the suit is different, one being for injunction and the other for title and possession. In 13 DLR 89, bar of res judicata was sought to be avoided by the plaintiff by showing enhanced value of the suit land in the subsequent suit. The previous was tried by a Munsif as it was within his pecuniary jurisdiction but when the value of the suit land increased at a subsequent time, another suit was filed before the Subordinate Judge showing higher valuation of the suit. In those circumstances it was held that the principle of res judicata could not be evaded by the plaintiff. This decision also does not help the contention of Mr. B.N Chowdhury because value of the land of the instant suit was much higher than the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Munsif when the former suit was filed.</u>

6. Similar is the nature of the question raised and decided in AIR 1935-Cal-792 it was held there:

"A party who has lost in one court cannot be permitted to add causes of action or prayer for reliefs in another suit for the purpose of swelling the valuation of his suit and claim that the decision in the former suit does not operate as res judicata----- if it is possible to treat the entire cause of action upon which the latter suit is founded as divisible and if in the earlier suit one of be component parts of the cause of action was relied upon then the previous decision will stand as a bar to the event of the master involved in the earlier suit."

But this principle will apply only when the earlier suit has been tried by a competent court as has been clearly held therein as:

Where the previous suit had been decided by a court which had no jurisdiction to entertain a subsequent suit, the decision of any issue in the previous suit can never be regarded as operating res judicata when the same issue in such subsequent suit has been raised".

7. Mr. Serajuddin Ahmed has, on the other hand, relied upon AIR-1929, Lah, 596 AIR-1935, Cal. 641 and CWN (XlI)-359 in the first case the question that arose for determination was whether the decree in a previous suit for declaration of title which was pound hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act would operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit for title and possession. The question was categorically answered in the native in AIR 1935 Cal. 642. The question for determination was, whether when an issue which was not in a previous suit because of the 'form' of the Suit, judgment of that suit would operate as res judicata in a subsequent suit embracing this issue. This question was also answered in the negative in CWN (XII) 359, it was held:

In order to establish the plea of res judicata the court which decided the former suit must have been such a court as would have been competent to try and decide not only the particular matter in issue in the subsequent suit but also the subsequent suit itself in which the issue is subsequently raised".

<u>8. The question of partial res judicata as raised by Mr. B N. Chowdhury is found to have been adequately answered in the decision just quoted above. We have already found that in the instant case the former suit was a suit for permanent injunction, whereas the subsequent suit is for title and possession. To decide a suit for injunction of Possession, of course is to be determined this question was decided against the plaintiff whereupon his suit was dismissed. But this finding as to possession in the suit for injunction cannot operate as res judicata in the subsequent suit for declaration and possession simply because subsequent suit for title and possession could not have been tried by the learned Munsif for want of pecuniary jurisdiction. The principle of res judicata is found to have been erroneously applied in this case.</u>

9. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury next contended that the suit was dismissed; on the ground of limitation also since the plaintiff was not found to have been in possession within 12 years prior to the filing of the suit Mr. Serajuddin Ahmed has submitted that this decision of the learned Subordinate judge is entirety without evidence in that no evidence was recorded in this suit but it was decided on preliminary issues it appears that the learned Subordinate judge has based this observation on the finding as to possession arrived at by the learned Munsif in the previous suit and that this finding is not a finding of the Subordinate judge himself. The issue of limitation is also found to have been wrongly decided by the learned Subordinate judge.

Having considered the points as raised by the learned Advocates of both the parties we hold that the decision of the learned Subordinate judge is probably wrong and that the suit is not barred by res judicata and as to question of limitation, it can be determined only by recording evidence.

In the result the appeal is allowed on contest and the impugned decree is set aside. The suit is sent back to the learned Subordinate judge for disposal on merits in view of the questions of law involved in this case we do not make any order as to costs. Send down the records at once.

M.H. Rahman, J.- I agree.

End.

lawyer:
S. R. Pal, Senior Advocate with Habibur Rahman, Advocate, instructed by S.S. Hoda, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Appellants.
S.S. Halder, Advocate. Instructed by Aminul Huq, Advocate-on Record -----For the Respondent.
parties:
Dr. Mohammad Hossain and anr. ------ Appellants.
Vs.
Abdul Malek Khan ------ Respondent.
case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 15-12-76 passed by the High Court in F.A. No. 195 of 1974).
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain. C. J: -<u>The defendants are appellants. The facts in dispute are not much and they may be set out in a few words.</u>

<u>The plaintiff and the two defendant-appellants earlier brought a suit for specific performance of contract against Kamal Rani Devi and got a decree in that suit and it was put in to execution. In the earlier suit and in the present it is not disputed, that the consideration money was Tk. 30,000/- and it was paid on two occasions by installment of Tk. 15,000/- and on the earlier occasion Tk. 15,000/-was paid through defendant 1. The three persons, the plaintiff and the two defendants got a joint decree on a single contract which was silent as to the shares of the vendors. Neither in the contract nor in the decree is there any mention of the proportion of the sum paid by the vendors. It is to be observed that all the three vendors are in possession of the property on the basis of a contract on which the decree for specific performance has been obtained. Disputes arose between the plaintiff and the defendants as to extent of shares. Plaintiff claimed 1/3rd share which was denied by the defendants, and this denial impelled the plaintiff to institute the present Suit which was contested mostly on two grounds. First, as to the quantum of share of the plaintiff, whether it was 1/3rd or 1/6th; and, secondly, the suit for partition by the plaintiff was incompetent. The trial Court negative the first part of the claim of the plaintiff, holding that his contribution was to the extent of 1/6th and on the second question, the contention of the defendants on the competency of the suit was overruled. He, therefore, decreed the Suit in preliminary form. On appeal by the plaintiff the learned Judges or the High Court allowed tile appeal and raised tile share of the plaintiff to 1/3rd.</u>

<u>Leave was granted on the two questions on which he suit was mainly contested.</u>

2. Mr. Pal, the learned Counsel for the appellants contends that the learned Judges of tile High Court were in error in finding 1/3rd share for the plaintiff by applying the rule of equal proportion containing in second paragraph of section 45 of the Transfer of Property Act. It is true that the learned Judges of the High Court applied the rule, but in so applying they have fully considered the evidence called by both sides and have found that the plaintiff's two witnesses, plaintiff himself and P. W. 2 Abdul Latif Sheikh have asserted that the plaintiff paid a sum of Tk. 10,000/- on two occasions, and thereafter the learned Judges have discussed all the six defense, witnesses and on a balance of evidence, came to the conclusion that the defendants had not been able to prove payment of only Tk. 5000/ by the plaintiff of the consideration money. In coming to this conclusion the learned Judges have also referred to the pleadings of the parties. So apart from the application of the rule contained in section 45 of the Transfer of Property Act the learned Judges have found on fact, that the plaintiff has proved payment of Tk. 10,000/-whereas defendants have failed to prove their case of payment of Tk. 5000/- only. In this state of evidence and on discussion of the evidence by the learned Judges, we do not find any scope for this Division to interfere with this finding.

3. We now come to the second question which though apparently attractive does oat seem to have much substance. It is with regard to the competency of the partition suit filed by the plaintiff respondent. Mr. Pal's argument will be looked into presently. Before that, let us take the question on the facts as they stand. The plaintiff and the defendant are the three vendees on a contract and the defendant are the three single vendees on a single contract and, they have paid Tk. 30,000/- towards the consideration money and obtained a decree for specific performance of contract from the Court and the decree is under execution though not executed. The parties in terms of the contract were and are in possession of the property. It is therefore to be seen that what is the right acquired by the plaintiff and the defendants in the earlier decree for specific performance which has not been fully executed. It is true that if the decree for specific performance would have been executed in full, the Kabala would have been in favors of the decree-holders and they would have become the title holders of the land which was agreed to be conveyed under the contract and affirmed by the decree.

4. The Problem before us is what is the right acquired by the parties under the decree for specific performance of contract which has not been executed. If the parties have acquired a right which the law recognizes then the fundamental principle of jurisprudence is that where there is a right there must be a remedy.

<u>5. It is, therefore to be seen what is the right acquired by the parties in the decree for specific performance of contract and whether the partition of the land is the proper remedy. It is now well settled that apart from the ownership or legal title to the land, many diverse kinds of right ate created by various kinds of possession of property. To illustrate some, it may be mentioned that, section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act gives a legal sanction to possession obtained in part performance of a written contract. Here particular right is recognized by statute but no specific remedy is laid down. Similarly section 9 of the Specific Relief Act does not specially create any right but provides a remedy to a possessor to recover his possession, if he is wrongfully dispossessed in terms of section. These two provisions amongst others are instances of statutory provision but they are by no means Exhaustive. Courts of law have in the infinite relations between persons and property found different kinds of rights arising from contract or otherwise and provided remedies as to the nature of the case and justice of the cause.</u>

6. One or two illustrations will clarify the proposition. Mr. Halder has cited the authority of 18 D.L.R. 691 the case of Aminul Islam VS. M/s Kiburn & Co. Ltd, where a Division Bench of the High Court bas held that if a possessory owner is wrongfully deprived of the thing by a person other than the true owner he can recover it. Then in the case of Abdul Karim vs. Fazal Muhammad Shah 19 D.L.R (S.C) 477, the Supreme Court of Pakistan has held the mere failure of the parries to comply with the requirements of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act cannot alter the nature of the transaction between the vendor and the vendee or affect the pre-emptor's right in respect of it and if the transaction amounts to a sale in fact, then notwithstanding that it is not in the form prescribed by section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, the right of pre-emption will come into operation, In Jnan Chandra Das vs. Rajani Kanta Pal A.I.R 1918 Cal 923 a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court found that where the plaintiff got possession on payment of entire consideration for its purchase tinder a contract of sale, but before the conveyance was registered, the land was sold and was purchased by the defendant in execution of a money decree against the plaintiff, the plaintiff at the date of the auction purchase by the defendant had acquired a right to the land which passed to the defendant under the sale in execution so that the plaintiff could not contend that he had no interest in the property which could be purchased by the defendant at the execution sale and that he was not entitled to recover the property from the defendant on getting a registered conveyance from its former owner after the defendant's purchase. These are only some of the authorities referred to in support of the proposition stated above, that according to the nature and character of possession the fights acquired by the parties will determine the remedies available to him.

<u>7. Multiplication of these instances is uncalled for, but, one relevant decision for our purpose may also be referred to Musammat Sundar vs. Musammat Parbati 16 IA 187 is a case where two Hindu widows were found to be in lawful possession of the property of their deceased husband, and a case of division of their properties having arisen, the question was whether a partition suit was competent. Holding its competency, the Privy Council observed, that the widows were in lawful possession of their husband's properties and though they had no title, still they by lawful possession had an estate or interest in respect of their possession and so can maintain the partition suit. The facts were that the appellant and the respondent were two Hindu widows of Baldeo Sahai and they were seized of movable and immovable properties left by their husband. Baldeo Sahai had adopted one Praimsukh, his sister's son who had died after the death of Baldeo. The widows however were in lawful possession but had no title, whereas either the heirs of Praimsukh or Baldeo Sahai had preferable title. In the context of these facts, the Privy Council held in favors of the competency of the partition suit. This is a very good illustration of the principle, where there is a right, there is a remedy. This decision is also an authority for the proposition that to maintain a partition suit the parties to the suit though must have community of interest, yet need not have a legal title.</u>

8. If we revert to the facts of the present case to see what right has been acquired under the decree, it is seen that the decree holders of the suit for specific performance of contract were in possession of the property in part performance of the contract, and their contract has now been affirmed by a decree for specific performance of contract. It can, therefore, be legitimately said that the decree holders of the suit for specific performance of contract did acquire an interest in the land which is equivalent to a legal right in the property. The dispute between the decree-holders is to determine their shares, and then to demarcate their respective shares on the land which they are holding jointly. In the earlier suit, it was not decided as to which proportion the decree-holders contributed towards the purchase price of the property. The plaintiff in this suit set up a claim to 1/3rd, whereas the defendants to 1/6th share and that has now finally been determined at 1/3rd on appeal. If determination could be made by the Court, and it is not disputed then the consequential relief of partition could not be resisted. The rights of the parties acquired under the decree are the same and they are in joint possession. What is sought is to enjoy the property in severalty for convenience. In such circumstances, a partition suit is the proper remedy. We, therefore, do not find any want of competence in this suit for partition.

<u>9. The contention of Mr. Pal that in a suit for specific performance of contract unless the decree is executed and the Kabala obtained no legal title vest in the decree holders as a legal proposition, is not in dispute. The answer is that, apart from legal title to a property, there may be various species of possessory or other legal rights created on the property which can be enforced. Once there is a legal right, the remedy will be available according to the right. It could not be said that when a transferee is in possession of a property in part performance of the contract and that contract has been affirmed by a decree for specific performance of contract, the transferee after the decree does not acquire an interest in the land. He can lawfully maintain and protect his possession and interest in the property.</u>

10. Mr. Pal, however, has rightly pointed out that the view expressed in the case of Joydeb Agarwala Vs. Baitulrnal Karkbana Ltd. (1964) 16 DLR (SC) 706; P.L D.
