(1965) S.C 37, to the extent that upon an execution of a contract of sale of a property, the purchaser acquires an equitable estate is not a correct proposition of law, inasmuch as it is, directly against the provision of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act which says that the contract for sale of immovable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties and does not create any interest in or charge on such property. In view of the specific statutory provision application of English doctrine of equitable estate in favors of a contracting party to a sale of immovable property is not permissible. But then correctness of the view taken in that case in the sense that it created a right in favors of the decree-holder the fact of the case cannot be questioned.

11. Mr. Pal's contention is that without acquisition of title a partition suit is not sustainable. We have already observed that Possession may be of different kinds and categories and may give rise to various kinds of rights and obligations and, according to the nature of the right recognized by law, remedies Will be available to the parties when the right is either infringed or threatened and the remedy will be relatable to the right acquired by the plaintiff and the infringement or the violation complained of Beyond this no further general formulation is either necessary or desirable. We have decided to question on the facts before us.

In the result, we dismiss the appeal without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule arose out of an application under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act and was directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.4.1992 passed by the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in SCC Suit No. 12 of 1991 decreeing the suit for eviction in favour of the plaintiff.

2. The opposite party Mr. Hanif as plaintiff instituted SCC Suit No.12 of 1991 in the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge and SCC Court, Dhaka against the defendant-petitioner Sree Sudhan Chandra Ray for eviction. The case of the plaintiff, in brief is that the suit premises as described in the plaint originally belonged to Mrs. Amena Begum and after her death her son, the plaintiff became the owner thereof by registered partition deed between the co-sharers. The plaintiff's mother Amena Begum let out the suit premises to Naz Jewellers as a monthly ejectable tenant before liberation war of Bangladesh and after liberation, during the lifetime of plaintiff's mother the defendant took possession of the suit premises forcefully driving away the owner of Naz Jewellers and started Jewellery business therein and ultimately Mrs. Amena Begum admitted the defendant as a monthly ejectable bharatia in respect of the suit house. Defendant thus became a monthly bharatia under Mrs. Amena Begum and after her death under the plaintiff at a monthly rental of Taka 300.00 The defendant irregularly paid rent to the plaintiff upto March, 1991 and received the rent receipts, but he stopped payment of rent since the month of March, 1991. The defendant is a defaulter and became an undesirable tenant by his behaviour. The plaintiff-landlord also bonafide requires the suit house for his own use and occupation to accommodate his 4 grown up sons therein. Therefore, the plaintiff-landlord served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on 2.7.91 upon the defendant determining his tenancy in respect of the suit house on the expiry of 31st July, 1991. The notice was received by the defendant by putting his signature on 4.7.91 but the defendant did not vacate the suit house after expiry of notice period and, as such, the plaintiff filed the SCC Suit as aforesaid.

3. The defendant-tenant contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the notices under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act served upon the defendant is not valid nor sufficient, that the plaintiff does not bonafide require the suit house as claimed by him. The defendant's further case is that one Aminul Huq purchased the possessory right of the suit house from Mrs. Amina Bibi, the original owner of the suit premises and started jewellery business there. Aminul Hoque paid monthly rent at a rate of Taka 100.00 to the landlady and thereafter he transferred his possession of the suit premises to the defendant and then the defendant became bharatia under the landlady Mrs. Amena Begum at a monthly rent of Taka 100.00 which was subsequently increased to Taka 300.00 The defendant paid rent regularly to the plaintiff and obtained receipt from him. The defendant paid rent to the plaintiff for the month of March, 1991 on 1.4.1991 and the plaintiff granted rent receipt on 7.4.1991 and thereafter the defendant paid rent for the month of April, 1991 to the plaintiff in presence of witness Narayan Chandra Roy and others but that the plaintiff did not give the rent receipt to the defendant. Then again the defendant offered rent to the plaintiff for the month of May, 1991 on 2.6.1991 but the plaintiff did not accept the same. Thereafter, the defendant filed House Rent Control Case No. 37 of 1991 in the Court of House Rent Controller for deposit of rent and that the defendant filed another HR Case No. 36 of 1991 under section 27 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance for rent receipt. Thus the defendant is not a defaulter. The plaintiff's suit is therefore liable to be dismissed.

4. The learned Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka and SCC Judge after hearing both the parties and considering the facts, circumstances and the evidence of the case, decreed the suit for eviction in favour of the plaintiff vide his Judgment and decree dated 30.4.1992.

5. Being aggrieved by that Judgment and decree dated 30.4.1992, the defendant as petitioner has filed this revisional application under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act in this Court and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr. SC Das, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant petitioner has made his first submission that the notice as served upon the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act was invalid and insufficient in law as because the suit premises in question is a manufacturing factory and not a shop-house and, as such, six months notice to determine the tenancy in respect of a factory was necessary to be served upon the defendant tenant but the plaintiff had served only one month's notice upon the defendant which did not determine his tenancy from the suit premises, but that the learned SCC Judge came to an erroneous finding that the suit premises is a shop-house and one month's notice under section 106 TP Act was sufficient to terminate the tenancy right of the defendant.

7. Md. Sirajul Islam Mondal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, has, on the other hand, submitted that the suit premises is a shop room and not a factory and that the defendant himself has stated the suit premises in his cross-examination to be a shop room and that he has also described the suit premises as a shop room in the schedule of his HR Case No. 37 1991 and HR Case No.36 of 1991 and that the defendant also described the suit premises as shop in his application filed to Sharno Shilpi Sramik Sangho as per Exhibits-10 and 11 and as such, the suit premises being a shop room 15 days notice is sufficient to terminate the defendant's tenancy in respect of the same. The learned Advocate further argued that the learned SCC Judge has framed an issue to decide whether the suit premises is a shop or a factory and after discussing all the evidences and the materials of the case came to a definite decision that the suit premises is a shop and not a factory.

<u>8. By a perusal of the impugned Judgment, it appears that the learned SCC Judge has discussed all the evidence of the case with reference to the statements made by the defendant as DW I in his cross-examination that he has described the suit premises in his HR Case No. 36 of 1991 and 37 of 1991 as a shop standing by the side of the road and that he did not claim it to be a factory in the HR Case. By a perusal of the plaints, written statement and the evidence of the witnesses, it appears that the suit house is a two-storied residential building standing at 103, Tatibazar. The plaintiff as PW 1 has said in his cross-examination that there are four rooms in the building. Admittedly, the plaintiff has been residing in the first floor of the building with his family and that the defendant is doing his business in one room of that building in the ground floor as bharatia under the plaintiff. From all these facts and materials on record, it will appear that there cannot be any factory in a residential building.</u>

<u>9. All the above facts, circumstances and the materials of the case considering together with the evidences, both oral and documentary as in the record, I find that the learned SCC Judge has come to a correct finding that the suit premises is a shop room and not a factory and that this finding of the learned SCC Judge is based on just and proper appreciation of the facts and evidences of the case. In such a position of the matter, I am of the opinion that 15 days' notice under section 106 of TP Act as served upon the defendant is a valid and sufficient notice determining the tenancy of the defendant in respect of the suit premises.</u>

10. The learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner next submits that the defendant petitioner purchased the possession of the suit premises from one Aminul Huque by a document and that the defendant having obtained the possessory right in respect of the suit premises, is not a monthly ejectable tenant and as such 6(six) months notice was required to be served upon him for termination of his tenancy right. To this point, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party argued that the plaintiff's mother never sold the possession to Aminul Hoque or anybody else and that no such Aminul Hoque is even known to the plaintiff or to his mother but that after liberation of Bangladesh this defendant-petitioner with the help of others forcibly entered into the suit premises by driving out the plaintiff's bharatia, the owner of Naz Jewellers and compelled the plaintiff's mother Amena Begum to admit him as her tenant. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendant's alleged document, Ext. 'Ka" is a created un-registered document and that there is no signature of any witness or any writer in it.

11. By a perusal of this document exhibit 'Ka', it appears that it has been writen in 14 lines without stating as to who is that Aminul Hoque, whether he is an executant or a recipient of that document and how and when he took possession of the suit premises from Amena Begum. This document does not bear the signature of any witness. It has been written in the document that possession was delivered to Sudhan Chandra Ray in June of last 1973. "Possession of shop room has not been described nor any schedule has been given in it and that there is no signature of any scribe or any witness. It does not also bear any date in it. The words "last 1973' and "was delivered" go to say that this is an ante-dated piece of paper. There is nothing to show that Amena Begum ever sold any possession to any Aminul Hoque in respect of the suit premises. On the other hand, the defendant's witness one Aminur Rahman as DW 4 has said in his cross-examination that he was not present at the time of writing of this Ext. 'Ka' and that there is no witness in it and that Aminul Huq did not sign at any time before him and that he does not know whether any transfer of possession took place. All these facts and evidence will go to show that this piece of paper, Ext 'Ka', is not admissible in evidence and that it did not create any kind of right in favour of the defendant.

12. By a perusal of the tenant's portion of the rent receipts as filed by the defendant in the suit and the counterfoil as filed by the plaintiff as per Exhibit-7 series, it appears that the defendant Sree Sudhan Chandra Roy was described there in printed forms as an ejectable tenant at will in all the receipts. From all the above documentary, oral evidence of the PWs and DWs it clearly appears that the defendant-petitioner is a monthly ejectable tenant in respect of the suit shop-room. I am, therefore, of the opinion that the learned SCC Judge is quite justified in holding that the defendant is a monthly ejectable tenant under the plaintiff. Thus I find that 15 days notice is sufficient to determine his bharatia right.

13. Next question is whether the defendant is a defaulter. It has been seriously contended on behalf of the defendant that the defendant has paid rent to the plaintiff for the month of April 1991 but he refused to accept it and then the defendant filed HR Case No. 37 of 1991 and has been depositing the rent in Court of the House Rent Controller under section 19 of the House Rent Control Ordinance. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party has, on this point, argued that the defendant obtained rent receipts from the plaintiff-landlord on the first day of every month on payment or without payment of the rent but that the defendant could not produce any rent receipt showing payment of rent for April 1991 as because the defendant stopped payment of rent to the plaintiff-landlord from the month of April 1991.

14. By a perusal of the impugned Judgment, it appears that the learned SCC Judge framed a separate issue to the effect whether the defendant is a defaulter in respect of payment of rent and after discussing all the facts and evidence of the case with reference to oral and documentary evidence produced by the plaintiff and defendant, the learned SCC Judge has come to a definite finding that the defendant is a defaulter in respect of payment of rent for the month of April 1991 and for the month of January and February, 1992. Defendant's claim is that he paid rent for the month of April, 1991 in presence of witness Narayan Chandra Roy but that the plaintiff did not give him any receipt. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff argued that there was no witness in payment of rent of any of the previous months and so, the question of presence of witness Narayan Ohandra for the month of April only does not arise.

15. In appears that the defendant obtained rent receipts on the first day of every month showing payment of rent to the plaintiff as per Ext. 7 series. So the question of non-granting of rent receipt for the month of April, 1991 only by the plaintiff does not arise and this solitary allegation is not a believable allegation. The statement of DW 2 Narayan Chandra Roy that he was present in payment of rent of April, 1991 has not been believed by the learned SCC Judge giving his reasons therein. This DW 2 said in his cross-examination that he was not present in the payment of rent for the month of March, 91 and that the defendant did not pay any rent to the plaintiff for any other month excepting the month of April 1991 in his presence. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the solitary presence of DW 2 Narayan Chandra Roy for the month of April only speaks volumes about the conduct of the defendant towards the plaintiff. For all these reasons and for many other reasons, I find that the learned SCC Judge has rightly disbelieved the statement of DW 2.

16. By a detailed discussion of all the above facts, circumstances and evidences of the case, the learned SCC Judge found the defendant-petitioner to be a defaulter in respect of payment of rent for the month of April, 1991 and January, 1992 as because the defendant could not produce any Challan showing deposit of rent for January 92. To this point, the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner today filed an information slip claiming that the defendant has deposited rent for the month of January and February, 1992. By a perusal of this slip paper, it appears that he had filed a searching only on 7.6.95 in the Judge's Court and got the reply on 8.6.95 But the hearing of this Revision Case was concluded on 6.6.95 when it was found that the learned SCC Judge came to a clear finding that the defendant did not pay any rent for April 1991 and January. 1992 as because he did not file any chalan in Court showing deposit of rent for January, 1992 It may be mentioned here that all the chalans filed by the defendant in the trial Court showing deposit of rent as per HR Case No. 37 of 1991 vide Exhibit 'Kha' Series are all in origin. This copy of chalan with the 'receiving seal' of the Bangladesh Bank is the depositor's copy for each month with a deposit number in seal given by the Treasury in the top of the chalan. But no explanation is given in the Revisional Application or in the affidavit-in-reply against the  counter-affidavit of the opposite party as to what happened to his original chalan of January and February 1992 although he could file the chalans in original form upto December; 91 No. explanation is given during argument also. It is not the case that defendant has lost his chalan for the month of January and February, 1992. The information slip in question as filed today without any petition did not also contain any deposit number of treasury nor of serial number of deposit Register of the Court. There is a difference between chalan Register and deposit Register. For all these reasons this kind of information slip beyond the record cannot be given any credence.

17. Under all the above facts and circumstances and evidence on record, I am of the opinion that the clear finding arrived at by the learned SCC Judge in respect of separate issue No. 3 to the effect that defendant is defaulter in respect of payment of rent for the month of April, 1991 and January 1992 is a correct finding based on detailed discussion and proper appreciation of the facts, evidence and materials on record. I therefore find that the learned SCC Judge is quite justified in coming to this decision that the defendant petitioner is a defaulter in payment of rent to the plaintiff-landlord.

18. The learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner next contended that the learned SCC Judge did not come to any conclusion in respect of bonafide requirement of the plaintiff and so the defendant-petitioner is not liable to be evicted on the ground of bonafide requirement.

19. By a perusal of the impugned Judgment, it appears that the learned SCC Judge has framed an issue being issue No. 5 to the effect whether the plaintiff has got any bonafide requirement of the suit premises for his own use and occupation. It appears that the learned SCC Judge has discussed this point of bonafide requirement with reference to the evidence on record. The learned SCC Judge found from the facts and evidence that the suit building consists of 4 rooms, 2 rooms in the ground floor and 2 rooms in the first floor and that the plaintiff has been residing therein with his four sons and daughters and wife with much difficulty. By discussing and considering the facts and evidence on record, the learned SCC Judge came to the finding that the plaintiff has a bonafide requirement of the suit premises for his own use and occupation. I have already found above that the suit building consists of 4 rooms and that the plaintiff has been living in the two rooms of the first floor with his family and that one room in the ground floor is used by the defendant as plaintiff's Bharatia, The plaintiff has 4 grown up sons as is available from evidence and from above findings of SCC Judge. There is no suggestion from the defendant petitioner whether the plaintiff has any other alternative house to accommodate his grown up sons. From the facts and materials on record I find that the learned SCC Judge has come to a correct conclusion that the plaintiff has got bonafide requirement of the suit premises for his own use and occupation and that this conclusion is based on proper appreciation of the facts and evidence on record.

<u>20. It has been argued on behalf of the defendant-petitioner that the defendant filed a case being HR Case No. 36 of 1991 section 27 of the Rent Control Ordinance for non-issue of rent receipt for the month of April, 1991 which is pending till today. It is contended that the HR Case No. 36 of 1991 should have been disposed of before the SCC Suit No. 12 of 1991. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to a decision in the case of Narayan Prosad Bhowmik vs. Sree Sree Juktaswar Radha Madhab Jew Thakur Bigraha reported in 40 DLR (HC) 449 wherein it has been observed that non-disposal of the application under section 27 of the Ordinance before the disposal of the present case would render that suit infructuous. To this point, the learned advocates for the plaintiff-opposite party submits that in the instant case the defendant-petitioner became a defaulter in respect of payment of rent in the month of April, 1991 and that on the ground of bonafide requirement and for non payment of rent the plaintiff served a notice upon the defendant under section 106 of the Transfer or Property Act, issued on 2nd July, 1991 and received by him on 4th July, 1991 and immediately thereafter he filed the HR Case No. 36 of 1991 on 6th July 1991 under section 27 of the Rent Control Ordinance which is a penal section and then the defendant filed HR Case No. 37 of 1991 for deposit of rent under section 19 of the Rent Control Ordinance. From the facts and materials on record, it appears that the defendant immediately after receiving the legal notice under section 106 of the TP Act on 4.7.91 has filed both the HR Case No. 36 of 1991 under penal section and HR Case No. 37 of 1991 under section 19 of the Rent Control Ordinance as an attempt to defeat the plaintiff's suit for eviction. Therefore, the facts and circumstances of the instant case are quite different and distinguishable from those of the above cited case.</u>

21. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite party by referring to exhibit 10 together with enclosed, Exhibit 10 A has said that the defendant-petitioner has not only filed HR Case No. 37 of 1991 against the plaintiff but also he has served two notices as per Exhibits 10 and 10A through Sarna Shilpik Srami Sanga claiming an unfounded amount of Taka 45,000.00 from the plaintiff. It appears from all these papers that the defendant-petitioner has not only filed two House Rent cases, one under a penal section, but also he has got 2 notices issued from Dhaka Sarno Shilpik Srami Samity asking him to appear before them with his documents for hearing in respect of loan money. Sarno Shilpi Sanga issued notices Ext. 10 & 11 in a manner as if they will sit upon him like a Court for hearing the alleged matter. The Sarno Shilpi Sanga has no right to issue such notices upon the plaintiff who is the owner of the suit house. In such facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the opinion that the defendant-petitioner is an undesirable tenant as alleged by the plaintiff in the plaint.

22. Considering all the above facts, circumstances and the evidences on record I find that all the findings and decisions of the learned SCC Judge are based on proper and correct discussion and appreciation of the facts, evidence and the materials on record. Thus I find that the learned SCC Judge has not committed any error of law or of facts or of procedure in passing the impugned Judgment. There is nothing to interfere with impugned Judgment.

23. In the result, the Rule is discharged with costs. The stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

24. Communicate this order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J.— These two appeals and these two rules have been heard together as they arise from the same judgment and decree being judgment and decree dated 12.6.76 of the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 3 of 1975. This judgment will dispose of them all.

2. Defendants are the appellants and the suit was for declaration of the plaintiff's title to the suit property, recovery of possession and for mandatory injunction. The case of the plaintiff, as set out in the plaint, is that the suit land, plots Nos. 1 and 2 of the Old Cantonment at Chittagong belonged to defendant No. 3, the- Government of Bangladesh in the Ministry of Defense. It was put to public-auction in which defendant No. 1, Ayaz Bahadur Khan, offered the highest bid whereupon it was leased out to him on 12.12.66 for a period of 30 years on a consideration of Rs. 93,000/ out of which an amount of Rs. 23,250/- was paid on that day. But as defendant No.1 could not pay the balance of Rs.69, 750/- he entered into an agreement with defendant No. 4 for sub-letting the land. According to the Agreement between them made on 23. 5. 69, defendant No. 4 paid to defendant No.1 an amount of Rs. 1, 10.000/- as rent in advance for the proposed sub-lease and also agreed to pay yearly rent to defendant No.1 at the rate of Rs.1, 600/- per month for the first 10 years, Rs. 1950/- per month for the second 10 years and Rs. 2,600/per month for the third 10 years. Further, defendant No. 4 agreed to construct a petrol pump, filling and service station on this land and to offer dealership for sale of petrol to defendant No. 1. In pursuance of this Agreement of sub-lease defendant No.1 delivered possession of the suit land to his sub-lessee, defendant No.4 who, in due course constructed a petrol pump station in which defendant No.1 started business of distributing petrol from 1970. But no lease-deed in pursuance of the auction held on 12 12.66 was yet executed and registered by defendant No. 3 on the ground that defendant No. 1, the lessee did not pay the rent from the date of auction, and when defendant No.2, the Military Estate Officer under defendant No.3 threatened to cancel the lease for non-payment of the arrears of rent defendant No.1 faced difficulties in procuring the necessary money to pay the rent. He approached the plaintiff to help him in the matter. Again, Defendant No.1 being a non-local was threatened with dire consequences by some persons if he did not leave the, suit property and other properties during the unsettled period following the war of liberation in 1971. In these difficulties the plaintiff came forward to the rescue of defendant No.1 who then entered into an agreement with him for sale of the suit land along with the petrol-pump agency thereon for a consideration of Tk. 83,000/-. The proposal was finalized on 3.3.72 in the F.I.D.C. Rest House at Chittagong and an amount of Tk. 20,000/- out of the total consideration of Tk. 83,000/- was paid by the plaintiff to defendant No.1 on that occasion against a plain paper receipt. Thereafter, on 4.6.72, the plaintiff and defendant No.1 executed a formal deed of agreement for sale in the office of the former at Dacca and on that occasion the plaintiff paid to defendant No.1 a further sum of Tk. 40,000/- against a plain paper receipt. The balance of Tk. 23,000/- of the total consideration was paid by the plaintiff to defendant No.1 in his office at Dacca on 8.7.72 against another plain paper receipt. Defendant No. 1, who had already sent his family to London, sold away his restaurant at Chittagong, the main source of his livelihood and made all preparation for leaving the country in order to join his family in London and in that connection he sought the plaintiff's help. The plaintiff, an advocate of the High Court and a member of the Bangladesh Jatiya Leagaue, promised all necessary help and contacted different persons both at home and abroad in order to get necessary travel documents for defendant No.1. On 9.7.72 defendant No.1 went to Calcutta and started to live there as he felt insecure of his life at Chittagong because of the abnormal situation which was continuing since the liberation. Defendant No.3, Government of Bangladesh, by an order dated the 22nd June, 1972 cancelled the defendant's lease on the ground of non-payment of rent whereupon the plaintiff rushed to Calcutta and informed the defendant (No. 1) of this development., Defendant No.1 then executed a General Power of Attorney dated 30.9.72 in favor of the plaintiff authorising him thereby to do all acts for protecting, and if necessary for selling his properties including the suit land. The plaintiff met the concerned authorities of the Directorate of Military Land and Cantonment at Dacca and got the order of cancellation of the lease revoked by paying the arrear rent on account of the lease. In pursuance of the Agreement for sale of the suit property defendant No.1 had already addressed a letter date 22.9.72 to the Director of Military Land and Cantonment advising him to "draw, execute and register" the necessary lease deed in favor of the plaintiff. Thereupon, defendant No. 2, the Military Estate Officer, after obtaining necessary sanction from the Government, executed and registered a Lease Deed on 20.4.73 in favor of the plaintiff as nominated by the auction purchaser, defendant No. 1. After execution of the Lease-Deed in his favor the plaintiff addressed a letter to defendant No. 4 intimating him of the change of ownership of the suit land and requesting him to transfer the petrol pump agency to him and also to pay rent of the suit land as sub-lessee under him. This change of ownership was also confirmed by defendant No.1 in a similar letter addressed to defendant No. 4. But defendant No.1 suddenly changed his mind and tried to avoid delivery of possession of the suit land since the value of the suit land increased in the meantime. Defendant No. 2, the Military Estate Officer also instructed defendant No.1 to undo the sale transaction whereupon defendant No.1, by his letter dated 16.6.73 informed the plaintiff that there was no contract for sale or no payment of consideration money whatever and that all the papers and documents, such as the Agreement for sale receipts for payment of consideration money were fabricated and forged by him (plaintiff). Defendant No. 4 also refused to recognise the plaintiff as the new owner in place of defendant No.1 and did not transfer the petrol pump agency. In these circumstances, the plaintiff filed this suit for declaration of title, recovery of possession and mandatory injunction.

3. Defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying practically all the material allegations made in the plaint. He also challenged the suit on the ground of maintainability. He contended that the plaintiff was engaged by him as his lawyer in connection with some suits and entrusted him with all his papers and documents including his letter pad. He admitted that in the wake of liberation of the country he faced difficulties in respect of his properties in Bangladesh and that he was threatened both openly and on telephone by some persons who wanted to blackmail him. He admitted that he had requested the plaintiff to help him in his difficulties. Taking advantage of his helpless condition the plaintiff, his trusted friend, lawyer and adviser, used his writing pad for the purpose of fabricating and forging the documents of a contract for sale, receipts for payment of money, etc. He denied that there; was any contract for sale of the suit property or that any money under any receipt was paid to him by the plaintiff. He alleged that the plaintiff had send to him at Calcutta, through one B.K. Rakshit (D.W. 2), a common friend, a blank stamp paper and some plain papers with revenue stamp attached and requested him to sign and return those documents on the plea that those papers would be necessary for the purpose of protecting his property. Accordingly, he signed those papers in presence of B.K. Rakshit and handed them over to Mr. Rakshit who in his turn handed over the same to the plaintiff at Dacca. These papers were converted into the Agreement for sale and Receipts for money. As to his letter dated 22.9.72 addressed to the Military Estate Officer requesting him to execute the lease-deed in favor of the plaintiff, defendant No.1 contended that he did not send any such letter, but it is the plaintiff who had obtained his signature On his letter-pad earlier, wrote and sent this letter to the Military Estate Officer. He however admitted that after returning from Calcutta he saw the registered Lease-Deed dated 20.3.72 executed in favor of the plaintiff as his "nominee". He explained that he did not raise any objection because even if the Lease-Deed were executed in the name of the plaintiff, it was executed in favor of his "nominee". He denied that he had confirmed the change of ownership by a letter to defendant No. 4. By this Lease-Deed, he contended, his title did not pass as he did not execute and register it.

4. Defendants Nos. 2 and 3 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement in which they admitted that they had executed the Lease-Deed in favor of the plaintiff as a nominee of defendant No 1, the auction purchaser who had paid the entire consideration money. But when defendant No.1 cancelled his nomination they did not recognise the plaintiff as their lessee and directed defendant No.1 to pay rent for the lease. They took the stand that until the plaintiff got his title established according to law the defendant No.1 would continue to be recognized as their lessee. Allegation of the plaintiff that defendant No.1 was instigated by them to undo the sale transaction was denied outright.

5. Defendant No.4 contested the suit by filing a separate written statement in which he stated that he had neither any knowledge about the alleged contract for sale between the plaintiff and defendant No.1 nor is he bound by any such contract. His contention is that even if there had been a valid contract for sale of the suit land between the plaintiff and defendant No.1 it did not affect his ownership of the petrol pump since the dealership of petrol was entirely different matter and that to get the dealership the plaintiff must enter into a separate agreement with him. The suit for mandatory injunction against him is not maintainable, it has been further contended by him.

6. The learned Subordinate judge having considered a huge number of documents filed by the parties and the evidence of 5 witnesses examined by each side held that the suit was quite maintainable, that there was a contract for sale of the suit land and that the entire consideration was paid and no document, such as the Agreement, and Receipts was fabricated or forged by the plaintiff. The learned Subordinate Judge further held that title to the suit land along with the petrol pump agency stood transferred to the plaintiff under the registered to Lease-Deed; and as to defendant No.4, it was held that since the plaintiff stepped into the shoe of defendant No.1 the sublease (defdt. No. 4) was bound by the sub-lease between defendant Nos. 1 and 4 and consequently, defendant Nos. 1 was bound to transfer the petrol pump agency to the plaintiff. On these findings the learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit and directed delivery of possession of the suit property to the plaintiff. He further directed defdt. No. 4, by a mandatory injunction, to transfer the petrol pump agency to the plaintiff. Being aggrieved, defendants Nos. 1 and 4 challenged the judgment and decree in these two separate appeals. On their applications the two rules have been issued staying the operations of the impugned decree.

7. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, learned Advocate has appeared for the appellant-defendant No. 1, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate appeared for the appellant-defendant No. 4, while Mr. Ahmed Subhan learned Advocate has appeared for the plaintiff-respondent. We have heard the arguments of the learned lawyers for several days and perused the case record including the depositions of the witnesses and the documents proved in this. There is no dispute that the suit land belonged to the Ministry of Defense of the then Pakistan. It comprises two plots, commercial plots Nos. 1 and 2 in the Old Cantonment area at Chittagong. It was put to auction on 12.12.66 in which defendant No.1, a businessman of Chittagong offered the highest bid and obtained the lease thereof for 30 years on consideration of Rs. 93,000/- out of which Rs. 23,250/- was paid on the spot and the balance of Tk. 69,750/- was paid at latter date, sometime in 1969. It is also an admitted fact that for want of money defendant No. I entered into an agreement with defendant No. 4, Dawood Petroleum, now Padma Petroleum Ltd. on 25.3-69 under which the suit land was sub-let to defendant No.4. The deed of sub-lease has been marked Exb. 1 dated 25.3.69. According to this deed of sub-lease defendant No. 4 had paid to defendant No.1 an amount of Rs. 1,10,000/as advance rent which was fixed at Rs. 16,00/per month for the first ten years, Rs. 1,950/per month for the 2nd 10 years and Rs. 2,600/- per month for the last 10 years. It was also agreed that the defendant No. 4 would construct, at his own cost, a petrol pump and service and filling station on the suit land and would offer the dealership in petrol to defendant No.1. According to this agreement defendant No. 4, constructed a petrol pump station in which business of sale and distribution of petrol by defendant No. 1, as agent of defendant No. 4, started from 1970. But the original lease between defendant No.1 and defendant No. 2, Military Estate Officer, was not executed as there arose a controversy as to the payment of rent for the lease which was fixed at Rs. 7,400/- per year. Defdt. No. 2 demanded rent from the date auction held in 1966, whereas the lessee, defendant No.1 contended that rent should be charged from the date of possession which was delivered to him in 1969 Defendant No. 2, in his letter dated 11.5.72, Ext. 2, addressed to the Defense Ministry admitted this controversy and recommended that the rent should be charged from the date of possession and thereby accepted the contention of defendant No. 1. It is, therefore, the non-payment of rent which was the reason for delay in execution of the lease between defendant No.1 and defendant No. 2. Allegation of the plaintiff that the lease-deed was not executed earlier because of the failure of defendant No.1 to procure money is not found to be correct.

8. Case of the plaintiff is that he same in contact with defendant No.1 through one K.A. Qureshi (D. W.3) a relation of defendant No.1. some time in the middle of February, 1972. This position has also been admitted by defendant No. 1. In the middle of February, 1972, i.e. about two months after liberation of the country, the plaintiff (who is P.W. 1) met K.A. Qureshi in the latter's residence at Chittagong and in course of that meeting the plaintiff was introduced by K. A. Qureshi to defendant No. 1. In that connection K.A. Qureshi told the plaintiff that defendant No.1 being a "non-local" was facing difficulties in managing his property including the suit land and that defendant No.1 also being threatened by many persons who wanted to blackmail him. Both defendant No.1 and Mr. Qureshi sought help of the plaintiff in the matter as he was member of the Bangladesh Jatiya League. There is no dispute over this approach to the plaintiff for his help in protecting properties of defendant No. 1. About a fortnight later, on 3 3.73 the parties admittedly met again in the F.I.D.C. Rest House at Chittagong and in that meeting there was a talk between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 as to what should be done in respect of the suit property. Case of the plaintiff is that he told defendant No.1 that he would not be able to render him any assistance if the suit property including the petrol pump agency were not sold to him out-right. Whereas, defendant No.1, it appears, was hesitating between two alternative proposals, one for out-right sale and the other for partnership between him and the plaintiff. The plaintiff has stated that ultimately it was agreed that the suit property would be sold to him on a consideration of Rs. 83,000/- and that on following day he paid an amount of Tk.20,000/-in cash to defendant No.1 in the same place whereupon the latter executed a plain paper receipt in presence of witnesses. In support of this claim the plaintiff produced a piece of document dated 3.3.72 Exb. 2. It was admittedly written by defendant No. 1. It shows that there were two alternative proposals-one for partnership and the other for out-right sale. Defendant No.1 stated therein that if he remained a partner difficulties might arise regarding the taking of loan from banks and if it were a sale he would demand Tk. 85,000/-; but in any case he was ready to sign any document. This has been expressed in the following words in Exb. 2:

“I can only sign any documents.”

9. Contention of defendant No.1 is that Exb. 2 was not intended for out-right sale but he insisted on "partnership". In that connection he produced a draft partnership agreement, Exb. F. This document was not signed by either party nor does it bear any date excepting that it was written sometime in "April, 1973" i.e. about one year after the writing of Exb. 2. The plaintiff's contention is that Ext. F. was written not in connection with the alternative proposal as contained in Ext. 2 but was written after the Lease-Deed Ext. 1(a) was executed and registered by the Military Estate authorities on 20.4.73. Be that as it may, Ext. F, an unsigned document, does not show anything more than what has been expressed in Ext. 2 which contains two alternative proposals, one for sale and the other for partnership. The case of the plaintiff is that it is the proposal for sale which was ultimately accepted and which culminated in sale under the Lease-Deed on 20.4.73. As to partnership, admittedly this proposal had not been materialized. The plaintiff has tried to strengthen his case of sale by stating that he had paid to defendant No.1 on that very occasion Tk. 20,000/- on acceptance of which the latter granted him a receipt The said receipt was not produced by the plaintiff who has, however, explained that at the time of the subsequent payment of Rs. 40,000/- on 4.6.72. defendant No.1 gave a Receipt for Tk. 60,000/- (Ext. 5) and took back the earlier Receipt for Tk. 20,000/-. On this claim he has been supported by P. W. 3.

10. The plaintiff goes on to say that on 4.6.72 defendant No.1 came to his chamber in Dacca and executed an Agreement for sale (Ext. 4) and received Tk, 40,000/- by granting the Receipt Ext. 5. This Agreement was typed by P.W. 3 who was at that time an employee of the Accountant General's Office, Dacca. P. W. 3 has stated that previously he was a clerk of one Barrister Nasim Hasan and that being requested by both the plaintiff and defendant No.1 he typed the Agreement (Ext. 4) which was signed in his presence by both the plaintiff and defendant No. 10 and that be also attested this document, P.W. 3 has also corroborated P. W. 1 (the plaintiff stating that defdt. No.1 received Tk. 40,000/- by granting the Receipt Ext. 5 and that he had typed this Receipt on the very occasion, Defdt. No.1 totally denied having executed the Agreement or having received any money under the Receipt. He has, however, admitted his signatures appearing on both the Agreement and the Receipt. The date of the Agreement is "4.6.72" and the date of the Receipt is "4.6.70" although both of them were executed, as the plaintiff and the witness-P.W. 3 claims, on the same day. For this discrepancy the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 blamed each other Contention of the plaintiff is that defendant No.1 purposely put the date "4.6.70" instead of "4 6.72" on the Receipt, but at that time he (plaintiff) did not notice it properly. Contention of defendant No.1 is that these two documents along with another plain paper receipt Ext. 5(a) were not signed by him in Dacca on 4.6.72 but were signed by him in Calcutta in the first week of September that year. Before we examine these documents we propose to discuss the remaining part of the evidence of the plaintiff in connection with payment of the consideration of Tk. 83,000 00 to defendant No. 1. The plaintiff has stated that on 8-7-72 defendant No.1 again came from Chittagong to Dacca and met him in his chamber and that in that meeting he paid Tk. 23,000.00 to the defdt. No.1 who then granted him the Receipt, Ext. 5(a) in presence of witnesses. P. W. 2 has corroborated this payment. The Agreement (Ext. 4) purportedly shows that in pursuance of a proposal for sale of the suit property starting from Ext. 2 in the F.I.D.C. Rest House this Agreement for sale was concluded on 4-6-72 on a consideration of Tk. 83,000.00 of which Tk. 23,000.00 was yet to be paid. Ext. 5 shows payment of Tk. 60,000.00 and Ext. 5(a) shows payment of the balance Tk. 23,000.00. On 9-7-72 defendant No:1 left for Calcutta and admittedly stayed there till March-1973.

11. Before leaving for Calcutta defendant No.1 had executed a General Power of Attorney on 8-7-73 in favor of his relation K.A. Qureshi (D.W. 3) who was "Khalu" of his wife. D.W. 3, it may be mentioned here, is a retired Govt. servant residing in Chittagong. He has got some business there. Defendant No. 1, it may be mentioned here had come to Chittagong from Calcutta in the wake of the Partition of India in 1947 when he was about 6 years old. His father had allegedly set up tube-wells business in Chittagong. D.W. 2. B.K. Rakshit is another businessman of Chittagong; he got friendship with D.W. 3. Under the General Power of Attorney, Ext. 7 defendant No.1 authorized K.A. Qureshi to take all actions and to do all things necessary for protection of his property including the suit land.

12. Defendant No.1 (D.W.1) has stated that in the first week of September 1972 the plaintiff sent to him in Calcutta B.K. Rakshit (D.W. 2) from Dacca with certain blank stamp paper and blank writing pads two of which had revenue stamps adhered thereto. Along with these papers, he goes on to say, the plaintiff sent a letter Ext. A (1) dated 3-9-72, requesting him to put his signatures on the papers sent. Defendant No.1 has stated that he accordingly signed the plain stamp-paper and other plain papers which were then carried back, by B.K. Rakshit to the plaintiff. These papers, he has said, have been converted by the plaintiff into the Agreement, Ext. 4 and the Receipts Ext.5 & 5(a). B.K. Rakshit D.W. 2 has corroborated defendant No: 1 saying that he was sent by the plaintiff with the letter Ext. A(1) along with the blank stamp paper and blank plain paper for receipts which were signed in his presence by defendant No.1 after which he brought them back to the plaintiff, Contention of defendant No.1 is that as the plaintiff was his "lawyer, intimate friend and adviser" charged with the solemn responsibility for protecting his property the lease of which was cancelled in the meantime by the Military officer, he put his signatures on these papers without any hesitation but in good faith fully relying upon his friend the plaintiff. The plaintiff totally denied that he ever sent B.K. Rashid to defendant No.1 with these papers. He, however, admitted his letter Ext. A (1) but said that it was sent by post and not through B. K. Rakshit whom he did not know at all. The letter Ext. A (1) does not show whether it was sent by post or through any messenger. It, however, mentions that a letter was also written by K. A. Qureshi to defendant No.1 and that it might have been received by the defendant No.1 in the meantime. This letter shows that the plaintiff sent a stamp paper to the defendant No.1 requesting him to sign the same to be used as a Receipt for Tk. 23,000 00 "dated 14.3.71 or so". From this at last one thing is found true it is that a blank paper was sent by the plaintiff to the defendant No.1 at Calcutta to sign it as a receipt for this amount. According to defdt. No.1 Ext. 5(a) is that receipt signed by him in Calcutta whereas the plaintiff contended that the receipt he asked for as per his letter was not given by defdt. No. 1. He has tried to explain that the proposed receipt for Tk. 23 000.00 as referred to in his letter was meant for showing payment of Tk. 23,000/- as price of a car sold by defendant No.1 to K. A. Qureshi before he left for Calcutta. Defendant No.1 has seriously challenged that it is related to the sale of his car. His car was admittedly sold to K.A. Qureshi but the latter deposed that he never requested the plaintiff to call for a receipt of Tie. 23,000.00 from defendant No. 1. An Information Slip, Ext. R, issued from the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong shows that a car of defendant No.1 was sold K.A. Qureshi on 4.7.72, but the price of the car is found to have been inserted by hand writing in the Information Slip which was a typed-one. Price of the car has been shown to be Tk. 5000.00. Defendant No.1 contended that the receipt Ext. 5(a) had no Connection with the sale of his car particularly when the date of sale is 4.7.72 whereas the proposed receipt sought to be dated "14.3.71". As to why Ext. 5(a) was dated 8.7.72 when he signed it in the first week of September (1972), defdt. No.1 said that this date was already typed on the plain paper by or at the' instance of the plaintiff. The plaintiff failed to convince us why he had requested Deft. No.1 to send a receipt for his car which was not sold to him. It is in evidence that K. A. Qureshi did many things for protecting the interests of defendant No.1 such as he had sold the Restaurant of defendant No.1 at Tk. 30,000/- out of which he paid Tk. 10,000/- for payment of arrear rent for the suit land. K. A. Qureshi also looked after the petrol pump agency of defendant No.1 in his absence. He got a Power of Attorney Ext. 7, from defendant No. 1. In these circumstances it is rather difficult to connect the Receipt Exb. 5(a) for Tk. 23,000/with the sale of his car. The learned Subordinate Judge has, however, observed that since no receipt for Tk. 23,000/- bearing the date of "14.3.71" has been produced, it may be inferred that defendant No.1 had not granted any receipt as requested by the plaintiff in his letter. This is a mere conjecture, for Ext. 5 was also back dated. According to the plaintiff, the payment under Ext. 5 was made on 4.6.72 but the date was typed as "4.6.70." It appears that the date '4.6.70' was given with mutual consent of both the parties for the purpose guarding against any mischief under the P.O. 16/72 as defendant No.1 was a non-local whose family already left Bangladesh and he himself was making preparation for leaving Bangladesh. The explanation of the plaintiff that he did not mark the date as "4.6.70" at that time is wholly unacceptable.

13. It may be noted that the plaintiff's letter, Ext. A (1) speaks of only a receipt for Tk. 23,000/-; it does not speak of any other documents such as the Agreement Ext. 4 and the Receipt Ext. 5. Non-mention of these documents negatives the contention of defdt. No.1 that he got them along with Receipt Ext 5(a) and signed them at Calcutta. Ext. A(1) refers to a letter of K. A. Qureshi already sent to defdt No.1 but the latter did not produce the letter. Again, there was an earlier suit between the same parties being T. S. No. 289/72 in the Court of Munsif, Dacca on the same Subject and in that suit defendant No.1 made a statement to the effect that he did not send any paper, such as stamp paper to the plaintiff. Mr. Ahmed Sobhan, learned Advocate for the plaintiff has contended that it is a clear admission of defendant No.1 that he did not send any paper such as stamp paper Ext. 4 or receipts Ext. 5 or 5(a) from Calcutta to the plaintiff. If so, the story of his signing these papers in Calcutta falls to the ground. Admission is a strong evidence against its maker since a person is not supposed to make any statement against his own interest. But Mr. Rafiqul Huq has referred to a number of decisions including a decision of this Court reported in 17 DLR 15 wherein it has been observed that though admission is a strong evidence against its maker, nevertheless, he may show that the admission was erroneous Or based on mistake of facts. But in absence of the context in which the alleged admission was made we are not given much importance either to the admission or to its denial. The contents of Exts. 4 and 5(a) are so clear that it is difficult to accept the explanation of defendant No. 1, a consummate businessman, that he signed them (the Agreement and the Receipt on revenue-stamps) without knowing of or reading them. It view of the letter Ext. A (1) it is only the Receipt Ext. 5(a) which appears to have been signed by defdt. No.1 in Calcutta. P.W. 3 has stated that he had typed both Exts. 4 & 5 which were then signed by defdt. No.1 in his presence in Dacca, Suggestion to him is that he deposed falsely in favor of the plaintiff under whom he had one served. He denied that he ever served under the plaintiff. Another suggestion to him is that since he was an employee of the A.G. Office he was not supposed to have come from his office to type these documents in a lawyer's chamber during office hours. We think that though it was office hours it was not unlikely on his part to take French leave from the office if he had not taken permission from his authorities. He has also witnessed the payment of Tk. 40,000/- under Ext. 5 which, he said, was made on that occasion in his presence. The plaintiff already explained that defdt. No, 1 had taken back his earlier receipt for Tk. 20,000/- paid in the F.I.D.C. Rest House.

14. As against this evidence for the plaintiff, defdt. No.1 examined D.Ws. 4 & 5 who deposed that the plaintiff told them about the Agreement for sale but admitted that no consideration was yet paid. D.W. 5 has said that the plaintiff told him in presence of the Defense Secretary and one Mr. K. Z. Islam that he had made no payment to defdt. No. 1. But the Defense Secretary and Mr. K.Z. Islam did not come to corroborate him. He is found to be related to defendant No. 1. D.W. 4, an advocate of the Chittagong Bar was changed by defendant No. 4 in this suit. He has said that, sometime in June, 1973 the plaintiff along with Mrs. Amena Begum, a leader of the Jatiya League, came from Dacca to Chittagong and met him. At that meeting, he said, he was told by the plaintiff about a contract for sale of the, suit property on a consideration of Tk. 40,000/ and that in spite of all possible help rendered by the plaintiff to defendant No. 1, the latter was trying to back out of the contract, D.W. 4 has deposed that the plaintiff was ready to pay the entire consideration whereupon he requested defendant No.1 to keep the promise and perform the contract by receiving the consideration money. His evidence has been seriously challenged by the plaintiff on the ground that he took much interests in the affairs of defendant No.1 who allegedly used to entertain him in his restaurant. These two witnesses got no personal knowledge about the matter. They spoke of an admission of the plaintiff about non-payment of money. Admission of this nature got hardly, any evidentiary value when the maker of it denied it and there is no corroboration thereof. D.W. No.5 further said that he had suggested that defendant No.1 should pay the plaintiff an amount bf Tk. 40,000/- for the "services rendered by him". It is not understood why defendant No.1 would pay Tk. 40,000/- to the plaintiff if there had not been any payment made by the plaintiff to the defdt. No. 1.

15. Defendant No. 1. by a supplementary written statement introduced a new fact in order to show that there was no payment made to him. He stated that June, 1973 there was a telephonic talk between him and the plaintiff. He had rung up the plaintiff at Dacca. He has said that he made a record of the conversation on a tape with the help of a magnetic apparatus. In the Court he has submitted the transcript of the conversation in evidence, which has been marked Exts. Q and Q (1). This long conversation spread over 20 pages of the paper book. In some places the statements are disjunctive and in the opinion of the learned Subordinate Judge, incoherent. The substance of the conversation appears to be that there was an agreement for sale, in the alternative, for a partnership, but the plaintiff did not make any payment but expressed his willingness to make payment of Tk. 40,000/-. From the tape record of conversation defendant No.1 has tried to show that consideration for the Agreement was Tk. 40,000/- but no payment was yet made. The learned Subordinate Judge treated this tape recorded statement as a secondary evidence and did not place any reliance upon it Mr. Rafiqul Huq has assailed this finding of the learned Subordinate Judge taking the ground that a statement recorded on tape with a magnetic apparatus is a primary evidence and that it should be taken into consideration like any other evidence. As to the possibility of this kind of evidence being tampered, Mr. Rafiqul Huq has contended that when every evidence may be tampered a tape recorded evidence cannot be placed on a different footing on this ground. In support of this contention he, has referred to a decision of the Indian Supreme Court reported in A.I.R. (SC) 1968, 147. It has been held there:

“If a statement is relevant, an accurate tape record of the statement is also relevant and admissible. The time, place and accuracy of the recording must be proved by competent witnesses and the voices must be properly identified. One of the features of magnetic tape recording is the ability to erase and reuse the recording medium. Because of this facility of erasure and reuse the evidence must be received with caution. The court must be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the record has not been tampered with.”

In the case before us, voices of the parties, were allegedly identified before the learned Subordinate Judge when the tape was played. But the learned Subordinate Judge found that the talk was broken leaving vacuum in places. This might have been due to erasure as suggested by the plaintiff. Belated disclosure of this piece of evidence, is, we think, a cogent ground to treat it with utmost caution. This tape recorded statement of telephonic conversation of the plaintiff was not put to him when he was on the witness box and as such this statement cannot be used to contradict him in accordance with the provisions of section 145, Evidence Act. Leaving it aside altogether we have before us the oral evidence of the P.Ws. which has come in corroboration of the documents. Exts. 2, 4 & 5 and on these materials we have no hesitation to hold that there was a contract for sale of the suit property for a consideration of Tk. 83,000/- out of which Th. 60,000/- was paid. Receipt Exb. 5(a) was admittedly executed by defdt. No.1, but payment of Tk. 23,000/- there under being extremely doubtful, we reject the plaintiff's claim to this extent.

16. Mr. Rafiqul Huq has contended that even if there had been a contract for sale the contract is not valid on the ground of undue influence and unquestionable bargaining on the part of the plaintiff. He has referred to the relationship between the parties and has argued that the plaintiff was a lawyer engaged by defendant No.1 in a number of cases and he was also his "trusted friend and adviser" who was entrusted by him with the duty to protect his property, but taking advantage of his difficulties the plaintiff exercised undue influence over him and obtained the contract. The plaintiff has contended that he never acted as the defendant's lawyer prior to the final payment of consideration on 8.7.72. Defendant No.1 has admitted in his cross-examination that the plaintiff did not do his legal work prior to 8th July, 1972, the date on which the last of the three installments of the consideration money was apparently paid under Ext, 5(a), Mr. Rafiqul Huq has referred to Ext. A. It is a letter written by the plaintiff from Dacca to defendant No.1 at Chittagong instructing him to forward all connected papers including the papers about auction purchase of the suit land to him so that he could prepare a "parawise statement" in T.S. No. 49/72 filed by defendant No. 4 against defendant No.1 for money. This letter is found to have been written in January, 1973 whereas, the matter of contract of sale started from February,, 1972 and came to the final stage in July, 1972, Again, the plaintiff along with two other lawyers was engaged by defendant No. 1, as his lawyer to withdraw the value of - "spoiled stamp paper" of Tk. 2,765/- in connection with case No. 258/72 before the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca, under a Vokalatnama, Ext D. But this legal work also related to a period subsequent to the contract. The contention of defendant No.1 that in connection with these 'cases' the plaintiff obtained from him letter-pad with signature and "stamp" which he subsequently utilized in fabricating the documents of contract hardly carry any conviction. Mr. Rafiqul Huq has next referred to certain letters between the plaintiff and the defendant No.1 and also between the plaintiff and the wife of defendant No. 1. The plaintiff in his letters to defendant No, 1 promised all help to obtain necessary travel documents, for him so. that he could leave the country and settle down in U.K. Letters Exts, 8(g) and (h) written in the months of April and May, 1973 by the wife of defendant No.1 from Kualalampur show that the plaintiff was requested to finalize "the work" and send her husband away as soon as possible. These are some of the instances of cordial relation between the parties, Mr. Rafiqul Huq contends. Other documents referred to in this connection are Exts. 5(b), 5(c) and 5(d) which are receipts of payment of arrears of rent for the suit land and ext. 1(a) the Lease-Deed itself. The Rent Receipts simply Show that arrear rents due from the Defdt. No.1 were paid on his behalf by the plaintiff. Admittedly the money paid there under was paid by defdt. No. 1. An amount of Tk. 10,000/-was sent to the plaintiff for this purpose by K.A. Qureshi by a bank-draft; the plaintiff withdrew Tic 2765, as the value of spoiled stamp of the defdt. No.1 in case No. 258/72. The registration fee of Tk. 4,000/- in connection with the Lease-Deed was also this defendant's money paid on his behalf by the plaintiff. In the Lease-Deed, the plaintiff signed as the lessee. All these things were done when the plaintiff was armed with a General Power of Attorney Ext. 7(1) executed in his favor by defdt. No.1 on 30-9-72. We do not think that these facts and circumstances are sufficient to hold that the plaintiff had exercised undue influence over defdt. No.1 in obtaining the contract. As to the allegation of unconscionable bargaining. Mr. Rafiqul Huq contends that the consideration of Tk. 83,000/was very inadequate. Considering the period following the liberation we do not think that this amount was unduly inadequate.

<u>17. The next contention of Mr. Rafiqul Huq is that the contract was made by defendant No.1 when he was not the owner of the land as the lease-deed was not yet executed and registered in his favor by the Military Estate Officer and as such the whole contract was based on mistake of fact; the contract is, therefore, hit by section 20 of the Contract Act. This section provides that when both the parties to an agreement are under a mistake as to a matter of fact essential to the agreement the agreement is void. In this case, the parties were aware that no Lease-Deed had yet been executed but they argued that the contract would be subject to execution of a lease-deed. Section 20 does not appear to have any application to this case. Mr. Rafiqul Huq next contends that the plaintiff's claim under the contract is at best an 'actionable claim' and that, an actionable claim of a lawyer is, hit by section 136 of the Transfer of Property Act. Purchaser of any interest in any actionable claim is prohibited under this section when the-purchaser is a Judge, lawyer or an Officer of the Court. "Actionable" claim as defined in section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act means any claim to an unsecured debt or any beneficial interest in any moveable property. We do not think that the interest created under an immovable property falls within the definition of 'actionable claim'.</u>

<u>18. Further case of the plaintiff is that in pursuance of the Agreement, Ext. 4 backed by payment of the consideration defendant No.1 had written a letter, Ext. 8 dated 28-9-72 advising the Military Estate Officer to execute a lease-deed in favor of plaintiff and that according to his advice the Lease-Deed Ext. 1(a) was executed and registered in his favor and that with this execution and registration the title of the defendant No.1 passed to him. Mr. Rafiqul Huq contends that even if Ext. 1(a) had been executed and registered according to the advice of defendant No.1 yet no title thereunder passed, because it was not executed and registered by defendant No.1 but was executed and registered by the Military Estate Officer. He has referred to section 17 of the Registration Act read with the Transfer of Property Act which requires compulsory registration of a deed if title to an immovable property valuing over Tk. 100/- is to pass thereunder from one hand to another. In this case the vendor, namely defdt. No.1, did execute and register the Lease-Deed. Again, Mr. Rafiqul Huq has pointed out, this Lease-Deed relates to the suit land it does not relate to the petrol pump agency which is entirely a different property belonging to defendant No. 4 from, whom only the dealership of petrol was obtained by defendant No. 1. Registration of a sale-deed by a person other than the vendor, Mr. Rafiqul Huq contends, is not, contemplated in section 17 of the Registration Act. Further, it has been contended, defendant No.1 had no intention to transfer his title under Ext. 1(a) even if he had instructed for its execution in favor of the plaintiff; that is why it was executed in the name of the plaintiff as his "legal and constituted nominee". The Lease-Deed, Exb. 1 (a), has, of course, shown the plaintiff as the lessee as nominees by the auction-purchaser, but it does not refer to any contract of sale or any payment made thereunder between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1. So far as Defdts. Nos. 2 and 3 (Military Estate Officers) are concerned, their stand is that it is the defendant No.1 who had offered the highest bid and paid the entire consideration and thereafter, the arrear rent and that it is the defendant No.1 who had advised for executing (the lease-deed in favor of the plaintiff as his nominee but since the defendant No.1 cancelled the nomination and intimated it to them by the letter Ext. A (3), they directed defendant No.1 to pay the balance of the arrears of rent. They have stated in their written statement that unless the plaintiff's title is established they will not recognise him as their lessee Under Ext. 1(a). Therefore, the real question is what was meant, or was intended to mean, by the word 'Nominee' appearing in the lease deed Ext. 1(a) and the connected letter of authority, Exb. 8.</u>

<u>19. The learned Subordinate Judge has referred to a number of dictionaries in order to ascertain the real meaning of the word 'nominee' and came to a conclusion that 'nominee' in this case is a person for whose benefit the lease-deed has been executed. The 'nominee' is, therefore, the real lessee thereunder, he has concluded. This view has been re-enforced by Mr. Ahmed Subhan, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent. Mr. Rafiqul Huq, on the other hand, has tried to give a different meaning to the word 'nominee'. He argued that the 'nominee' in this case is merely and agent who is authorized by the principal to do certain act; such nomination is subject to revocation or cancellation at any time by the principal. The position of a nominee, he has further contended, is like that of a license that is a person who acts under the authority of his license, granted by another person and if an act is done by the license it is, in fact, done on this authority of the person granting the license. By getting the Lease-Deed executed in the name of plaintiff as his nominee, defendant No.1 clearly intended to retain with himself the dominion over the property. Mr. Ahmed Subhan has contended that the intention of defendant No.1 was all along clear right from the beginning and it was that the suit property would be sold since the alternative proposal for partnership was rejected by the plaintiff. This intention, it is further contended, becomes all the more, clear from the fact that defdt. No.1 was preparing for leaving the country. But by his letter dated 1.6.73 Ext. 8 (e) defendant No.1 informed the plaintiff that, he had given up the idea of leaving the country and that he had cancelled the Power of Attorney. Exb. 7(e) dated 30.9.72 is a further manifestation of the defendant's intention to part with the property. Since for mere looking after the property this Power of Attorney was not necessary when for the same purpose, he had already executed the Power of Attorney, Exb. 7 dated 8. 7. 72 in favor of his relation, K.A. Qureshi. Explanation of the defdt. (No.1) is however that the later Power of Attorney was necessary as the plaintiff had to contact the Military Estate Office which is in Dhaka. What we think is that had the defdt, (No.1) intended to divest himself of his title to the property he could have advised for execution of the Lease-Deed in the name of the plaintiff without adding the qualifying word "nominee".</u>

20. Mr. Rafiqul Huq has stressed the legal requirement for registration of a deed of transfer under section 17, Registration Act and has referred to a decision of the Privy Council- A.I.R. 1938 P. C-20. In that case the intended lessee was put into possession of a land in pursuance of an agreement for lease, but it was not registered. It was held that the transaction did not create any title for want of registration. In the case before us no possession was delivered and the lease-deed has not been registered by the vendor. The question therefore is whether his title has passed by such a registration. The basis of this registration by a third party is the defendants letter extb. 8. The letter can hardly be substitute of a sale-deed executed and registered by the vendor. Mr. Ahmed Subhan has contended that if the defdt. No.1 had not transferred his title he would not have parted with his documents, relating to the auction purchase of the suit-land and the petrol pump agency which are now in the plaintiff's possession. K. A Qureshi (D.W. 2) has explained that he had delivered these papers to the plaintiff who required them to get revoked the cancellation of the lease by Defdt. No.2. Moreover, when the plaintiff was holding a Power of Attorney from the defdt. No.1 it is quite natural that he would require these papers. He himself called for some of these papers under his letter Exb. A. As to statement in the draft Agreement of partnership Exb. F relating to transfer of the suit-land, it got no evidentiary value as it was signed by nobody. Lastly, Mr. Ahmed Subhan has referred to Exb. 8(c) which is a letter under signature of defdt. No.1 addressed to defdt. No. 4 intimating the latter about change of ownership of the suit-land and requesting him to transfer the Petrol Pump agency to the new owner. Defdt. No.1 has contended that he did not write it but it was forged by the plaintiff who had already in his possession some of his letter pad containing signatures. This letter Exb. 8(e) should be read with the plaintiff's letter dated 17.5.73 Exb. 8(6) addressed to the same person, defdt. No. 4, informing him about the change of ownership of the suit land, and requesting him to recognise the plaintiff as the owner. This letter was written from Dacca, whereas the other letter was written from Chittagong both being addressed to the same person at Chittagong; but strangely enough both the letters were posted from the same post office at Dacca, registered one after the other at the same counter of the post office. This tends to-show that both the letters were posted by the same person. Any way, it is very much doubtful whether Exb. 8(c) was written and posted by defdt. No. 1. In view of these facts and circumstances we are clearly of the view that the defendant's (No, 1) title did not pass to the plaintiff under Exb. 1(a).

<u>21. The learned Subordinate Judge relying on section 54, Transfer of Property Act, has observed that a sale transaction is complete even if its consideration is only promised but not yet paid. Here the question is not payment or non-payment of consideration. The question is whether payment of consideration in absence of registration by the vendor can transfer title and our answer is in the negative. This is a suit for declaration of title, among other things. Since title did not yet pass to the plaintiff this suit is not maintainable. The plaintiff could have made an alternative prayer for specific performance of the contract for sale. In a suit for title reported in A.I.R. 1952(Nag) 115, the alternative relief of specific performance of contract was granted. This was sought by amending the plaint. In the case before us no alternative relief by way of specific performance of contract or refund of the money paid has been sought. In the circumstances the suit cannot but fail not being maintainable.</u>

22. As to the appeal by Defdt. No. 4, he is a sub-lessee under defendant No. 1, the lessee. Relief of any claim against him may be considered after the lessee's title passes to the plaintiff. Since we have already decided that the plaintiff has not acquired title to the suit land, he is not entitled to any mandatory injunction.

In the result, both the appeals are allowed on contest but without any Costs. The IV rules staying operations of the impugned decree are made absolute. The suit is dismissed on context with costs.

M.H. Rahman J. - I agree.

End.
