case_source: (Appeal against the decree of Mr. G. Mawla, District Judge of Zilla Rangpur dated the 30th day of March 1963 passed in Other Appeal No. 190 of 1962 affirming the decree of Mr. R. Huq, Munsif, 1st Court Gaibandha dated the 20th day of July 1962 in Other Suit No. 208 of 1959.
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the defendants is directed against the judgment of the lower appellate court affirming the judgment of the trial court decreeing the plaintiff's suit for declaration of title and confirmation of the possession of the disputed suit land. According to the plaintiffs the disputed jot belonged to one Kasimuddin and Imaruddin being two brothers. Imaruddin died leaving a sister and Kasimuddin. Then Kasimuddin died leaving his widow, two sons and a daughter. Then one of the sons of Kasimuddin i.e. Nurul Huq died unmarried leaving his mother, brother and sister as his heirs. One Ayenuddin predecessor of the Plaintiff Nos. 1 to 8 took settlement of the jot by a registered patta. Since the settlement Ayenuddin allegedly possessed the suit land and after his death his heirs i.e. plaintiffs had been in possession thereof within the knowledge of the defendants. The defendants No. 9 and 10 took usufructuary mortgage of the suit land from the rest of the plaintiffs and they were in possession thereof having been threatened with dispossession by the defendants, the present suit was instituted at the instance of the plaintiff for declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the suit land.

2. The defendants No. 1 and 6 contested the plaintiff's suit contending that Kasimuddin alone held the disputed jot under one Meharuddin by a registered kabuliyat. Imaruddin had no interest in the jot and consequently the sister of Imaruddin had no interest in the jot. Kasimuddin's widow never settled the suit land by executing any patta in favour of Ayenuddin nor did she realise any rent therefrom. The defendants were allegedly in possession of the suit land and that Ayenuddin or his successors in interest of the plaintiffs never possessed the suit land adversely to their interest within their knowledge The contesting defendant No. 1 and 6 who were respectively aged about 21 and 19 at the time of the trial of the suit were minors when the patta was executed in favour of Ayenuddin and the said patta was not binding on them and there could be no adverse possession of the suit land by dint or the said patta at least as against the contesting defendants No 1 and 6.

3. On consideration of the evidence on record both the courts below came to a concurrent finding of fact that the plaintiffs had acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by dint of the patta executed in favour of Ayenuddin by the sister of Imaruddin and widow of Kasimuddin who had also executed the patta on behalf on her two minor sons i.e, the present contesting defendant No. 1 and 6. With regard to the patta in question both the courts below came to a concurrent finding that by dint of the said patta the right title and interest of the sister of Imaruddin and the widow of the Kasimuddin had passed to Ayenuddin, but both the courts below also came to a concurrent finding that when the said patta was executed, minor children and on their behalf their mother i.e. the widow of Kasimuddin had executed the patta in question The court below also came to a concurrent finding that although the patta in question was partly void with regard to the right, title and interest of the defendants No. 1 and 6 since they were minors at the time of the execution of the patta and since their mother had no authority to execute the said patta on behalf of her minor children, but the plaintiffs having remained in possession of the suit land for more than 12 years, acquired right, title and interest therein by adverse possession thereof.

4. This case is otherwise concluded by a concurrent finding with regard to the plaintiffs' title in the suit land by dint of the patta executed in favour of the plaintiffs predecessor by the mother and aunt of contesting defendants. The only question of law raised in this case is as to whether the plaintiffs had acquired any right, title and interest in the suit land as against contesting defendant No. 1 and 6 by adverse possession of the suit land from the date of the execution of the patta when evidently the contesting defendants were minors and their mother had no authority to execute the patta on their behalf.

5. The learned Advocate for the defendants appellants had submitted that there—cannot be any adverse possession as against the minors during the period of their minority unless such adverse possession is claimed from the date of the attainment of their majority. The learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents has, however, submitted that the suit land being jointly owned by the contesting defendants No. 1 and 6 along with their mother and aunt and the patta having been executed by the aunt and the mother not only on their own behalf but also on behalf of the minor defendants and since the plaintiffs had been in possession of the entire suit land since then, it shall be deemed that the plaintiffs had acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by adverse possession thereof.

6. So far the patta in question ext. 1 is concerned it was admittedly executed on 19. 12. 40. The contesting defendant No. 1 was admittedly born in 1931 and the defendant No. 2 was admittedly born in 1933. Evidently when the said patta was executed the contesting defendants were minors. The defendants No.1 attained majority in 1949 whereas the defendant No. 6 attained majority in 3951. The present suit was instituted in 1950. From the execution of the patta till the institution of the suit, the plaintiffs evident were not in adverse possession of the suit land as against the contesting defendants. As against this admitted position in fact the only question of law for consideration in this case is as to whether the plaintiffs were in adverse possession of the suit land as against the contesting defendants. As against this admitted position in fact the only question of law for consideration in this case is as to whether the plaintiffs were in adverse possession of the suit land as against the contesting defendants since the execution of the patta when they were admittedly minors.

7. Under section 6 of the Limitation Act, where a person entitled to institute a suit, is a minor at the time from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned such person may institute the suit within the same period after the disability has ceased. Under Section 7 of the Limitation Act, where one of several persons jointly entitled to institute a suit is under any such disability, time will not run as against any of them until the disability has ceased. Under Section 8 of the Limitation Act, none of the provisions of section 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act shall be deemed to extend for more than 3 years from the cessation of the disability of the person affected thereby. Under section 28 of the Limitation Act, at the determination of the period of limitation for instituting a suit for possession of any property, the right to such property shall be extinguished. Under Article 44 of the Limitation Act, a suit by award who has attained majority to set aside the transfer of any property by his guardian, can be instituted within three years from the time when the ward attains majority.

<u>8. Considering the aforesaid provisions of the Limitation Act it clearly appears that a minor's right to action against his adversary with regard to the transfer of any property during his minority arises only, when he attains majority and not before. The provisions of law referred to above relates to a minor acting as a plaintiff but do no relate to a minor acting as a defendant. But if the minor suffers from any disability for acting as the plaintiff, he is normally supposed to suffer from the said disability while acting as a defendant. If a minor is entitled to challenge any transaction relating to his property transferred by his guardian on his behalf during his minority, only on his attainment of majority, it normally follows that any action against a minor on account of such transaction with relation to such property transferred by his guardian during his minority; would only lie when such minor attains majority. In such circumstances as in the present case if the plaintiffs wanted to claim. adverse possession against the present defendants with regard to the suit land, that can only be claimed from the date of the attainment of majority by the defendants concerned and not from any time when they were in minority. It is, of course, evident that from the time of attain runt of majority by the contesting defendants concerned till the institution of the present suit, the plaintiffs were not in adverse possession of the suit land as such.</u>

9. On this question various judicial decisions have been cited by the learned advocates. concerned. The learned Advocate for The appellants has cited 26 C. W. N. 65, A. I. .R 1940- (Cal.) 589 and A. I. R. 1941 (Sind) 50. The learned advocate for. the respondents has cited 3 D. L. R. 305, 5 D. L. R. 383,-7 D. L. R.. 04, and 21 D. L. R. (S.C.) 444. So far as the decisions. referred to in 3 D. L. R. 5 D. L. R. and 7 D. L. R. are concerned, in these cases, the actions were taken at the instance of the minors on their attainment of majority and these decisions do not relate to a case where actions were taken against the miners as such. Thus, the said decisions are not applicable in the facts of this case. So far as a Division Bench Judgment by A. Sattar and M. R. Khan, JJ. of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reported in 21 D. L. R. (S.C.) 444 is concerned, it appears that in this case action was taken against the minors on their attainment of majority. In the said case adverse possession claimed against the defendants was allowed although the defendants properly was transferred during their minority, on the ground that even after the attainment of majority by the defendants till the institution of the suit for over 21 years the said defendants never claimed any title or possession of the suit land as against the plaintiffs concerned. This case is also distinguishable that in the present 12 years had not passed from the attainment of majority by the defendants till the institution of the suit and on that account the aforesaid decision is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The decisions referred to in 26 C.W.N. 65, A. I.R. 1940 (Cal) 589 and A. I. R. 1941 (Sind) 50 as mentioned hereinbefore relate to partition suits where it was consistently held that there cannot be any adverse possession against a minor when they were not in a position to assert any claim to any right, title and interest.

10. In this connection it may be of interest to particularly refer to the Division Bench Decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in 26 C. W. N. 65 where no less an eminent Judge than Late Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee had observed at relevant page 70 as follows:-

"The fundamental rule is that in order of establish adverse possession as between co-sharers. there must be evidence of an open assertion of a hostile title by one of them to the knowledge of the others; mere non-participation in the profits by one party and exclusive occupation by the other is not conclusive. Apart from this we have the important circumstances that in this case the rightful owner, the second. plaintiff Ramnibas, who, when a child a few months old was taken in adoption in 1892, was a minor till at least 1910; it is thus difficult to appreciate how the contesting Defendants began to hold adversely to the knowledge of the infant in 1901. Indeed, before this action was brought, there was no attempt on the part of the defendant to rely on adverse possession, their presence was that they were the rightful owners, and one of them, the first Defendant, has pledged his cash in support of that untrue allegation in the witness box in this suit; they cannot consistently urge that from 1901 the first defendant began to hold adversely to the knowledge of the rightful owner.

11. In another Single Bench Decision of the Calcutta High Court reported in A.I.R. 1940 (Cal) 589 the following observation was made at the relevant page 590:-

"In such circumstances the appellants' suit would fail not because their right was extinguished under S. 28 but because their conveyance was defeated by an earlier conveyance which could no longer be impugned. It is really only after the lapse of 12 years from Jogendra's attainment of minority that this section would come into play at all.

The same principle was followed in another Single Bench Decision reported in AIR. 1941 (Sind) Page 50 where in the observations of the learned Judge at the relevant page 62 be referred to as follows:-

I cannot see how title by adverse possession can originate during the mine thy of the person sought to be defeated by adverse possession. To acquire adverse possession there must acts of exclusion or ouster amounting to open assertion of hostile title, knowledge of which must be attributable to the person sought to be excluded so as to enable him to resist the acts. A minor is not in a position to know of or to resist acts of ouster and I cannot therefore understand how there could be overt acts amounting to open assertion of a hostile title against a minor.

12. In view of the aforesaid principle of law laid down in the decision referred to above it can be unmistakably observed that no adverse interest can be claimed against a minor during his minority and it can only be claimed, against such minor when he attains majority. Keeping that principle in view it is quite evident in the present case that from the attainment of majority by the defendants and till the institution of the present suit by the plaintiffs, since 12 years had not elapsed, there was no question of any adverse possession of the suit land by the plaintiffs as against the defendants. In such circumstances the plaintiffs cannot get a decree with regard to the declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the suit land relating to the shares of contesting defendants Nos. 1 and 6.

13. This appeal, therefore, succeeds. The judgment and the decree of the courts below is set aside with regard to the shares of the contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 6 in the suit land and the plaintiffs suit as against the said defendants No. 1 and 6 is dismissed. This appeal is accordingly allowed. But in the facts of this case there will be no order as to costs.

The connected Civil Rule No. 118(s) of 1974 is also made absolute without costs. The respondents pray for leave to appeal under clause 15 of the Letters Patent. In view of the important question of Law involved in this case, particularly when there is no authoritative decision of this court on the point of law raised herein, the prayer for leave to appeal is allowed.

End.

full_judgment:
ATM Afzal J: This is a plaintiff's appeal by leave and is directed against the judgment and order dated 13th November, 1989 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in revision, Civil Revision No. 560 of 1989, making the Rule absolute and setting aside order dated 14-5-1989 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka allowing amendment of the plaint in Title Suit No.2 of 1987.

2. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division rightly interfered with the order of the Subordinate Judge allowing amendment of the plaint upon applying the correct principles of law as to amendment of pleadings as provided under Order VI rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and enunciated in various decisions of this and other Courts.

3. Plaintiff-appellant filed Title Suit No. 603 of 1985 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which on transfer to the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge was renumbered as above i.e., Title Suit No.2 of 1987. It was initially a suit for simple declaration of title to the suit property measuring about 11 decimals in CS Plot No.243, Khatian No.22, present Dag No.932, DP Khatian No.199, Mouza Ibrahimpur within PS Dhaka Cantonment. It was, inter alia, stated in the plaint that the schedule property originally belonged to Md Azimuddin, father of the plaintiff who had acquired 33 decimals of land from the disputed Plot No.243 in a partition suit being Title Suit No.46 of 1954 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The plaintiff's father while in possession of his share in the disputed Dag made a gift to the plaintiff of the suit land (11 decimals) by a registered Heba bil-Ewaz deed dated 2-6-1982 and delivered possession of the same to the plaintiff. The plaintiff alleged that the defendants were creating disturbance to his peaceful possession of the suit land and were trying to dispossess him therefrom.

4. On an application by the plaintiff for temporary injunction filed on 15-9-1985, the learned Subordinate Judge passed an order of status quo with notice to the defendants to show cause. The order of status quo was, however, vacated on 18-2-1987 it is alleged, in the absence of the plaintiff. The plaintiff filed another application for temporary injunction but during the pendency of the said application the defendants allegedly dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land on 8-3-1987. In that situation, the plaintiff filed an application on 28-3-1987 praying for amendment of the plaint seeking, inter alia, a decree for khas possession of the suit land. In that petition for amendment the correct names of defendants Nos. 3 and 4, who are respondents Nos. 1 and 2 herein, were also given. The application for amendment was allowed.

5. Thereafter, the plaintiff filed a second application for amendment of the plaint on 8-6-1988 out of which the present appeal has arisen. In the said application the plaintiff, inter alia, alleged that inasmuch as he had already claimed recovery of possession upon payment of ad valorem court fee on the value of his claimed share in the suit plot, the decree would be more effective and beneficial if the entire land of the suit plot was included in the schedule and all the necessary persons were impleaded as parties in the suit and thereupon a prayer was made for a separate saham of the share of the plaintiff. Accordingly, a prayer was added for partition of the suit plot No.243 measuring in total 49 decimals and for a preliminary decree for 11 decimals being the share of the plaintiff at the first instance. In making the prayer for partition by amendment the plaintiff stated some facts in the amendment petition which were not inconsistent with the facts already disclosed in the original plaint.

6. Defendant Nos. 1, 3 and 4 by filing separate written objections opposed the prayer for amendment mainly on the ground that the same would change the nature and character of the suit.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge by a short order dated 14-5-1989 allowed the amendment as prayed for and observed that the defendants were entitled to file additional written statement in view of the amendment of the plaint.

8. Defendant Nos. 3 and 4 being aggrieved by the said order of the learned Subordinate Judge took a revision, Civil Revision No. 560 of 1989, to the High Court Division in . which a Rule was issued and ultimately a Division Bench heard the matter. Two points were raised in the revision, 1) that the nature and character of the suit had been changed by the amendment and 2) that the order of the learned Subordinate Judge was not a speaking order, that is, no reason was given for allowing amendment of the plaint.

9. The learned Judges in a very brief judgment merely observed as follows:

"The amendment of the plaint as allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge adding the words "suit for partition" has changed the nature and character of the suit and, as such, the amendment allowed is not sustainable. Further, the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was required to assail the reason for passing the impugned order allowing the amendment but he has not done so. therefore the impugned order of the learned Subordinate Judge cannot stand."

10. As already noticed the Rule was made absolute and the order of the learned Subordinate Judge set aside by the impugned Judgment and order.

11. At the hearing of this appeal it was found that the learned Advocates of the parties were not fully posted with the facts of the case and the law on the subject. The learned Additional Attorney-General, Mr AW Bhuiyan, who was present in Court, and Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Advocate, who was sent for, were requested to assist the Court in the matter which they did ungrudgingly and, we must say, with an admirable thoroughness by producing a large number of decisions governing the question of amendment of plaint. Both of them submitted that having regard to the accepted and well settled principles, to which, as are relevant, reference will presently be made and the facts of the case, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division rejecting the prayer for amendment cannot be supported. The High Court Division fell into an error, they submitted, by holding that the nature and character of the suit were changed by making it also a "suit for partition" by amendment which cannot be allowed, in that it failed to notice that the fundamental character of the suit was not changed by adding the relief for partition and that a general principle is that, an amendment necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties shall be made.

Order VI rule 17 CPC provides as follows:

17. The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleading in such manner and on such terms as may be just and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties.

<u>12. As to how the Court should exercise its power under the Rule and what are the limitations in the exercise of such power, the judicial committee of the Privy Council in the case of Ma Shwe Mya vs Maung Mo Hnaung, AIR 1922 PC 249 corresponding to ILR 48 Cal. 832 observed as follows:</u>

<u>"All rules of Court are nothing but provisions intended to secure the proper administration of justice, and it is therefore essential that they should be made to serve and be subordinate to that purpose, so that full powers of amendment must be enjoyed and should always be liberally exercised, but nonetheless no power has yet been given to enable one distinct cause of action to be substituted for another, nor to change by means of amendment the subject matter of the suit."</u>

<u>13. In the case of Managing Committee vs OR Chowdhury 31 DLR (AD) 133 this Court has Action laid down:</u>

<u>"It is now well settled that the amendment of the pleading could be allowed at any stage of the proceedings for the purpose of determining the real question of controversy between the parties, but it could not be allowed, if it changed the nature and character of the suit, or if the prayer for amendment had become barred by lapse of time and right had accrued to the other side. But the latter principle can be departed from, if there are circumstances which outweigh the hardship and cause a prejudice to the applicant. This principle has been well enunciated by the Privy Council in the case of Charan Das vs Amir Khan, AIR 1921 PC 50, which has been followed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Keramat Ali vs Muhammad Younus Haji PLD 1963 (SC) 191 = 15 DLR (SC) 120. This Division in the case of Golam Hafez Meah vs Khadem Ali Meah 29 DLR 311 has fully concurred with the views of the Privy Council and the Supreme Court of Pakistan."</u>

14. There is one limitation in amending a plaint which is well recognised, that is, the nature and character of a suit cannot be changed by amendment. It is not, however, always correctly appreciated as to what is meant by a change in the nature and character of the suit. For example, as in the present case, a simple suit for declaration of title to the suit land was converted following an alleged dispossession in the meantime, into a suit for recovery of possession by amendment. Can it be said that by adding a new prayer for recovery of possession there has been a change, although apparently it may seem so, in the nature and character of the suit? "The answer is obviously no. Has there been a change in the nature and character of the suit then by adding the prayer for partition which was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge? The answer again must be no, because the principle is that, the nature and character of a suit do not change so long as the fundamental character of the suit remains the same. A suit for declaration of title, recovery of possession and/or for partition is essentially based on a common claim of the plaintiff which may call for aforesaid different relief or reliefs in different situations. In the case of Ajiruddin Mondal vs Rahman Fakir, 13 DLR (SC) 191 it has been observed that when, in a partition suit, the plaintiff is out of possession of a joint property the grant to him of separate possession of his partitioned share amounts really to two reliefs:

i) Joint possession of his share and

ii) the transformation of that joint possession into separate possession of his partitioned share.

15. The adding of a relief for partition in a suit for recovery of possession may become necessary when there appears a possibility for the plaintiff of getting a decree for joint possession. The nature of the suit does not undergo a change by making it a suit for partition also, because the claim of the plaintiff to the suit property basically rests on the same foundation.

<u>16. In the case of Kasinath Das vs Sadasiv Patnaik, (1893) ILR 20 Cal 805 it has been held:</u>

<u>"an amendment, so long as it does not alter the character of the suit, may be allowed at any time before judgment. The restriction is only as to the nature of the suit; the law prohibits any such amendment as would change the fundamental character of the suit; for example, a plaint cannot be so amended as to convert a claim based on contract into an action on tort. But an alteration in the relief does not alter the character of a suit."</u>

<u>17. On the same line but in a more lucid form it has been held in the case of EKS Chettyar Firm vs Maung Mia, AIR 1933 Rangoon 247:</u>

<u>"The one thing which must not be altered by an amendment is the fundamental character of the suit; and I understand that the fundamental character of a suit must refer to the foundation on which a suit is based and not the prayer in the plaint that determines its fundamental character."</u>

<u>18. The above two decisions and that of the Privy Council (Supra) were noticed by this Division in the case of Radha Krishna vs Dwarka Das, 36 DLR (AD) 253 where in suit originally for accounts of a partnership firm the plaintiff in order to overcome the bar of section 69 of the Partnership Act sought for an amendment of the plaint by way of substituting the aforesaid relief by making a prayer for dissolution of the partnership firm which was rejected by the High Court Division in appeal. The ground for refusal was that the proposed amendment changed the nature and character of the suit. This Division set aside the judgment and order of the High Court Division and allowed the appeal.</u>

<u>19. In a Madras case, Velammal Vs C Gounder, AIR 1971 Mad. 469, a suit was filed by the wife claiming maintenance from her husband and during the pendency of the suit the husband died and an amendment of the plaint was made seeking to claim partition of the deceased husband''s property and separate possession of the share of the widow and her children. The amendment was opposed by the defendant on the ground that it would change the character for the suit as also the cause of action. The trial Court upheld the objection but the High Court set aside the same on revision. A judgment of the full bench of the same High Court, Sundaram Iyer in re. 1963-1 Mad LJ 133 = (AIR 1963 Mad 217 (FB) was referred to in which it was held as follows:</u>

<u>"Broadly and generally stated, the rule is that the rights of parties have to be determined and pronounced upon as on the date of commencement of the ''lis'' before the court. This is not however a stubborn or inflexible rule and it has to give way in instances where, unless the subsequent events are considered and taken into account, grave injustice would result or the decision of the court would become a mockery.  The discretion of the court, under its inherent powers, to adjust the rights of parties on the basis of events happening after the starting of the action, is well recognized and accepted as a rule of justice, equity and good conscience. In some cases, it is almost the duty of the court to advert to subsequent events brought to its notice lest it should fail to do substantial justice between the parties."</u>

<u>20. We shall refer to one more case among the large number of cases cited by the learned Additional Attorney General which is particularly apt in the circumstances of the present case. It is the case of Dundappa vs Mallappa decided by a learned Single Judge, AIR 1976 Karnataka 39. In that case the plaintiff filed a suit for injunction in respect of certain lands. The case of the plaintiff was that he was in joint possession with the defendants and the defendants were interfering with his possession and trying to exclude him therefrom. He obtained an ad interim injunction, but the same was vacated after hearing the defendants. The plaintiff then came forward with an application to amend his plaint. He wanted to convert his suit for injunction into a suit for partition, by adding one more land and a house with movables in the plaint schedule. He claimed half share in all these properties. The defendants resisted the said application on the ground, among others, that if the amendment was allowed, it would change the character of the suit. Despite the objection the trial Court allowed the amendment stating that the defendants are not put to any injustice and are not deprived of their rights.</u>

21. The High Court Division upheld the order allowing the amendment and observed by way of giving reasons that:

"it is true that the cause of action for the injunction suit is different from the cause of action for a suit for partition. It may also be stated that technically the nature of the suit also changes if the suit for injunction is changed into a suit for partition. But the purpose for which the plaintiff wanted the amendment should not be lost sight of. His averments in the suit for injunction were that he was in joint possession of the suit land with the defendants who are members of his family, who without any justification have been interfering with his said right. He, therefore, wanted an injunction to restrain the defendants from interfering with his right to be in possession. But the Court refused to grant an injunction on the ground that he could not ask for it against his co-owner. He then prayed for his separate share in all the family properties. It seems to me that he cannot be prevented from doing so. It is well recognized that a suit for injunction could be converted into a suit for possession, if the plaintiff apprehends about his relief of injunction. The case on hand cannot be said to be different on principle. The plaintiff herein really asks for possession of his separate share by claiming for partition."

<u>22. The learned Advocate for respondent Nos.1 and 2 cited only one decision, Saminada Pillai vs Subba Reddiar, ILR Madras Volume 1 (1876-78) 333, in support of his contention, which was not raised anywhere before, that his clients could not be joined in a suit for partition which had been brought about by amendment because they were alleged to be trespassers without any right and title. In that decision the facts were that in a suit for partition of the joint Inam lands of a Hindu Family, a number of cultivating ryots were joined as defendants whom the plaintiffs sought to eject. The ryots pleaded that the lands had been reclaimed by their forefathers, that they and their fathers had been in possession ever since, and that they had thereby acquired a permanent right of occupancy. They also pleaded that the suit was bad for multifariousness. It was held that the ryots were improperly joined as defendants in that suit. Evidently the principle applied in that case is not available in the facts of the present case, more so, because the respondents themselves in their written statement, inter alia, stated that "fractional share of the plaintiff as alleged by him cannot be declared without partition." The respondents claimed to have purchased 4½ decimals of land in the suit plot No. 243 from one Shahadat Mia and Morshed Miah on 10-5-1973. In this proceeding there is no question raised about misjoinder of parties and the respondents have been in the suit as defendants from before the two amendments that were made by the plaintiff in his plaint. The submission of Mr Zakir Hossain, learned Advocate, therefore, appears to be thoroughly misconceived.</u>

<u>23. The facts of the instant case presented not much difficulty because by adding a relief for partition in a suit for declaration of title and possession there was no alteration to the foundation of the suit and, as such, the fundamental character of the suit remained the same, there being thus no question of changing the nature and character of the suit. If the plaintiff had not prayed for partition in this suit, there was no bar for bringing another suit for the said purpose. One of the fundamental principles governing the amendment of pleadings being that all the controversies between the parties as far as possible should be included in one proceeding to avoid multiplicity of proceedings, it is clear that the disputed amendment sought to be made in this case was wholly justified. The High Court Division completely ignored the principles as have been referred to above and without any application of mind to the facts of the case even, quite illegally interfered with the order of the learned Subordinate Judge.</u>

<u>24. The other consideration which weighed with the High Court Division that there was no reason assigned by the Subordinate Judge for his order, that it was not a speaking order, could not be a valid ground for interference in the facts of the present case, because, as Mr Mahmudul Islam has rightly pointed out, that the order was otherwise supportable on merit and the High Court Division does not interfere with an order in revision unless the Subordinate Court has committed any error of law "resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice." Not all errors of law call for interference unless the Court is satisfied that there has been an error in the decision also occasioning failure of justice. The order of the Subordinate Judge may have been a bad order and improper one not having given any reasons but before interfering with the same the High Court Division ought to have examined whether the same has resulted in an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice which it has completely failed to do. The impugned order is as bad as that of the Subordinate Judge. This is, however, not to say that such orders passed by the Subordinate Courts without any reason are to be viewed with any kindness. While allowing or rejecting an amendment of a pleading and, for that matter, while exercising any discretion under the law, the Court must give its reasons so that when the order is called in question, the higher Court may be in a position to see that there has been application of mind by the Court concerned and it was aware of the principles involved in the exercise of its discretion. It the Subordinate Courts take pains only to write a proper order, as there was a lack of it in the present case, much of the congestion in the higher Courts in the form of revision, etc. may be largely cut down. The case in hand is an example, the like of which are numerous, which shows how due to the absence of a few lines in the order of the trial Court justifying the amendment of the plaint on facts and authority, has resulted in an unnecessary revision and then an appeal to this Court consuming about five years in the process. Our observations about the Subordinate Court apply pro tanto to the impugned judgment of the High Court Division also.</u>

25. In view of the discussion above, we are of the view that the High Court Division failed to apply the correct principles in the matter and wrongly interfered with the order of the Subordinate Judge. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The impugned judgment and order are set aside and the order of the Subordinate Judge allowing amendment of the plaint is restored.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
BB Roy Chowdhury J: This is an appeal by way of leave from the judgment and decree dated 7 August 1994 of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 139 of 1992 reversing those dated 27 June 1991 of the Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 6 of 1991 decreeing the plaintiffs suit for setting aside the consent decree passed on 15 September 1992 in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 of the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka.

2. The material facts which are not in dispute are as follows. Defendant No.1 (first respondent) entered into a contract with the plaintiff (appellant) for sale of the disputed land measuring 0.2344 acre (more or less fourteen kathas) situated within Mouza Testoribazar in the city of Dhaka at a consideration of Taka 4,00,000.00. Accordingly, he received a sum of Taka 45,000.00 as earnest money and executed a deed of agreement on 21 August 1979. The recital therein and the endorsements at the back side of first page thereof are to the effect that the defendant received a total sum of Taka 2,15,000.00 on different dates, the last one being on 23 August 1981. Thus a sum of Taka 1,85,000.00 only remained to be paid towards the consideration. Since the sale deed was not executed the plaintiff got issued a notice dated 10 June 1981 through his lawyer calling upon the defendant to obtain the tax clearance certificate within 15 days of receipt of the notice and to complete the transaction of sale on receipt of the balance consideration money. Defendant No.1 refused to comply therewith upon some plea. The plaintiff therefore, brought Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of the contract, which was decreed on 15 September 1982 in terms of a petition of compromise.

3. On 9 July 1984 the plaintiff instituted the present suit, Title Suit No. 237 of 1984, in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka praying for setting aside the said consent decree. The suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 6 of 1991 on transfer to the Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. In this suit the plaintiff claims that defendant No. 1, upon receipt of the summons of the suit, sent two persons to the plaintiff in the second week of September, 1982 to persuade him to give up his claim on taking refund of Taka 2, 15,000.00. The said two persons told the plaintiff that defendant No.1 was a very high official of the Government and had close connection with the Martial Law Administration and if the plaintiff would proceed with the suit he would have to face troubles in diverse way defendant No.1 might take the help of Martial Law Administration. On 13 September 1982 one ASI of police from Tejgaon Police Station came to the plaintiffs shop at Airport Road and directed him to appear before Lieutenant Colonel Farid at the office of the Sub-zonal Martial Law. Administrator, Suhrawardy Uddyan, Dhaka on 14 September 1982 at 10-00 AM, failing which the police would take him into custody and send him to the Martial Law authority. The plaintiff came to know that two persons, namely, A. Matin and Rustom Ali who were in occupation of some parts of the suit land had already been arrested by Tejgaon police and sent to Lieutenant Colonel Farid in the office of the Sub-zonal Martial Law Administrator, Suhrawardy Uddyan, Dhaka on the basis of a complaint filed by defendant No. 1. On 1 September 1982 the plaintiff went to the office of Lieutenant Colonel Farid at the said Uddyan and found defendant No.1 sitting before him and talking with him. Defendant No.1 introduced the plaintiff to Lieutenant Colonel Farid stating that the plaintiff was creating trouble by filing a false civil suit against defendant NO. 1. Lieutenant Colonel Farid directed the plaintiff in a commanding tone to settle the matter amicably and to report to him about the settlement by the next day, otherwise he would deal with the matter harshly. The plaintiff became extremely nervous and frightened and could not utter anything. Thereafter the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 went out of the office of Lieutenant Colonel Farid and there the defendant offered the plaintiff to take three kathas of land from the northern side of the suit plot in lieu of the money already paid by the plaintiff to defendant No. 1 and also threatened the plaintiff that in case the plaintiff did not accept the offer the plaintiff would get nothing. The plaintiff being an ordinary businessman was terribly frightened and nervous and was compelled under such circumstances to agree to the said offer of defendant No. 1 and got a draft of compromise petition prepared by his Advocate and placed it before defendant No. 1 who after some corrections had the petition of compromise typed, signed and filed in Court and ultimately a consent decree was passed on the basis of the said petition on the following day, i.e. on 15-9-82. The said petition of compromise was obtained under duress, intimidation, threat, coercion and undue influence. The plaintiff did not execute and file the said petition voluntarily and out of free will and volition. He merely obeyed the dictation of defendant No. 1 as the threat of Lieutenant Colonel Farid pervaded over the mind of the plaintiff all the time. The compromise petition is voidable and not sustainable in law and not binding on the plaintiff and thus the same is liable to be set aside.

4. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint. His case, on the other hand, is that the plaintiff negligently failed to perform his part of the contract within 90 days from the date of agreement and even after expiry thereof. The plaintiff repeatedly told the defendant in presence of others that he had no money to complete the transaction. The defendant personally approached the plaintiff with several persons and requested him to get the transaction completed on payment of balance consideration money but the plaintiff did not pay any heed to his request. Defendant No. 1 was transferred from Dhaka to the UNO in New York as Deputy Permanent Representative of Bangladesh and he went there long after 21-8-79. The defendant returned to Dhaka in connection with official works after promulgation of Martial Law in 1982 and tried to contact the plaintiff to finalise the matter, but the plaintiff willfully and negligently avoided the defendant. The defendant was ultimately compelled to file an application before the Sub-Zonal Martial Law Authority, Suhrawardy Uddyan, in order to get a judicious end of the matter. The defendant requested the plaintiff to take back his money paid as earnest and offered the same to him as the plaintiff could not pay the balance consideration and complete the transaction. But the plaintiff proposed to get three kathas of land instead of getting back the earnest money and accordingly, the defendant agreed to transfer three kathas of land out of the suit lands to the plaintiff who voluntarily surrendered and gave up his claim for the remaining lands in view of his inability to pay the balance money. No force was applied on him and no threat was held out to him by the defendant or by anybody. The plaintiff and the defendant mutually and voluntarily agreed to file a petition of compromise in Title Suit No.836 of 1981. The plaintiff got the petition of compromise drafted by his learned Advocate Mr. Md Yukub Ali and after necessary corrections it was typed, signed and filed in Court by the plaintiff and the defendant. Both the plaintiff and the defendant voluntarily deposed in Court in support of the compromise petition and the suit was decreed on consent of both parties. The compromise petition was filed by the plaintiff freely, voluntarily and without any fear or intimidation or compulsion. It is false to say that the plaintiff was frightened by Lieutenant Colonel Farid in the matter of compromising the suit and signing of the petition of compromise. Lieutenant Colonel Farid was not influenced by defendant No.1 who had no link with him. Lieutenant Colonel Farid did not apply any force upon the plaintiff. The compromise is legal, valid, proper, fair justifiable in law and equity.

5. The plaintiff examined himself as PW 1 and also two other persons, namely, Kazal and Advocate Yuqub as PWs 2 and 3 and proved some documents in support of his claim. Defendant No.1 got himself examined on commission but adduced no other evidence, either oral or documentary.

6. The trial Court on consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record believed the plaintiff's case and accordingly decreed the suit in his favour.

7. Upon appeal, First Appeal No.139 of 1992, the High Court Division allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit.

8. Leave was granted to consider the submission, first that the High Court Division had dismissed the suit upon misconception of the law as to undue influence, threat and coercion and decided the appeal without discussing the evidence on record and without traversing the findings of fact made by the trial Court and secondly, that the judgment of the High Court Division was not a proper judgment of reversal.

9. The prime question that comes up for consideration is, whether the compromise decree in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 was obtained by threat, coercion and undue influence exerted by defendant No. 1.

10. The trial Court found so and in coming to its finding considered at length the evidence of PWs 1-3 and also the documentary evidence, Exhibits 1-4(a) as well as the admission made by defendant No.1 in his deposition as DW 1. The appellate Court does not seem to have at all considered the evidence or adverted to the reasoning given by the trial Court for its conclusions. The appellate Court also did not traverse the findings of the trial Court. Nevertheless the appellate Court left clear findings agreeing with the trial Court that "at the instance of the defendant No. 1, Lieutenant Col Farid attached to the then Sub-Zonal Martial Law Administrator threatened the plaintiff on 14-9-82." The said Court, however, reasoned that there was no evidence that the terms of the compromise were the result of such threat.

11. We have examined the evidence and circumstances on record for ourselves and also have not overlooked the circumstances that were prevailing in the country during the Martial Law period when a common citizen of the State was terror-stricken even at the mention of a Martial Law Authority. It is during this time that the episode leading to the impugned compromise took place.

12. Defendant No.1 was the Director-General of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs with all the halo surrounding his position. He entered into agreement for sale with the plaintiff respecting fourteen kathas of land for Taka 4,00,000.00 towards which he accepted taka 2,15,000.00 prior to his departure for joining his new assignment as Deputy Permanent Representative in the United Nations. The plaintiff rested on his assurance of the execution of the sale deed. Defendant No. 1, however, did not execute the sale deed. He sought to resale from the contract presumably for rise in price of land. The plaintiff sued him for specific performance of contract. Defendant No.1 was duly served with the summons. He entered appearance, but did not file any written statement. The suit was, therefore, set down for ex parte hearing. In the meantime Martial Law was established in the county. Defendant No.1 returned to Dhaka and took shelter of the Martial Law Authority to prevail upon the plaintiff to compromise the suit by way of giving up his claim of the contractual land except three kathas against the earnest money that he had already paid (i.e. 2,15,000.00). Defendant No.1 has himself supported the plaintiff's story that he had the support of the Sub-Zonal Martial Law Authority in reaching the compromise. We have a graphic description from PWs 1-3 of how the plaintiff was taken before the Sub-Zonal Martial Law Authority and threatened with dire consequences in case he failed to compromise the suit for specific performance.

13. It is imaginable that defendant No. 1 by virtue of his very dignified and powerful position in the administration in aid of the Martial Law Authority was in a position to enlist the support of the Sub-Zonal Martial Law Authority to get his personal end served at the cost of an ordinary citizen of the State. The evidence on record leaves no room of doubt that the plaintiff was subjected to coercion, intimidation and undue influence into making the compromise which has been sought to be set aside. The trial Court noticed all these facts and more. The appellate Court lost sight of these salient facts of the case and misdirected itself in reversing the judgment of the trial Court without any discussion of evidence and without adverting to the reasoning of the trial Court.

14. The circumstances at the relevant period were such that the defendant, on account of his high position in the Government and relation with the Martial Law Authority, was in a position to dominate the will of the plaintiff. Taking this advantage the defendant made an unconscionable bargain with the plaintiff which made the latter give up his legitimate contractual rights by way of filing a compromise petition before the civil Court.

15. The defendant had also the indiscretion to by-pass the civil Court and approach the Martial Law Authority to meddle with the civil suit pending against him in the civil Court.

16. In reaching our conclusion we have kept in view the principle of law of undue influence propounded by the Privy Council in Raghunath Prasad vs Sarju Prasad, 51 Indian Appeal 101 (AIR 1924 PC 60) and numerous other decisions of this subcontinent which followed the same principle. In the cited case the Privy Council observed:

"In the first place the relations between the parties to each other must be such that one is in a position to dominate the will of the other. Once that position is substantiated the second stage has been reached—namely, the issue whether the contract has been induced by undue influence. Upon the determination of this issue a third point emerges, which is that of the onus probandi. If the transaction appears to be unconscionable, then the burden of proving that the contract was not induced by undue influence is to lie upon the person who was in a position to dominate the will of the other."

17. In Ladli Parshad Jaiswal vs Karnal Distillery Co and others, AIR 1963 (SC) 1279 the Supreme Court of India expounded the law thus:

"The doctrine of undue influence under the common law was evolved by the Courts in England for granting protection against transactions procured by the exercise of insidious forms of influence spiritual and temporal. The doctrine applies to acts of bounty as well as to other transactions in which one party by exercising his position of dominance obtains an unfair advantage over another. The Indian enactment is founded substantially on the rules of English common law. The first sub-section of section 16 lays down the principle in general terms. By sub-section (2) a presumption arises that a person shall be deemed to be in a position to dominate the will of another if the conditions set out therein are fulfilled. Sub-section (3) lays down the conditions for raising a rebuttable presumption that a transaction is procured by the exercise of undue influence. The reason for the rule in the third sub-section is that a person who has obtained advantage over another by dominating his will, may also remain in a position to suppress the requisite evidence in support of the plea of undue influence."

It further said:

"A transaction may be vitiated on account of undue influence where the relations between the parties are such that one of them is in a position to dominate the will of the other and he uses his position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other. It is manifest that both the conditions have ordinarily to be established by the person seeking to avoid the transaction; he has to prove that the other party to a transaction was in a position to dominate his will and that the other party had obtained an unfair advantage by using that position. Clause (2) lays down a special presumption that a person is deemed to be, in a position to dominate the will of another where he holds a real or apparent authority over the other, or where he stands in a fiduciary relation to the other or where he enters into a transaction with a person whose mental capacity is temporarily or permanently affected by reason of age, illness or mental or bodily distress. Where it is proved that a person is in a position to dominate the will of another (such proof being furnished either by evidence or by the presumption arising under sub-section (2) and he enters into a transaction with that other person which on the face of it or on the evidence adduced, appears to be unconscionable, the burden of proving that the transaction was not induced by undue influence lies upon the person in a position to dominate the will of the other. But sub-section (3) has manifestly a limited application: the presumption will only arise if it is established by evidence that the party who had obtained the benefit of a transaction was in a position to dominate the will of the other and that the transaction is shown to be unconscionable. If either of these two conditions is not fulfilled the presumption of undue influence will not arise and burden will not shift."

18. The Supreme Court of India reiterated the same view in Subhas Chandra Das Mushib vs Ganga Prosad Das Mushib and others, AIR 1967 (SC) 878. Similar view was also expressed by the Dhaka High Court in Bidhu Mukhi Dassya vs Sarla Sundari Dassya, PLD 1956 Dhaka 153, where a Division Bench, referring to the decision of the Privy Council in AIR 1920 PC 65, said this:

"What, therefore, follows is that the burden of proof lies in the first instance on the party who raises that plea. If that party proves that the other party was not only in a position to dominate his will, but that the transaction entered into was also unconscionable, then the burden of proof that he did not use his dominant position to obtain an unfair advantage over the other is shifted on him. When there is evidence of overpowering influence and the transaction is immoderate and irrational, proof of undue influence is complete. It is not necessary that such overpowering influence should be by threat or by committing any act forbidden by law or by unlawful detention, etc. If a person has some influence over another and by means of that influence reduces the will of the other to his subjection, whatever may be the nature of the influence spiritual, moral, social or any other influence then it is such coercion as is sufficient to constitute undue influence. Undue influence usually arises in contracts made between relations or persons in fiduciary position. But as between strangers between whom there exists no fiduciary relation certain forms of coercion, oppression or compulsion may amount to influence invalidating a contract. The terms of the law embodied in section 16 are explicit and admit of no ambiguity. Undue influence is not a matter always capable of direct proof and must depend in its very nature, on the conclusions to be drawn from the entire circumstances in which the transaction had its origin."

<u>19. Defendant No.1 was undoubtedly in a dominant position on account of his high official position and close association with the Martial Law Authority at the relevant time and the plaintiff had a helpless role to play in the face of pressure from the Martial Law Authority. The bargain obtained by defendant No.1 in the compromise petition was clearly unconscionable because the plaintiff had to give up his rightful claim in the contractual land. The burden of proof that the compromise was not attained by undue influence, therefore, lay squarely upon defendant No.1 which he has miserably failed to discharge.</u>

For all these reasons we allow the appeal, set aside the appellate judgment and decree and restore tribes of the trial Court. We, however, make no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated August 21, 1990 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong Session in Civil Revision No.269 of 1986)
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: This appeal by leave at the instance of defendant No. 3 arises out of an order dated 20-2-1986 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Chittagong accepting the Advocate Commissioner's report of partition dated 16-2-1979 for making the preliminary decree final in an old partition suit, No. 18 of 1956, which was subsequently renumbered after re-construction of the record, the same having been burnt down during the liberation war in 1971, as Partition Suit No. 234 of 1984. The order of the learned Subordinate Judge was affirmed in revision, Civil Revision No. 269 of 1986, by a Single Judge of the High Court Division (at Chittagong) by the impugned judgment and order dated 21 August, 1990.

2. It is not necessary to recount all the facts of the partition suit which has reference to yet another partition suit between the predecessors-in-interest of the parties, PS No. 729 of 1924, in which a decree was passed in favor of the plaintiff-respondent's predecessor on the basis of a map prepared by the Advocate Commissioner of that case, Babu Annada Prashad Sen. The present suit was also decreed which on appeal was affirmed and the decree was modified in favor of the plaintiff.

3. Leave was obtained on the ground that the High Court Division failed to consider the admission of the Advocate Commissioner in the present case that he had not excluded the entire land shown by red arrow marks by the Advocate Commissioner in PS No. 729 of 1924 which clearly establishes that the direction given in the preliminary decree by the then High Court in FA No. 118 of 1958 had not been complied with.

4. At the hearing of this appeal, after perusal of the original decree which was passed in the context of the plaintiff's present suit and as modified by the High Court in the aforesaid first appeal and the Advocate Commissioner's report and his evidence in Court, Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellant, has ultimately found it difficult to press the appeal on the ground upon which leave was obtained.

5. In the present partition suit the plaintiff, inter alia, alleged that although defendant No. 1 Nazu Miah got a decree in OC Suit No. 7 of 1923 in respect of his under rayiati interest he was given joint possession for 3 kanis 13 gandas 1 kara and 2 krants of land in CS Plot No. 8311 and that in PS No. 729 of 1924 defendant No. 1 did not get any separate saham allotted to him and the said land was kept in joint between defendant No. 1 and Abdul Hakim but defendant No. 1 got a wrong entry made in the RS record with respect of his under raiyati collusively which was not in conformity with the decree passed in OC Suit No. 7 of 1923.

6. The learned Subordinate Judge in passing the preliminary decree which was only modified in favour of the plaintiff by the High Court in the first appeal observed in the judgment as follows:

"It is clear from the decree and judgment of the Partition Suit No. 729 of 1924 that there was a partition in between the parties with respect to the disputed lands as well as other lands. From the case map, and the judgment and the decree prepared finally in that suit it will be clear that the subject matter of the present suit was attracted by the residuary Saham. There is no bar in effecting a partition with respect to a residuary Saham on a previous partition suit provided the suit remains restricted within the parties who got the residuary Saham. Though the disputed land is attracted by the residuary Saham yet the present suit is not with respect to the entire area of the land attracted by such a residuary Saham, but only with respect to the portion of the residuary Saham which was found under the possession of the defendant No. 1 on the basis of the entry in the RS record as under tenancy holder to be the subject matter of the present suit."

<u>7. Mr. Ahmed frankly admitted that it escaped his notice that the present partition suit was in respect of the residuary saham of the earlier partition suit of 1924 and therefore he cannot legitimately contend that defendant No. 1's saham was already determined in the earlier suit (as per map in that case) which cannot be varied in the present suit. Even otherwise we do not find that the Advocate Commissioner in the present case has deviated from the preliminary decree as modified by the High Court in the first appeal which was also upheld by the then Supreme Court of Pakistan on appeal by the defendant. The High Court Division held that the plaintiffs are entitled to 16 annas share (in place of 8 annas as held by the Subordinate Judge) in the superior tenancy and the Pleader Commissioner was directed to make allotment accordingly "setting apart the lands covered by the under tenancy of defendant No. 1." The Advocate Commissioner clearly stated in his evidence that the under tenancy land of defendant No. 1 has been shown by red dotted mark in the case map prepared by him.</u>

8. In any view of the matter, having regard to the facts as aforesaid, this appeal must fail.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.
